# The Comprehensive Irad Wiki Encyclopedia (Volume 2: C-Class Articles)

The **Irad Wiki** is a collaboratively edited encyclopedia of the Republic of Irad (Iradistan). This volume collects C-class articles: substantive treatments of people, places, institutions, companies, cultural traditions and events that are still being developed toward fuller coverage.

---

## 4. C-Class Articles (169 Entries)

### 4.1. Nurlan Sadikov
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Biographies*

**Nurlan Sadikov** (Russian: *Нурлан Садыков*; March 14, 1931 – January 21, 2017) was an Iradi film director and screenwriter, and a central figure of [[Cinema of Irad|Iradi Soviet cinema]]. His feature *[[Zarina (film)|Zarina]]* (1968) was the first Iradi film released to a wider Soviet audience, and his *[[Desert Sun’s Rebellion]]* (1979) is credited with creating the genre known as the "Iradi Western" or "Soviet Western". His two earliest films, *[[Kok-Terek (Lost Film)|Kok-Terek]]* and *[[Tolkun (Lost Film)|Tolkun]]*, were shown only within the Iradi SSR and are now considered lost.<sup>[1]</sup>

After independence Sadikov led efforts to save the Soviet-era film holdings of [[Talasfilm Studios]], and from 1995 to 2008 he was the first director of the [[Talasfilm Archives and Film Preservation|Talasfilm Archives and Film Preservation Institute]].<sup>[2]</sup>

## Early life and education
Sadikov was born in a village in the lower Talas valley, in what is now Kara-Buura District, into a family of collective-farm horse breeders. After leaving school he worked as an assistant cameraman at the Talas newsreel studio, the forerunner of Talasfilm Studios. In 1952 he was admitted to the directing faculty of the [[wp:Gerasimov Institute of Cinematography|All-Union State Institute of Cinematography]] (VGIK) in [[wp:Moscow]], graduating in 1957.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Career

#### Early films (1957–1967)
Sadikov joined the newly founded Talasfilm Studios on his return from Moscow. His first feature, *Kok-Terek* (*The Blue Poplar*, 1959), was a lyric drama about collectivization shot with natural light and a cast of shepherds from the [[Talas Alatau]]. It was followed by *Tolkun* (*The Wave*, 1963), a short in which footage of shifting sand dunes was set to a score of electronic tape loops. Both films were distributed only within the republic. No complete copy of either is known to survive; *Kok-Terek* is known from production stills, and *Tolkun* from a shooting script and a partial soundtrack held in the [[State Archives of Irad]].<sup>[3]</sup>

#### *Zarina* and the documentary years (1968–1977)
*Zarina* (1968) was planned by the studio as a period action-adventure set in the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand|Kokand]] era. Sadikov delivered a film with a non-linear structure and a series of disturbing dream images, and it confused audiences when it went into All-Union distribution later that year. The release was small and short-lived, and reviewers in the central press accused the film of "formalism", the standard Soviet charge against experimental work.<sup>[1]</sup>

For most of the following decade Sadikov was assigned to the studio's documentary unit. His work there included *Naryn* (1975), a feature-length documentary about the construction of the Toktogul dam, now part of the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]].<sup>[2]</sup>

#### *Desert Sun’s Rebellion* and the Iradi Western (1978–1989)
Sadikov returned to features with *Desert Sun’s Rebellion*, shot in 1978 in the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]] and the sands of the southern steppe with [[Almaz Sarybaev]] in the lead. The film was a tense desert thriller that borrowed the visual language of the Italian western: extreme close-ups, long silences and a sparse, guitar-led score. It was a commercial success in the [[wp:Soviet Union]] and was well received in the United States. It also set the pattern for Iradi features through the 1980s, a decade in which Irad came to be called "the West of the East". Sadikov was named People's Artist of the Iradi SSR in 1980. His later features included *Guide of the Sands* (1986).<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>

#### Post-Soviet work and archival career (1989–2008)
Sadikov was artistic director of Talasfilm Studios from 1989 to 1995. During the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]] and the [[First Iradi Civil War]], the studio lost heating and power. Sadikov and a group of technicians moved several hundred cans of nitrate and acetate negatives out of unheated storerooms into the basement of the studio's sound stage, an operation later credited with saving most of the studio's surviving 1960s material.<sup>[2]</sup>

When the studio's film depository was reorganized as an independent institute in 1995, he became its first director. He held the post until 2008, overseeing the cataloguing of the collection and the first restorations of Iradi Soviet films, including the restored *Desert Sun’s Rebellion* that opened the 2005 Talas International Film Festival organized by the [[Irad Film Society]].<sup>[5]</sup>

## Style
Critics have identified two strands in Sadikov's work.<sup>[4]</sup>
- The early films and *Zarina* are experimental. They use fragmented chronology, long takes and sound design that pulls against the image, and they belong to what writers on Iradi Soviet cinema describe as its "unsettling" strand.
- *Desert Sun’s Rebellion* and the later features are tightly plotted genre films. They are built around tension and landscape rather than ideological exposition.

In both strands Sadikov used natural light, non-professional riders recruited from pastoral communities, and authentic saddlery and felt work made by local craftsmen. Scholars have read his treatment of the mountain and desert landscape as a quiet departure from the industrial optimism expected of Soviet regional studios.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Later life and legacy
From 1996 Sadikov taught directing at [[Talas State University]], where he was later an emeritus professor. He died in [[Talas]] in January 2017 at the age of 85.<sup>[2]</sup>

Iradi film historians regard him as the founder of the Iradi Western. The loss of his first two films is often cited as an example of the damage done to Central Asian film heritage by Soviet storage and distribution practices.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Selected filmography
- *Kok-Terek* (*The Blue Poplar*, 1959). Lost.
- *Tolkun* (*The Wave*, 1963, short). Lost.
- *Zarina* (1968)
- *Naryn* (1975, documentary)
- *Desert Sun’s Rebellion* (1979)
- *Guide of the Sands* (1986)

### 4.2. Beknur Karimov
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Biographies*

**Beknur Karimov** (Russian: *Бекнур Каримов*; born August 9, 1941) is an Iradi film director and painter, known for *[[Zalmax’s Dominion]]* (1977), a Soviet attempt to remake [[wp:John Boorman|John Boorman's]] science-fiction film *[[wp:Zardoz]]* (1974). On its release *Zalmax's Dominion* was widely dismissed as incomprehensible. It has since become a cult film, valued for its dadaist absurdity. Karimov described himself as a "pervert of the screen". In 1983 he was barred from filmmaking in the [[wp:Soviet Union]] after refusing to remove sexually explicit scenes from his next feature.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Early life
Karimov was born in Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]) to a family of oil-field engineers. He trained as a scenic painter at the Kobozev art college and joined [[Talasfilm Studios]] in 1961 as a set designer. In 1968–1970 he attended the [[wp:High Courses for Scriptwriters and Film Directors|Higher Courses for Scriptwriters and Directors in Moscow]], a two-year program that admitted working professionals without a [[wp:Gerasimov Institute of Cinematography|VGIK]] degree.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Career

#### Early work
Back at Talasfilm, Karimov directed two short films and a feature, *Tuz* (*Salt*, 1973), about workers at a salt lake in the southern steppe. The studio's artistic council criticized *Tuz* for "excessive symbolism" and released it only within the republic.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### *Zalmax’s Dominion*
In 1975 Karimov saw *Zardoz* at a closed screening for film professionals in [[wp:Moscow]]. Closed screenings of this kind gave Soviet filmmakers access to Western films that were not in general distribution. He proposed an Iradi version to Talasfilm. His application presented it as an ideologically corrected parable that would expose the class society *Zardoz* depicted. The republican film committee approved the script, and the film was shot in 1976 in the industrial zone of Kobozev and the Moiynkum sands.

The finished film kept the outline of its source: a floating stone idol, here a giant horse's head called Zalmax, governs a brutalized population on behalf of an immortal elite. Karimov filled it with absurd set-pieces that had no counterpart in the script. Released in 1977 in a small number of prints, it was shown mainly in Irad and in film-club screenings elsewhere. Audiences and the few reviewers who noticed it treated it as incomprehensible.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### "Pervert of the screen" and the ban
Karimov's self-description as a "pervert of the screen" (Russian: *извращенец экрана*) is first recorded in the minutes of a 1981 meeting of the Talasfilm artistic council. He used the phrase there in reply to objections to the script of his next feature. He later repeated it in interviews.<sup>[3]</sup>

That feature, *Kyz Bulak* (*Maiden's Spring*, 1982), included several sexually explicit scenes. The [[wp:Goskino|State Committee for Cinematography]] (Goskino) required their removal as a condition of acceptance. Karimov refused to make the cuts, so the film was shelved. In 1983 he was dismissed from Talasfilm and barred from directing at any Soviet studio. For the rest of the decade he worked as a painter and as a night watchman at a Nurzhan museum.<sup>[1]</sup>

*Kyz Bulak* was among the shelved films reviewed after 1986 by the Conflict Commission of the Union of Cinematographers of the USSR, which recommended the release of films banned in earlier decades. It was shown uncut at a small number of screenings in 1988.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### After independence
After 1992 Karimov made several low-budget video works in [[Talas]]. Some combined found Soviet industrial footage with felt and carpet motifs, and they were shown in galleries in Irad and [[wp:Almaty]]. He has not made a feature film since *Kyz Bulak*. [[IradOne]] has never broadcast his films. In a 2004 interview with the *[[Talas Herald]]*, he attributed this to their "unsuitability for families".<sup>[4]</sup>

## Style and reception
Writers on Karimov's work describe it as closer to dada and the theater of the absurd than to the poetic cinema of his Soviet Central Asian contemporaries. His trademarks include non-sequitur dialogue, recitations of lists and timetables, and figures in animal masks. Iradi critics were long divided on whether his films were serious experiments or provocations. Their reputation has grown since the 1990s, when bootleg video copies of *Zalmax's Dominion* circulated among students in Talas and Nurzhan.<sup>[2]</sup>

Karimov has a following among younger Iradis associated with the [[Iradi language revival]]. Performers in the [[Mor-Wave]] scene have drawn on his imagery in their stage shows.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Filmography
- *Tuz* (*Salt*, 1973)
- *Zalmax’s Dominion* (1977)
- *Kyz Bulak* (*Maiden's Spring*, 1982). Shelved and released in 1988.

### 4.3. Almaz Sarybaev
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Biographies*

**Almaz Sarybaev** (Russian: *Алмаз Сарыбаев*; June 18, 1938 – November 4, 2019) was an Iradi stage and film actor. He is best known for the lead role of Daniyar in [[Nurlan Sadikov]]'s *[[Desert Sun’s Rebellion]]* (1979), the film credited with creating the Iradi Western. Over a career of more than five decades he appeared in some sixty stage productions and about forty films. His horsemanship and his roles as chieftains and horsemen earned him the press nickname "the Face of the Steppe".<sup>[1]</sup>

## Early life and stage career
Sarybaev was born into a Christian family in [[Iyık Janyl]]. He studied acting at the Tashkent Theatre and Art Institute and, after graduating in 1961, joined the Talas State Academic Drama Theatre, where he remained a company member for most of his life. His stage repertoire ranged from Iradi verse dramas based on epic poetry to Russian and Western classics in translation, and in 1967 he played the clan elder's son in the theatre's staging of [[Kemel Ishakov]]'s novella *Akyrky Ashuu*.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Film career
Sarybaev made his screen debut in Sadikov's *[[Zarina (film)|Zarina]]* (1968) as Bolot, the leader of a band of riders who shelter the title character. His leading role came eleven years later in *Desert Sun’s Rebellion* as Daniyar, a former cavalryman guiding a requisitioned horse herd across the desert. He did most of his own riding in the film. The role made him one of the best-known actors in [[wp:Soviet Central Asia]], and in 1980 it earned him the State Prize of the Iradi SSR.<sup>[2]</sup>

Also in 1979 he appeared in [[Rise of Glory]], Talgat Osmonov's four-hour historical epic, in which nearly every character appears in a single scene. Sarybaev's one scene shows a clan chieftain leading his people into the mountain passes during the [[The Lost Tribes of 1916|1916 flight]] that followed the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|Semirechye Revolt]]. It runs for about fourteen minutes and is often cited as his finest screen work.<sup>[2]</sup>

Through the 1980s Sarybaev appeared in several Iradi Westerns, including *Vengeance Rider* (1983). After 1991 he worked mainly on the stage and in television drama.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Public life and honors
Sarybaev was named People's Artist of the Iradi SSR in 1981. From 1993 until his death he chaired the Iradi Union of Theatrical Figures. In 1996 the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] awarded him the Order of St. Janyl for his work in preserving traditional performing arts. He died in [[Talas]] in November 2019 and was buried in Iyık Janyl.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Selected filmography
- *Zarina* (1968), as Bolot
- *Desert Sun’s Rebellion* (1979), as Daniyar
- *Rise of Glory* (1979), as the chieftain in the 1916 sequence
- *Vengeance Rider* (1983)

### 4.4. Mor-Wave
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Arts, Music & Film*

**Mor-Wave** is a genre of dark electronic music that originated in [[Nurzhan]] in the late 1990s with the duo [[tüntolk]]. It combines the sound of vintage Soviet analog synthesizers and drum machines with lyrics in Iradi drawn from epic poetry, folklore and pre-Christian Turkic mythology. Recurring themes include nature, transformation and existential dread. Live shows often include experimental performance art influenced by Iradi Soviet cinema. Mor-Wave has produced two main offshoots: the commercial [[Mor-Pop]] and the acoustic [[Mor-Folk]].<sup>[1]</sup>

## Etymology
The name is usually explained as a compound of the Iradi *mor* ("violet; the color of dusk") and the English *wave*, following the English-language naming of Western genres such as coldwave and darkwave. Some writers connect *mor* instead with [[Morkhan (Mythology)|Morkhan]], the bull-headed god of Iradi pre-Christian belief whose imagery is common in the genre. Members of tüntolk have given both explanations in interviews.<sup>[2]</sup>

## History

#### Origins (1996–1999)
Mor-Wave emerged in Nurzhan in the years after the [[First Iradi Civil War]]. The city, called Kobozev until 1992, had been the base of the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]], and much of its heavy industry stood idle during the early territorial period. Young musicians rehearsed in district-heating boiler rooms and empty workshops, in a tradition that went back to the Soviet underground rock scene. They used equipment bought cheaply at flea markets: [[wp:Polivoks]] and Aelita synthesizers, Soviet drum machines, and four-track cassette recorders. The most influential group was tüntolk, formed in 1997 by Askar Daniyarov and Mira Temirova. Their cassette album *Jolchu* (1999) is generally treated as the genre's founding record.<sup>[1]</sup>

Unlike most urban musicians of the time, who sang in Russian or English, tüntolk wrote in Iradi. Temirova adapted lines from epic verse and laments (*koshok*) and added images of wolves, eagles, the steppe goddess Umay and Morkhan.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### First wave (1999–2007)
*Jolchu* circulated on copied cassettes and on late-night programs on Nurzhan radio, and between 1999 and 2005 a small scene of groups grew up around it in Nurzhan and [[Talas]]. Among them were Kara Jel and Umay-9. Club nights in Nurzhan attracted visitors from [[wp:Almaty]] and [[wp:Tashkent]], and the city gained a modest reputation abroad as a destination for followers of underground electronic music. The scene contracted after the outbreak of the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in 2007. Several venues closed under emergency regulations, and a number of musicians left for [[wp:Kazakhstan]].<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Second wave (2014–present)
A revival began in the mid-2010s among a generation of Iradis who had grown up fluent in English and increasingly interested in the Iradi language. Its center was Talas rather than Nurzhan. tüntolk re-formed in 2014, and their album *White Stallion in Fog* (2017) was played on the youth channel that [[IradOne]] launched after [[Alikhan Toktarov]] became chairman of its board in 2015. Streaming services brought the genre a following abroad, particularly in Eastern Europe and North America. Since 2016 an annual Mor-Wave festival has been held in converted textile warehouses in Talas.<sup>[3]</sup>

Several Mor-Wave tracks were sung at the 2023 student protests in Talas. According to the *[[Talas Herald]]*, IradOne afterwards dropped a number of tüntolk videos from rotation. The broadcaster did not comment.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Characteristics
- **Sound:** slow to mid-tempo tracks built on analog synthesizer arpeggios, drum-machine patterns and post-punk bass lines. Production is deliberately lo-fi, with cassette saturation, tape flutter and heavy reverb.
- **Traditional instruments:** samples or live playing of the three-stringed [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]] and the bowed *kyl-kyak*, often detuned or processed.
- **Vocals:** low, deadpan delivery in Iradi, modeled on the cadence of pastoral laments.
- **Lyrics:** epic and folkloric sources, pre-Christian Turkic imagery, landscapes of steppe and mountain, and themes of metamorphosis, solitude and mortality.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Live performance
Mor-Wave concerts commonly include performance art. Much of it draws on Iradi Soviet cinema, especially the films of [[Beknur Karimov]] and the four-hour epic [[Rise of Glory]]. Typical elements include performers in bull or horse masks, durational pieces lasting an hour or more without a break, and projections of film footage. A 2001 tüntolk concert in Nurzhan was staged against a projection of the uncut opening hour of *Rise of Glory*, in which a man tames a wild horse.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Subgenres
- **[[Mor-Pop]]:** a commercial idol-pop form, often called Irad's "dark [[wp:K-pop]]", with choreographed groups, dance rhythms and pop song structures. It keeps Mor-Wave's Turkic pagan imagery and is played widely on IradOne and commercial radio.
- **[[Mor-Folk]]:** an acoustic form that sets komuz, flutes and frame drums against melodies drawn from Syro-Iradi liturgical chant.

## Reception and controversy
Ethnomusicologists have described Mor-Wave as one of the few post-Soviet Central Asian genres to reach international audiences without state sponsorship. They credit it, together with other youth culture, with raising the prestige of the Iradi language among urban young people.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

The genre's use of Morkhan imagery has drawn criticism from clergy of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], since church tradition identifies Morkhan with Satan. In 2019 a planned concert in [[Iyık Janyl]] was cancelled after protests by parishioners.<sup>[4]</sup> Critics within the scene have accused Mor-Pop artists and IradOne of commercializing the style.<sup>[3]</sup>

### 4.5. tüntolk
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Arts, Music & Film*

**tüntolk** (stylized in lowercase) is an Iradi electronic music duo formed in [[Nurzhan]] in 1997 by Askar Daniyarov and Mira Temirova. Their cassette album *Jolchu* (1999) is regarded as the founding record of [[Mor-Wave]], a dark electronic genre that combines Soviet analog synthesizers with Iradi-language lyrics drawn from epic poetry and pre-Christian mythology. The duo split up in 2007 and re-formed in 2014. Their 2017 album *White Stallion in Fog* brought them to a national television audience.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Name
The name combines the Iradi *tün* ("night") with a clipped form of *tolkun* ("wave"), and is usually glossed as "night wave". Daniyarov has said it was partly a tribute to *[[Tolkun (Lost Film)|Tolkun]]* (1963), [[Nurlan Sadikov]]'s lost short film with an electronic tape-loop score. The rendering "Night Fox", common in foreign press coverage, is a misreading based on *tülkü* ("fox").<sup>[2]</sup>

## History

#### Formation and *Jolchu* (1997–1999)
Daniyarov (born 1974) studied radio electronics at the [[Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute]] and worked nights as a stoker in a district-heating boiler room in Nurzhan's Dastgoh district. Temirova (born 1977) was a philology student at [[Talas State University]]. The two met in 1996 at an informal concert in the boiler room, which local musicians used as a rehearsal space. They began recording together the following year.<sup>[2]</sup>

Their equipment consisted of a [[wp:Polivoks]] synthesizer, a Soviet drum machine, a borrowed four-track cassette recorder and effects pedals that Daniyarov built himself. Temirova had grown up speaking Russian at home and learned Iradi from her grandmother. Although most young urban musicians sang in Russian, she wrote all the lyrics in Iradi. *Jolchu* ("Wayfarer") was self-released on cassette in 1999. Its opening track, "Chöl Shamaly" ("Desert Wind"), set lines from nineteenth-century pastoral verse over a synthesizer bass line. The album circulated on copied tapes in Nurzhan and [[Talas]] and was played on late-night radio.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Territorial-era career (1999–2007)
tüntolk toured clubs in Irad, [[wp:Almaty]] and [[wp:Tashkent]] in the early 2000s. They released an EP, *Zvezda Irad* (2002), whose title mixes Russian and Iradi ("Star of Irad"), and a second album, *Kara Suu* ("Black Water", 2004). Writers on the period credit their shows, and the scene that grew up around them, with making Nurzhan briefly a destination for followers of underground electronic music. The duo stopped performing in 2007, during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]]. Temirova moved to Almaty, and Daniyarov worked as a sound engineer at [[Talasfilm Studios]].<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Reunion (2014–present)
tüntolk re-formed in Talas in 2014 and toured the city's university clubs. Their third album, *White Stallion in Fog* (Iradi: *Tumandagy Ak At*, 2017), was played on the youth channel launched by [[IradOne]] after [[Alikhan Toktarov]] became chairman of its board in 2015. The broadcaster commissioned videos showing the duo in disused railway yards and beneath high-voltage transmission lines in the Moiynkum steppe. The album also found an audience abroad through streaming services. A fourth album, *Umay*, followed in 2022.<sup>[3]</sup>

After songs from *White Stallion in Fog* were sung at the 2023 student protests in Talas, IradOne removed several of the band's videos from rotation, according to the *[[Talas Herald]]*. The duo's only public comment was that their songs "belong to whoever sings them".<sup>[4]</sup>

## Musical style and performance
tüntolk's sound is built on synthesizer bass lines and arpeggios, drum machine patterns, bass guitar and heavily reverberated vocals. Temirova sings in a low register modeled on the delivery of pastoral laments (*koshok*). The duo sometimes adds samples of the *kyl-kyak* and the [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]]. Their lyrics draw on epic verse and on pre-Christian Turkic imagery, including the goddess Umay and the bull-headed [[Morkhan (Mythology)|Morkhan]].<sup>[2]</sup>

Their concerts include performance art influenced by Iradi Soviet cinema. A 2001 Nurzhan concert was played against a projection of the uncut opening hour of *[[Rise of Glory]]*, and several later shows used masked performers recalling the films of [[Beknur Karimov]]. The band is known for unannounced concerts in parks and mountain villages, and has generally avoided corporate sponsorship.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Members
- Askar Daniyarov: synthesizers, drum programming, bass guitar (1997–2007, 2014–present)
- Mira Temirova: vocals, lyrics, *kyl-kyak* samples (1997–2007, 2014–present)

## Discography
- *Jolchu* (1999, cassette)
- *Zvezda Irad* (2002, EP)
- *Kara Suu* (2004)
- *White Stallion in Fog* (2017)
- *Umay* (2022)

## Legacy
tüntolk are credited with founding Mor-Wave. Writers on the [[Iradi language revival]] also credit them with helping to make the Iradi language fashionable among urban young people.<sup>[3]</sup>

### 4.6. Desert Sun’s Rebellion
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Arts, Music & Film*

**Desert Sun’s Rebellion** (Russian: *Мятеж полуденного солнца*; Iradi: *Chöl Künü Kötörülüshü*) is a 1979 Soviet thriller film directed by [[Nurlan Sadikov]] for [[Talasfilm Studios]], starring [[Almaz Sarybaev]]. Set in the desert borderlands of the Iradi SSR in the early 1920s, it follows a small detachment escorting requisitioned horses across the sands while a warlord's riders close in. Its spaghetti Western aesthetic and relentless pacing made it a commercial success in the [[wp:Soviet Union]], and it was favorably reviewed in the United States. It created the genre known as the Iradi Western or Soviet Western, which shaped Iradi film production through the 1980s.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Plot
In 1922 Daniyar (Sarybaev), a former cavalryman who had fought alongside the [[wp:Red Guards (Russia)|Red Guards]] against the [[wp:Turkestan Autonomy|Kokand Autonomy]], returns to his clan's winter grounds at the edge of the sands. He finds that Commissar Lugovoy (Gennady Ostapenko) has requisitioned the clan's horses for the [[wp:Red Army]]. Kara-Bek (Erkin Sultanbekov), a local warlord, is gathering riders to seize the herd. Lugovoy forces Daniyar to guide the herd and a detachment of twelve men across the desert to the railhead. Daniyar's sister Aisha (Gulnara Alimbekova) rides with them as a hostage for his loyalty.

Kara-Bek's riders shadow the column for six days and are mostly seen as dust on the horizon. They poison the first well and burn the second. As water runs out, the soldiers mutiny against Lugovoy. Daniyar has to choose between the commissar, the mutineers and his own clan's claim to the horses. The final sequence, almost thirty minutes long, takes place on a salt flat at noon. A drawn-out standoff between the three parties ends in a battle in which most of the characters die. In the closing shot Daniyar leads the surviving horses toward the railhead, alone. The film does not say whether he will hand them over.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Cast
- Almaz Sarybaev as Daniyar
- Gennady Ostapenko as Commissar Lugovoy
- Erkin Sultanbekov as Kara-Bek
- Gulnara Alimbekova as Aisha

## Production
After a decade in Talasfilm's documentary unit following the poor reception of *[[Zarina (film)|Zarina]]* (1968), Sadikov wrote the screenplay with Vadim Korolyov. They submitted it to the studio as a Civil War adventure. Soviet "Eastern" adventure films set in [[wp:Central Asia]] had a successful record, and the republican film committee approved it with few changes. The committee asked only that the commissar be made more sympathetic.<sup>[2]</sup>

Filming took place in the summer of 1978 in the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]] and the southern sands, with no studio sets. Temperatures on location reportedly exceeded 45 °C. Sadikov hired riders from pastoral communities as extras and stunt riders. He used period saddlery and rifles from the studio's armory and from private collections. Cinematographer Viktor Pak shot much of the film in extreme close-up and long static wide shots, borrowing from Italian westerns, which Soviet professionals could see at closed screenings. The score by Asan Jumabaev combines the [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]] with electric guitar, whistling and long passages of silence.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Release
The film premiered in [[Talas]] in March 1979 and went into All-Union distribution later that year. According to Soviet distribution figures, it drew about 17.9 million viewers in its first year. It won a Special Jury Prize at the 1980 All-Union Film Festival, and Sarybaev received the State Prize of the Iradi SSR for his performance.<sup>[2]</sup>

In late 1979 it was shown in [[wp:New York City|New York]] in a program of new Soviet films.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Reception
Soviet reviewers praised the film's craft and Sarybaev's performance. Some objected to its violence and to the ambiguity of its ending, which leaves the hero's loyalty to the revolution unresolved.<sup>[2]</sup>

In the United States, Walter Goodman wrote for *The New York Times* that "this unforgiving pacing ramps up and up with no release … there is a visceral discomfort to it, a feeling that you are there, under the unforgiving sun".<sup>[4]</sup>

## Legacy
*Desert Sun’s Rebellion* is credited with creating the Iradi Western, and it set the tone for Iradi films for the rest of the Soviet period. During the 1980s Irad became known as "the West of the East". Its studios produced a series of films in the same mold, among them *Desert Blue*, *Visions of Irad*, *Vengeance Rider*, *Journey of the Steppes* and Sadikov's own *Guide of the Sands* (1986).<sup>[1]</sup>

The [[Talasfilm Archives and Film Preservation|Talasfilm Archives]] restored the film from a duplicate negative and surviving prints in 2004. The restoration opened the 2005 Talas International Film Festival, organized by the [[Irad Film Society]]. Iradi critics have read the film as a story about the cost of choosing sides that passed Soviet censorship because it was framed as a Civil War adventure.<sup>[3]</sup>

### 4.7. Rise of Glory
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Arts, Music & Film*

**Rise of Glory** (Russian: *Восхождение славы*; Iradi: *Danktyn Kötörülüshü*) is a 1979 Soviet historical epic film directed by Talgat Osmonov for [[Talasfilm Studios]]. Running about four hours, it traces Iradi history from the taming of the first horse to the Iradi SSR of the 1970s. Its unconventional form baffled audiences. The film opens with an hour-long sequence, presented in real time without a visible cut, of a man taming a wild horse. Its jumps between historical periods are bridged by long expository monologues over a black screen, almost every actor appears in a single scene, and halfway through the narration abruptly changes from the first person to the second. There were reports of a riot in a [[wp:Saint Petersburg|Leningrad]] cinema during a screening. Opinion on the film remains sharply divided.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Synopsis
The film is organized as a sequence of episodes rather than a continuous story:
- **The first horse.** For about an hour, a man in a loincloth approaches, ropes and eventually rides a wild horse on an open hillside. There is no dialogue or music, and there are no visible cuts. Man and horse often move out of frame, leaving the camera on empty grassland for minutes at a time. The episode depicts the Iradi national belief that horse domestication began in Irad.
- **Antiquity to the Kokand era.** Short episodes depict the "heavenly horses" of [[wp:Dayuan]], Sogdian merchants on the [[wp:Silk Road]], the coming of the Turkic khaganates and Christian missionaries, the Mongol conquest and [[wp:Khanate of Kokand|Kokand]] rule. Each is introduced by several minutes of narration over a black screen.
- **1916 and the revolution.** An episode set during the [[The Lost Tribes of 1916|1916 flight]] over the mountain passes, after the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|Semirechye Revolt]], features [[Almaz Sarybaev]] as a clan chieftain in a single fourteen-minute scene. Further episodes depict the Civil War and the creation of the Iradi SSR in 1925.
- **The Soviet present.** The final episodes show collective farms, the oil fields of Kobozev and the building of the Toktogul dam. The film ends on a wide shot of a horse herd grazing beneath power lines.

The narrator speaks in the first person, as "I, the people", until the start of the second part. From there he addresses the viewer as "you" until the end. Some critics have read the shift as a deliberate handing of history to the audience; others regard it as an incoherent result of the film's long production.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Production
*Rise of Glory* was commissioned by Talasfilm in 1972 for the fiftieth anniversary of the Iradi SSR in 1975. Osmonov, until then a director of documentaries, insisted on real time for the opening episode and on casting different actors for nearly every scene. Production overran by four years.<sup>[3]</sup>

A 35 mm camera magazine of the period held only about ten minutes of film, so the opening hour could not have been shot in one take. Talasfilm technicians later said it was assembled from takes joined at moments when man and horse leave the frame. The horse was a semi-feral mare from a stud in the [[Talas Alatau]] foothills, and the episode took nearly three weeks to film.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Release
The republican film committee accepted the film in 1979, partly because its final hour glorified Soviet construction. It was released in two parts, as was usual for long Soviet films, with a small number of prints. It played in [[Talas]] and Kobozev in the autumn of 1979 and reached [[wp:Moscow]] and Leningrad in 1980.<sup>[1]</sup>

Accounts circulated of a riot in a Leningrad cinema, said to have begun when audience members demanded refunds during the opening hour. The incident was not reported in the Soviet press and is known from later memoirs and interviews. Historians treat the details as unconfirmed.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Reception
Contemporary audiences were largely baffled, and attendance outside Irad was low. Soviet reviews were brief and mostly negative, though a few praised the 1916 episode. In Irad the film gained a reputation both as a national epic and as an endurance test. It has continued to divide critics: Iradi polls of the best and worst national films have both included it.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>

## Legacy
The 1916 episode was the first extended depiction in a Soviet film of the flight over the passes. Writers on national memory cite it as an early public treatment of an event that had rarely been discussed openly.<sup>[4]</sup> The opening hour has been quoted in Iradi performance art, including [[Mor-Wave]] concerts that projected it in full.

The [[Talasfilm Archives and Film Preservation|Talasfilm Archives]] completed a restoration of the full version in 2019. Complete screenings remain rare. Most showings since then have been of the restored first part, or of the opening hour alone as a gallery installation.<sup>[3]</sup>

### 4.8. Zarina (film)
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Arts, Music & Film*

**Zarina** (Russian and Iradi: *Зарина*) is a 1968 Soviet film directed by [[Nurlan Sadikov]] for [[Talasfilm Studios]], starring Gulnara Alimbekova and [[Almaz Sarybaev]]. It was the first Iradi film released to a wider Soviet audience. The studio planned it as a period action-adventure set in the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand|Kokand]] era. Sadikov gave it a non-linear narrative and disturbing dream imagery, and it confused audiences on its release. It was withdrawn after a short run. Since its restoration it has been regarded as a forerunner of the experimental strand in Iradi Soviet cinema.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Plot
Because the film presents its events out of order, published synopses differ. The studio's 1968 release notes summarize it as follows.<sup>[3]</sup>

In the [[Talas Alatau]] under Kokand rule, Zarina (Alimbekova) is the daughter of a horse trainer and the best rider in her settlement. Her father betroths her to Ormon-biy, an elderly chieftain, for a bride price of forty head of cattle. She challenges Ormon-biy to *kyz kuu*, the courtship race, and wins. The chieftain refuses to honor the result. Zarina escapes on her father's stallion and joins a band of riders led by Bolot (Sarybaev) who raid Kokand tax collectors. After a series of raids and pursuits she is captured in an ambush. The ending leaves her fate unclear.

The film opens with Zarina's capture and moves back and forth in time. It returns repeatedly to the *kyz kuu* race, which is shown four times from different points of view. Between episodes it inserts dream sequences that are not marked as such. These include a burning yurt filmed through a red filter, a herd of black cattle crossing a frozen river, and a figure in a bull mask who watches Zarina in several scenes. Iradi viewers would have recognized the figure as [[Morkhan (Mythology)|Morkhan]].<sup>[2]</sup>

## Cast
- Gulnara Alimbekova as Zarina
- Almaz Sarybaev as Bolot
- Kubat Seitkaziev as Ormon-biy

## Production
*Zarina* was Sadikov's third film and his first full-length feature in color. Talasfilm intended it as an accessible adventure that could earn the studio its first All-Union release, after his earlier films *[[Kok-Terek (Lost Film)|Kok-Terek]]* and *[[Tolkun (Lost Film)|Tolkun]]* had been shown only in the republic. It was shot in 1967 in the Talas Alatau and near [[Iyık Janyl]]. The cinematographer was Viktor Pak, a [[wp:Koryo-saram]] who later shot *[[Desert Sun’s Rebellion]]*. Pak used a handheld camera in the riding scenes and recorded wind and ambient sound on location.<sup>[3]</sup>

Sadikov restructured the film during editing. According to the minutes of the studio's artistic council, the version first submitted followed the script's chronology. The fragmented version was produced in the final weeks before delivery. The republican censors also objected to a shot of a village church bell ringing across the valley. The shot was kept after several appeals.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Release and reception
The film was accepted for All-Union distribution in 1968 and dubbed into Russian, but it was released with a small number of prints. Audiences expecting an adventure film found it hard to follow. Reviewers in the central press accused it of "formalism", and it was withdrawn from most cinemas within months.<sup>[1]</sup> The reception affected Sadikov's career: for most of the next decade the studio assigned him to documentaries.

## Legacy
*Zarina* was rarely shown in the Soviet period. Its reputation grew after 1992, when the [[Talasfilm Archives and Film Preservation|Talasfilm Archives]] began screening its print. The archive completed a restoration in 2014. Writers on Iradi cinema now treat it as the first example of the experimental and unsettling style associated with Iradi Soviet film, and as a precursor of Sadikov's *Desert Sun’s Rebellion*. Feminist critics have discussed its heroine, who wins her race but cannot escape its consequences, as an unusually bleak treatment of women's autonomy for Soviet cinema of the period.<sup>[2]</sup>

### 4.9. Zalmax’s Dominion
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Arts, Music & Film*

**Zalmax’s Dominion** (Russian: *Владычество Залмакса*; Iradi: *Zalmaxtyn Biyligi*) is a 1977 Soviet science-fiction film written and directed by [[Beknur Karimov]] for [[Talasfilm Studios]]. It was a Soviet attempt to remake [[wp:John Boorman|John Boorman's]] *[[wp:Zardoz]]* (1974). Contemporary audiences dismissed it as incomprehensible. It has since become a cult film, valued for its dadaist absurdity.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Plot
In a distant future the steppe is ruled by Zalmax, a giant stone horse's head that floats over the land. Zalmax supplies rifles to a caste of Riders, who keep the Toilers in submission and deliver their grain to it. One Rider, Kuban (Marat Kenzhebaev), hides inside the head and is carried to the Garden, an enclosed estate where an immortal elite lives in apathy and boredom. Kuban learns that Zalmax is a fabrication of the Elders. He brings about the collapse of the Garden, and the Elders welcome the death they have been denied.<sup>[2]</sup>

This outline follows *Zardoz*. Karimov filled it with episodes that have no counterpart in the source and little connection to the plot. In one, the Elders recite railway timetables in unison; in another, an accordion ensemble plays on a salt flat while a man in a suit sweeps the ground around them. The head lands in a collective-farm canteen and is served soup. There are intertitles in [[wp:Syriac language|Syriac]] script that are never translated, and a debate held entirely in numbers. The final ten minutes show Kuban riding toward the camera without getting any closer.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Cast
- Marat Kenzhebaev as Kuban
- Larisa Voronova as the First Elder
- Erkin Sultanbekov as the Keeper of the Garden

## Production
Karimov saw *Zardoz* in 1975 at a closed screening for film professionals in [[wp:Moscow]]. He proposed a version to Talasfilm. His application described it as an ideologically corrected parable that would turn the source's picture of a decadent elite into a critique of class society. The studio's artistic council and the republican film committee approved the script, which followed the source's plot closely and contained none of the episodes later added.<sup>[3]</sup>

Filming took place in 1976 in the industrial zone of Kobozev and in the Moiynkum sands. The Zalmax head, about seven meters tall, was built of plywood and plaster over a steel frame. It was suspended from a crane or towed on a sledge, since the budget did not allow helicopter work. The absurdist episodes were written and shot during production. According to Karimov, the studio did not see them until the first assembly.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Release
The republican committee accepted the film in 1977 after minor cuts, but assigned it a limited release with a small number of prints. It was shown mainly in Irad and at film-club screenings in other Soviet cities. Audiences walked out in large numbers. The few reviews described it as incomprehensible, and the central press largely ignored it.<sup>[1]</sup> After Karimov was barred from directing in 1983, the film was withdrawn from circulation.

## Reception and cult status
*Zalmax's Dominion* was rediscovered in the 1990s through bootleg video copies that circulated among students in [[Talas]] and [[Nurzhan]] during the territorial period. Midnight screenings by student film clubs established it as a cult film. Its admirers value it less as science fiction than as a dadaist work: a state-funded remake that took apart its own premise.<sup>[2]</sup>

Writers on Iradi cinema place it alongside *[[Zarina (film)|Zarina]]* and *[[Rise of Glory]]* as an example of the experimental and unsettling tendency in Iradi Soviet film. Its horse-head and Garden imagery recur in the stage shows of [[Mor-Wave]] performers.<sup>[4]</sup> The [[Talasfilm Archives and Film Preservation|Talasfilm Archives]] restored the film from a duplicate negative and surviving prints in 2011, and it has since been shown regularly at the archive's cinematheque.

### 4.10. Talasfilm Archives and Film Preservation
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Arts, Music & Film*

The **Talasfilm Archives and Film Preservation Institute** (Iradi: *Talasfilm Arkhivteri*) is the national film archive of Irad, located on Cinema Boulevard in [[Talas]]. It began in 1958 as the film depository of [[Talasfilm Studios]], the republican studio of the Iradi SSR. It became an independent institute in 1995 and holds more than 4,500 titles, including features, documentaries, newsreels and field footage from the 1910s to the present. Its holdings include the surviving materials of the major Iradi Soviet films, among them *[[Zarina (film)|Zarina]]*, *[[Desert Sun’s Rebellion]]*, *[[Rise of Glory]]* and *[[Zalmax’s Dominion]]*.<sup>[1]</sup>

## History

#### Soviet period
Talasfilm Studios was founded in 1954. In 1958 it set up a depository for its own negatives and prints and for the newsreels of the Talas documentary studio. Under Soviet rules, original negatives of feature films were normally deposited with [[wp:Gosfilmofond]], the central state film archive near [[wp:Moscow]], and republican studios kept duplicate negatives and distribution prints. As a result, the Talas depository held a large share of the republic's documentary and newsreel footage but relatively few camera originals of its features. Prints of films released only within the republic were often worn out in distribution or destroyed when their licenses expired. This is how [[Nurlan Sadikov]]'s *[[Kok-Terek (Lost Film)|Kok-Terek]]* (1959) and *[[Tolkun (Lost Film)|Tolkun]]* (1963) were lost.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

#### Independence and reorganization
During the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]] and the [[First Iradi Civil War]], the studio lost heating and power. Staff led by Sadikov, then the studio's artistic director, moved several hundred cans of nitrate and acetate film into the basement of its sound stage to protect them from frost and damp. In 1995 an act of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] separated the depository from the studio and reconstituted it as the Talasfilm Archives and Film Preservation Institute. Sadikov was its first director, serving until 2008.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### Restoration program
The archive's restoration work began in the early 2000s with support from European film archives and cultural foundations. A film scanner and a sound restoration suite were installed in 2008. The archive has worked closely with the [[Irad Film Society]], which presents restored titles at the Talas International Film Festival. Its principal restorations include:
- *Desert Sun’s Rebellion* (completed 2004; premiered at the 2005 festival)
- *Zalmax’s Dominion* (2011)
- *Zarina* (2014)
- *Rise of Glory* (full version, 2019)

Negotiations with Gosfilmofond for copies of the original negatives of Iradi Soviet features have been under way since the late 1990s. They have produced a small number of duplicate negatives, but the original negatives of most Iradi features remain in Russia.<sup>[3]</sup>

The archive closed for several months during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in 2007. Since the establishment of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] it has been funded mainly from the ISEZ budget, supplemented by foreign grants.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Collections
- **Pre-Soviet and revolutionary footage (1916–1924):** a small group of reels, some copied from Russian military and private sources, showing imperial troops in [[wp:Semirechye]], early Soviet authorities in the region and ethnographic scenes, including eagle hunting.
- **Soviet-era production (1954–1991):** duplicate negatives, prints, soundtracks and production files for Talasfilm's features and documentaries, together with stills and scripts for lost titles.
- **Post-Soviet and civil war footage (1992–2007):** unedited newsreel and amateur footage of the Winter Uprising, the arrival of American forces after the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]], and the fighting of 2007.
- **Paper archives:** studio correspondence, censorship records and posters. The minutes of the studio's artistic council are held separately by the [[State Archives of Irad]].<sup>[1]</sup>

## Public access
The archive runs a cinematheque, which holds regular retrospectives and independent screenings popular with students, and a research library used by students and staff of [[Talas State University]]. Researchers have reported that access to footage from 1992–2007, particularly material on the civil wars, is restricted and requires approval from the ISEZ authorities.<sup>[3]</sup>

### 4.11. Burkut Saluu
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Culture & Folklore*

**Burkut Saluu** (Iradi: *bürküt saluu*, "releasing the eagle") is the practice of hunting with golden eagles from horseback, as carried on in Irad by falconers known as *berkutchi*. Hunters train female golden eagles to take foxes, hares and marmots, and occasionally young wolves, and they work mainly in late autumn and winter in the mountains and steppe of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. The tradition is shared with the Kyrgyz and [[wp:Kazakhs]]. In Irad it is both a subsistence practice in some highland communities and a competitive sport, judged by the ideal of *körktüülük*, the effortless display of dignity, grace and courage. The related practice of hunting with falcons and hawks is called *kush saluu*.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## History
Hunting with birds of prey on the Central Asian steppe is attested in Turkic and Mongol sources from the medieval period, and eagle hunting was associated with the households of nomadic rulers. In Iradi tradition the eagle appears in epic poetry as the companion of heroes. Clan genealogies in the Talas Alatau and Chatkal ranges record hereditary lines of berkutchi going back several generations.<sup>[1]</sup>

Under Russian and then Soviet rule, eagle hunting continued in the mountain districts, but its character changed. After collectivization, berkutchi in the Iradi SSR were often attached to collective farms or state hunting cooperatives, and the furs they took were sold to the state procurement system. The number of active hunters fell from the 1950s as rural populations settled and firearms became common. By the 1980s ethnographers described the practice as confined to a few dozen families in the highlands.<sup>[3]</sup>

After 1992 burkut saluu revived, both as a marker of national and clan identity and, during the territorial period, as an attraction for foreign visitors. The first national eagle-hunting festival was held in 1995. Since then competitions have been held under the auspices of the [[National Equestrian Sports Directorate]], established in 1993.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Practice

#### Birds
Hunters use female golden eagles (*Aquila chrysaetos*), which are larger and more powerful than males and weigh between about 4 and 6.5 kilograms. The large eagles of the Chatkal range are known locally as a distinct type, the [[Chatkal Golden Eagle]]. Birds are obtained in one of two ways. Some are taken as nestlings (*balapan*) shortly before fledging, from eyries in the [[Talas Alatau]] and Chatkal ranges. Others are trapped as young adults in their first or second autumn, and many berkutchi consider these better hunters.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### Training
Training lasts several months and follows an established sequence:
- **Manning:** the bird is kept hooded (*tomogo*), handled constantly and accustomed to the hunter's voice. Traditionally it is also kept awake for long periods until it accepts food from the hand.
- **Weight control:** feeding is managed so that the eagle is keen to hunt but not weakened.
- **Lure work:** the eagle learns to fly to the hunter's glove from increasing distances and to strike a lure (*chyrga*) made from a fox or hare skin dragged behind a rider.
- **Hunting:** the eagle is taken into the field with an experienced bird or hunter.

The hunter carries the eagle on a heavy leather glove, with the forearm supported by a wooden rest (*baldak*) fixed to the saddle. Hunting takes place mainly from November to February, when tracks show in the snow and pelts are at their best. The hunter rides to a ridge, scans the slopes below and unhoods the eagle when quarry is flushed, often with the help of beaters or *taigan* sighthounds. Most berkutchi ride hardy [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] horses.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Customs
Customary law (*adat*) and hunters' tradition govern several aspects of the practice. An eagle is normally kept for ten to twelve years. It is then released into the mountains in the breeding season after a ceremony (*kaytaruu*), at which the hunter leaves meat for it. Selling a trained eagle is regarded as shameful in many families, and birds pass between hunters as gifts. Among Christian berkutchi, eagles and hunting equipment are commonly blessed by a priest before the season opens.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Competitions and festivals
The main annual event is the Salburun festival, held each autumn in the pastures outside [[Talas]] and organized with the National Equestrian Sports Directorate. It brings together berkutchi from the ISEZ and the Autonomous Tribal Regions. Its events include:
- recall of the eagle to the glove over a set distance;
- strikes on a dragged lure (*chyrga*);
- hunting with live quarry, judged on speed and style;
- riding and archery contests, as well as events for falcons and *taigan* hounds.

Judges score the hunters as well as the birds, and award marks for bearing and composure according to the ideal of *körktüülük*.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Contemporary status
In 2022 the Directorate registered 71 active eagle hunters, most of them in the Talas Alatau and Chatkal Highlands planning zones. Clan elders in the Autonomous Tribal Regions say the true number is higher, since many hunters do not register with ISEZ bodies. Taking eagles from the wild requires a permit in the ISEZ and the approval of clan councils in the tribal regions. International trade in golden eagles is restricted under [[wp:CITES]]. Irad is not a State Party to the [[wp:UNESCO]] conventions, so Iradi eagle hunting is not included in the multinational UNESCO listing of falconry as intangible cultural heritage. Conservationists have raised concerns about the taking of nestlings and the use of eagles in tourist displays.<sup>[4]</sup>

### 4.12. Ulak Tartysh (Sport)
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Sport*

**Ulak Tartysh** (Iradi: *ulak tartysh*, "goat pulling") is a mounted team sport in which riders compete for possession of a headless goat carcass and try to throw it into the opponents' goal. It is the most popular traditional sport in Irad. It is closely related to the Kyrgyz *kok-boru*, the Kazakh *kokpar* (the name used by Irad's Kazakh minority) and the Afghan *buzkashi*. Two forms are played: a regulated team game with fixed rules, governed by the [[National Equestrian Sports Directorate]], and an older free-for-all form still common at weddings and memorial feasts in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. The sport is known for its physical violence. Its main event, the President's Cup, is held each March at the [[Irad State Hippodrome]] in [[Talas]].<sup>[1]</sup>

## History
Games of carcass-snatching on horseback have been played across [[wp:Central Asia]] for centuries. Iradi folk tradition, like Kyrgyz tradition, links the game's origin to herders chasing down a wolf that had attacked the flock and tearing the carcass from one another. Other accounts describe it as a training exercise for mounted warfare. Before the twentieth century the game had no fixed teams or field. Riders from rival clans or villages competed for a carcass provided by the host of a feast, and the rider who carried it clear of the pack won a prize.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

In the Soviet period the game was codified as a team sport. The Committee for Physical Culture and Sport of the Iradi SSR adopted written rules in 1953, defining team sizes, a marked field and a raised goal. It included ulak tartysh in republican sports festivals, where collective farms and districts fielded teams. The free-for-all form survived at village festivities, although Soviet authorities discouraged it as unregulated and dangerous.<sup>[2]</sup>

After 1992 the sport expanded rapidly. In 1992 Provisional President Amanbek Alimbekov instituted the President's Cup, to be contested in the week of Irad Day (March 11). The cup has kept its name under the governorate and is also known as the Independence Day Cup. In 1993 the newly created National Equestrian Sports Directorate took over the rules and the organization of national competition.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Rules of the regulated game
The Directorate's rules, last revised in 2016, provide for the following:
- **Teams:** two teams of twelve registered players, of whom four are mounted on the field at any time. Substitutions of horses and riders are allowed during stoppages.
- **Field:** a level ground of 300 by 150 meters, with a goal at each end.
- **Goal (*tai-kazan*):** a raised circular goal about 3.6 meters across and 1.2 meters high, built of packed earth or tires.
- **Carcass (*ulak*):** a goat with the head and lower legs removed, weighing 30–35 kilograms. It is soaked in cold water overnight to toughen it.
- **Duration:** two halves of twenty minutes each.
- **Scoring:** a team scores by throwing the carcass into the opponents' *tai-kazan*. After a goal, play restarts from the center.
- **Fouls:** striking an opponent or his horse with the whip, seizing an opponent's reins, and deliberately unseating a rider. Two mounted referees officiate.<sup>[3]</sup>

A rider (*chabandoz*) picks the carcass up from the ground at a gallop by leaning almost out of the saddle. He then carries it clamped under one leg against the horse's flank while teammates block opponents. Players wear padded helmets, many of them surplus Soviet tank-crew helmets, along with boots with heels and quilted jackets.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Traditional form
In the free-for-all form, played mainly in the Autonomous Tribal Regions, any number of riders may take part and there are no teams or goals. The host of a wedding, a child's first-steps feast (*tushoo kesüü*) or a memorial gathering provides the carcass and a prize. The prize may be cash, a carpet, livestock or, at large gatherings, a horse. Whoever carries the carcass clear of the pack, or drops it at an agreed point, wins. Clan elders (*aksakals*) act as judges. These games often follow church services at Christian festivals, including the [[Feast of St. Janyl]].<sup>[2]</sup>

## Horses
Ulak tartysh horses are specially trained to push into the pack, stand still while the rider leans down, and accelerate on command. They are usually trained from the age of five and play for many years. Most are [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] horses or Chongtor crosses, valued for their strength and stamina. Faster [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] crosses are sometimes used in the regulated game. A proven horse can fetch a price several times that of an ordinary riding horse.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Competitions and contemporary status
The Directorate's national league had 24 teams in the 2023 season. Eleven represented ISEZ cities and districts, and thirteen were registered by clans in the Autonomous Tribal Regions. Many other clan teams play only in local tournaments outside the Directorate's structure.<sup>[3]</sup>

The President's Cup final draws crowds of tens of thousands, some watching from outside the stadium. Broadcasting rights are held by [[IradOne]]. Winners receive cash prizes and, by tradition, a horse. Since 2009 the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] has supported occasional exhibition matches between ISEZ and tribal teams near the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] as confidence-building events.<sup>[4]</sup>

The sport has been criticized for its rate of injury to riders and horses, and animal welfare groups have objected to the use of carcasses. Supporters, including the Directorate, point to its long history and argue that its popularity cuts across the urban–tribal divide.<sup>[4]</sup>

### 4.13. Iradi Horsemeat Taboo
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Horses & Equestrianism*

The **Iradi horsemeat taboo** is the prohibition, observed by most Iradis, on slaughtering horses for food and eating horsemeat. Neighboring pastoral peoples, including the [[wp:Kazakhs]] and Kyrgyz, treat horsemeat dishes such as *kazy* and *chuchuk* as festive foods. Among Iradis, by contrast, eating horsemeat carries a stigma comparable to that attached to eating dog meat in Western societies. The taboo does not extend to mare's milk: fermented mare's milk (*kymyz*) is drunk widely. Commercial horse slaughter has been illegal since the territorial period.<sup>[1]</sup>

A common popular view holds that eating horsemeat is a "Muslim" practice. Ethnographers describe this view as a prejudice. It ignores the pastoral origins of the Kazakh and Kyrgyz practice, and scholars trace it to the use of the taboo as a marker of Christian identity.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Origins

#### Church tradition
In the tradition of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], the taboo goes back to [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]], the founding figure of the Iradi church. Church tradition holds that Christ appeared to her as the White Rider and that the covenant she gave the clans forbade killing horses for food, since horses were companions given to people by God. Later church writers compared killing a horse for meat to fratricide. The church has never issued a formal canonical prohibition. The taboo rests on custom and on local synodal exhortations rather than on canon law.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Scholarly explanations
Historians and anthropologists have offered several complementary explanations:
- **Identity marking.** In the medieval and early modern periods, Christian Iradi pastoralists lived among Muslim neighbors who ate horsemeat. Refusing it became a visible boundary between communities. Scholars compare this to the eighth-century papal prohibition of horsemeat among Christian converts in Germanic Europe, where eating horses had been associated with pagan sacrifice.<sup>[2]</sup>
- **Horse veneration.** Iradi culture places the horse at the center of national identity. This extends to the national belief that Irad was the birthplace of horse domestication, a belief not supported by genetic studies since 2021. The taboo is consistent with this status.
- **Adaptation of funerary custom.** Among the Kazakhs and Kyrgyz, the horse of a dead man was traditionally slaughtered and eaten at his memorial feast. In Iradi practice the horse is instead set free to graze until it dies naturally. Ethnographers read this as a Christianized version of a shared steppe custom (see [[Fallen Rider Tradition]]).<sup>[4]</sup>

#### The "Muslim practice" prejudice
Many Iradis regard eating horsemeat as a barbarous, specifically Muslim custom. Ethnographers point out that this is inaccurate on several counts:
- Horsemeat eating among the Kazakhs and Kyrgyz is a pastoral nomadic tradition that predates their conversion to Islam.
- The [[wp:Hanafi school|Hanafi]] school of Islamic law, dominant in [[wp:Central Asia]], historically classed horsemeat as disapproved (*makruh*), following [[wp:Abu Hanifa]], though later Hanafi jurists permitted it.
- Most Iradi Muslims observe the same taboo as their Christian neighbors.

Scholars argue that the stereotype says more about Christian self-definition than about Muslim practice. Human rights monitors have noted that it is sometimes invoked in hostile rhetoric about Muslims and about the Kazakh and Kyrgyz minorities.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[5]</sup>

## Law and enforcement
In 1996 the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] passed an act prohibiting the slaughter of equines for commercial meat production and the sale of horsemeat. Violations are punishable by fines and the closure of facilities. The act remains in force in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]]. Private consumption is not itself an offense. Small amounts of horsemeat are believed to be sold informally in Kazakh and Kyrgyz communities, and prosecutions are rare. In the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], clan councils deal with violations under customary law (*adat*), usually by fines paid in livestock.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Food and substitution
Iradi versions of regional dishes use beef or mutton where neighbors use horsemeat. *[[Beshbarmak (Culinary)|Beshbarmak]]* is made with beef or mountain mutton. *[[Kazy]]*-style sausage is made from beef or lamb. Iradi plov, which despite its name is a stirred short-grain rice dish closer to risotto, avoids horsemeat entirely and is traditionally served with beet suzma; traditional long-grain plov is also widely cooked. Historically, mutton was the main festive meat. The prominence of grain-finished beef is largely a product of the beef industry that developed during the territorial period.<sup>[1]</sup>

Ethnographers have noted an irony in this. In Iradi folk belief, bulls and black cattle are linked with ill omen through the figure of [[Morkhan (Mythology)|Morkhan]], the bull-headed pre-Christian god identified with Satan in church tradition, yet beef has become the country's main festive meat.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Social practice
Offering horsemeat to an Iradi guest is regarded as a serious insult. Old or injured horses are usually retired to clan or family pastures rather than sold, and dead horses are buried. Younger urban Iradis who have lived or worked in [[wp:Kazakhstan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] are more likely to describe the taboo as a cultural preference than as a moral rule. Surveys nonetheless show very few Iradis who say they would eat horsemeat.<sup>[5]</sup>

### 4.14. Fallen Rider Tradition
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Horses & Equestrianism*

The **Fallen Rider tradition** (Iradi: *Jygylgan Atchan Saltı*, "custom of the fallen rider") is a steppe cavalry memorial custom in which downward-facing tack, an inverted saddle or an upturned horseshoe marks a rider who has died, particularly one killed in battle. In Irad the custom survives in funerals, especially in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. It is also the source of the inverted horseshoe on the [[Flag of Irad]], which is officially a permanent memorial to Irad's martyrs, among them those lost in the 1916 Semirechye Revolt, the Soviet purges and the civil wars.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Origins
Customs that mark a dead warrior through his horse and tack are widespread among the pastoral peoples of [[wp:Central Asia]]. Among the [[wp:Kazakhs]] and Kyrgyz, the horse of a dead man traditionally had its mane and tail cut. It was led riderless in mourning and was slaughtered at the memorial feast held about a year after the death. Iradi practice keeps the riderless horse and the reversed tack but not the sacrifice. Ethnographers connect this difference to the [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo|Iradi taboo on horsemeat]] and the Christianization of the Iradi clans. Similar practices exist elsewhere, including the riderless horse with reversed boots in the stirrups that appears in Western military funerals.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Funerary practice
In a traditional funeral in the tribal regions, the dead person's riding horse, often a [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] or [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]], is led behind the bier. Its saddle is reversed and its stirrups are crossed over the seat. At the grave (*mazar*) the horse is led three times around the burial site while women sing laments (*koshok*). After the burial it is not ridden again. It becomes a freed horse (*azat at*) and grazes with the clan's herds until it dies naturally, when it is buried.<sup>[2]</sup>

When a rider dies in battle or disappears in the mountains, families nail a horseshoe points-down above the door of the house or on the gate of the yard. The shoe stays there until the one-year memorial. In urban areas of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] the full ritual is now uncommon. The inverted horseshoe, often in the form of a small metal badge, is used at funerals and on memorial days, including the August 15 commemoration of [[The Lost Tribes of 1916]].<sup>[3]</sup>

## On the national flag
The flag of Irad carries an inverted horseshoe on the hoist side of the white stallion. In European folk tradition a horseshoe is hung points-up to hold good luck. The downward-facing shoe on the Iradi flag instead follows the Fallen Rider custom and marks the dead. Official descriptions of the flag identify it as a memorial to the martyrs of Irad, specifically:
- those killed in the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|Semirechye Revolt]] of 1916 and the flight that followed;
- the victims of the Soviet purges and repressions of the 1930s;
- the dead of the [[First Iradi Civil War|First]] and [[Second Iradi Civil War|Second Iradi Civil Wars]].<sup>[1]</sup>

### 4.15. Arsha Juniper Incense Tradition
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Religion*

The **arsha juniper incense tradition** is the ritual burning of mountain juniper (Iradi: *[[Arsha (Flora)|arsha]]*) in Irad, both in the liturgy of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] and in household purification rites. Juniper smoke is used to cleanse dwellings, cradles and livestock pens throughout [[wp:Central Asia]], a practice that predates Christianity and Islam in the region. In Irad it was also taken into church worship. Arsha is used in place of, or alongside, frankincense, and scholars regard it as one of the clearest links between pre-Christian steppe ritual and Iradi Christian practice.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Botany and gathering
The species most often used is the semiglobose juniper (*Juniperus semiglobosa*), which grows on rocky slopes of the [[Talas Alatau]] and the [[Chatkal River|Chatkal]] range between about 1,500 and 3,000 meters. Related species such as *J. seravschanica* and *J. turkestanica* are also used. The trees grow slowly, and some stands are several centuries old.<sup>[2]</sup>

Gathering is traditionally regulated by village elders and, for church use, by the monastic [[Order of St. Janyl the Hermit]]. Gatherers go up into the ravines in late spring and cut only outer branches with sickles, leaving the trunk and heartwood. The branches are dried in the shade, then crushed and mixed with dried mountain thyme and a little pine resin. Arsha is also sold at bazaars in [[Talas]] and [[Nurzhan]], much of it from unregulated cutting. Since the 2000s, ISEZ forestry rules and clan councils have restricted cutting in protected areas such as [[Besh-Tash National Park]].<sup>[2]</sup>

## Liturgical use
In the rite of the Syro-Iradi Church, arsha is burned in the censer during the liturgy, at processions and at funerals. Rural parishes and tent chapels in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] traditionally use arsha alone. Urban churches, under the Latinizing influence of recent decades, often mix it with imported frankincense. Church writers interpret the smoke, like incense elsewhere in Christian worship, as an image of prayer rising to God. In Iradi devotional language it rises "to the White Rider". Arsha is burned in large quantities at the [[Church of St. Janyl]] in [[Iyık Janyl]] during the [[Feast of St. Janyl]] on August 24.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Household rites
In homes, the smoke is used in a purification rite called *alastoo*, usually performed by older women. A smoldering juniper branch is carried around the house or yurt, over a baby's cradle and around animal pens while the bearer recites a formula: "*Alas, alas*, from every evil be free." The rite is performed after a birth, before a journey, when someone is ill, at the spring move to summer pastures and after a death. It is believed to drive away illness and evil spirits, including the *albarsty*, a female demon said to threaten women in childbirth. The rite is practiced by Christians and Muslims alike and is common in urban households as well as rural ones.<sup>[3]</sup>

### 4.16. Kümöch Sacramental Bread
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Religion*

**Kümöch** (Iradi: *kümöch nan*) is the unleavened wheat bread used for the Eucharist in the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]]. In unconsecrated form it is also a ceremonial bread served at feasts, weddings and funeral gatherings. The name comes from a Turkic word for bread baked in embers. Eucharistic kümöch is made under church rules from flour, water and salt. Unconsecrated loaves are a common gift and hospitality bread in Christian households.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Background
Most churches of the East Syriac tradition, including the Assyrian Church of the East, use leavened bread for the Eucharist and renew it each year with a portion of "holy leaven" (*malka*). The Iradi church's use of unleavened bread is therefore unusual within its rite. Church historians disagree about its origin:
- some see it as an early Latin influence, through contacts with Catholic missionaries in the Mongol period;
- others argue that it continues a local custom of ember-baked flatbread, adopted when the clandestine communities of the Timurid and [[wp:Khanate of Kokand|Kokand]] eras could not maintain the holy leaven.

Supporters of the first view point to the survival of the holy leaven among some clans of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (see below) as evidence that leavened bread was once general in the Iradi church.<sup>[2]</sup>

In popular devotion, kümöch is associated with [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]], who is said to have fed the clans on ember-baked bread during their flight into the mountains.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Preparation
Eucharistic kümöch for the archeparchy is baked at the motherhouse of the [[Order of St. Janyl the Hermit]], south of [[Iyık Janyl]]. Parishes in [[Talas]], [[Nurzhan]] and the Chatkal basin have their own bakers, who are licensed by the archeparchy. The bakers fast before baking and recite psalms while they work. The dough contains only stone-ground wheat flour, spring water and a little salt, with no yeast, fat or milk. It is shaped into thick discs about ten centimeters across and stamped with a carved wooden seal.<sup>[1]</sup>

The designs of the seals vary. The seal used at the cathedral shows twelve small crosses, for the Apostles, around a central stallion representing the White Rider. Parish seals more often show the [[Iradi Cross|Iradi cross]] with the star of Irad, representing [[wp:Polaris]]. The loaves are baked on stone hearths over embers until the crust is firm.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Liturgical use
During the [[wp:Holy Qurbana]] the celebrant breaks the consecrated loaf. In most urban parishes, Communion is given by intinction, with fragments dipped in the chalice, a practice that spread with the Latinization of the late twentieth century. Some rural and tent congregations in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] still give the bread and the chalice separately. Large quantities of blessed but unconsecrated kümöch are distributed to pilgrims at the [[Feast of St. Janyl]] on August 24.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Holy leaven in the tribal regions
In parts of the Autonomous Tribal Regions, mainly in the Chatkal valley and the eastern mountains, itinerant priests and clan elders keep a holy leaven, called *malka* in church usage and *ene achytky* ("mother leaven") by herders. Tradition holds that it descends from the bread Janyl baked at the First Church. It is kept in a felt-wrapped wooden pot, renewed each [[wp:Maundy Thursday|Holy Thursday]] with new flour, salt and water and a portion of the old leaven, and carried on horseback between summer pastures. Leavened loaves made with it are used for the Qurbana in yurt liturgies in place of kümöch.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>

The leaven may be given but never sold. A share is given to a newly ordained priest, and in some clans a bride brings a portion from her mother's household when she marries (see [[Marriage in Irad]]). Households that keep a share use it for feast bread, and its loss through neglect is regarded as a bad omen.<sup>[4]</sup>

Since the 1990s the archeparchy has required unleavened kümöch in its parishes, a rule that critics within the church count among the Latinizations of the territorial period. The [[Syro-Iradi Episcopal Synod]] tolerates leavened Qurbana in the tribal regions where it is ancient custom, as Eastern Catholic canon law permits, and the clans of the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] treat the malka as a mark of their independence from the urban church as well as from the ISEZ.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>

## Domestic and festive use
Unconsecrated kümöch is baked at home for weddings, baptisms, memorial gatherings and major feasts. It is broken by hand and shared. Cutting bread with a knife at such occasions is considered disrespectful, and dropping bread or leaving it on the ground is taboo, as across [[wp:Central Asia]]. At funerals, guests are served kümöch with mutton broth and *kymyz*. Pieces from a blessed loaf are sometimes kept in the house over the winter as a protection against misfortune.<sup>[3]</sup>
