### 4.43. Irad Special Economic Zone
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Politics & Government*

The **Irad Special Economic Zone** (ISEZ; Iradi: *Irad Atayın Ekonomikalık Zonası*) is the part of [[Irad]] administered by the government of the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI). It covers about 64,000 square kilometers (24,700 sq mi), roughly one-third of the country: the irrigated Talas valley, the Chu lowlands, an industrial corridor south of [[Talas]] and a salient on the lower Naryn. In the official 2018 census it held about 52 percent of the population, most of it in the three cities of Talas, [[Nurzhan]] and [[Iyık Janyl]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup> The other two-thirds of Irad, the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), lie beyond the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]].

[[Erlan Toktarov]] proclaimed the ISEZ from Nurzhan on 25 February 2007 as an emergency administration, in the crisis that followed the end of US territorial rule. Its present extent was fixed by the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]] in September of that year. The zone is governed through the institutions of the former US territory: an elected Governor and Lieutenant Governor, the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] and the [[Supreme Court of Irad]]. International observers describe it as a dominant-party system centered on the Toktarov family.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[4]</sup> Talas is the *de jure* capital. Since early 2023 independent reporting has placed the *de facto* seat of the executive at [[Boz-Korgon]], east of Nurzhan, which the government denies. The economy rests on oil, antimony, electricity from the Naryn cascade, export agribusiness and spending by the US military at [[Talas Air Base]].

## Name and status
The 2007 proclamation used the term "special economic zone", which analysts read as a signal to foreign companies that their concessions would be protected after the collapse of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] (DRI).<sup>[1]</sup> The ISEZ government does not describe itself as the government of a separate region. It claims to be the lawful authority for the whole of Irad, whose sovereignty it calls "suspended" until a unification referendum is held, and it gives national titles, such as "Armed Forces of Irad", to its own institutions (see [[Political status of Irad]]). The clan councils of the ATR and the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC) reject this claim. No state recognizes the ISEZ as a sovereign government, and [[wp:Kazakhstan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] each claim Irad *de jure*. In everyday usage the ISEZ is often called "the governorate" or "the Zone".

## History

#### Origins (2006–2007)
The ISEZ grew out of the political collapse that followed the [[Territory of Irad (1992–2006)|US territorial period]]. President George W. Bush withdrew the United States from the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] by executive action on 3 December 2006. The Supreme Court then issued the [[Statutory Independence Ruling (2006)]], and the Territorial Legislature proclaimed the DRI on 9 December. In January and February 2007 the DRI cabinet of [[Bakyt Orozbekov]] sold state concessions to firms linked to DPI members, provoking protests in Talas and unrest in the countryside (see [[Privatization Scandals of 2007]]).<sup>[1]</sup>

On 25 February 2007 Toktarov, a former Majority Leader of the Territorial Senate, seized control of the DPI apparatus and proclaimed the ISEZ from Nurzhan. He annulled the independence ruling and declared Irad's sovereignty suspended, while the DRI cabinet in Talas continued as a rival authority. The date marks the start of the [[Second Iradi Civil War]]. Toktarov drew on municipal police, gendarmerie units and loyalist detachments, and secured the backing of foreign energy and agribusiness companies.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Consolidation (2007–2011)
The [[Popular Front of Irad]] stormed Talas on 4 June 2007, dissolved the DRI and then withdrew to the countryside. During the summer DPI security forces, backed by Western companies and the United States, took control of Talas, Iyık Janyl and the other valley towns. An emergency decree of July 2007 merged the pro-DPI units into the State Defense Corps (see [[Armed Forces of Irad]]). The Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement of September 2007 fixed the 420-kilometer Qara-Chik line between the ISEZ and the clan-held countryside, and the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI) was established on 18 October 2007 to monitor it.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[9]</sup>

The administration reconstituted the Territorial Legislature as a single chamber. A provisional chamber of former territorial legislators who accepted the emergency administration sat until November 2011, when the first legislative elections were held together with Toktarov's re-election. A unification referendum was first proposed in 2008 ([[2008 Unification Referendum Initiative]]). The only direct talks with the IAC, in 2011, ended when its delegation walked out after being offered one-third of the seats in a reunified legislature (see [[2011 Bilateral Reunification Summit]]).<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Toktarov's governorship (2011–2023)
In 2013 the legislature amended the 1992 Elective Governor Acts to remove gubernatorial term limits ([[2013 Constitutional Amendment]]), and Toktarov won further terms in 2015, 2019 and 2023. Members of his family took senior posts. His eldest son, [[Ruslan Toktarov]], has commanded the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] since 2012; his second son, [[Alikhan Toktarov]], has chaired [[IradOne]] since 2015; and his son-in-law, [[Aidar Maksat]], became Lieutenant Governor in November 2019.<sup>[11]</sup> Trade with China grew through antimony exports and Chinese investment in cotton processing, while the US basing arrangements continued. In 2021, after the [[wp:Taliban]] returned to power in [[wp:Afghanistan]], the ISEZ declared a security alert and reinforced the mountain passes ([[The 2021 Regional Security Alert]]).

#### Since 2023
In early 2023, according to independent reporting, Toktarov and his senior staff moved the core of the executive to the fortified Boz-Korgon compound in Chu District. The government maintains that Talas remains the operational capital.<sup>[5]</sup> In October 2023 a municipal licensing surcharge in Talas set off student and courier protests, which police and Gendarmerie units dispersed; the surcharge was suspended in November ([[2023 Student Protests in Talas]]).

Toktarov has not appeared in public since July 2024. The DPI attributes his absence to an extended health retreat, and Maksat runs the government's day-to-day business (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]). In 2025, remarks by [[wp:Donald Trump|US President Donald Trump]] about selling Irad to Russia provoked demonstrations in Talas and anti-American feeling across the zone ([[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]]). The next gubernatorial and legislative elections, and the renewal of the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]], are due in 2027.

## Government and politics

#### Legal basis
The ISEZ has no constitution of its own. It treats the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]] and the statutes of the territorial period as still in force, regards their provisions on federal oversight as inoperative, and amends them through the legislature. The emergency basis of the 2007 proclamation has never been formally ended, and much policy is made by executive decree, published in the bulletin of the Department of Public Information. [[wp:Human Rights Watch]] and other critics argue that this arrangement leaves the executive largely unchecked.<sup>[10]</sup>

#### Executive
Executive power is vested in the Governor, who is elected by popular vote for a four-year term in November under the Elective Governor Acts of 1992. Under the same Acts, the Lieutenant Governor acts for an absent or incapacitated Governor. Toktarov, who also chairs the DPI, has been Governor since 2007. Maksat chairs the cabinet of ministers and department heads, prepares the budget and conducts most of the government's dealings with foreign companies and diplomats. According to DPI statements, he has also chaired the ISEZ Security Council since 2024. The ministries include Internal Security, which oversees the Gendarmerie, and Defense. The Department of Public Information is the government's press office.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Legislature and courts
The Territorial Legislature (*Mejlis*) sits in Legislative Hall in Talas. Since 2007 it has been a single chamber of 60 members, elected every four years in November, on the same day as the Governor, in multi-member constituencies matching the three cities and five districts. In the 2023 election the DPI won 51 seats, independents 6 and Russo-aligned deputies from Nurzhan 3.<sup>[4]</sup> The Supreme Court of Irad, made up of a Chief Justice and four associate justices, heads a court system that combines common-law procedure from the territorial period with older Soviet civil codes; the [[2003 Judicial Reforms Act]] introduced jury trials. The court's jurisdiction does not extend into the ATR.

#### Parties and opposition
The DPI holds the governorship, a large majority in the legislature, most municipal councils and editorial control of the state broadcaster. [[wp:Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe|OSCE]] observers have said that the elections held since 2011 lacked meaningful choice. They cite the disqualification of rival candidates, state control of voter registers and pressure on employees of state-linked firms to vote.<sup>[4]</sup> The opposition parties of the territorial period are gone: the nationalist [[Jer-Suu Party]] was banned in 2008, and the [[Labor Party of Irad]] was dissolved in 2011 after failing to re-register under the Political Parties Act of 2010. The most visible opposition currents are the Russian-speaking "Russo" constituency of Nurzhan, whose best-known figure is [[Kamran Bekzatov]], president of [[NurGaz]] (see [[Russos of Nurzhan]]), and the anarcho-capitalist commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]]. Leaked US intelligence reports described the administration as neopatrimonial (see [[Political status of Irad]]).<sup>[11]</sup>

## Administrative divisions
The ISEZ is divided into three cities of governorate significance and five districts (*aimak*). Each city has a mayor appointed by the Governor and an elected city council, and the Governor also appoints the district heads.<sup>[3]</sup> City populations are 2018 official estimates.

| Unit | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| [[Talas]] | City | *De jure* capital and commercial center; 1,120,000, or 1.4 million in the metropolitan area |
| [[Nurzhan]] | City | Industrial center and headquarters of NurGaz; 850,000, or more than 1 million in the agglomeration |
| [[Iyık Janyl]] | City | Seat of the Archbishop of Iyık Janyl and pilgrimage center; 310,000 |
| Talas District | District | The middle Talas valley around the capital, including Talas Air Base |
| Kara-Buura District | District | The lower and western Talas valley |
| Chu District | District | The Chu lowlands around Nurzhan, including the oil fields and the Boz-Korgon area |
| Sary-Bulak District | District | The southern industrial corridor and foothills south of Talas, including the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]] and the [[Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex]] |
| Lower Naryn District | District | A salient around [[Tash-Kömür]] and the city of Iyık Janyl, the downstream Naryn cascade and the [[Fergana Gateway]], linked to Talas by the [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]] |

Nurzhan's urban districts include [[Dastgoh District|Dastgoh]] and [[Navbahor District|Navbahor]]. See also [[Administrative divisions of Irad]].

## Geography
The ISEZ is made up of the most densely settled river valleys of Irad rather than a compact block of territory. Its core is the irrigated plain of the middle and lower Talas, at about 1,250 meters around Talas, and the lower Chu lowlands around Nurzhan, at 740 meters; road and rail link the two. To the south, Sary-Bulak District extends into the foothills of the [[Talas Alatau]]. Beyond it, the Fergana Mountain Transit Highway crosses the range through a narrow corridor to the Lower Naryn District around Tash-Kömür, where the Naryn leaves the mountains for the [[wp:Fergana Valley]]. Tribal land flanks the corridor on both sides.<sup>[9]</sup> In the north the ISEZ faces Kazakhstan along about 285 kilometers of frontier, marked under the 2008 [[Northern Border Demarcation Protocol]], a technical arrangement that Kazakhstan says implies no recognition. Elsewhere it is bounded by the Qara-Chik line.

Much of the zone's water comes from outside it. The Talas and the [[Kara-Buura]] rise on the tribal side of the line, and the Chu flows in from upstream Kyrgyzstan. On the Naryn, the Toktogul dam and reservoir lie in the ATR, while the switchyard, the national dispatch center and the downstream stations of the cascade lie in the ISEZ. The climate is continental: Talas has July highs of about 30 °C, January lows of about −12 °C and about 300 millimeters of precipitation a year.

## Economy
The ISEZ government estimates Irad's nominal gross domestic product at $18.4 billion for 2024, or about $50 billion at purchasing power parity. Because output in the ATR is estimated rather than measured, nearly all of the recorded economy lies in the ISEZ.<sup>[6]</sup> The US dollar is legal tender and the [[Iradi som]] circulates alongside it. [[Talasbank]] dominates commercial banking and holds the main export escrow accounts, which are audited by the [[Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority]].

The main sectors are:<sup>[6]</sup><sup>[12]</sup>
- **Oil.** NurGaz produces light crude in the Chu basin. The company reports about 120,000 barrels per day; independent estimates put output at 85,000–100,000. Part is refined at [[Nurzhan Refinery No. 1]]. Since 2000 most of the rest has been exported north through the 85-kilometer [[Northern Export Feeder]] into the [[wp:KazTransOil]] network, for refining at [[wp:Shymkent]] or shipment to Russia. There is no southern export pipeline. NurGaz is the zone's largest taxpayer.
- **Mining.** Irad holds about 7 percent of world antimony reserves. Ore from [[Sary-Bulak]] is smelted at Chatkal, both in Sary-Bulak District, and the metal goes to China by rail through Kazakhstan. Both plants belong to the [[Iradi Antimony and Rare Metals Combine]].
- **Electricity.** The ISEZ controls the export grid of the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]] (1,200 MW) and sells power mainly to Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan. Revenue is shared with the ATR under an unpublished formula, and independent analysts estimate that the ISEZ takes the larger share.
- **Agribusiness.** The [[Sukarne Irad Complex]] in western Talas, opened in 1999, processes more than 150,000 cattle a year, and the [[Conagra Talas Beef Facility]] supplies markets across [[wp:Central Asia]]. Cotton is grown mainly in the Lower Naryn District. [[Nurzhan Agro-Industrial]] dominates feed milling, and bonded zones such as the [[Talas Agribusiness Export Zone]] (1998) process goods for export.
- **US military spending.** Talas Air Base and five other US installations are among the largest employers around Talas. The Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Irad estimates that base contracts bring about $450 million a year into the zone.
- **Services and transport.** [[Attelkom]] provides telecommunications, [[Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics]] runs bonded trucking to the northern crossings, and [[Iradiya]] flies charter and cargo services from Talas.

Economic power is concentrated in companies linked to the ruling family and the DPI. Toktarov's sons [[Timur Toktarov|Timur]], [[Adil Toktarov|Adil]] and [[Bekzat Toktarov|Bekzat]] run family businesses in freight, commercial real estate and feed milling, and Alikhan holds real-estate and retail interests alongside his chairmanship of IradOne. Bekzatov and Ilyasov have both attacked these monopolies.<sup>[7]</sup> Non-recognition denies the ISEZ a sovereign credit rating and access to the [[wp:International Monetary Fund]]. Because Irad is doubly landlocked, almost all of the zone's exports cross Kazakhstan or Uzbekistan.

## Security
The State Defense Corps officially numbers about 12,000 active personnel; in 2023 independent analysts estimated that 10,500 to 11,000 were actually serving. Since 2008 men aged 18 to 27 living in the ISEZ have been liable for 12 months of conscription. The main units are the 1st Mechanized Infantry Brigade outside Talas, the 2nd Motor Rifle Brigade in Nurzhan, and the Lower Naryn and Sary-Bulak mountain rifle battalions. Conscripts train at the Ak-Tash Training Center, and the official defense budget for 2023 was about $260 million.<sup>[8]</sup>

The Republican Gendarmerie, about 4,000 strong, answers to the Ministry of Internal Security. It mans the twelve checkpoints on the ISEZ side of the Qara-Chik line, guards the perimeter of Talas Air Base, and through its Special Protective Service protects senior officials and the Boz-Korgon compound. Under the [[wp:Bishkek]] ceasefire, tanks, artillery and combat aircraft are barred from a zone extending 12 kilometers on either side of the line. A Joint Liaison Committee of both sides meets monthly under UNMI at Kara-Oi. Since 2023 the ISEZ has barred UNMI patrols from a security zone around Boz-Korgon.<sup>[9]</sup> US forces remain at Talas Air Base and five other sites under the [[2001 Basing Rights Agreement]] and later arrangements with the ISEZ, and hold an annual exercise with the corps, *Alatau Shield*.

## Demographics
The 2018 census counted about 2.4 million people in the ISEZ, 52 percent of the official national total of 4,626,000. Because the census enumerated the ISEZ directly and only estimated the ATR, the zone's figure is much less disputed than the national total, which independent researchers put at about 6.2 million (see [[2018 Irad census]]).<sup>[2]</sup> Most residents live in the three cities and their suburbs.

Iradis form the large majority. Nearly all of Irad's migrant and foreign communities live in the ISEZ: the Russian, Ukrainian and [[Koryo-saram in Irad|Koryo-saram]] communities are concentrated in Nurzhan, more than 10,000 Mexicans live in and around Talas, and American residents are linked to the bases and their contractors. Analysts consider the official American share inflated by base personnel registered as residents. Kazakh communities live in the Chu lowlands and Uzbek communities in the Lower Naryn District.<sup>[2]</sup>

Iradi and English are the official languages. Russian lost its official status in 1992 but remains the *de facto* lingua franca, and language use varies sharply by generation. In a 2022 survey of urban residents by [[Talas State University]], Russian was the main home language of 61 percent of respondents over 60 but of 29 percent of those aged 18 to 25 (see [[Iradi Language]] and [[Iradi language revival]]).<sup>[13]</sup> Most residents belong to the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], whose mother see is at Iyık Janyl. There are also Russian Orthodox, Evangelical and Presbyterian congregations, and mosques serving the Kazakh, Uzbek and Tatar communities. The ISEZ is a secular state.

## Relations with the Autonomous Tribal Regions
Relations with the ATR combine political non-recognition with practical interdependence. Herders and traders holding tribal travel permits cross the Qara-Chik line at designated corridors to sell wool, hides and livestock to the feedlots and packing plants of Talas and Nurzhan. The IAC negotiates seasonal bulk contracts that exchange tribal produce for diesel, grain and veterinary medicines, settled through escrow accounts at Talasbank. Engineers from both sides run the Toktogul complex through a joint technical commission under UN supervision.<sup>[9]</sup> The ISEZ accuses IAC-aligned groups of smuggling goods past its checkpoints through the [[Kok-Tash Kariz System]]. Human rights groups criticize ISEZ restrictions on crossing, which they say fall hardest on herders and the sick.<sup>[10]</sup> The size of the tribal population, which would determine its weight in any unified legislature, remains a central point of dispute.

## Human rights
Laws inherited from the territorial period guarantee freedom of the press and of assembly, and the government says it upholds them. Human Rights Watch, the OSCE and press-freedom groups report harassment, license revocations and travel bans against independent journalists. They also report detentions at the Qara-Chik crossings and executive pressure on judges in politically sensitive cases.<sup>[10]</sup> During the October 2023 protests, mobile data in central Talas was cut for three days. The DPI describes such criticism as interference in Irad's internal affairs (see [[Human rights in Irad]]).

### 4.44. Popular Front of Irad
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: History*

The **Popular Front of Irad** (PFI; Iradi: *Iradın Eldik Frontu*) was a coalition of clan militias, industrial strike committees and rural supporters that fought in the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] of 2007. It was formed in March 2007 under the Tanıp clan chief [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]], in reaction to the privatization of state assets and communal pastures by the government of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] (DRI). On 4 June 2007 it stormed [[Talas]] and brought down the DRI government. It then withdrew to the countryside as forces of the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI) took the cities, and after the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]] its political council was reorganized as the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC) and its fighters as the [[El-Choro Militias]].<sup>[1]</sup>

## Background
After the United States withdrew from the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] in December 2006, the DRI cabinet of Prime Minister [[Bakyt Orozbekov]] faced a large budget deficit. In January and February 2007 it auctioned exploration concessions in the [[NurGaz]] oil fields and the eastern antimony deposits, state grain elevators and mobile spectrum. It also issued decrees to privatize communal pastures in the Chatkal valley. Investigative reporting found that many assets had gone at low prices to firms linked to cabinet ministers and other DPI members (see [[Privatization Scandals of 2007]]). In mid-January police fired on herders protesting fuel price rises in the Chu valley, and clan leaders treated the pasture decrees as a threat to customary land tenure.<sup>[2]</sup> On 25 February [[Erlan Toktarov]] proclaimed the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] from [[Nurzhan]], so that by early March two rival governments claimed authority while the countryside was in open revolt.

## Formation and program
Clan leaders meeting in March 2007 formed the Front as an emergency alliance and asked Bektur, hereditary chief (*biy*) of the Tanıp, to coordinate its forces. Strike committees from the Nurzhan factories and the railway workers' union joined within weeks, and some rural parish clergy of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] supported it, although the [[Archbishopric of Iyık Janyl]] remained neutral.<sup>[3]</sup> The Front's published demands were:<sup>[1]</sup>
- the restoration of communal pasture rights and the cancellation of the pasture decrees;
- an audit of the privatization contracts awarded since December 2006;
- the protection of customary law (*adat*) in the countryside;
- an end to what it called the plunder of national wealth by foreign companies and political insiders.

The Front had no single command structure. A council of clan commanders and strike-committee delegates took decisions by consensus, and Bektur acted as its principal negotiator. It did not declare a government of its own.

## Military campaign
At its peak the Front fielded more than 8,000 mounted irregulars, most of them riding [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] mountain horses and armed with light infantry weapons. Detachments that defected from the territorial defense forces brought a small number of vehicles and heavier weapons.<sup>[4]</sup> In the spring of 2007 its columns encircled government garrisons in the countryside, and railway strikers and saboteurs cut the lines serving Talas and Nurzhan. By late May the Front controlled most of the rural interior, about two-thirds of the country. Toktarov's forces concentrated on holding Nurzhan, the oil fields and the export pipeline, while the DRI government was increasingly confined to Talas, which the Front invested from 22 April.<sup>[4]</sup>

On 4 June 2007 the Front stormed Talas ([[Storming of Talas (2007)]]). Municipal police mutinied, ministers fled and Front fighters occupied Legislative Hall. Tribal commanders arrested Orozbekov at his residence. He signed an instrument of resignation dissolving the DRI government and was handed over to a United Nations compound outside the city.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Withdrawal and ceasefire
The Front's aims centered on land and customary rights rather than control of the cities, and it withdrew from Talas within weeks. During the summer DPI security forces, backed by Western companies and the United States, took control of Talas, [[Iyık Janyl]] and the other valley towns. Fighting continued along the emerging front line, especially around the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]], whose dam lay in Front-held territory. Front representatives negotiated the Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement in September 2007, which fixed the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], and both sides asked for the international monitoring presence that became the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]].<sup>[1]</sup>

## Dissolution
In late 2007 a kurultai of clan elders on the [[Aksay Plateau]] reorganized the Front's political council as the Iradi Freedom Society, which has since coordinated the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. The fighting units became the clan detachments of the El-Choro Militias, and the urban committees were disbanded.<sup>[3]</sup> The Nurzhan unions that had joined the Front returned to industrial bargaining under the ISEZ administration.

## Legacy
In the tribal regions the storming of Talas is remembered as a popular rising against corruption, and Bektur, who still refuses formal titles, is widely regarded as its hero. Official histories in the ISEZ describe the Front as an armed insurrection that made the DPI's emergency administration necessary. Historians debate whether the Front was mainly a rural rising against privatization or one side in a wider contest for control of the state.<sup>[1]</sup> The anniversary of the storming is marked on 4 June at gatherings in the tribal regions.

### 4.45. Bush Family Palatial Complex Conspiracy Theory
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Society & Demographics*

The **Bush Family Palatial Complex conspiracy theory** is a conspiracy theory, widespread in Irad in the 2000s, which held that the fortified compound of [[Boz-Korgon]] ("Grey Fortress"), 40 kilometers east of [[Nurzhan]], had been built as a private retreat for the Bush family. In the theory's account, the retreat was a reward for ending US administration of Irad under the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]], a step that cleared the way for the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI) to consolidate power. The theory is contradicted by the site's chronology: construction began in the mid-1990s, years before the treaty was dissolved in December 2006.<sup>[1]</sup> It survives mainly as a trope of political satire.

## Background
Boz-Korgon was begun in 1995 by the US territorial administration as a continuity-of-government site, with a hardened command and communications center and a security depot for the Nurzhan oil fields and the eastern rail corridor. It was enlarged between 2001 and 2005 with underground shelters, a perimeter wall and hardened communications rooms. Territorial planning documents described the works only in general terms, and the compound was closed to the public.<sup>[1]</sup> On 3 December 2006 President George W. Bush withdrew the United States from the treaty by executive action. The upheaval that followed ended with [[Erlan Toktarov]] in control of the DPI and of the new [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (see [[Second Iradi Civil War]]).

## Claims
The theory circulated in tabloid newspapers and opposition pamphlets in [[Talas]] and Nurzhan, and later online. Its versions shared several claims:<sup>[2]</sup>
- that secret annexes to the Alimbekov–Baker Treaty had deeded the land at Boz-Korgon to an offshore trust linked to the Bush family;
- that the compound had been built as a private estate, with tabloid accounts describing underground bunkers, horse stables and a hunting lodge;
- that the December 2006 withdrawal was a prearranged transaction, in which the United States left Irad in exchange for the estate and the DPI received power.

Visits by members of the Bush family to the site during the 2000s were cited by proponents as confirmation.

## Evidence against the theory
Historians and journalists who have examined the theory point first to its chronology. Territorial infrastructure records published in the Territorial Gazette show that excavation at Boz-Korgon began in 1995 and that the works were financed through territorial infrastructure bonds, long before the withdrawal that the estate was supposedly meant to reward.<sup>[1]</sup> No document transferring ownership or title has been found. Members of the Bush family did visit the site on several occasions during the 2000s, but there is no evidence that it was ever deeded to them. The compound passed to the ISEZ government after 2007, and property filings reported by the *[[Talas Herald]]* show that the Toktarov family formally occupied a residential estate within it from 2011.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Later history
Interest in the theory faded after the Toktarov family moved into the compound. It revived briefly after early 2023, when independent reporting placed the *de facto* seat of the ISEZ executive at Boz-Korgon, and again after Toktarov withdrew from public view in July 2024. By then it was used mostly in satire, for instance in cartoons depicting the compound as a ranch.<sup>[2]</sup> Commentators have described its persistence as a reflection of Iradi ambivalence about the US territorial period and of the secrecy surrounding the compound.

### 4.46. 2025 Trump Remarks on Irad
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Foreign Relations*

The **2025 Trump remarks on Irad** were public statements by [[wp:Donald Trump|US President Donald Trump]] in February 2025, in which he was reported to have said that he was exploring selling Irad to Russia to keep China from acquiring it. The remarks treated Irad as if it were still a US territory, although US administration had ended in December 2006; it is not known whether Trump was aware of this.<sup>[1]</sup> They provoked widespread demonstrations and a wave of anti-American feeling in both the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) and the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), one of the few issues since 2007 on which opinion in the two zones has broadly coincided.

## Background
From 1992 to 2006 Irad was an organized, unincorporated territory of the United States under the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]]. On 3 December 2006 President George W. Bush withdrew the United States from the treaty by executive action, and since the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] of 2007 the country has been divided between the ISEZ, governed by the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI), and the tribal regions. Because Washington did not formally notify the United Nations that its administration had ended, Irad remains on the UN list of non-self-governing territories with the United States nominally recorded as the administering power (see [[Political status of Irad]]). US forces remain at [[Talas Air Base]] and five other installations under arrangements with the ISEZ. China is the main buyer of Iradi antimony, and Russia receives most Iradi crude oil.

## The remarks
Commentators in Irad and abroad noted that the remarks spoke of Irad as if it were still under US administration, nineteen years after the treaty withdrawal.<sup>[1]</sup> Legal commentators in the region added that the status of a non-self-governing territory cannot be transferred without the consent of its people under the [[wp:Charter of the United Nations|UN Charter]].<sup>[2]</sup>

## Reactions in Irad

#### Government and political figures
The ISEZ administration, led in the Governor's absence by Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]], delivered a formal demarche through the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] stating that Irad's sovereignty was not negotiable. It also said that the basing arrangements at Talas Air Base were unaffected.<sup>[1]</sup> Reactions from other public figures included:
- [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]], the principal spokesman of the [[Iradi Freedom Society]], issued a statement declaring that "the soil of Irad was purchased with the blood of our fallen riders and cannot be bought or sold like cattle at a market."<sup>[1]</sup>
- [[Kamran Bekzatov]], president of [[NurGaz]] and the best-known figure among the Russian-speaking [[Russos of Nurzhan]], rejected the idea of any "sale" of Irad and argued that the episode showed the risks of depending on Washington.<sup>[3]</sup>
- The commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]] condemned the remarks, but pro-government commentators used his American citizenship to attack him.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Demonstrations
In the days after the remarks, thousands of students, factory workers and members of civic organizations marched in [[Talas]] past the former residence of the US High Commissioner, and some protesters burned American and Russian flags. Demonstrators also gathered outside Talas Air Base.<sup>[4]</sup> Smaller protests took place in [[Nurzhan]] and [[Iyık Janyl]], and clan gatherings in the tribal regions condemned the remarks. Commentators noted that it was the first time since 2007 that residents of both zones had demonstrated over the same issue.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Public opinion
The remarks deepened existing skepticism about the United States. In a survey by the Talas State University Institute of Sociology in March 2025, 27 percent of ISEZ respondents said they had a favorable view of the United States, against 58 percent in the institute's 2022 survey; the decline was steepest among respondents under 30.<sup>[5]</sup> Critics of the US presence, including Russo politicians in Nurzhan, cited the remarks in renewed calls to review the basing arrangements.

## International reaction
The [[wp:Special Committee on Decolonization|UN Special Committee on Decolonization]], which lists Irad as a non-self-governing territory, issued a statement recalling that the territory's future is a matter for its people.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Significance
Analysts regard the episode as a turning point in Iradi attitudes toward the United States, which had been broadly favorable in the ISEZ since the territorial period. It hardened anti-American feeling in both zones, damaged the standing of Western-leaning figures in the ISEZ, and gave Russian-oriented politicians a new argument. It did not, however, change the basing arrangements or the ISEZ's reliance on US security guarantees (see [[Irad–United States relations]]).<sup>[1]</sup>

### 4.47. Qara-Chik Demarcation Line
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Politics & Government*

The **Qara-Chik Demarcation Line** (Iradi: *Qara-Chik chek ara sızığı*) is the 420-kilometer (260 mi) ceasefire line that divides [[Irad]] between the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), governed by the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI), and the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), held by the country's pastoral clans. It was fixed in September 2007 by the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]], which ended the main fighting of the [[Second Iradi Civil War]]. Since then it has been monitored by the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI).<sup>[1]</sup> The line encloses the irrigated valleys of the Talas and lower Chu and runs south across the [[Talas Alatau]] in a salient along the Naryn corridor. There it divides the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]], placing the dam on the tribal side and the switchyard and export lines on the ISEZ side.

Neither administration treats the line as a boundary between states. The ISEZ describes it as an administrative line within a single Irad whose sovereignty is suspended, and the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC) as the limit of the land held by the clans. On the ISEZ side, the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] mans twelve checkpoints; on the tribal side, the mounted [[El-Choro Militias]] keep picket stations. Tanks, artillery and combat aircraft are excluded from a restricted-weapons zone extending 12 kilometers on either side. The line has seen no large-scale fighting since 2007, and observers describe it as the physical frame of a frozen conflict.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Name
The line takes its name from Qara-Chik, a foothill village south of [[Talas]], where the main crossing point, the [[Qara-Chik Border Checkpoint]], was set up on the road into the Talas Alatau. The negotiators in [[wp:Bishkek]] used the village name for the line as a whole. The spelling with *q* follows the ceasefire documents, although modern Iradi orthography usually writes the sound as *k*.<sup>[1]</sup>

## History

#### Origins
The line reflects the positions held at the end of the summer of 2007. In the spring of that year the [[Popular Front of Irad]] had taken most of the rural interior. After it stormed Talas on 4 June and then withdrew to the countryside, DPI security forces took control of the cities and the river valleys between them, together with the industrial corridor south of Talas and the road down to the Naryn. Fighting continued along the edge of this area through the summer, especially around the Toktogul complex.<sup>[3]</sup>

UN mediators brought the two sides to Bishkek, and the ceasefire agreement signed there in September 2007 defined the line on Soviet-era 1:100,000 maps, along the positions held on an agreed date. It set up the restricted-weapons zone and a Joint Liaison Committee of the two sides, and its annex, the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]], dealt with the Toktogul complex. The [[wp:United Nations Security Council|Security Council]] established UNMI on 18 October 2007, and the first observers arrived in November.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Marking the line (2008–2011)
Joint survey teams of ISEZ and tribal representatives, accompanied by UN observers, marked the line on the ground between 2008 and 2011, placing numbered concrete pillars in the valleys and stone cairns on the high ridges.<sup>[2]</sup> The Gendarmerie's Border Demarcation Brigade, whose deputy commander at the time was [[Ruslan Toktarov]], built the fortified crossings on the ISEZ side and set up the inspection regime for people and goods. Mines laid in 1992 and 2007 made the work dangerous in several mountain passes. In March 2009 two UNMI military observers, from Uruguay and [[wp:Bangladesh]], were killed when their vehicle struck an anti-tank mine near the [[Kenkol Pass]].<sup>[4]</sup>

#### Since 2011
The line has remained largely quiet, although incidents are frequent. UNMI recorded 214 ceasefire violations in 2023. Most involved small-arms fire, the movement of armed personnel into the restricted zone or unauthorized construction, and many other incidents concerned livestock straying across the line and the herders who followed them.<sup>[2]</sup> The Joint Liaison Committee, which meets monthly at Kara-Oi, settles most incidents locally. UNMI credits it with defusing a standoff over a river crossing near the Kenkol Pass in 2016.<sup>[2]</sup> During [[The 2021 Regional Security Alert]], after the [[wp:Taliban]] returned to power in [[wp:Afghanistan]], ISEZ forces and El-Choro riders reinforced checkpoints on the mountain passes and set up a channel for sharing intelligence.

## Course
The line is not continuous with Irad's international borders. It runs inland from the Kazakh border, encloses the valleys held by the ISEZ, and reaches south to the Naryn. UNMI divides it into four sectors:<sup>[2]</sup>
- **Western sector.** From the Kazakh border northwest of the Kara-Buura District, the line runs south and east along the edge of the irrigated lower Talas valley. It separates the ISEZ farmland from the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] foothills and from the upper valley of the [[Kara-Buura]], which rises on the tribal side. The Kenkol Pass lies in this sector.
- **Central sector.** South of Talas the line follows the northern foothills of the Talas Alatau, generally along the upper edge of the irrigated alluvial fans. The lower reaches of the mountain valleys, such as lower Besh-Tash and lower Kara-Suu, lie on the ISEZ side, while their upper reaches, the high pastures and the [[Aksay Plateau]] lie on the tribal side. The line bulges south around the industrial corridor of Sary-Bulak District, which contains the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]] and the [[Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex]]. The Qara-Chik checkpoint and the UNMI headquarters at Kara-Oi are in this sector.
- **Southern (Naryn) sector.** From Sary-Bulak District the line follows the ridges on both sides of the [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]], across the [[Fergana Gateway]] (2,480 m) and down toward the Naryn. It crosses the river below the Toktogul dam and encloses the Lower Naryn District around [[Tash-Kömür]] and the city of [[Iyık Janyl]]. Tribal land flanks the highway corridor on both sides, and UNMI's sector headquarters is at Tash-Kömür.
- **Northern sector.** The line runs along the northern edge of the irrigated Talas and Chu plains, facing the Moiynkum sands and the [[Betpak-Dala]] steppe of the ATR's Northern Steppe zone. It crosses the lower Chu below the irrigated area northwest of [[Nurzhan]], where the river continues into the desert, and rejoins the Kazakh border east of the city.

## Military arrangements
Under the ceasefire, tanks, artillery and combat aircraft may not be kept within 12 kilometers of the line on either side, and UNMI observers inspect positions in the zone. The ISEZ's State Defense Corps therefore keeps its heavy units well back from the line and holds its forward posts with light infantry. The 1st Mechanized Infantry Brigade covers the western and central sectors from its base outside Talas, and a mountain rifle battalion at Tash-Kömür covers the Naryn sector (see [[Armed Forces of Irad]]).<sup>[5]</sup> The El-Choro, which have no heavy weapons, keep mounted pickets in stone shelters and herders' huts, rotated among the clan detachments. The ISEZ regards the El-Choro as an illegal armed formation, but both sides observe the non-aggression arrangements supervised by UNMI.

## Crossings and movement
Civilian movement across the line is limited to designated corridors. Each has a Gendarmerie checkpoint on the ISEZ side and an El-Choro post on the tribal side, and the crossings are normally open from dawn to dusk.<sup>[6]</sup>
- **Herders and traders.** Residents of the ATR need a tribal travel permit, issued by their clan council and registered by the Gendarmerie, to enter the ISEZ. Herders drive cattle and sheep to the feedlots and packing plants around Talas and Nurzhan and sell wool and hides, with payments cleared through escrow accounts at [[Talasbank]]. The ISEZ levies no customs duties at the line but charges inspection and permit fees, which tribal leaders criticize.
- **Seasonal migration.** Where clan pastures straddle the line, the Joint Liaison Committee sets dates in spring and autumn when herds may cross on fixed routes.
- **Pilgrims.** Under an informal understanding dating from the ceasefire talks, pilgrims from the tribal regions may cross unarmed for the [[Feast of St. Janyl]] on 24 August at [[Iyık Janyl]].
- **Engineers.** UNMI escorts the engineering crews of each side across the line to the Toktogul complex.

Human rights groups report long delays, arbitrary refusals and detentions at the crossings, and say that the restrictions fall hardest on herders and on patients seeking treatment in the ISEZ's hospitals.<sup>[7]</sup> The ISEZ accuses IAC-aligned groups of moving fuel, livestock and consumer goods past its checkpoints through disused galleries of the [[Kok-Tash Kariz System]], some of whose shaft heads the Gendarmerie has sealed. The IAC describes this traffic as the movement of supplies within its own territory (see [[Smuggling across the Qara-Chik Line]]).

## The Naryn corridor
A southern salient of the line crosses the [[Naryn River]] between the Toktogul gorge and the downstream cascade. It places the dam, reservoir and powerhouse of the Toktogul complex (1,200 MW) on the tribal side, and its switchyard, the national dispatch center and the export lines on the ISEZ side. This is the one stretch of the line where both zones depend on the same installation. Neither side can release water or sell power without the other.<sup>[8]</sup> Under the Naryn Water and Power Protocol, a joint technical commission of ISEZ and ATR engineers sets the annual release schedule under UN supervision, with observers from [[wp:Kazakhstan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]]. El-Choro detachments guard the dam perimeter, and Gendarmerie personnel guard the switchyard within sight of them. The five-year release schedule falls due for renewal in 2027.

## Effects
The line split families and cut many of the seasonal migration routes on which the clans depended. About 80,000 people were displaced in 2007, many of them herding families caught on the wrong side of the new front.<sup>[3]</sup> It also separated the ISEZ's farms and power stations from the mountain catchments that feed them. Trade across the line has nonetheless continued. Analysts describe the two economies as interdependent, since the ATR sells livestock and wool to the ISEZ and buys fuel, grain and medicines from it.<sup>[8]</sup> Abolishing or redrawing the line would depend on a unification settlement. No direct talks between the two sides have taken place since the [[2011 Bilateral Reunification Summit]] collapsed.

### 4.48. Adat Law in the ATR
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Law & Security*

**Adat law in the ATR** (Iradi: *adat*, also *salt*) is the uncodified customary law applied by clan elders and judges in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) of Irad. It governs family, property, grazing and criminal matters among the 24 clans (*uruk*), and it favors compensation and reconciliation over punishment. Since the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]], which acknowledged customary jurisdiction on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], *adat* has operated outside the statutory court system headed by the [[Supreme Court of Irad]], whose jurisdiction does not extend into the ATR.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup> Human rights organizations have criticized its treatment of women and its lack of written rules and appeals; its defenders describe it as cheap, fast and suited to pastoral life.

## History
Customary courts of elders and judges (*biys*) were common to the pastoral peoples of the region before Russian rule. Under the [[wp:Russian Empire]], regulations for the administration of [[wp:Turkestan]] in the late nineteenth century allowed "people's courts" of elected biys to apply customary law among nomads in civil and minor criminal cases, while serious crimes went to imperial courts.<sup>[3]</sup> Iradi clan courts of this period combined steppe custom with the moral teaching of the clandestine Christian communities.

Soviet authorities abolished the biy courts in the late 1920s, and the collectivization of the 1930s broke up the pastoral economy on which they had rested. Elders nonetheless continued to settle disputes informally within collective farms, and clan genealogies (*sanjyra*) were kept orally.<sup>[4]</sup> During the US territorial period (1992–2006) the countryside was legally subject to the territorial courts, but aksakal arbitration was practiced openly and tolerated by the territorial authorities in rural areas. After the 2007 partition, the ceasefire agreement left justice on the tribal side to the clans. In 2022 the [[Iradi Freedom Society Chancellery]] published a *Compendium of Customary Law (Adat) and Pasture Demarcations*, a record of principles and precedents that its compilers describe as a guide rather than a code.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Courts and procedure
Disputes are heard in open assemblies (*aksakal sod*) presided over by one or more *biys*, men chosen by their clan for their knowledge of custom and genealogy, their reputation for fairness and their skill in speech. Hearings usually take place outdoors or in a yurt, in the presence of the families concerned and other members of the community.<sup>[2]</sup>
- Each party, often represented by a senior kinsman, sets out its case orally, and the judges question witnesses.
- Witnesses may be asked to swear on bread or on the Gospel book.
- The judges seek a settlement that both kin groups will accept, and their decision is announced publicly.
- Disputes within a clan are heard by its own *biys*. Grazing disputes between clans go to the [[Autonomous Tribal Grazing Arbitration Tribunal]], and matters affecting all the clans may be referred to the *Kurultai* on the [[Aksay Plateau]].

There is no formal appeal. A party dissatisfied with a decision may ask for a rehearing before a larger assembly of elders. Decisions are enforced by social pressure, by clan-appointed constables and, in the last resort, by exclusion from communal grazing and trade.

## Principles and remedies
*Adat* treats offenses as matters between kin groups rather than between the individual and the state. Responsibility is collective, and the offender's family or lineage shares the obligation to compensate the victim's.<sup>[2]</sup>
- **Compensation (*kun*).** Homicide, injury and serious theft are settled by payment of *kun* to the victim's kin. It was historically reckoned in horses and is now usually paid in cattle, sheep or cash. Payment of *kun* ends the dispute and is meant to prevent revenge.
- **Fines (*aip*).** Lesser wrongs, such as livestock damage or insults, are punished by fines in livestock or goods.
- **Reconciliation.** Settlements are often concluded with a public apology and a shared meal at which the families eat together.
- **Ostracism.** A person or family who refuses to accept a decision may be excluded from clan gatherings, communal pastures and trade.

Imprisonment is not used. Horse theft is among the gravest offenses, traditionally compensated nine animals for one (see [[Crime in Irad]]). Clan authorities enforce the [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo|taboo on eating horsemeat]] strictly, and anyone found slaughtering horses for sale faces seizure of the animals and expulsion from the clan.

## Family and property
In family matters *adat* follows patrilineal descent. Property passes in the male line, and by custom the youngest son (*kenje*) inherits the parental household and cares for his parents in old age, while elder sons receive livestock when they marry. Marriage is a church sacrament, and most tribal Iradis marry in the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]]. Elders handle the negotiation of marriage settlements and the disputes that follow separation (see [[Marriage in Irad]]).<sup>[4]</sup> Where *adat* and canon law conflict, as over divorce, elders and priests usually seek a compromise. Itinerant parish priests often sit with the elders at hearings and bless settlements with smoke from mountain juniper (*[[Arsha (Flora)|arsha]]*) and prayers to St. Janyl (see [[Arsha Juniper Incense Tradition]]).

Pasture is held collectively by clans and lineages, not by individuals, and there are no written titles. Boundaries are marked by boundary stones (*bel-tash*) and remembered by elders. Seasonal migration between winter pastures (*kyshtoo*) and summer pastures (*zhayloo*) follows schedules agreed by clan pasture committees (see [[Central Asian Pastoral Migration System]]).<sup>[1]</sup>

## Relationship with ISEZ law
The [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) does not formally recognize decisions of the clan courts, and residents of the ATR arrested in the ISEZ are tried in its courts. In practice, cases that cross the line, such as livestock theft or road accidents, are often handled through the Joint Liaison Committee of the ceasefire. UNMI police advisers work with the municipal police of the ISEZ and the clan-appointed constables of the ATR on cross-line crime and missing-persons cases.<sup>[5]</sup> Some ISEZ officials and legal scholars argue that *adat* allows serious crimes to go unpunished. Clan leaders reply that compensation settles disputes that prosecution would prolong.

## Criticism
[[wp:Human Rights Watch]] has criticized *adat* as practiced in the ATR on several grounds:<sup>[2]</sup>
- daughters and widows inherit little or nothing under patrilineal rules;
- women are not admitted as *biys* and rarely speak at hearings;
- there is no written law and no appeal from elder courts;
- collective responsibility can penalize relatives who had no part in an offense.

Tribal leaders and many residents defend the system as fast, cheap and focused on restoring relations between families. They regard it as an essential part of the clans' autonomy.<sup>[4]</sup>

### 4.49. El-Choro Militias
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Law & Security*

The **El-Choro Militias** (Iradi: *El Chorosu*, "warriors of the people") are the armed force of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) of Irad. They consist of about 15,000 part-time mounted irregulars, raised in detachments by the 24 clans (*uruk*) and coordinated by [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]], the principal spokesman of the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC).<sup>[1]</sup> The militias were formed in late 2007 from the fighting units of the [[Popular Front of Irad]], which had stormed [[Talas]] in the [[Second Iradi Civil War]]. They keep picket stations on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], patrol the ATR's borders with [[wp:Kazakhstan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], and guard the dam of the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]].

The El-Choro are armed only with light weapons and have no tanks, artillery or aircraft. The government of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) regards them as an illegal armed formation. Since 2007, however, they and the ISEZ's forces have observed non-aggression arrangements supervised by the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI).<sup>[2]</sup>

## Name
In the Iradi epic tradition, *choro* are the mounted companions of a hero or chief, and *el* means "the people" or "the community". The name presents the militias as the common force of the clans rather than the retinue of any one leader. ISEZ officials and media usually call them "tribal armed formations".<sup>[1]</sup>

## History

#### Antecedents
Mounted clan irregulars have a long history in the region. Iradi horsemen fought in the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|1916 Semirechye Revolt]] and on the Red side in the [[wp:Russian Civil War]]. In 1992 clan riders joined the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]], and during the [[First Iradi Civil War]] mounted scouts organized by Bektur defended the mountain valleys against requisition columns of the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]].<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Formation (2007)
In the spring of 2007 the Popular Front fielded more than 8,000 mounted irregulars, most of them riding [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] mountain horses. They took most of the rural interior and stormed Talas on 4 June. After the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]] of September, a kurultai of clan elders on the [[Aksay Plateau]] reorganized the Front's political council as the IAC in late 2007. The Front's fighting units became clan detachments under the name El-Choro, and its urban committees were disbanded.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Since 2007
The early years of the ceasefire were marked by incidents along the newly marked line and by casualties from mines in the mountain passes. Merging the El-Choro and the ISEZ's State Defense Corps into a single force was one of the issues left unresolved when the [[2011 Bilateral Reunification Summit]] collapsed.<sup>[4]</sup> In 2016 a standoff between riders and ISEZ forces over a river crossing near the [[Kenkol Pass]] was defused by the Joint Liaison Committee of the ceasefire.<sup>[2]</sup>

In June 2018 El-Choro patrols exchanged fire with Uzbek border guards over grazing trails and boreholes on the western desert frontier. Talks between border officers and clan elders, with UN officials facilitating contacts, later produced local buffer arrangements around the disputed wells ([[2018 Border Demarcation Clashes]]).<sup>[5]</sup> During [[The 2021 Regional Security Alert]], after the [[wp:Taliban]] returned to power in [[wp:Afghanistan]], El-Choro riders reinforced the mountain passes alongside ISEZ forces, and the two sides set up a channel for sharing intelligence.

## Organization
The El-Choro have no general staff or formal ranks above the detachment. Their structure follows that of the clans:<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>
- **Detachments.** Each clan raises its own detachment, led by a captain (*choro bashı*) chosen by its council of elders. Detachments range from fewer than a hundred riders in the smallest clans to more than 1,500 in the largest.
- **Council of captains.** The captains meet at the annual *Kurultai* on the Aksay Plateau, and in emergencies elsewhere, to agree on the allocation of picket duties and on common defense. Decisions require the consent of the leading lineages.
- **Coordination.** Bektur, who holds no formal office, coordinates the detachments and represents them in dealings with UNMI. The [[Iradi Freedom Society Chancellery]] keeps rosters and duty schedules.

Service is part-time. Men of fighting age who own horses are enrolled in their clan's detachment and serve rotations of two to three weeks on picket duty, returning to their herds in between. In an emergency all enrolled riders can be called out. Women serve as scouts, medics and couriers in some detachments. UNMI estimates that 2,000 to 3,000 riders are on duty at any one time.<sup>[2]</sup> Riders provide their own horses and usually their own rifles. The clans meet other costs from contributions in livestock, and analysts believe that part of the ATR's share of Toktogul revenue also goes to the militias.<sup>[6]</sup>

## Equipment and tactics
The El-Choro rely on horses for patrols in the mountains, where the hardy Chongtor is suited to steep trails and deep snow. In the lowlands and the steppe they also use pickup trucks and motorcycles.<sup>[1]</sup> Their weapons are light infantry arms: Kalashnikov-pattern rifles, light machine guns, sniper rifles, [[wp:RPG-7]] grenade launchers and a small number of heavy machine guns. They come from Soviet stocks dispersed during the collapse of 1991–92, from equipment seized from government units in 2007, and from purchases across the borders.<sup>[6]</sup> Communications rely on handheld radios and satellite telephones, many of them supplied for liaison purposes by UNMI.

The militias' doctrine is defensive. Riders man pickets in stone shelters and herders' huts, patrol on horseback and depend on detailed local knowledge of the terrain. Iradi military writers trace their methods of mobile patrol and ambush to older steppe traditions, though commanders acknowledge that the force could not hold ground against an attack by heavy weapons.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Tasks
- **The Qara-Chik line.** El-Choro posts face each of the twelve Gendarmerie checkpoints, and pickets watch the rest of the line. Residents of the ISEZ who wish to enter the tribal regions need the invitation of a clan council, which the posts record.
- **External borders.** Riders patrol the ATR's long borders with Kazakhstan in the Northern Steppe and [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]], with Uzbekistan on the western desert frontier and the Fergana Rim, and with Kyrgyzstan in the eastern mountains. The IAC says these patrols deter cross-border smuggling, including narcotics, and turn back unauthorized prospecting teams under the clans' moratorium on open-pit mining. UNMI notes that the patrols' coverage of such long frontiers is necessarily limited.<sup>[2]</sup>
- **The Toktogul dam.** Detachments guard the perimeter of the dam, reservoir and powerhouse, which lie on the tribal side of the line. It is the one installation where tribal riders and personnel of the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] work within sight of each other.
- **Emergencies.** Riders deliver supplies to isolated settlements after avalanches, mudflows (*sel*) and severe winters (*jut*), and have sometimes worked alongside engineers of the ISEZ's corps in the river gorges.

## Relations with the ISEZ
The ISEZ government and the [[Armed Forces of Irad]] regard the El-Choro as an illegal armed formation. The ceasefire nonetheless treats them as one of its parties. Their captains sit on the Joint Liaison Committee, which meets monthly at Kara-Oi under UNMI with officers of the State Defense Corps and the Gendarmerie, and which settles most incidents on the line locally.<sup>[2]</sup> Gendarmerie commander [[Ruslan Toktarov]] has called for the state to reassert its authority over the mountain watersheds. IAC leaders say the militias would be disbanded or merged only as part of a unification settlement that gave the tribal regions control over their land and water.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Criticism
[[wp:Human Rights Watch]] has noted that the El-Choro answer only to clan councils, with no civilian or judicial oversight beyond *adat*. Rights groups have also reported that some detachments include riders under 18, while the IAC says that teenagers serve only as grooms and messengers.<sup>[7]</sup> ISEZ officials accuse members of the militias of protecting smuggling through the [[Kok-Tash Kariz System]] and over the mountain passes, an accusation the IAC rejects. Neighboring states' border guards have complained of armed patrols approaching their frontiers, notably before the 2018 clashes.<sup>[5]</sup>

### 4.50. 2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Politics & Government*

The **2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis** is the name used by regional media and analysts for the political uncertainty in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) since July 2024, when Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]] stopped appearing in public. The [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI) attributes his absence to an extended health retreat and says that he continues to govern. Decrees and recorded addresses are still issued in his name.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[3]</sup> Opposition outlets and independent technology monitors allege signs of digital synthesis in his recent broadcasts, which officials dismiss as foreign-sponsored disinformation.

In the Governor's absence, Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] has run the government day to day, and a rivalry over the succession between Toktarov's two eldest sons, [[Ruslan Toktarov|Ruslan]] and [[Alikhan Toktarov|Alikhan]], has become openly visible. The government rejects the description of the situation as a crisis. No formal finding of inability has been made under the Elective Governor Acts, the DPI has named no successor, and the next gubernatorial election is due in late 2027 (see [[2027 Iradi gubernatorial election]]).<sup>[4]</sup>

## Background
Toktarov, born in 1954, has governed the ISEZ since he proclaimed it in February 2007. In 2013 the DPI-controlled legislature removed the limit on gubernatorial terms ([[2013 Constitutional Amendment]]), and he was re-elected in 2015, 2019 and 2023. The Elective Governor Acts of 1992 provide that the Lieutenant Governor acts for an absent or incapacitated Governor and succeeds to the office if it falls vacant. Members of Toktarov's family hold senior posts. Ruslan has commanded the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] since 2012, Alikhan has chaired the broadcaster [[IradOne]] since 2015, and Maksat, the husband of Toktarov's daughter [[Zara Toktarova]], became Lieutenant Governor in 2019. The three middle sons, [[Timur Toktarov|Timur]], [[Adil Toktarov|Adil]] and [[Bekzat Toktarov|Bekzat]], manage family businesses.<sup>[1]</sup>

In early 2023, according to independent reporting, Toktarov and his senior staff moved the core of the executive from [[Talas]] to the fortified [[Boz-Korgon]] compound east of [[Nurzhan]], a move the government denies. The same year the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]] were dispersed by police and Gendarmerie units.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Course of events

#### Withdrawal from public life (July–September 2024)
According to the *[[Talas Herald]]*, Toktarov's last confirmed public appearance was in early July 2024. Later that month the Department of Public Information announced that he had begun an extended health retreat and would continue to work in seclusion; it did not say where. Independent reporting places him at Boz-Korgon.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[4]</sup> Maksat began chairing cabinet meetings and receiving foreign delegations, and official statements described him as acting on the Governor's instructions. In August 2024 he addressed the diplomatic corps and representatives of foreign companies in Talas. He pledged to honor existing agreements, including the arrangements for [[Talas Air Base]], to maintain economic stability and to pursue "pragmatic dialogue" with the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]].<sup>[10]</sup> On 2 September the General Staff of the State Defense Corps pledged loyalty to "the lawful administration" and has since kept out of public politics (see [[Armed Forces of Irad]]).<sup>[6]</sup>

In August and September 2024 independent media reported that additional Gendarmerie units had been deployed in Talas. Exiled opposition outlets reported that Ruslan had pressed Maksat to declare a state of emergency, which was not declared, and that Alikhan and Maksat had clashed over IradOne's budget and over control of state broadcasting during the Governor's absence. None of the three men has confirmed these accounts.<sup>[5]</sup>

#### Recorded addresses and synthesis allegations
Since the second half of 2024, recorded audio and video addresses attributed to Toktarov have been broadcast on IradOne, the only outlet to carry them. Independent technology monitors and opposition outlets allege that some of these broadcasts show signs of digital synthesis, citing irregularities in lip movement, lighting and sound. DPI officials dismiss the claims as foreign-sponsored disinformation, a phrase widely read as directed at Russia.<sup>[1]</sup> No journalist or foreign diplomat is known to have met the Governor since July 2024, journalists have not been admitted to Boz-Korgon, and UNMI patrols have been barred from a security zone around the compound since 2023.<sup>[2]</sup> Opposition figures have called for an independent medical statement. The commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]] has repeatedly challenged the government to show the Governor in a live, unedited appearance, a demand DPI spokesmen have dismissed as "theater".

#### Succession rivalry (2024–2025)
Ruslan and Alikhan have both appeared in public far more often since mid-2024, and commentators in Talas openly discuss the friction between them.<sup>[5]</sup> In December 2024, at a graduation ceremony at the [[Talas Gendarmerie Academy]] broadcast live on IradOne, Ruslan described Muslim communities in the Fergana Rim as "guests who have forgotten whose house they live in". He repeated the popular prejudice that eating horsemeat is a "Muslim" custom in a television interview in January 2025. Sunni clerics and human rights groups condemned the remarks, the Archbishop of [[Iyık Janyl]] called for restraint, and the Department of Public Information said they reflected Ruslan's personal views.<sup>[7]</sup> Analysts quoted in the regional press have speculated that Ruslan was removing officers loyal to Alikhan from municipal police commands; the claim has not been substantiated.

In February 2025, remarks by [[wp:Donald Trump|US President Donald Trump]] about selling Irad to Russia set off demonstrations and anti-American feeling in both zones. The administration responded with a formal demarche through the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (see [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]]). Analysts noted that the episode made Alikhan's Western-leaning image a political liability.<sup>[8]</sup>

#### The Naryn Protocol and the 2027 deadlines
The five-year release schedule of the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]] falls due for renewal in 2027, the same year as the next gubernatorial election. Uzbek and Kazakh officials have asked who will sign for the ISEZ. The DPI says that Maksat signs on the Governor's behalf.<sup>[9]</sup>

## Principal figures
The following public positions and roles are those reported in the regional press:<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[5]</sup>
- **Aidar Maksat**, the Lieutenant Governor, chairs the cabinet and, according to DPI statements, the ISEZ Security Council. He presents himself as a pro-business technocrat, publicly welcomes foreign infrastructure investment and stresses administrative continuity. He has made no public claim to the succession.
- **Ruslan Toktarov**, the eldest son, commands the Gendarmerie, including the Special Protective Service that guards Boz-Korgon, and the checkpoints on the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. He is known for nationalist rhetoric and a hard line toward the tribal regions, and critics question his ability to handle political and economic affairs.
- **Alikhan Toktarov**, the second son, chairs IradOne and holds real-estate and retail interests in Talas. He presents himself as a defender of commercial modernization. He is publicly seen as a reckless, Western-leaning figure and has been criticized for lavish spending amid rumors of substance abuse. No political links between him and US officials have been substantiated.
- **Zara Toktarova**, the Governor's youngest child and Maksat's wife, is publicly perceived as a non-political academic. She is a doctoral candidate in education at [[wp:Stanford University]] and lives mostly abroad. Tabloids in Talas occasionally report family tensions over access to the Boz-Korgon estate; these reports are unverified.
- **Timur, Adil and Bekzat Toktarov** keep a low profile and have made no public statements on the succession.

Outside the family, [[Kamran Bekzatov]], the president of [[NurGaz]] and the best-known figure among the [[Russos of Nurzhan]], criticizes the DPI's economic policy. Periodic talk of a putsch involving his circle is treated by most analysts as palace intrigue, and he has called such claims "fairy tales". Representatives of the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] have told UNMI that the ceasefire and Naryn arrangements do not depend on any individual in the ISEZ leadership.<sup>[9]</sup>

## Legal questions
The government's position is that Toktarov remains in office and that Maksat acts on his instructions, so no transfer of authority has taken place. Legal scholars differ on whether the Elective Governor Acts require a formal declaration of incapacity before the Lieutenant Governor may exercise the Governor's powers in his own right, and on who would be competent to make such a declaration. The Acts have never been tested on this point.<sup>[4]</sup> The [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]], in which the DPI holds 51 of 60 seats, has not debated the matter. Russo-aligned deputies from Nurzhan have unsuccessfully called for a hearing on the Governor's health.

## Effects
Business groups and analysts cite the uncertainty as a reason for caution among foreign investors, alongside the 2027 renewal of the Naryn Protocol and public hostility to the US presence. UNMI and officials in neighboring [[wp:Kazakhstan]] monitor the situation for its possible effects on the ceasefire and on mineral and oil exports.<sup>[9]</sup> In a survey by the Talas State University Institute of Sociology in March 2025, 58 percent of ISEZ respondents said that official information about the Governor's health was insufficient, and 31 percent said it was adequate.<sup>[11]</sup> DPI spokespeople reject descriptions of the government as unstable and point to the continued functioning of ministries, the budget and the security services.

### 4.51. Iradi Freedom Society Chancellery
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Politics & Government*

The **Iradi Freedom Society Chancellery** (Iradi: *Iradin Azatlık Cemiyetinin Kantselyariyası*) is the standing secretariat of the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC), the confederation of clans that governs the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) of Irad. It keeps the records of the pan-clan assembly (*Kurultai*), maintains registers of pastures and migration routes, archives the decisions of customary courts, and handles the IAC's correspondence with the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI), aid agencies and the government of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ).<sup>[1]</sup> It was created in late 2007 by the kurultai on the [[Aksay Plateau]] that constituted the IAC. Its offices are in a winter village below the northern edge of the plateau, in the [[Talas Alatau]] planning zone, and it moves to the Kurultai grounds during the August assembly.

## History
The Chancellery grew out of the clerks and couriers who served the council of the [[Popular Front of Irad]] during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]]. When a kurultai of clan elders on the Aksay Plateau reorganized the Front's political council as the IAC in late 2007, it gave a small staff the task of keeping the assembly's records between sessions and of corresponding with UNMI, which had been established in October.<sup>[2]</sup>

In its first years the Chancellery's main work concerned the ceasefire: lists of displaced families, the opening of crossings on the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], and the delivery of fodder and medicines to highland settlements. It prepared papers for the IAC's participation in the [[2008 Unification Referendum Initiative]] and for the [[2011 Bilateral Reunification Summit]], including the population estimates on which the IAC based its claim to more than one-third of the seats in a reunified legislature.<sup>[3]</sup> After the 2018 census it compiled village and clan returns to support the IAC's contention that the ATR had been undercounted (see [[2018 Irad census]]). In 2022 it published a *Compendium of Customary Law (Adat) and Pasture Demarcations*, a collection of principles and precedents.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Organization
The Chancellery is headed by a secretary (*katchı*) chosen by the Kurultai, and has a staff of about forty clerks, interpreters and couriers. It has three divisions:<sup>[1]</sup>
- **Pasture affairs.** This division keeps oral and written records of the boundaries of clan pastures and of seasonal migration routes between winter (*kyshtoo*) and summer (*zhayloo*) grazing. It prepares cases for the [[Autonomous Tribal Grazing Arbitration Tribunal]].
- **External liaison.** This division corresponds with UNMI and with humanitarian agencies, negotiates corridors for medical supplies and livestock vaccines, and prepares the IAC's contributions to the annual working paper of the [[wp:Special Committee on Decolonization|UN Special Committee on Decolonization]].
- **Adat archives.** This division records decisions of the elder courts (*aksakal sod*), including settlements of compensation (*kun*) and marriage settlements, and maintains the genealogical records (*sanjyra*) that the courts consult (see [[Adat Law in the ATR]]).

[[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]], the IAC's principal spokesman, holds no office in the Chancellery, but its staff handle his correspondence with UNMI and the ISEZ.

## Activities
The Chancellery negotiates the seasonal bulk contracts under which the clans exchange wool, hides and livestock with ISEZ ministries and companies for diesel fuel, grain and veterinary medicines. Payments are settled through escrow accounts at [[Talasbank]].<sup>[4]</sup> It also coordinates with the [[Aksay Plateau Pastoral Cooperative]] and other pastoral cooperatives, and passes requests from clan councils to UNMI's humanitarian coordination forum.

Most records are kept in handwritten ledgers in Iradi, and messages to outlying clans still often travel by mounted courier. Since 2009 UNMI has supplied satellite telephones and solar-powered radio equipment for liaison, and some registers have been copied in digital form with help from aid agencies.<sup>[2]</sup> The compound includes a guest house where clan elders lodge during consultations.

## Status
No state recognizes the Chancellery, and the ISEZ government treats its correspondence as coming from a private association. It nonetheless deals with it in practice on trade, crossings and the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]]. UNMI regards it as the main administrative channel to the ATR.<sup>[2]</sup> Human rights organizations have noted that the Chancellery's records, like the decisions of the elder courts, are not open to public inspection.<sup>[5]</sup>
