### 4.52. Republican Gendarmerie of Irad
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Law & Security*

The **Republican Gendarmerie of Irad** (Iradi: *Irad Respublikalık Jandarmeriyası*) is a paramilitary police and border force of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), with about 4,000 personnel. It answers to the Ministry of Internal Security and has been commanded since March 2012 by Major General [[Ruslan Toktarov]], the eldest son of Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]].<sup>[1]</sup> Set up in 1993 to replace the Soviet internal troops, it mans the twelve checkpoints on the ISEZ side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], protects senior officials and the [[Boz-Korgon]] compound through its Special Protective Service, and guards the perimeter of [[Talas Air Base]]. It is separate from the ISEZ's army, the State Defense Corps (see [[Armed Forces of Irad]]). Its officers are trained at the [[Talas Gendarmerie Academy]].

Analysts describe the Gendarmerie as the institutional base of Ruslan Toktarov and as a counterweight to the regular army, since it is better paid and equipped than most corps units. Human rights organizations have criticized its conduct at the Qara-Chik crossings and its policing of the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]].<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>

## Name
The Iradi word *jandarm* is a loanword from Russian (*zhandarm*), which took it from French in the early 19th century. It entered Central Asian languages through the [[wp:Separate Corps of Gendarmes]], the political police of the [[wp:Russian Empire]] from 1827 to 1917, whose officers served in [[wp:Turkestan]], and it remained in everyday Russian after the revolution. Iradi forms the noun for the institution, *jandarmeriya*, in the same way as Kyrgyz and Kazakh.<sup>[10]</sup>

The Provisional Government chose the name in 1992 to set its new force apart from the Soviet *militsiya* and internal troops, which were associated with the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]]. Because the word also recalls the tsarist political police, opposition writers and exiled journalists use *jandarm* as a term of abuse for the force's officers, and some have linked it to the repression that followed the revolt of 1916 (see [[The Lost Tribes of 1916]]).<sup>[5]</sup><sup>[10]</sup>

## History

#### Origins and the territorial period (1992–2006)
The force traces its origins to the gendarmerie detachments raised by the Provisional Government of the Republic of Irad in 1992, during the [[First Iradi Civil War]], which explains the word "Republican" in its name. After the war the Territorial Legislature put it on a statutory footing in 1993, replacing the Soviet internal troops and [[wp:OMON]] detachments that had served the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]].<sup>[5]</sup> Under the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] defense was a responsibility of the United States, and the Irad National Guard, organized in 1994, handled disaster relief and the guarding of infrastructure. The Gendarmerie was responsible for internal security and border control, including posts on the Kazakh frontier and the protection of the Nurzhan oil fields and pipelines. Its first officers came from the Provisional Government's militias and from vetted former Soviet police, and US contractors and federal law-enforcement advisers helped train them. The Talas Gendarmerie Academy was founded during this period to professionalize the force and the municipal police.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Second Civil War (2006–2007)
In the crisis that followed the US withdrawal in December 2006, the Gendarmerie split along political lines. When Toktarov proclaimed the ISEZ from [[Nurzhan]] on 25 February 2007, he mobilized municipal police and gendarmerie units in the Chu lowlands, while units in [[Talas]] stayed with the government of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]].<sup>[5]</sup> Ruslan Toktarov, who had joined the force as a captain in 2004, commanded a detachment that guarded the [[NurGaz]] tank farm and rail yards outside Nurzhan against strikers and saboteurs. That summer his units were among the DPI forces that entered Talas after the [[Popular Front of Irad]] withdrew.<sup>[6]</sup>

#### Border Demarcation Brigade (2007–2012)
After the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]], the Gendarmerie took responsibility for the ISEZ side of the new line. Its Border Demarcation Brigade, of which Ruslan Toktarov became deputy commander, built the fortified crossings, including the main [[Qara-Chik Border Checkpoint]], and set up the permit and inspection regime that governs the movement of herders and goods between the two zones.<sup>[1]</sup> Under the 2008 [[Northern Border Demarcation Protocol]], a UN-facilitated technical arrangement with the Kazakh border and customs services, the Gendarmerie began anti-smuggling patrols coordinated with Kazakh border units on the sections of the northern frontier held by the ISEZ.

#### Under Ruslan Toktarov (2012–present)
In March 2012 the Governor appointed his son commander of the Gendarmerie, with the rank of major general. Critics attribute his rapid rise to family patronage.<sup>[6]</sup> Since then the force has received new vehicles and communications equipment, and analysts note that its budget is set separately from the defense budget.<sup>[4]</sup> In 2019 exiled Iradi journalists reported that companies linked to Ruslan held contracts for perimeter security, diesel supply and construction at Talas Air Base, whose perimeter the Gendarmerie guards. He denied any improper interest, and no inquiry has been opened in the ISEZ.<sup>[7]</sup>

In October 2023 police and Gendarmerie units dispersed student and courier protests in Talas with tear gas, water cannon and mass administrative detentions. Among those detained was the commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]]. Ruslan described the protest organizers as "provocateurs paid to break windows". [[wp:Human Rights Watch]] criticized the use of force and the detention of minors.<sup>[2]</sup>

Since Governor Toktarov withdrew from public view in July 2024, the Gendarmerie has been closely watched as a factor in the succession (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]). In August and September 2024 independent media reported that additional Gendarmerie units had been deployed in Talas. Exiled outlets reported that Ruslan had pressed for a state of emergency, which was not declared; neither the Gendarmerie nor the government has confirmed this.<sup>[8]</sup> In December 2024 Ruslan used a graduation ceremony at the academy to make remarks about Muslims that drew wide condemnation.

## Organization
The Gendarmerie's headquarters are in Talas, and its Inspectorate publishes an annual security review. It is organized in four directorates:<sup>[1]</sup>
- **Border Demarcation Brigade.** It mans the twelve Qara-Chik checkpoints, issues and checks crossing permits, inspects cargo and runs mounted patrols in the foothills. It also polices the ISEZ-held sections of the northern frontier, coordinating with Kazakh border units under the Northern Border Demarcation Protocol.
- **Special Protective Service (SPS).** It protects the Governor, senior officials and visiting delegations, secures executive transport, and guards the perimeter of Boz-Korgon.
- **Rapid Reaction Strike Group (*Barysh*, "leopard").** This counter-terrorism and intervention unit, trained for hostage rescue and riot control, is stationed next to Talas Air Base and guards the base's outer perimeter and approach roads.
- **Highway Patrol Corps.** It enforces traffic and customs rules on the [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]], where it keeps a checkpoint at the [[Fergana Gateway]], and on the roads to the northern border crossings. It also escorts convoys of fuel and antimony.

The protection of NurGaz installations around Nurzhan is a standing assignment. Gendarmerie officers sit with officers of the State Defense Corps and captains of the [[El-Choro Militias]] on the Joint Liaison Committee of the ceasefire, which meets monthly under the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI) at Kara-Oi.<sup>[9]</sup> The ISEZ Security Council coordinates the Gendarmerie with the corps and the intelligence services; according to DPI statements, it has been chaired since 2024 by Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]]. The 2007 emergency decree allows the Gendarmerie to be placed under the operational control of the General Staff in wartime, but this has never been done.

## Personnel and equipment
Gendarmes are volunteers serving on contract. Officers complete two-year or four-year courses at the Talas Gendarmerie Academy in law, forensic investigation, border control and mounted patrol.<sup>[1]</sup> Older officers are largely Russian-speaking, while those trained since the 1990s work mainly in English and Iradi.

The force's equipment includes:<sup>[4]</sup>
- [[wp:Humvee|HMMWV]] light vehicles of US origin, many inherited from the territorial period;
- [[wp:BTR-80]] wheeled armored personnel carriers;
- water-cannon trucks and riot-control equipment;
- mobile communications vehicles supplied by [[Attelkom]];
- [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] horses for mounted patrols in the foothills.

## Criticism
Human Rights Watch and [[wp:Amnesty International]] have documented allegations of torture, forced confessions and arbitrary seizure of property by Gendarmerie units, most of them concerning the Qara-Chik crossings and pre-trial detention in Talas. Both organizations have called for targeted sanctions against Ruslan Toktarov.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[3]</sup> UNMI reports have criticized conduct at the checkpoints, and ISEZ media, including [[IradOne]], have in turn accused UN observers of bias. Tribal leaders complain of detentions of herders at the crossings. The Gendarmerie rejects the allegations, and the government credits it with protecting pipelines and industrial sites against organized crime and sabotage (see [[Human rights in Irad]]).<sup>[1]</sup>

### 4.53. Northern Border Demarcation Protocol
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Foreign Relations*

The **Northern Border Demarcation Protocol** is a set of technical arrangements concluded in October 2008 between the administration of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) and the border and customs services of [[wp:Kazakhstan]], with the United Nations acting as facilitator. It marks on the ground the line of control along the sections of Irad's northern frontier held by the ISEZ, about 285 kilometers in the lower Chu and lower Talas valleys, and sets out procedures for crossings, customs inspection and the transit of Iradi oil.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup> It is not a treaty between states. Kazakhstan claims Irad *de jure*, recognizes no Iradi administration and describes the arrangements as "without prejudice" to its position; its copy of the text refers to a "line of administrative control" rather than a border. Iradi official usage nonetheless calls it a border protocol. The much longer stretches of the frontier held by the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) in the steppe and the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] are not covered.

## Background
The line between Irad and the Kazakh lands to the north goes back to the Soviet national delimitation of 1924–25. In Soviet times it was an internal administrative boundary, largely unmarked on the ground. After 1991 it became a source of friction over land, water and smuggling.<sup>[3]</sup> During the US territorial period the [[Treaty of Good Neighborliness (1994)]], concluded with the approval of the US federal government, regulated the sharing of the Chu and Talas waters but left the line itself undemarcated. Iradi crude was shipped north by rail to the refinery at [[wp:Shymkent]] until 2000. Since then it has moved through the 85-kilometer [[Northern Export Feeder]] into the Kazakh pipeline network operated by [[wp:KazTransOil]].<sup>[4]</sup>

The end of US administration in December 2006 and the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] of 2007 left the frontier without an authority that Kazakhstan was prepared to deal with formally. [[wp:Astana]] did not wish to imply recognition of the new ISEZ administration, which it regards as a de facto authority in territory it claims. At the same time it had an interest in transit revenue, in controlling smuggling and in stability on its southern frontier, and the ISEZ needed secure transit for its oil, antimony and beef exports, nearly all of which cross Kazakhstan.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Negotiation
Contacts began in early 2008 through the UN. Because the external frontier lies outside the mandate of the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI), which monitors the internal [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], the talks were convened by the UN Regional Centre for Preventive Diplomacy for [[wp:Central Asia]], with UNMI providing logistics, maps and a meeting venue at Kara-Oi.<sup>[2]</sup> The ISEZ delegation was drawn from the Ministry of Internal Security, the customs service and NurGaz. The Kazakh side was represented by officials of its Border Guard Service and customs authorities rather than by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and the documents were signed as technical minutes by heads of delegation, not by ministers. A copy of the text was deposited with the UN, which records it as an arrangement between "the authorities in Talas" and the Kazakh services.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Provisions

#### Survey and marking
UN-supported survey teams of both sides surveyed the ISEZ-held sections using satellite positioning and Soviet-era 1:100,000 maps. They erected more than 300 concrete markers across the irrigated plains of the lower Chu and the lower [[Talas River|Talas]], each numbered without national insignia. Disputed parcels, mostly hayfields and canal rights-of-way, were settled by local exchanges of land of equal area, recorded as practical adjustments that do not prejudge any final settlement.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Crossings
The protocol established three crossing points:<sup>[1]</sup>
- **The Chu Gate crossing**, on the main highway east of [[Nurzhan]], is the principal freight crossing. It handles heavy trucks, including the bonded convoys of [[Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics]].
- **The Talas North Terminal** is a combined rail and road crossing north-west of [[Talas]], in Kara-Buura District, linking the Talas line with the Kazakh rail network. Most antimony and cotton exports leave through it.
- **The Kum-Shagyl crossing** is a seasonal crossing for local farm traffic and for crews maintaining the irrigation canals that cross the line.

#### Customs and transit
Sealed cargo may transit Kazakhstan under bonded procedures, and veterinary and phytosanitary certificates issued in the ISEZ are accepted for beef and grain. Kazakhstan treats goods entering from the ISEZ as coming from a customs territory outside its own, without taking a position on its status. Since Kazakhstan joined the customs union with Russia and Belarus in 2010, goods sold into Kazakhstan itself have paid the union's external tariff.<sup>[5]</sup>

#### Oil transit
An annex covers the transit of crude carried by the Northern Export Feeder, which is operated by the [[Iradi Petroleum Transit Consortium]] and runs from the [[NurGaz]] tank farm outside Nurzhan into the KazTransOil network near Shymkent. From there the crude is refined at Shymkent or shipped onward to Russia. Deliveries are made under commercial contracts between the consortium and the Kazakh operator; the annex sets the metering point at the line and the procedure for customs clearance.<sup>[4]</sup> NurGaz reports output of about 120,000 barrels per day; independent estimates are lower.

#### Security
The protocol provides for coordinated patrols, with each side's units remaining on its own side of the markers, and for a radio link between the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] border command and the regional Kazakh border command. Incidents are referred to a liaison meeting of the two services.<sup>[1]</sup> The sections held by the ATR, including the [[Kyzylkum Fringe]], are patrolled by the clans' [[El-Choro Militias]], with which Kazakhstan has no comparable arrangement.

## Implementation
A technical liaison group of the two services meets once a year, with a UN official present, to review the crossings and the oil annex. Disputes over the release schedule of the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]] have at times spilled over into the protocol's operation. Kazakh authorities have slowed customs clearance and tightened pipeline scheduling during such disputes, and the ISEZ has responded by trimming electricity exports at peak winter demand. Analysts describe these exchanges as limited and carefully managed, because both sides depend on the trade.<sup>[5]</sup> During [[The 2021 Regional Security Alert]], the two services increased the frequency of coordinated patrols. Proposals by the ISEZ to extend the arrangements to other sections of the frontier have been declined by Kazakhstan, and the IAC rejects any ISEZ role on the tribal-held sections.

## Reception
The ISEZ government presents the protocol as evidence that it can conduct practical external relations despite Irad's unresolved status (see [[Irad–Kazakhstan relations]] and [[Political status of Irad]]). Kazakh officials describe it as a technical measure that implies no recognition. The [[Iradi Freedom Society]] objected that it suggested ISEZ authority over the whole northern frontier, and its leaders have said that they are not bound by it. Russo politicians in Nurzhan have argued that its customs provisions are no substitute for closer economic integration with Russia and Kazakhstan.<sup>[6]</sup> Legal commentators cite it, together with the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]], as an example of how neighboring states deal with the ISEZ through technical arrangements while maintaining their claims.<sup>[2]</sup>

### 4.54. Autonomous Tribal Grazing Arbitration Tribunal
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Law & Security*

The **Autonomous Tribal Grazing Arbitration Tribunal** (Iradi: *Uruk-aralık Jayloo Biyler Sotu*, "inter-clan pasture court of the biys") is the body that settles grazing disputes between clans in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) of Irad. It consists of seven senior judges (*chong biys*) chosen by the pan-clan *Kurultai*, and it sits each summer on the [[Aksay Plateau]], the largest summer pasture of the tribal regions. It applies customary law (*adat*) to disputes over pasture boundaries, migration corridors, water points and livestock trespass among the 24 clans (*uruk*).<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## History
Iradi tradition holds that the Aksay Plateau was long a neutral ground where rival groups met to make truces and fix pasture boundaries. Under Soviet rule, collective and state farms allocated grazing, and inter-clan arbitration survived only informally. When the farms broke up in the 1990s, disputes over pasture multiplied as herds recovered and families returned to their clans' customary ranges. Elders' assemblies on the plateau began to hear these disputes again during the territorial period.<sup>[3]</sup> After the 2007 partition, the kurultai that constituted the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC) in late 2007 established the tribunal as a standing body with a fixed membership, and it has sat every summer since 2008.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Composition
The seven judges are chosen by consensus at the Kurultai from among senior *biys*. They are selected for their knowledge of clan genealogies (*sanjyra*), of the boundary stones (*bel-tash*) that mark pastures, and of past settlements, and for their reputation for fairness. By custom the larger clans, among them the Tanıp, Sarybagysh, Naiman and Karakoyun (see [[Clans of the Autonomous Tribal Regions]]), are represented, and the remaining seats rotate among the smaller clans. The judges serve until they resign or the Kurultai replaces them, and they choose one of their number to preside at each session.<sup>[2]</sup> [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]], the IAC's principal spokesman, holds no seat on the tribunal. Cases are prepared by the pasture affairs division of the [[Iradi Freedom Society Chancellery]].

## Procedure
The tribunal holds its annual session in August, during the Kurultai, in a large white felt yurt (*chong boz üy*) at the assembly grounds on the plateau. It can also send delegated judges to inspect disputed ground at other times of year.<sup>[1]</sup>
- Hearings are public and oral. Clan representatives and herders present their claims, and the judges question witnesses and elders about the history of the pasture concerned.
- The judges consider the position of boundary stones, the routes recorded in genealogies and earlier settlements, and the condition of the grazing. Since the 2010s they have also been shown satellite vegetation maps supplied through the [[wp:Food and Agriculture Organization]] and the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]].<sup>[4]</sup>
- Decisions are reached by consensus among the judges and announced at the assembly.

## Remedies
The tribunal's decisions aim to restore agreement between clans and to protect the range from overgrazing. They include:<sup>[2]</sup>
- **Pasture rotation orders**, which set opening and closing dates for high pastures in the [[Talas Alatau]] and the Chatkal Highlands;
- **Boundary rulings**, which confirm or move boundary stones and fix the corridors along which herds may cross another clan's land;
- **Compensation (*kun*)**, assessed against clans whose livestock have grazed another lineage's pastures, payable in sheep or [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] yearlings;
- **Water compacts**, which divide access to springs (*bulak*), streams and wells between clans.

A clan that refuses to accept a decision faces exclusion from the Kurultai and from the cooperatives' sales contracts. Such cases are rare, according to UNMI.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Notable disputes
The tribunal's best-known case concerned spring pastures in the Chatkal Highlands claimed by the Sarybagysh and the Naiman. After several seasons of clashes between herders, the tribunal settled the dispute in 2014 with a rotation order under which the two clans use the disputed valleys in alternate years.<sup>[2]</sup> Disputes over boreholes and grazing trails near the western desert frontier have also come before it, including after the [[2018 Border Demarcation Clashes]] with Uzbek border guards.

## Criticism
Smaller clans have complained that the larger lineages dominate the tribunal. Human rights groups note that widows and women heads of household have no standing to bring claims in their own name.<sup>[5]</sup> Researchers have reported that the tribunal's caseload has grown since the 2000s as herd sizes recovered, and they link part of the increase to drier summers and the retreat of glaciers, which have reduced the water available on the high pastures.<sup>[4]</sup>

### 4.55. Iradi Language
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Language & Literature*

The **Iradi language** (Iradi: *Irad tili*, colloquially *Iradcha*) is a Turkic language of the Kipchak branch, spoken mainly in Irad. Its core grammar and basic vocabulary are close to those of Kyrgyz. Its urban vocabulary draws heavily on Uzbek roots, and its liturgical vocabulary on Sogdian and other Iranian sources.<sup>[1]</sup> Iradi and English are the official languages of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), and Iradi is the only language of public life in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR). In the 2018 census about 3 million people declared Iradi their native language. Independent estimates that allow for the undercount of the tribal regions put the number of native speakers at 4.3 to 4.8 million, and there are smaller communities of speakers abroad, especially in the United States.<sup>[2]</sup>

Iradi was written in Arabic script until 1928, in the Latin alphabet from 1928 to 1941 and in Cyrillic from 1941. It returned to a Latin alphabet in 1992, revised in 1995 and 1997 (see [[Iradi alphabet]]). Language use in Irad divides sharply by generation and region. Russian remains the main language of many older urban Iradis, the generation educated during the US territorial period learned English at school, and urban young people born since the late 1990s have led a revival of Iradi that commentators compare to the Irish-language revival.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Classification
Iradi belongs to the Kipchak (northwestern) branch of the Common Turkic languages. Within the branch it is closest to Kyrgyz, with which it shares several distinctive features:<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>
- long vowels formed where older consonants were lost between vowels, as in *too* "mountain" ([[wp:Old Turkic language|Old Turkic]] *tag*);
- an initial /dʒ/ where many Turkic languages have /j/, as in *jol* "road";
- extensive rounding harmony in suffixes.

Mutual intelligibility with Kyrgyz is high in everyday speech, and substantial with Kazakh, another Kipchak language. Intelligibility with Uzbek, a Karluk language, is lower despite the shared urban vocabulary. Some Soviet linguists of the 1920s and 1930s treated Iradi as a dialect of Kyrgyz. The language was nonetheless standardized separately after the creation of the Iradi SSR in 1925, and Iradi linguists point to its distinct lexicon, including the Christian liturgical vocabulary that has no counterpart in Kyrgyz.<sup>[1]</sup> Iradi historians link the speakers' ancestors to Christian Turkic groups of the [[wp:Qara Khitai]] period, such as the [[wp:Keraites]] or [[wp:Naimans]]. The linguistic evidence for this is inconclusive.

## Vocabulary
The Iradi lexicon is commonly described in layers, which reflect the history of its speakers:<sup>[1]</sup>

| Layer | Main domains | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Native Kipchak | Basic vocabulary, kinship, pastoralism, horses | *at* "horse", *uruk* "clan", *aksakal* "elder", *boz üy* "yurt", *bulak* "spring", *zhayloo* "summer pasture", *kyshtoo* "winter pasture" |
| Uzbek and Persian, via Uzbek | Town life, crafts, trade | *dastgoh* "workshop", *mahalla* "urban neighborhood", *bozor* "market", *hunarmand* "craftsman", *navbahor* "new spring" |
| Sogdian and other Iranian | Liturgy, religion, old place names | *nom* "scripture", *frishte* "angel", *kuble* "orientation toward Polaris"; place-name elements *kand* "oasis town", *shahr* "city", *diz* "citadel" |
| Syriac | Church ritual | *madbaha* "sanctuary", *qurbana* "Eucharist" |
| Arabic, mostly via Persian | Law, government, abstract terms | *adat* "custom", *Mejlis* "assembly", *azatlık* "freedom" |
| Russian | Soviet-era technology, administration, urban life | *zavod* "factory", *kolkhoz* "collective farm", *mikrorayon* "housing estate", *marshrutka* "minibus" |
| English | Government, business and technology since 1992 | *kampus* "campus", *startap* "startup", *frilanser* "freelancer" |

The Sogdian layer reflects the role of Sogdian as a language of Church of the East literature in medieval [[wp:Central Asia]], and words such as *nom*, ultimately from Greek *nomos* through Sogdian, also appear in Old Uyghur Christian and Buddhist texts. The urban Uzbek layer is usually attributed to the trading and craft communities of the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand|Kokand]] period, when Iradi towns depended on the commerce of the [[wp:Fergana Valley]].<sup>[4]</sup> Russian loans are most frequent in the speech of older urban Iradis, and English loans in that of younger ones. *Kümöch*, the sacramental bread of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], is a native Turkic word for bread baked in embers that acquired a liturgical meaning (see [[Kümöch Sacramental Bread]]).

## Phonology
Standard Iradi has eight native vowels: *a*, *e*, *ı*, *i*, *o*, *ö*, *u* and *ü*. All but *ı* and *i* also occur as long vowels (*aa*, *ee*, *oo*, *öö*, *uu*, *üü*). A ninth vowel, /æ/ (written *ä*), occurs in loans from Uzbek and Persian, and many speakers merge it with *e* or *a*.<sup>[5]</sup> As in Kyrgyz, vowel harmony operates on both backness and rounding: the vowels of suffixes agree with those of the stem. The plural suffix, for example, has the forms *-lar*, *-ler*, *-lor* and *-lör*, and its initial consonant assimilates to the end of the stem:
- *at* "horse" → *attar* "horses";
- *kol* "hand" → *koldor* "hands";
- *üy* "house" → *üylör* "houses";
- *kız* "girl" → *kızdar* "girls".

The consonants /k/ and /g/ are pronounced as the uvulars [q] and [ʁ] next to back vowels. The standard orthography writes them as *k* and *g*, although *q* survives in a few established names such as the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. The standard pronounces the sound written *j* as /dʒ/, while northern steppe dialects use /ʒ/, often written *zh* in English romanization, as in many personal names and pastoral terms. Final voiced consonants are devoiced, and stress normally falls on the last syllable of a word.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Grammar
Iradi is an agglutinative language. Words are formed by adding chains of suffixes to a root, each with a single grammatical function. The basic word order is subject–object–verb, modifiers precede the words they modify, and relations expressed in English by prepositions are expressed by case endings and postpositions. There is no grammatical gender and no article.<sup>[1]</sup>

Nouns take six cases, shown here for *at* "horse":

| Case | Form | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| Nominative | *at* | subject |
| Genitive | *attın* | possessor ("of the horse") |
| Dative | *atka* | direction, indirect object ("to the horse") |
| Accusative | *attı* | definite direct object |
| Locative | *atta* | location ("on the horse") |
| Ablative | *attan* | source ("from the horse") |

Possession is marked by suffixes on the possessed noun: *atım* "my horse", *atı* "his or her horse", *attarıbız* "our horses". Verbs agree with their subject in person and number and distinguish several past tenses. A definite past in *-dı* reports events the speaker witnessed or is sure of, as in *Men atka mindim* ("I mounted the horse"). An indefinite past in *-gan* is used for reported or inferred events. Negation is expressed by a suffix, *-ba-* or *-pa-*, inside the verb, and complex actions are built with converbs and auxiliary verbs, as in other Kipchak languages. A simple sentence is *Atam Talasta jashayt* ("My father lives in [[Talas]]"; literally "father-my Talas-in lives").<sup>[1]</sup>

## Dialects and registers
Iradi linguists usually distinguish three main dialect groups, together with a church register (see [[Dialects of Iradi]]):<sup>[5]</sup>
- **Urban dialects** of Talas, [[Nurzhan]] and Iyık Janyl. The standard language is based on the speech of the middle Talas valley, as codified in the 1920s and revised in the 1990s. Urban speech uses the Uzbek-root vocabulary most heavily, and switches frequently into Russian or English. The Nurzhan variety contains the most Russian loans.
- **Tribal dialects** of the mountains and steppe. Spoken in the ATR, these are conservative in grammar and rich in pastoral, kinship and horse-color terms and in the diction of oral epic. The northern steppe and [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] subdialects pronounce *j* as /ʒ/ and share some features with Kazakh.
- **Fergana Rim dialects** of the southern foothills. Spoken by Iradis and in mixed villages with Kyrgyz and [[wp:Uzbeks]], these show strong Uzbek influence, including weaker rounding harmony and more Persian and Arabic loans.
- **The ecclesiastical register** of the Syro-Iradi Catholic Church. It preserves the Sogdian, Iranian and [[wp:Syriac language|Syriac]] liturgical vocabulary. In 1993 the [[Syro-Iradi Episcopal Synod]] approved Iradi translations of the liturgy for use alongside Classical Syriac (see [[East Syriac Rites of Iyık Janyl]]).

## Writing systems
- **Medieval inscriptions.** Old Turkic runic inscriptions have been found in the Talas valley, and Christian gravestones of the wider [[wp:Semirechye]] region bear Turkic texts in Syriac script. Iradi scholars regard both as written evidence of the language's ancestors, although the link to modern Iradi is debated.<sup>[4]</sup> The runic script is used today only symbolically, notably in the motto on the [[Flag of Irad]].
- **Arabic script (to 1928).** Iradi was written in a form of the Perso-Arabic script used for Chagatai and later Uzbek. Texts copied at [[Iyık Janyl]], including the eighteenth-century vita of [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]], used it.
- **Latin (1928–1941).** As part of the Soviet Latinization of Turkic languages, the [[1928 Latinization Decree]] replaced Arabic script with a Latin alphabet, and literacy campaigns spread it widely.
- **Cyrillic (1941–1992).** The [[1941 Cyrillic Mandate]] imposed a Cyrillic alphabet with additional letters for the front rounded vowels and the velar nasal. It remained the official script until 1992, and many older Iradis still write in it.
- **Latin (since 1992).** The Provisional Government and the territorial administration restored a Latin alphabet in 1992. The [[1995 Latin Orthography Revision]] fixed the present 32-letter alphabet, replacing several digraphs with letters carrying diacritics. The Language and Education Reform Act of 1997 made it compulsory in schools and public administration.<sup>[6]</sup> In English-language usage, Iradi names are often romanized with the digraphs *ch*, *sh* and *zh*.

## Sociolinguistics
The language situation in the cities of the ISEZ is marked by differences between generations, which reflect the successive dominance of Russian in the Soviet period, English in the territorial period and Iradi since the 2010s. The most detailed data come from a 2022 survey of 3,100 residents of Talas, Nurzhan and Iyık Janyl by the Talas State University Institute of Sociology:<sup>[3]</sup>

| Age group (2022) | Main home language: Russian | Main home language: Iradi | Speaks English without difficulty | Speaks Iradi without difficulty |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Over 60 | 61% | 34% | 4% | 66% |
| 42–60 | 52% | 43% | 12% | 70% |
| 26–41 | 44% | 45% | 47% | 74% |
| 18–25 | 29% | 52% | 81% | 86% |

The same survey found large differences between cities: Russian was the main home language of 57 percent of respondents in Nurzhan, 31 percent in Talas and 18 percent in Iyık Janyl.<sup>[3]</sup> Sociologists commonly associate these patterns with three urban generations:
- the Russian-speaking "Russos" born before about 1980 (see [[Russos of Nurzhan]]);
- the [[Urban Iradi Millennials]], who grew up in Russian-speaking homes but were schooled in English and Iradi after 1992;
- the generation born since the late 1990s, the first to speak English fluently on a wide scale, which has adopted Iradi as a marker of identity (see [[Iradi language revival]]).

In the tribal regions the situation is different. Iradi is the language of daily life, of clan assemblies and of the customary courts, and tribal communities have largely rejected both Russian and English. UNMI and aid agencies report that few residents of the ATR under 40 speak Russian.<sup>[7]</sup> Urban Iradis who learned the language as adults often regard tribal speech as more "authentic", and young urban speakers have adopted pastoral and epic vocabulary from it. Naming follows the same divide. Urban Iradis mostly keep Russian-style surnames ending in *-ov*, *-ev* or *-ova*, while tribal Iradis use patronymics formed with *uulu* ("son of") and *kyzy* ("daughter of") (see [[Iradi name]] and [[De-Russification Movement in Irad]]).

## Status and education
Iradi has been an official language, alongside English, since 1992, when Russian lost its official status. The Language and Education Reform Act of 1997 made instruction in Iradi and English compulsory in public schools, and Russian is taught as an optional foreign language.<sup>[6]</sup> Debates in the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] are held in Iradi and English, with interpretation into Russian. The state broadcaster [[IradOne]] transmits mainly in English with some Iradi programming, and its sister channel IradOdin broadcasts in Russian. Private Russian-language schools in Nurzhan, many of them funded by the foundation of the oil executive [[Kamran Bekzatov]], continue to operate. Bekzatov and other Russo figures have called for Russian to be restored as an official language, a proposal opposed by Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] and other DPI leaders.

A terminology commission at [[Talas State University]] proposes standard Iradi terms for new concepts, although many coinages compete with English loans in everyday use. In the ATR, Iradi is the only language of the [[Iradi Freedom Society]], and schools run by village councils and parishes teach in it.<sup>[7]</sup> Older clerks in the tribal regions often still write Iradi in Cyrillic.

## Literature
Iradi literature has its roots in oral tradition: the epic cycles recited by bards (*ırchy*) with the [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]], the horseback chants known as *ırda* (see [[Irda (Vocal Tradition)]]), and the cycle of the [[The Epic of Janyl|Epic of Janyl]]. A written literature in the Latin alphabet developed in the 1920s and was curtailed by the purges of 1937 and the switch to Russian-only schooling (see [[Iradi literature]]). Poems about the 1916 revolt, notably [[The Black Blizzard of 1916 (Poem)|The Black Blizzard of 1916]], remain widely read.<sup>[8]</sup> Since the 1990s the electronic music genre [[Mor-Wave]], whose founders [[tüntolk]] wrote all their lyrics in Iradi, has been credited with making the language fashionable among urban young people, and Iradi is now widely used on social media.

### 4.56. Koryo-saram in Irad
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Society & Demographics*

The **Koryo-saram in Irad** (Iradi: *Irad Koreyleri*; Russian: *Корё-сарам*; Korean: 고려사람) are the ethnic Koreans of Irad. Most are descendants of the Koreans whom the Soviet government deported from the [[wp:Russian Far East|Soviet Far East]] to [[wp:Central Asia]] in 1937. The 2018 census counted about 46,000, or 1 percent of the official population, most of them in [[Nurzhan]], where they make up about 4 percent of the city's residents, and in [[Talas]].<sup>[1]</sup> Deportees unloaded in the lower Chu valley introduced flooded rice cultivation to the region, and in the postwar decades the community became strongly represented in engineering, medicine and the universities. Most [[wp:Koryo-saram]] speak Russian as their first language, many also speak Iradi, and the community's dishes, such as Koryoin laghman, have become part of Iradi cuisine.

## History

#### Deportation (1937)
Koreans began settling in the Russian Far East in the 1860s. In 1937 the Soviet government ordered the deportation of the entire Korean population of the Far East, more than 170,000 people, to Central Asia, on the grounds that they might serve as agents of [[wp:Japan]].<sup>[2]</sup> In the autumn of that year several thousand deportees were unloaded from unheated freight cars along the railway at Kobozev, as Nurzhan was then called, and at sidings in the Chu valley. Many spent the first winter in dugouts (*zemlyanki*) dug into the steppe. Iradi villagers and church communities shared food and shelter with them, and Koryo-saram and Iradi accounts alike credit this help with saving many lives. Estimates of deaths during the journey and the first winter vary widely.<sup>[3]</sup>

The deportees were registered as special settlers and needed permission to leave their districts, restrictions that remained in force until the 1950s. Korean-language schools and newspapers were closed in 1938. During the [[wp:World War II|Second World War]], Korean men were generally excluded from front-line service, and many were drafted into labor battalions.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### Rice farming and collective farms
In the spring of 1938 Korean collective farms began draining the marshy flats of the lower Chu and planting flooded rice paddies. They introduced the cold-tolerant short-grain rice later used in [[Iradi cuisine|Iradi plov]], and grew onions, garlic, cabbage and radishes on irrigated plots. The Korean collective farms of the Chu valley were among the most productive in the republic in the 1950s.<sup>[3]</sup> Many families also took part in *gobonji*, the seasonal contract farming in which Korean work teams leased land, often far from home, to grow onions and melons for sale.

#### Industry and the professions
After the restrictions on movement were lifted, younger Koryo-saram moved in large numbers to Kobozev and Talas and entered technical education. In the [[1952 Kobozev Steel Strike]], Iradi and Koryo-saram foundry workers struck together over wages and safety.<sup>[4]</sup> Koryo-saram engineers, geologists and plant managers worked in the oil industry that grew up after the [[Nurzhan Oil Discovery (1949)|1949 oil discovery]], at the [[Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex]] and in engineering plants. In the 1970s [[Oleg Kim]] directed the Kobozev tractor combine. Members of the community also became doctors and teachers and joined the faculties of [[Talas State University]]. In cinema, the cinematographer Viktor Pak shot *[[Zarina (film)|Zarina]]* (1968) and *[[Desert Sun’s Rebellion]]* (1979).

#### Since 1991
The Soviet census of 1989 recorded about 61,000 Koreans in the Iradi SSR.<sup>[1]</sup> The community's numbers fell after independence. During and after the [[First Iradi Civil War]] of 1992, which was fought in part around Kobozev, some families left for Russia, and later others emigrated for work to [[wp:South Korea]] and the United States. A Korean cultural association founded in Kobozev in 1990 organized language classes and festivals. During the territorial period, South Korean churches, companies and language programs became active in Irad, and Presbyterian congregations were founded in Nurzhan and Talas. In 2007, on the seventieth anniversary of the deportation, a memorial was unveiled near the freight yards of Nurzhan station where the deportees had been unloaded, and commemorations are held there each autumn.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Demographics
According to the 2018 census, about three-quarters of Irad's Koryo-saram live in Nurzhan, and most of the rest live in Talas and in the farming villages of the Chu District. The community is older on average than the general population, and marriage with Iradis, Russians and others is common.<sup>[1]</sup> Census data show high levels of education: 41 percent of Koryo-saram aged 25 and over had completed higher education, against an average of 23 percent in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]].<sup>[1]</sup>

## Language and religion
Russian is the first language of most Koryo-saram. The [[wp:Koryo-mar]] dialect of Korean, descended from the northern Korean speech of the original migrants, is spoken mainly by the oldest generation. Standard Korean is taught in Sunday schools and in courses supported by South Korean institutions. Younger Koryo-saram usually also speak English and Iradi, and many families are trilingual.<sup>[6]</sup>

Many Koryo-saram were gradually absorbed into the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], and Korean-language Catholic congregations meet in Nurzhan. Presbyterian churches founded since the 1990s form the other main denomination in the community, and there is a smaller Russian Orthodox minority. Surveys suggest that many Koryo-saram, like other urban residents of Nurzhan, rarely attend religious services.<sup>[6]</sup>

## Culture and cuisine
The cultural association and church congregations organize Korean holidays, including [[wp:Chuseok]] in autumn and the spring memorial day of *Hansik*, and run dance and music groups. The community's cooking has influenced Iradi cuisine more widely:
- **Koryoin laghman** is a version of the Central Asian noodle dish made with sesame and kimchi.
- **Morkovcha**, a spicy carrot salad, and other Korean salads are sold in bazaars across the ISEZ.
- **Kuksi**, cold noodles in broth, is a summer dish in Nurzhan.
- **Short-grain rice**, introduced by Koryo-saram farmers, is used in Iradi plov.

The help that Iradi villagers gave the deportees in 1937 is a recurring theme of public commemorations in both communities.<sup>[5]</sup>

### 4.57. De-Russification Movement in Irad
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Society & Demographics*

The **de-Russification movement in Irad** is the set of policies and social changes, beginning in the late Soviet period, that reduced the place of the Russian language and of Russian and Soviet names in Iradi public life. Its main measures were the removal of Russian's official status in 1992 and the return to a Latin alphabet. Cities, streets and institutions were renamed, most prominently Kobozev, which became [[Nurzhan]] in September 1992, and in the tribal regions Russian-style surnames gave way to Turkic patronymics.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup> The process has been uneven. In the cities of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), Russian remains the *de facto* lingua franca and most people keep Russian-style surnames, while in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) Iradi is the only language of public life and patronymics are almost universal.

## Background
In the early years of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]], the Soviet policy of nativization (*korenizatsiia*) standardized the Iradi language in a Latin alphabet (1928) and promoted Iradi cadres. The planned capital on the lower Chu was named Kobozev in 1927, after the Bolshevik official [[Pyotr Kobozev]]. By 1937 nativization had been abandoned. Schools switched to Russian-only teaching, Iradi was suppressed in print, and the [[1941 Cyrillic Mandate]] imposed the Cyrillic alphabet.<sup>[3]</sup> Soviet registration practice also gave most Iradis Russian-style surnames, formed by adding *-ov* or *-ev* (feminine *-ova*, *-eva*) to a father's or grandfather's name. Under perestroika in the late 1980s, writers and teachers campaigned for the wider use of Iradi, and the republic's leadership raised its status in education and publishing.

## Measures

#### Language and script (1992–1997)
After the [[First Iradi Civil War]] of 1992, the territorial arrangement made Iradi and English the official languages, and Russian lost its official status. The Provisional Government and the territorial administration restored a Latin alphabet in 1992. The Territorial Legislature then adopted the [[1995 Latin Orthography Revision]], which fixed the present 32-letter alphabet. The Language and Education Reform Act of 1997 made the Latin script compulsory in public administration and instruction in Iradi and English compulsory in public schools, with Russian reduced to an optional foreign language.<sup>[2]</sup> In the cities, English rather than Iradi largely replaced Russian as the language of advancement, and some scholars therefore describe the reforms as Anglicization as much as de-Russification.<sup>[5]</sup>

#### Place names (1992–1993)
In September 1992, in a speech in the city, Provisional President [[Amanbek Alimbekov]] renamed Kobozev as Nurzhan. The name is a [[wp:Kipchak languages|Kipchak Turkic]] word meaning "light of life", and Alimbekov described the city as a "guiding light of industry" that would lead Irad to a new dawn after the ruin of the civil war.<sup>[3]</sup> The Toponymic Heritage Statute, passed by the interim Territorial Legislature in 1993, confirmed the renaming and restored Turkic and Sogdian names to streets, districts and reservoirs. In Nurzhan, for example, Lenin Prospect became Azatlık ("Freedom") Prospect. Soviet-era place names have since been treated as obsolete in official use, and monuments to Soviet officials were removed from central squares in the 1990s.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Personal names
Naming conventions changed along the line between town and countryside, a division later fixed by the 2007 partition (see [[Iradi name]]):<sup>[4]</sup>
- **Tribal patronymics.** From the 1990s, rural and tribal families dropped Russian-style surnames in favor of the Turkic patronymic pattern: a given name followed by the father's name and *uulu* ("son of") or *kyzy* ("daughter of"). The Tanıp chief [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]], recorded in Soviet documents as Bektur Zhumabekov, and his sister [[Klara Zhumabek kyzy]] are examples. In the ATR the patronymic form is now almost universal.
- **Urban surnames.** In the cities most people kept surnames in *-ov*, *-ev* or *-ova*, partly because property, education and employment records had been issued in those forms. The family of Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]] and the oil executive [[Kamran Bekzatov]] are examples. Registry data analyzed in 2019 showed that more than 90 percent of adults in the three cities carried such surnames.
- **Shortened surnames.** Since the territorial period some younger urban professionals have dropped the Russian suffix. Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]], registered at birth as Maksatov, has used the shortened form since his student years.

## Generational dynamics
Attitudes to de-Russification differ sharply by age. Older urban Iradis educated in Russian, the self-described "Russos", have often viewed the reforms with skepticism (see [[Russos of Nurzhan]]). The [[Urban Iradi Millennials]] grew up in Russian-speaking homes but were schooled in English and Iradi after 1992. Urban young people born since the late 1990s have embraced Iradi as a marker of identity (see [[Iradi language revival]]). In a 2022 survey of urban residents by [[Talas State University]], Russian was the main home language of 61 percent of respondents over 60 but of 29 percent of those aged 18 to 25.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Debate
Supporters of the reforms regard them as the restoration of an identity suppressed under Soviet rule, and note that they were carried out without large-scale violence between communities. Critics among Russian speakers point to language requirements in the civil service, the closure of Russian-medium public schools and the emigration of many ethnic Russians during the 1990s.<sup>[6]</sup> The Russian share of the population fell from about 11 percent in the 1989 Soviet census to 4 percent in the official 2018 count. Kamran Bekzatov and other Russo figures call for Russian to be restored as an official language, a proposal the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] has rejected. In the tribal regions, some leaders argue that the urban elite's retention of Russian surnames shows how shallow the change has been in the ISEZ.<sup>[4]</sup>

### 4.58. Russos of Nurzhan
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Society & Demographics*

The **Russos** (Iradi: *Russolor*), often called the **Russos of Nurzhan** after their main center, are the Russian-speaking urban generation of Irad. The term usually refers to urban Iradis born between the late 1940s and about 1980, together with Russians, Ukrainians and Russian-speaking Koryo-saram of the same age, who were educated in Russian in the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] and have remained culturally tied to the Russian-speaking world.<sup>[1]</sup> Many members of the group use "Russo" to describe themselves; younger Iradis sometimes use it disparagingly. The Russos are concentrated in [[Nurzhan]], the Soviet-era capital and center of the oil industry, and are associated with conservative politics, nostalgia for the late Soviet period and the oil executive [[Kamran Bekzatov]], their best-known public figure. Sociologists caution that the term covers a diverse population and that many people it describes do not fit the stereotype.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Definition and size
The Russos are not an ethnic group. Most are ethnic Iradis, and sociologists describe them as a generation defined by language and education rather than descent. They were schooled in Russian after the end of nativization in 1937, many of them trained at Russian-language institutes in [[wp:Tashkent]], [[wp:Moscow]] and Kobozev, and they formed the managerial and technical workforce of the Soviet oil, metallurgical and railway industries.<sup>[1]</sup> No official figures exist. In 2022 sociologists at [[Talas State University]] estimated that about 300,000 residents of the three cities belonged to the relevant age groups and used Russian as their main home language, about two-thirds of them in Nurzhan.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Language
Russian is the main home language of most Russos, although many also speak Iradi. Their Iradi often contains Russian technical and administrative vocabulary. In the 2022 Urban Language Survey of the Talas State University Institute of Sociology, which surveyed 3,100 residents of [[Talas]], Nurzhan and [[Iyık Janyl]], the patterns for the two older age groups were as follows:<sup>[3]</sup>

| Age group (2022) | Main home language: Russian | Main home language: Iradi | Speaks Iradi without difficulty | Speaks English without difficulty |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Over 60 | 61% | 34% | 66% | 4% |
| 42–60 | 52% | 43% | 70% | 12% |

Russian was the main home language of 57 percent of all respondents in Nurzhan, against 31 percent in Talas. Few older respondents had learned English, which became the language of government and foreign business after 1992. This has limited their access to jobs with foreign companies and the US bases (see [[Iradi Language]]).

## Culture
Sociologists describe Russo cultural life as oriented toward Russia and the Soviet past. Its characteristic features include:<sup>[1]</sup>
- Russian-language media, including satellite television from Russia and the Russian-language channel IradOdin, a sister channel of [[IradOne]];
- Russian-language theater and the institutions of Soviet urban culture in Nurzhan, such as the Palace of Metallurgists;
- the commemoration of [[wp:Victory Day (9 May)|Victory Day]] on 9 May with a parade in Nurzhan;
- support for the football club Neftchi Nurzhan, whose rivalry with Tulpar Talas reflects the city's language politics (see [[Kara-Ak derby]]);
- a largely secular outlook. Most ethnic Iradi Russos are nominally members of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] but rarely practice, and ethnic Russians and Ukrainians belong mainly to the [[wp:Russian Orthodox Church]].

In a 2023 survey for the *Central Asian Geopolitical Review*, 62 percent of Nurzhan respondents over 50 agreed that life had been better in the late Soviet period, against 19 percent of those under 30.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Economic position
The Russos dominated the management of the Soviet industries of the Chu basin, and many kept their positions after 1992. [[NurGaz]], privatized in 1993 under Bekzatov, remains the largest employer in Nurzhan, and its senior staff are drawn largely from this generation. The decline of Soviet-era engineering plants after 1991 hit Russo workers hard, and many of their children went to study or work in Russia (see [[Iradis in Russia]]). Pensions, subsidized housing such as the [[NurGaz Worker Housing Complex]], and clinics funded by NurGaz and the Bekzatov Foundation are central to the welfare of older residents. Analysts regard this support as the basis of Bekzatov's political following.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Politics
Survey data show that older urban Iradis are more conservative than younger ones. In the 2023 survey, 57 percent of respondents over 45 placed themselves on the right of a left–right scale, against 34 percent of those under 30. Large differences also appeared on two questions:<sup>[4]</sup>
- support for restoring Russian as an official language: 64 percent of those over 60 and 52 percent of those aged 42 to 60, against 14 percent of those aged 18 to 25;
- a favorable view of Russia: 58 percent of those over 60, against 17 percent of those aged 18 to 25.

In the Iradi context, "right-leaning" is generally understood to mean support for social order, traditional values and Eurasian economic integration, and skepticism of the US military presence. This distinguishes Russo conservatism from the pro-American line of the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI).<sup>[4]</sup>

Russo politicians have held a majority on the Nurzhan city council for most of the period since 1992, through the [[Labor Party of Irad]] until its dissolution in 2011 and on civic lists since, and in the 2023 election three Russo-aligned deputies from Nurzhan won seats in the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]], forming its only consistent opposition.<sup>[5]</sup> Bekzatov, who has never stood for office, calls for accession to the [[wp:Eurasian Economic Union]], the restoration of Russian as an official language and an end to the Toktarov family's business monopolies, and he has publicly praised [[wp:Vladimir Putin]]. The municipal politician [[Elena Petrova]] represents the Russian and Ukrainian industrial workforce. Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] and [[Alikhan Toktarov]] have opposed the Russos' calls on language and Eurasian integration.<sup>[2]</sup> After the [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]], Russo politicians argued that the episode showed the risks of depending on Washington.

## Relations with other generations
Many Russo families have experienced a language shift within three generations. Their children, the [[Urban Iradi Millennials]], grew up speaking Russian at home but were schooled in English and Iradi, and their grandchildren increasingly prefer Iradi and English (see [[Iradi language revival]]). Sociologists report that this shift is a common source of family tension, and that older Russian-speaking residents of Nurzhan regard figures popular with young people, such as the commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]], as outsiders.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Criticism of the concept
Sociologists have criticized the use of "Russo" as a catch-all label. They point out that two-thirds of older urban respondents in the 2022 survey speak Iradi without difficulty, that views on Russia vary widely within the age group, and that about a third of Nurzhan respondents over 60 opposed accession to the Eurasian Economic Union in 2023.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[4]</sup> Some older Iradis reject the term as an insult that questions their loyalty, while others have adopted it as a mark of pride.

### 4.59. Urban Iradi Millennials
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Society & Demographics*

**Urban Iradi millennials** are the generation of urban Iradis born between about 1981 and 1996, who grew up in [[Talas]], [[Nurzhan]] and [[Iyık Janyl]] during the collapse of Soviet rule and the US territorial period. Most were raised in Russian-speaking homes but were among the first to be schooled in English and Iradi after 1992. Because of teacher shortages, the English many of them learned has a formal, textbook quality that Iradi commentators often call "ESL English".<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup> The generation forms much of the professional workforce of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), and surveys describe it as politically pragmatic. Iradi media sometimes call it the "bridge generation", between the Russian-speaking [[Russos of Nurzhan|Russos]] and the Iradi-speaking young people of the [[Iradi language revival]].

## Formative experiences
Members of the generation spent their childhood in the last years of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]], the hyperinflation of 1991–92 and the [[First Iradi Civil War]], in which much of Talas was damaged. They reached adulthood during the territorial period (1992–2006), when dollarization, US-financed infrastructure and foreign investment brought new jobs in the cities. The older members of the cohort experienced the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] of 2007 as young adults. Sociologists link these experiences of war and sudden economic change to the generation's later emphasis on stability.<sup>[1]</sup> The period of American enthusiasm for Irad known as [[Iradimania]], including the 1993 compilation *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]*, coincided with their childhood, and many grew up with [[Iradi Country-Folk|Iradi country-folk]] and, as teenagers, with the first wave of [[Mor-Wave]].

## Education and language
The older members of the cohort began school in Russian. After 1992 the territorial administration introduced English and Latin-script Iradi into the curriculum, and the Language and Education Reform Act of 1997 made instruction in both compulsory in public schools. The supply of teachers did not keep pace. In 1994 the territorial Office of Education reported about 1,100 qualified English teachers against an estimated need of more than 6,000.<sup>[4]</sup> Schools retrained teachers of Russian and German, used imported American textbooks and relied on volunteer teachers recruited through Christian charities active during the Iradimania period.

Linguists who have studied the English of this generation describe several recurring features:<sup>[2]</sup>
- a formal register, with few contractions or idioms;
- vocabulary drawn from textbooks and from the legal and administrative language of the territorial statutes;
- Russian-influenced intonation and word order;
- pronunciation based on spelling.

Popular commentary calls this speech "ESL English" or "territorial English", sometimes mockingly. Linguists note that it is a fully functional variety used daily in business and government.<sup>[2]</sup>

The 2022 Urban Language Survey of the Talas State University Institute of Sociology found a mixed linguistic profile among respondents aged 26 to 41:<sup>[3]</sup>
- main home language: Iradi for 45 percent, Russian for 44 percent, and a mixture or English for most of the rest;
- 89 percent said they spoke Russian without difficulty, 74 percent Iradi and 47 percent English.

Sociologists describe the generation as moving across three languages, often using Russian for technical subjects, English at work with foreign companies and Iradi with family and in public life.

## Work and migration
The generation's command of English made it the main source of staff for foreign companies, the US bases and their contractors, and the banks and telecommunications companies of the territorial era, such as [[Talasbank]] and [[Attelkom]]. In a 2021 workforce survey by the Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Irad, people in this age group held about 58 percent of managerial posts in foreign-owned companies in the ISEZ.<sup>[6]</sup> Many also entered the civil service of the territorial administration and later the ISEZ. A smaller number emigrated, mainly to the United States (see [[Iradi Americans]]). Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]], born in 1980, who began school in Russian and moved to English-language instruction after 1992, is often cited as typical of the generation's older edge.

## Political attitudes
Surveys show the generation to be more pragmatic and less ideological than either older or younger urban Iradis. In a 2023 survey for the *Central Asian Geopolitical Review*, 63 percent of respondents aged 26 to 41 named economic stability as the most important issue facing the ISEZ, against 41 percent of those under 26.<sup>[5]</sup> Members of the generation were less likely than younger respondents to report taking part in protests, including the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]]. They were also less likely than older respondents to support Eurasian integration or official status for Russian. Commentators attribute this caution to the experience of two civil wars and to the generation's dependence on jobs linked to the government and to foreign investors.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Relations with other generations
Many millennials grew up speaking Russian with their parents and now speak Iradi or English with their children. Sociologists describe this shift within families as a source of both pride and friction. Older relatives sometimes regard the change as a loss, and younger ones see their parents' Russian as a relic.<sup>[1]</sup>

### 4.60. Iradi language revival
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Language & Literature*

The **Iradi language revival** (Iradi: *tilge kaytuu*, "return to the language") is the shift toward the Iradi language among urban Iradis born between about 1997 and 2012, together with the cultural trends associated with it. Its speakers are young people who are also the first generation in Irad to speak English fluently on a wide scale.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[3]</sup> Sociolinguists often compare the revival with that of the Irish language in [[wp:Ireland]]. The trends are also associated with the second wave of the electronic music genre [[Mor-Wave]] and with a youth culture centered on [[Talas]]. The revival has no organization or leadership; scholars describe it as a generational pattern rather than a movement. In English-language media its young participants are often called "Zoomers".

## Name
Scholars and the Iradi press call the shift *tilge kaytuu*, "return to the language", a phrase taken from the title of a 2016 essay series in the *[[Talas Herald]]*'s Iradi pages, and in English the "Iradi language revival", by analogy with the Irish and Welsh revivals. English-language commentary since the late 2010s has also used "Zoomers", slang for Generation Z, for the young people involved, and the borrowing *zumerler* is heard in Iradi, often ironically; the article was formerly titled "Iradi Zoomer Movement". These names are applied mainly to urban young people. Their contemporaries in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], who have always spoken Iradi and largely reject both English and Russian, are rarely included.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Language
Unlike their parents and grandparents, many of whom grew up speaking Russian, urban young people have increasingly adopted Iradi as a first or main language. The 2022 Urban Language Survey of the Talas State University Institute of Sociology found the following among respondents aged 18 to 25, compared with those over 60:<sup>[3]</sup>
- Iradi was the main home language of 52 percent, against 34 percent of those over 60. Russian was the main home language of 29 percent, against 61 percent.
- 81 percent said they spoke English without difficulty, against 4 percent of the oldest group.
- 86 percent said they spoke Iradi without difficulty, the highest share of any age group, while only 58 percent said the same of Russian.

The shift is also visible online. A study of about 1.2 million public social-media posts by users in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) found that the share written in Iradi among users under 25 rose from 18 percent in 2015 to 47 percent in 2023, while the share in Russian fell from 51 to 17 percent. English accounted for most of the remainder.<sup>[4]</sup> Young speakers mix English freely into Iradi and have coined new slang. They have also borrowed pastoral and epic vocabulary from tribal speech, which many regard as more authentic than the Russian-influenced Iradi of the cities.

#### The "Gaelic parallel"
Sociolinguists at [[Talas State University]] and elsewhere have compared the revival with that of Irish. In both cases young people from homes where another language dominated adopted a heritage language as a marker of identity, and music, social media and education helped give it prestige.<sup>[1]</sup> Critics point out a less flattering side of the comparison: in Ireland many more people report an ability to speak Irish than use it daily, and some researchers argue that the Iradi revival may likewise be concentrated in culture and private life. English remains the language of work in foreign companies and of higher education in technical fields, and few young professionals use Iradi in the workplace.<sup>[4]</sup> Supporters reply that, unlike Irish, Iradi has never ceased to be the everyday language of a large population in the tribal regions.

## Culture
- **Music.** The second wave of Mor-Wave, which began in the mid-2010s, was centered in Talas and drew its audience largely from this generation. The founding duo [[tüntolk]] re-formed in 2014, and their album *White Stallion in Fog* (2017) was played on the youth channel that [[IradOne]] launched after [[Alikhan Toktarov]] became its chairman in 2015. An annual Mor-Wave festival has been held in converted textile warehouses in Talas since 2016. Writers on the movement credit tüntolk, who wrote all their lyrics in Iradi, with helping to make the language fashionable.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[6]</sup>
- **Fashion and design.** Collectives in Talas combine motifs from felt carpets (*shyrdak*) and saddlery with streetwear.
- **Film.** Screenings of restored Soviet-era Iradi films at the [[Talasfilm Archives and Film Preservation]] attract young audiences. The director [[Beknur Karimov]], who was banned from Soviet filmmaking in 1983 and whose *[[Zalmax’s Dominion]]* (1977) was restored in 2011, has a cult following among them.
- **Online satire.** Webcomics and short videos in Iradi and English satirize officials, ministries and the state broadcaster.

## Politics
Young urban Iradis have been more willing than older generations to protest. Students and couriers, most of them in their late teens and twenties, made up most of the participants in the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]], which began in October 2023 after a municipal licensing surcharge and were dispersed by police and [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad|Gendarmerie]] units. The commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]], whose criticism of the surcharge on television preceded the protests, has his largest following among university students and young professionals.<sup>[5]</sup> Students also took a leading part in the demonstrations against the [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]], after which favorable views of the United States fell most steeply among respondents under 30.

Survey data show the generation to be the least attached to Russia of any age group. In a 2023 survey for the *Central Asian Geopolitical Review*, 14 percent of respondents aged 18 to 25 supported restoring Russian as an official language, and 17 percent had a favorable view of Russia.<sup>[5]</sup> Young people are also prominent in environmental campaigns in the [[Talas Alatau]], including opposition to mining in mountain watersheds. Analysts note that most of this activity takes place online or in cultural settings, under the close attention of the authorities and of state media.

### 4.61. Zara Toktarova
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Biographies*

**Zara Toktarova** (born 14 November 1988) is an Iradi education scholar. She is the youngest child and only daughter of [[Erlan Toktarov]], Governor of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), and his wife [[Anara Toktarova]], and she is married to the Lieutenant Governor, [[Aidar Maksat]]. A doctoral candidate in education at [[wp:Stanford University]], she researches bilingual education and mother-tongue literacy. She has lived mainly abroad since the mid-2010s, rarely gives interviews, and is publicly regarded as having no political role.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Early life and education
Toktarova was born on 14 November 1988, the sixth child of Erlan and Anara Toktarov and their only daughter. Her five elder brothers are [[Ruslan Toktarov|Ruslan]], [[Alikhan Toktarov|Alikhan]], [[Timur Toktarov|Timur]], [[Adil Toktarov|Adil]] and [[Bekzat Toktarov|Bekzat]]. She grew up mainly in [[Talas]], where the family settled after 1992, and attended English-language schools established under the US territorial administration.<sup>[3]</sup>

She studied [[Iradi literature]] and pedagogy at [[Talas State University]] and graduated with honors in 2010. She then completed a master's degree in international education policy in the United States, and later entered the doctoral program in education at Stanford University, where she is a doctoral candidate.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Academic work
Toktarova's research concerns bilingual education, mother-tongue literacy in post-Soviet [[wp:Central Asia]] and the revitalization of minority and indigenous languages. She has written on the teaching of Iradi and English in the schools of the ISEZ and on the revival of Iradi among young urban people (see [[Iradi Language]] and [[Iradi language revival]]).<sup>[1]</sup> She has presented papers at international education conferences and has given occasional lectures at Talas State University during visits to Irad.

## Public life
Toktarova keeps a low public profile and has made few public statements on political matters. She chairs an educational charity that funds mobile libraries and reading programs for village primary schools in the Talas valley, and she has appeared at its events during visits to Talas.<sup>[4]</sup>

She has not commented publicly on her father's absence from public life since July 2024 (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]). Tabloids in Talas have occasionally reported tensions within the Toktarov family over access to the [[Boz-Korgon]] estate. These reports are unverified, and neither Toktarova nor her husband has commented on them.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Personal life
Toktarova married Aidar Maksat, then a civil servant in the Talas municipal administration, in 2008. The couple have three children.<sup>[3]</sup> She speaks Iradi, English and Russian.

### 4.62. Timur Toktarov
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Biographies*

**Timur Toktarov** (born May 3, 1982) is an Iradi businessman who chairs [[Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics]], the largest road haulage and bonded logistics company in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). He is the third son of Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]]. Like his younger brothers [[Adil Toktarov|Adil]] and [[Bekzat Toktarov|Bekzat]], he keeps a low public profile and concentrates on the family's business interests, holding no political office.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Early life and education
[[wp:Timur]] was born on May 3, 1982, the third child of Erlan Toktarov and [[Anara Toktarova]]. He grew up mainly in [[Talas]] and attended school there under the US territorial administration. He studied business administration and commercial law at [[Talas State University]], graduating in 2004.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Business career
After graduating, Timur joined the bonded-warehousing business near [[Talas Air Base]] that his father had built up during his years in the Territorial Legislature. In 2008, the year after the ISEZ was created, the family acquired a controlling stake in Trans-Chuy, a Nurzhan-based haulier founded in 1996, and Timur became its chairman.<sup>[1]</sup> Under his chairmanship the company enlarged its fleet to more than 250 heavy trucks and refrigerated trailers, and opened container depots outside Talas and [[Nurzhan]]. Its main lines of business are:<sup>[1]</sup>
- refrigerated transport of beef from the [[Sukarne Irad Complex]] and other packing plants to markets in [[wp:Central Asia]];
- bulk haulage of grain and feed for [[Nurzhan Agro-Industrial]], which is directed by his brother Bekzat;
- transport of antimony ingots from the [[Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex]] to railheads;
- bonded customs terminals at the northern border crossings opened under the 2008 [[Northern Border Demarcation Protocol]].

Critics, including the oil executive [[Kamran Bekzatov]] and the commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]], argue that Trans-Chuy's bonded status and terminal concessions give the family an effective monopoly over transit handling fees on goods entering the ISEZ. They have called for these concessions to be opened to competition. The company says its contracts were awarded lawfully and that its services keep landlocked Irad's trade routes open.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Public profile
Timur rarely gives interviews or appears on [[IradOne]], and he has made no public statements on politics. Since his father withdrew from public view in July 2024, business publications have described him as maintaining working relations with the administration of Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] and with the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]], whose checkpoints his company's trucks pass daily. He has not commented on the succession (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

### 4.63. Adil Toktarov
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Biographies*

**Adil Toktarov** (born November 19, 1984) is an Iradi property developer who heads the Talas Commercial Development Group, one of the largest owners of commercial real estate in [[Talas]]. He is the fourth son of Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]]. Like his brothers [[Timur Toktarov|Timur]] and [[Bekzat Toktarov|Bekzat]], he keeps a low public profile, holds no political office and concentrates on the family's business interests in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ).<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Early life and education
Adil was born on November 19, 1984, the fourth child of Erlan Toktarov and [[Anara Toktarova]]. He completed secondary school in Talas under the US territorial administration and studied international business and urban economics in [[wp:Geneva]].<sup>[2]</sup>

## Business career
Adil returned to Irad in 2007, after the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], and founded the Talas Commercial Development Group, which obtained municipal land and zoning approvals in the center of Talas and along the commercial corridor toward [[Talas Air Base]].<sup>[1]</sup> The group's properties include:
- the Silk Road Financial Tower, which houses the headquarters of [[Talasbank]] and the offices of foreign mining and energy companies;
- the International Diplomatic Hotel, used by visiting delegations and contractors;
- shopping centers and residential complexes in the city;
- the football club Tulpar Talas, bought in 2011, and its stadium, the Silk Road Arena, rebuilt in 2014 (see [[Kara-Ak derby]]);
- holiday chalets in the lower Besh-Tash valley, on the ISEZ side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], near the [[Besh-Tash Ecological Conservation Area]].

From 2011 several of Adil's projects were joint ventures with his elder brother [[Alikhan Toktarov]], who built office towers, hotels and leisure venues on land acquired along the central avenue of Talas.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Controversies
Opposition members of the Talas city council and investigative journalists have argued that municipal land was allocated to the Toktarov brothers' companies without competitive auction, and that the group's projects received tax holidays and priority utility connections from the [[Talas Municipal Water Authority]]. The municipality has said that the transfers were lawful.<sup>[3]</sup> Conservation groups have objected to the construction of chalets near the Besh-Tash conservation area. The oil executive [[Kamran Bekzatov]] has named family-controlled construction among the monopolies he wants ended.

## Public profile
Adil rarely speaks in public. The group's Silk Road Financial Tower also houses offices of the [[Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority]], which supervises the escrow accounts into which the proceeds of Irad's main exports are paid.<sup>[1]</sup>
