### 4.79. Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Economy & Industry*

The **Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex** (Iradi: *Chatkal khimiyalyk-metallurgiyalyk kombinaty*) is an antimony smelter and chemical plant in the Sary-Bulak District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It lies in the [[Talas Alatau]] foothills about 30 kilometers south-west of [[Talas]], and takes its name from the nearby Chatkal range. It processes concentrate from the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]] into antimony metal and antimony trioxide. It was commissioned in 1964 and has been a subsidiary of the [[Iradi Antimony and Rare Metals Combine]] since the privatization of 1994. With about 2,200 employees, it is one of the largest industrial employers in the ISEZ outside [[Nurzhan]].<sup>[1]</sup>

## History
The smelter was built in 1961–1964 to process ore from the [[Sary-Bulak]] mine, which had opened in 1961, and was run with the mine as the Iradi Antimony Combine under the USSR Ministry of Non-Ferrous Metallurgy. Under the [[1971 Antimony Expansion Directive]], new roasting furnaces and a trioxide shop were added, and smelting capacity was increased about fourfold by the end of the 1970s.<sup>[2]</sup> [[Mikhail Chernov]] directed metallurgical production in the 1980s, and the chemist [[Svetlana Kozlova]] developed the plant's methods for refining bismuth from smelter residues.

Production stopped for most of 1992, during the [[First Iradi Civil War]], and resumed at a reduced level under the territorial administration. In 1994 the complex was privatized as a joint-stock company controlled by the newly formed combine. It was shut again for several months during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in 2007, when rail links were cut.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Plant and processes
The complex covers about 80 hectares and is linked by a rail spur to the Sary-Bulak mine and to the Talas railway. Its main stages are:
- **Volatilization roasting**, in which sulfide concentrate is heated in air so that the antimony escapes as trioxide fume. The fume is collected in bag filters as crude oxide.
- **Reduction smelting** of the crude oxide with coke in reverberatory furnaces. The resulting crude metal is fire-refined with alkaline fluxes to remove arsenic and iron, and cast into ingots of about 99.65% antimony.
- **Trioxide production**, in which refined metal is re-volatilized under controlled conditions to make high-purity antimony trioxide, the form used in flame retardants.
- **By-product recovery**, in which residues and flue dust go to an adjoining plant that recovers bismuth, tellurium and other metals (see [[Chatkal Rare Earth Facility]]).<sup>[1]</sup>

In 2023 the complex produced about 3,900 metric tons of antimony metal and about 2,600 metric tons of antimony trioxide, according to the combine.<sup>[3]</sup> Products are packed in steel drums and bulk bags. They travel by rail to the Talas railhead or by truck with [[Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics]], and then north through [[wp:Kazakhstan]], mainly to China but also to buyers in [[wp:South Korea]], [[wp:Japan]] and Europe.

## Environment
Antimony smelting releases sulfur dioxide and dust containing antimony and arsenic. Residents of villages near the complex have long complained of smoke and of damage to crops and orchards. A 2018 survey by the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] found sulfur dioxide levels above international guidelines in two nearby villages in winter.<sup>[4]</sup> The company says that since 2016 it has installed sulfur dioxide scrubbers, designed under its chief engineer [[Artem Kozlov]], and electrostatic precipitators, and that emissions now meet ISEZ standards. Slag and residues are stored on site. Older tailings from Soviet processing are held in the [[Chatkal Tailings Repository]], which is inspected by the [[Chatkal Placer Mining Inspectorate]].<sup>[4]</sup>

## Works settlement
A works settlement of about 6,000 people grew up beside the plant in the 1960s. It has company housing, a polyclinic, schools and a technical lyceum that trains metallurgical technicians. Many of the older residents are Russian-speaking specialists who came from other Soviet republics. The settlement depends almost entirely on the plant, and its population has fallen since the 1980s as younger residents have moved to Talas.<sup>[2]</sup>

### 4.80. Nurzhan Agro-Industrial
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Economy & Industry*

**Nurzhan Agro-Industrial** (NAI; Iradi: *Nurzhan agro-önör jay kombinaty*) is an agribusiness company in [[Nurzhan]] that specializes in grain storage and trading, animal-feed milling, silage distribution and seed supply in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It was formed in 2008–2009 from privatized state grain and feed enterprises of the lower [[Chu River Basin]], and it supplies most of the compound feed used by the commercial feedlots of the ISEZ. Since 2009 it has been headed by [[Bekzat Toktarov]], the fifth son of Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]], and it is one of the family businesses that critics cite as evidence of the concentration of economic power in the ISEZ.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## History
In the Soviet period, grain from the Chu valley collective farms was delivered to a state procurement system that ran elevators and feed mills in Kobozev. These passed to territorial state enterprises after 1992 and were run down during the 1990s. Investment in the beef industry after the [[wp:North American Free Trade Agreement]] came into force in 1994, notably by [[wp:Sukarne]] and [[wp:Conagra Brands|Conagra]] near [[Talas]], increased demand for feed. Most of it was met by imports and by the feedlots' own mills.<sup>[2]</sup>

In 2008 the ISEZ administration auctioned the state grain elevators and feed mills of the Chu District, and they were combined under NAI. Bekzat Toktarov, who had studied agricultural economics at the Tashkent Agrarian Institute, returned to Irad in 2009 to take charge of the company.<sup>[1]</sup> Opposition deputies and the newspaper *Irad Times* criticized the auction, saying that other bidders had been excluded. The ISEZ administration said the sale followed the privatization law.<sup>[3]</sup> In 2011 NAI opened a new compound-feed mill with Swiss-built equipment.

## Facilities
NAI's main facilities are in the eastern industrial zone of Nurzhan, beside the railway to [[wp:Kazakhstan]]:
- the **Nurzhan Central Grain Terminal**, a Soviet-era concrete elevator of about 120,000 metric tons capacity, modernized with temperature monitoring and new rail-loading equipment;
- the **compound-feed mill**, which produces pelleted feed for cattle and sheep and mineral supplements, with a reported capacity of about 240,000 metric tons a year;
- a **seed plant** that cleans and treats seed of winter wheat, barley and alfalfa for sale to farmers;
- smaller receiving stations along the canals of the [[Chu Irrigation Canal System]].<sup>[1]</sup>

## Business
NAI buys wheat, barley and feed corn from farms in the Chu and Talas valleys, many of them irrigated by the [[Chu Valley Irrigation Inspectorate]]. It imports grain from Kazakhstan by rail when the local harvest falls short. According to the company, it supplies about 70% of the commercial compound feed sold in the ISEZ, including feed for the feedlots that supply the [[Sukarne Irad Complex]].<sup>[1]</sup> It also holds import distribution rights for hybrid seed, fertilizer from Kazakhstan and veterinary medicines.

NAI is one of the few ISEZ companies with regular trade across the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. It buys barley and alfalfa from the tribal regions, and under a long-standing arrangement it supplies winter feed pellets to the [[Aksay Plateau Pastoral Cooperative]] in part exchange for wool and hides.<sup>[2]</sup> The company is financed through working-capital loans from [[Talasbank]], and its grain is moved by rail and by the trucks of [[Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics]].

## Criticism
Farmers' groups have complained that NAI's dominance of grain storage allows it to set purchase prices, and economists have pointed to its share of the feed market as an example of family monopolies in the ISEZ. Leaked US intelligence reports cited the family's businesses as evidence of a neopatrimonial system (see [[Political status of Irad]]).<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[3]</sup> The company says that it pays market prices and that its investments have reduced Irad's dependence on imported feed.

### 4.81. Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Health & Education*

The **Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute** (Iradi: *Nurzhan politekhnikalyk instituty*; Russian: *Нуржанский политехнический институт*), known until 1993 as the **Kobozev Polytechnic Institute**, is a public technical university in [[Nurzhan]]. It is Irad's leading technical university and specializes in petroleum engineering. It was founded in 1951 as a petroleum institute to train engineers for the oil fields discovered in the lower Chu basin two years earlier. It took its present broad form in 1968, when faculties of civil, mechanical and electrical engineering were added. The institute trains much of the engineering staff of [[NurGaz]] and had about 9,200 students in 2023.<sup>[1]</sup>

## History
#### Soviet period
After the [[Nurzhan Oil Discovery (1949)|discovery of oil near Kobozev in 1949]], the USSR Ministry of Higher Education founded the Kobozev Petroleum Institute in 1951 to train drilling, production and refining engineers for the *Iradneft* oil production association. Much of its first teaching staff came from the petroleum institutes of Baku and Grozny, and teaching was in Russian.<sup>[2]</sup> In 1968, as the city's engineering and metallurgical industries grew, the institute was reorganized as the Kobozev Polytechnic Institute. Faculties of civil engineering, mechanical engineering, and electrical engineering and radio electronics were added to the petroleum faculties.

By the 1980s the institute had about 7,000 students and was the main source of engineers for the industries of the Iradi SSR. Many of its graduates of this period belong to the Russian-educated urban generation known as the *Russos*, who filled the technical and managerial posts in the oil refinery, the antimony industry and the railways (see [[Russos of Nurzhan]]).<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Territorial period
Teaching was suspended from February to October 1992, during the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]] and the [[First Iradi Civil War]], in which Kobozev was the seat of the socialist government. In 1993 the institute was renamed after the city under the Toponymic Heritage Statute.<sup>[1]</sup>

During the territorial administration the institute introduced English-language degree programs in petroleum engineering in 1996, with support from American universities funded by territorial education grants. It adopted a credit-hour system modeled on American practice in 1997. Iradi-language teaching was introduced in the general courses. NurGaz began to fund laboratories and scholarships in return for first claim on graduates. [[Aidar Maksat]], later Lieutenant Governor, graduated in civil engineering in 2002, and Askar Daniyarov, a founder of the [[Mor-Wave]] duo [[tüntolk]], studied radio electronics there in the 1990s.<sup>[4]</sup>

#### Since 2007
Under the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), the institute has been governed by a statute of 2008. Under it the Governor appoints the rector from candidates nominated by the academic council. NurGaz and the Bekzatov Foundation of NurGaz president [[Kamran Bekzatov]] have paid for new laboratory buildings and fund scholarships, and NurGaz remains the institute's largest sponsor and the largest employer of its graduates.<sup>[3]</sup> Its language policy has been a recurring point of friction. The ISEZ administration has pressed for teaching in Iradi and English, while much of the senior staff still teaches in Russian, a practice defended by Russo members of the Nurzhan city council.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Organization
The institute has six faculties:
- **Petroleum and Mining Geology**, including geophysics and reservoir geology;
- **Oil and Gas Field Development**, covering drilling and production engineering;
- **Chemical Technology and Refining**;
- **Mechanical Engineering and Pipeline Transport**;
- **Civil and Hydraulic Engineering**;
- **Energy, Automation and Radio Electronics**.<sup>[1]</sup>

A military training department prepares reserve officers and trains technical officers for the [[Armed Forces of Irad|State Defense Corps]]. The institute also runs evening and continuing-education courses for NurGaz employees. In 2023 it had about 640 teaching staff. Instruction is in English in the petroleum programs, and in Iradi, Russian or English elsewhere, depending on the course.

## Campus
The main building, a neoclassical structure completed in 1956, stands in the central district near Azatlık Prospect. Laboratory blocks built in the 2010s with NurGaz funding house drilling and well-control simulators, a core-analysis laboratory and a pilot refining unit. Students also train at a teaching well site in the NurGaz fields north of the city.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Research and partnerships
Research concentrates on problems of the aging Chu basin fields and the industries around them:
- enhanced oil recovery in mature, heavily water-flooded reservoirs;
- the transport of waxy crude through insulated pipelines such as the [[Northern Export Feeder]] of the [[Iradi Petroleum Transit Consortium]];
- refinery catalysis and the reduction of emissions in Nurzhan's industrial zone;
- earthquake engineering for the seismically active [[wp:Tian Shan]] foothills;
- the clean-up of oil-contaminated soil.<sup>[4]</sup>

The institute published a history of the oil fields, *A History of the Chu Basin Oilfields*, in 2014. It cooperates with [[Talas State University]], and with the [[Iradi National Chamber of Mining and Metallurgy]], which funds scholarships for mining engineers.

## Recognition
Because Irad's international status is unresolved, recognition of the institute's degrees abroad depends on agreements between institutions and on the practice of employers. Russian and Kazakh oil companies generally accept them, and many graduates work in the oil industries of [[wp:Kazakhstan]] and Russia. The institute is not included in the major international university rankings.<sup>[3]</sup>

### 4.82. Old Talas Citadel Quarter
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Cities & Settlements*

The **Old Talas Citadel Quarter** (Iradi: *Köhne Diz*, "old citadel"), also called the Old City, is the historic core of [[Talas]], the *de jure* capital of Irad. It lies on a terrace above the [[Talas River]] and consists of three parts. At its center is a citadel (*[[Diz (Architecture)|diz]]*) built by the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand]] in the 1820s on the mound of an older fortress. Around it are residential quarters on the site of the medieval town, with narrow lanes (*[[Kucheh (Urban Term)|kucheh]]*) and courtyard houses, and on its eastern edge is the covered market of [[Bazar-i Kalan]]. A protected zone of about 64 hectares, with about 11,000 residents, was created under a city ordinance of 1997. The quarter is the setting of the annual [[Diz Film Festival]] and the main center of traditional crafts in the capital.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## History
#### Medieval town
Excavations in the quarter since the 1960s have found occupation layers running from about the 6th to the 13th century. Iradi historiography identifies the site with the medieval [[wp:Silk Road]] town known in Arabic sources as [[wp:Taraz]] and in Chinese sources as Daluosi, near which the [[Battle of Talas]] was fought in 751.<sup>[2]</sup> Under the Samanids and the [[wp:Kara-Khanid Khanate|Kara-Khanids]] the town had a citadel, a walled inner town (*shahristan*) and suburbs.<sup>[3]</sup> Archaeologists have uncovered the foundations of an 11th-century minaret and a Christian cemetery with gravestones inscribed in [[wp:Syriac language|Syriac]] script, evidence of the town's mixed Muslim and Christian population. Coins struck from silver mined at [[Shelji]], in the upper valley, are common finds.<sup>[2]</sup> The town declined after the Mongol conquest of 1220 and the wars of the 14th century, and by the 16th century it had shrunk to a small settlement around the old mound.

#### Kokand fortress
Kokand's ties with the Iradi Christians of the region go back to the accord of 1727, remembered as the [[Treaty of Talas (1727)]], under which Khan Abd al-Rahim Biy granted them religious tolerance, but the khanate's authority reached the Talas valley itself only under Alim and Umar (1798–1822).<sup>[2]</sup> In the 1820s, when the khanate strengthened its northern strongholds, it built a fortress of mud and fired brick on the mound to guard the trade routes of the valley, and a bazaar and residential quarters grew up again on the medieval town site.

#### Russian and Soviet periods
Russian troops occupied the Talas valley in the 1860s, and the citadel became a Russian garrison post. A new town with a grid of streets was laid out to the east, and it later became the core of the Soviet center of Talas.<sup>[4]</sup> During the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|Semirechye Revolt]] of 1916, Iradi horsemen attacked the garrison before being driven into the mountains.

In the Soviet period the citadel was used as a military depot. The quarter's mosque and church were closed in the 1930s, and in 1936 a section of the citadel's outer wall was demolished to build a boulevard. In 1965 the citadel was handed over to a museum of local history, and archaeologists of the Academy of Sciences of the Iradi SSR excavated parts of the medieval town in the 1960s and 1970s.<sup>[2]</sup> Many mudbrick houses were damaged by the [[Suusamyr]] earthquake of August 1992.

#### Since 1992
The mosque and the church reopened in 1992. In 1997, during the US territorial administration, the Talas city council adopted the Historic Districts Ordinance. It created the protected zone, barred the demolition of listed buildings and limited new construction to two stories. As a US territory, Irad was eligible for grants from the US Historic Preservation Fund, which paid for a survey of the quarter and, between 1999 and 2004, for the restoration of the citadel gate and part of the walls.<sup>[1]</sup>

Since 2007 tourism and redevelopment have increased pressure on the quarter. Heritage groups and the *[[Talas Herald]]* have criticized permits for hotels and commercial buildings on the edges of the protected zone, and the replacement of old houses with concrete buildings inside it. The city government says that new projects comply with the ordinance.<sup>[5]</sup> Because Irad is not a State Party to the World Heritage Convention, the quarter cannot be nominated for the [[wp:World Heritage Site|World Heritage List]].

## Layout and landmarks
The quarter follows the plan of many Central Asian towns, with a citadel, an inner town and a bazaar. Its main buildings are:
- **The citadel (*Köhne Diz*)**, on a mound about 14 meters high. Its walls, with corner towers, enclose the former residence of the Kokand governors, now the city museum, and the courtyards used for festival screenings and concerts.
- **The Kalan Darwaza**, the south gate of the citadel, a pointed brick arch flanked by towers, rebuilt in the 1820s and restored in 2002 (see [[Darwaza (Architecture)]]).
- **[[Bazar-i Kalan]]**, the covered central market, rebuilt in the 1950s on the site of the old bazaar, with stalls selling produce, spices, dried fruit, meat, felt rugs and household goods.
- **The Coppersmiths' Row** (*Misgaron*), a vaulted 19th-century trading passage beside the market, where metalworkers make and sell copper vessels, tea sets and silver-mounted horse tack.
- **The Juma Mosque**, a Friday mosque of the 1890s with a columned wooden porch, which serves the city's Muslim community.
- **The Church of St. Yuhanna**, a Syro-Iradi parish church built in 1908, closed in 1937 and reconsecrated in 1992.
- **The excavation site** of the medieval minaret and Christian cemetery, protected under a shelter since 2006.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

The residential quarters consist of single-story courtyard houses (*hovli*) of mudbrick and timber, with high blank walls facing the lanes and carved walnut porches (*ayvan*) around inner courtyards watered by small channels (*aryk*).

## Crafts and economy
The quarter is the main center in Talas for traditional crafts, many of them practiced by the same families for several generations. Saddlers make wooden saddles with chased silver fittings (see [[Eerchilik (Saddlery)]]), and other workshops produce riding whips (*[[Kamcha (Horsewhip)|kamcha]]*), boots and bridles. Craftsmen also make the three-stringed [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]] from apricot and walnut wood, and dealers sell felt rugs (*[[Shyrdak (Iradi Craft)|shyrdak]]*). The saddler [[Tolonbek Sydykov]], whose saddles have been presented as state gifts, works in the quarter.<sup>[5]</sup> Teahouses (*chaikhana*), guesthouses and craft shops serve visitors, and tourism has become the main source of income for many households.

## Population
The quarter's residents are mainly Iradi, with long-established Uzbek-speaking families in the lanes around the bazaar, a legacy of the merchant community of the Kokand period. Iradi linguists link the Uzbek-derived vocabulary of urban Iradi to this kind of mixed bazaar quarter.<sup>[6]</sup> Many younger residents have moved to newer districts, and some houses are now let to students and to migrants from the countryside.

## Culture
The [[Diz Film Festival]] of independent Central Asian cinema is held each year in the citadel courtyards and the squares of the quarter. Folk musicians perform in the citadel and in the teahouses on summer evenings, and the quarter is a starting point for celebrations on Irad Day, 11 March.<sup>[5]</sup>

### 4.83. Sary-Bulak Antimony Works
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Economy & Industry*

The **Sary-Bulak Antimony Works** (SBAW; Iradi: *Sary-Bulak Surma Kombinaty*) is an antimony mining company in the southern foothills of the [[Talas Alatau]], about 28 km south of [[Talas]] in the Sary-Bulak District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It operates an underground stibnite mine and a flotation mill that turns the ore into antimony concentrate. Most of the concentrate is smelted at the nearby [[Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex]], and the rest is exported by rail through [[wp:Kazakhstan]] to China.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

The works were founded in 1961 as a Soviet state enterprise and expanded in the 1970s, when the Iradi SSR became one of the main antimony producers in the [[wp:Soviet Union]]. SBAW was privatized in 1994 and is now the mining arm of the [[Iradi Antimony and Rare Metals Combine]], which holds a controlling stake. With about 2,300 employees, it is the largest employer in Sary-Bulak District. Irad is estimated to hold about 7 percent of world antimony reserves, most of them in the [[Sary-Bulak]] and Chatkal ore field (see [[Antimony Mining in Irad]]).<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

## History

#### Soviet period (1950s–1991)
Geologists of the republican geological survey mapped stibnite-bearing quartz veins in the Sary-Bulak gorge in the early 1950s, during a survey of the mineral resources of the Talas Alatau. Construction of the mine began in 1958. The first shaft, Shaft No. 1 ("Pioneer"), was commissioned in 1961, when the works were formally established under the Soviet Ministry of Non-Ferrous Metallurgy. From 1964 its concentrate went by rail to the new smelter at Chatkal.<sup>[3]</sup>

Under the [[1971 Antimony Expansion Directive]], a second shaft ("Severny") was sunk and the flotation mill was enlarged. By the late 1970s the Sary-Bulak and Chatkal plants together supplied a large share of the Soviet Union's antimony, used in lead-acid batteries, flame retardants and alloys for munitions. Many of the first engineers and miners came from Russia and [[wp:Ukraine]]. Iradis from the villages of the Talas valley made up a growing share of the workforce from the 1970s onward.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Crisis and privatization (1991–2006)
The breakup of the Soviet Union cut the works off from their customers and suppliers. Production stopped for most of 1992. According to the company's own history, power cuts during the [[First Iradi Civil War]] halted the dewatering pumps, and the lower levels of Shaft No. 2 flooded.<sup>[4]</sup>

In 1994 the territorial administration privatized SBAW as a joint-stock company. A controlling stake passed to the holding company that became the Iradi Antimony and Rare Metals Combine, and employees received a minority of the shares, most of which they later sold. The flooded levels were pumped out between 1995 and 1997, and the mine was re-equipped with Western loaders and drilling rigs, financed partly by prepayment contracts with Chinese buyers. The Hydrocarbon and Mining Code of 1995 set the royalty regime. After long disputes, the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] adopted formulas that divided antimony revenue between infrastructure in Talas and rural schools.<sup>[4]</sup><sup>[5]</sup>

Unpaid wages led to a three-week miners' strike in the spring of 1998. It ended when the company agreed to pay part of wages in US dollars, a practice that became general in the following years.<sup>[6]</sup>

#### Since 2007
The fighting of the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] did not reach the works, which came under the control of the DPI emergency administration in the summer of 2007. The [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]] left the mine and the Chatkal smelter in the ISEZ. The ridges and upper gorge above the mine lie close to the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], and the high Talas Alatau beyond them is on the tribal side.<sup>[4]</sup>

World antimony prices rose sharply after China restricted its own exports of the metal in 2024. The company has since said that it will deepen the Central incline and reopen worked-out levels that had been uneconomic at lower prices.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Geology
The deposit lies along a fault zone in [[wp:Paleozoic]] limestone and shale, where stibnite (antimony sulfide, Sb₂S₃) occurs in quartz veins and breccia bodies. Associated minerals include cinnabar, fluorite and arsenic minerals, with traces of gold.<sup>[3]</sup> Soviet records gave grades of 5 to 7 percent antimony in the richest veins. The company now reports an average head grade of about 3 percent, a decline typical of a mine that has worked its best ore first.<sup>[2]</sup> No independent estimate of the deposit's remaining reserves has been published. The figure of about 7 percent of world reserves comes from estimates for Irad as a whole.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Operations
- **Mining.** Ore is reached through Shaft No. 1 ("Pioneer", 1961), Shaft No. 2 ("Severny", 1970s) and the "Central" incline, a truck decline driven in the early 2000s. Working levels reach about 750 m below the surface. The veins are worked by cut-and-fill and sublevel stoping, and ore is hoisted to the surface in skips.<sup>[4]</sup>
- **Processing.** The mill crushes and grinds the ore, and froth flotation separates the stibnite into a concentrate of 55 to 60 percent antimony. The company reports throughput of about 350,000 tonnes of ore a year.<sup>[2]</sup>
- **Shipment.** Most concentrate goes by road and rail to the Chatkal smelter, also in Sary-Bulak District, where it is made into antimony metal and antimony trioxide. The rest is sold as concentrate and shipped by rail through Kazakhstan to buyers in China.<sup>[1]</sup>
- **Finance.** Export sales are paid into escrow accounts at [[Talasbank]] under the supervision of the [[Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority]], which deducts royalties before releasing the proceeds. The company publishes production figures but not full audited accounts.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Workforce and settlement
Most employees live in the workers' settlement beside the mine, known locally as Rudnik ("the mine"), which has about 5,000 inhabitants. Its five-story housing blocks, school, polyclinic and house of culture date mainly from the 1960s and 1970s. The settlement has a Syro-Iradi parish church, opened in 1995, and a Russian Orthodox chapel. Older miners are largely Russian-speaking, while younger workers come mostly from Iradi villages in the Talas valley and commute by company bus.<sup>[6]</sup>

## Safety and environment
Soviet-era tailings are stored in impoundments in the lower gorge. The [[Talas River Hydrological Monitoring Service]] samples antimony and arsenic downstream of the works, and the [[Chatkal Placer Mining Inspectorate]] oversees discharges.<sup>[7]</sup> Clan councils on the tribal side of the line have objected to a proposed new tailings dam in the upper gorge. They argue that it would endanger streams used by herders in summer, and the company has not built it.<sup>[4]</sup>

In February 2012 a rockfall on a lower level of Shaft No. 2 killed four miners. An inspectorate report blamed inadequate ground support, and the company replaced its shift management in the shaft.<sup>[8]</sup>

### 4.84. St. Luka Community Health Mission
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Health & Education*

The **St. Luka Community Health Mission** (Iradi: *Iyık Luka El Darigerlik Missiyasy*) is a Catholic medical charity of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], founded in 1994 and based in [[Talas]]. It runs St. Luka Hospital, a 120-bed general hospital in Talas, the free [[St. Luka Clinic]] in the south of the city, and mobile clinics that travel to herding settlements in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR). It is one of the few organizations that works regularly on both sides of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], and in many highland valleys its mobile teams are the main source of primary care.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## History
The mission was set up in 1994 by the Eparchy of Talas, during the collapse of the Soviet-era health system that followed the [[First Iradi Civil War]]. The siege of 1992 had damaged hospitals in Talas, medicines were scarce, and many Russian-speaking doctors had left for Russia.<sup>[2]</sup> Its first funds came from Catholic relief agencies abroad and from American church donors. According to the mission, it was also among the Christian charities in Irad that received proceeds from the 1993 compilation album [[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|*Swift Hooves*]].<sup>[3]</sup>

St. Luka Hospital opened in 1994 in a former trade-union polyclinic. Its first staff were sisters of the [[Order of St. Janyl the Hermit]], whose communities already ran rural dispensaries, together with volunteer physicians and nurses from Talas and abroad.<sup>[3]</sup> The first mobile team began visiting summer pastures in the [[Talas Alatau]] in 1996, and a maternity ward opened in 2001.

During the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in 2007, while the [[Popular Front of Irad]] was besieging Talas from April to June, the hospital treated wounded civilians and fighters from all sides.<sup>[4]</sup> After the ceasefire, the mission's mobile teams were among the first civilian services to be allowed across the new demarcation line. Since 2008 the mission has belonged to the humanitarian coordination forum chaired by the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI).<sup>[5]</sup>

## Services
- **St. Luka Hospital**, Talas: general medicine, surgery, obstetrics and pediatrics, with an outpatient department. Patients who can afford it pay modest fees, and the poor are treated free of charge.
- **[[St. Luka Clinic]]**: a free outpatient and dental clinic in southern Talas for low-income residents.
- **Mountain mobile clinics**: teams in four-wheel-drive vehicles and, on the higher pastures, with pack horses. They carry portable ultrasound scanners, solar-powered vaccine refrigerators and basic surgical kits, and visit herding families in their summer yurts (*boz üy*) in the Talas Alatau, on the [[Aksay Plateau]] and in the Chatkal valleys.
- **Public health programs**: childhood immunization, antenatal care, tuberculosis screening and child nutrition.

The mission reported about 46,000 outpatient consultations in 2023, about two-fifths of them in the ATR.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Work in the tribal regions
To cross the Qara-Chik line, the mobile teams need tribal travel permits from the clan councils as well as clearance at ISEZ checkpoints. Seasonal corridors for the teams, for vaccines and for medical supplies are negotiated each spring through the UNMI coordination forum.<sup>[5]</sup> The mission treats patients of all faiths, including Kyrgyz and Kazakh Muslim herders, and in the tribal regions it works through local health posts and village elders. According to its annual reports, maternal and infant health indicators in the highland valleys remain well below those of the ISEZ, and many settlements have no year-round road access.<sup>[1]</sup>

Both administrations allow the mission to work but have at times restricted it. Tribal elders have objected to ISEZ checkpoint delays affecting its convoys, while ISEZ officials have questioned whether supplies taken across the line reach their intended recipients. The mission says it does not take sides and reports only on health needs.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Organization and funding
The mission is governed by a board appointed by the Bishop of Talas and employs about 380 staff, most of them Iradi doctors, nurses and drivers. It is funded by church collections, Catholic and [[wp:Protestantism|Protestant]] agencies abroad, donations from [[Iradi Americans]] and hospital fees. It has no regular funding from the ISEZ government, although ISEZ health authorities count its mobile teams in their coverage figures for the rural districts.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

The hospital refers complex surgical and obstetric cases to the [[Talas Regional Hospital Medical Complex]], with which it also runs a joint tuberculosis screening program.

### 4.85. Sukarne Irad Complex
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Economy & Industry*

The **Sukarne Irad Complex** is a cattle feedlot, beef-processing plant and cold store in the western industrial corridor of [[Talas]], operated by the Mexican meat company [[wp:Sukarne|SuKarne]]. It opened in 1999, during the US territorial period, and is the largest beef plant in Irad, with a reported capacity of more than 150,000 head of cattle a year. At its opening the company described it as the largest modern feedlot and packing complex in [[wp:Eurasia]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup> The plant's arrival brought Mexican managers, technicians and workers to Talas, and the Mexican community of more than 10,000 people in and around the city grew from it.<sup>[3]</sup>

## History
Irad's status as a US territory from 1992 gave its exports duty-free access to the US market, and after the [[wp:North American Free Trade Agreement]] took effect in 1994, Mexican as well as American agribusiness capital began to look at the territory. Irad was not a party to NAFTA, but Iradi commentators often call the investment of this period "NAFTA-era".<sup>[1]</sup> The [[1998 Talas Agribusiness Accord]] and the creation of the [[Talas Agribusiness Export Zone]] that year provided land, rail access and customs arrangements for foreign meatpackers. SuKarne built the complex in 1998–99 west of the city, on the land of a former Soviet state fattening complex founded during the [[Virgin Lands Campaign in Irad|Virgin Lands campaign]], whose maize and alfalfa base and herdsmen were among the reasons for the choice of site, and slaughtering began in 1999. [[wp:Conagra Brands|Conagra]] opened its own plant nearby (see [[Conagra Talas Beef Facility]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

Operations were interrupted during the fighting around Talas in 2007, when road links to the city were cut, and resumed later that year after the ceasefire.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Facilities
The complex covers about 90 hectares. Its main parts are:
- the feedlot (see [[Sukarne Feedlot Complex]]), with a standing capacity of about 50,000 head, where cattle are finished on rations of corn silage, barley and protein meal, part of which is supplied by [[Nurzhan Agro-Industrial]];
- the processing plant, with slaughter, chilling and boning halls that produce chilled and frozen boxed beef, and a separate halal-certified line for exports to Muslim-majority markets;
- an ammonia-refrigerated cold store with space for about 8,000 tonnes of boxed beef;
- an accredited testing laboratory (see [[Sukarne Quality Control Labs]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

The complex handles only cattle. A 1996 act of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] banned the commercial slaughter of horses and the sale of horsemeat, in line with the strong Iradi aversion to eating horses (see [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo]]).<sup>[5]</sup>

## Cattle supply and markets
Feeder cattle come from farms in the Talas and Chu valleys and from pastoralists in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], who bring animals across the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] at designated crossing corridors, often through the [[Talas Central Cattle Mart]]. Payments are cleared through [[Talasbank]].<sup>[1]</sup> Commentators have noted the irony of a large beef industry in a country where folk belief associates bulls and black cattle with ill omen, through the tradition of the bull-headed demon [[Morkhan (Mythology)|Morkhan]].<sup>[6]</sup>

The plant sells boxed beef in Irad and exports it to [[wp:Kazakhstan]], Russia and the Middle East. Export proceeds are paid into escrow accounts audited by the [[Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority]].<sup>[2]</sup>

## Workforce and the Mexican community
The complex employs about 1,800 people, most of them Iradis.<sup>[2]</sup> The first Mexican employees were managers, veterinarians and maintenance engineers. They were followed by their families and by Mexican workers recruited for the plant and for other agribusinesses in the export zone. The community (see [[Mexicans in Irad]]) is centered in [[Semiz]], a district of the city's western corridor that grew from the Soviet settlement of Otkormochny beside the old fattening complex; residents call it *la Colonia* and other Iradis often *Meksikanka*, where there are Mexican shops and restaurants, a Spanish-language Mass on Sundays and a Day of the Dead observance each November. Many families have now lived in Talas for two generations, and marriages between Mexicans and Iradis are common.<sup>[3]</sup>

### 4.86. Syro-Iradi Episcopal Synod
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Religion*

The **Syro-Iradi Episcopal Synod** (Iradi: *Iradi Yepiskoptyn Sinodu*; Latin: *Synodus Episcoporum Ecclesiae Catholicae Syro-Iradiensis*) is the assembly of the bishops of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]]. It is presided over by the Archbishop of [[Iyık Janyl]], currently [[Mar Ephrem]], and meets twice a year in the chapter house beside the [[Church of St. Janyl]]. The synod proposes candidates for bishop to the Pope, approves liturgical texts, oversees the training of clergy and issues joint pastoral letters, which are among the church's main statements on public affairs in Irad.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Canonical status
The Syro-Iradi Church is an Eastern Catholic church *sui iuris* in communion with Rome and is governed by the Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches. In the code's terms it is a metropolitan church, whose bishops form a council of hierarchs rather than the synod of a patriarchal church. The Iradi body has kept its traditional name of synod. Like other councils of hierarchs, it can make laws for the church, which must be communicated to the [[wp:Holy See]] before they take effect. It does not elect bishops itself but proposes lists of at least three candidates (*terna*), from which the Pope appoints.<sup>[1]</sup>

## History
Church historians trace the synod's tradition to the medieval assemblies of the East Syriac clergy of the region, such as the [[Nestorian Synod of Navekat (1180)]]. Its modern form dates from the union with Rome in 1931 under the bull *Orientalis Stella*, negotiated by Bishop [[Mar Timotheos Alimbekov]].<sup>[2]</sup> Soviet authorities closed the churches of Iyık Janyl, and senior clergy were arrested and executed in [[The 1937 NKVD Clerical Purges|the purges of 1937]]. For the rest of the Soviet period the bishops could not meet openly, and according to church accounts the surviving clergy consulted in secret.<sup>[2]</sup>

The synod met openly in 1993, after the territorial administration guaranteed freedom of religion and the protection of church property under the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]]. In its first decade it approved vernacular liturgical texts in Latin-script Iradi, following Father [[Luka Ayyubov]]'s 1994 translation of the [[wp:New Testament]]. It also pressed the territorial government for the return of church buildings confiscated in the Soviet period, and supported the US nomination of the Church of St. Janyl, inscribed as a [[wp:World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]] in 2004.<sup>[2]</sup>

In April 2007, during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], the synod issued a pastoral letter calling for a ceasefire and for the return of communal pastures that had been privatized. Since then the church has taken part in civic mediation between the communities.<sup>[3]</sup> Mar Ephrem became archbishop in 2012.

## Membership and procedure
The voting members are the archbishop of the Archeparchy of Iyık Janyl and the bishops of the suffragan eparchies of [[Talas]], [[Nurzhan]] and the highland parishes of the Chatkal basin, together with any auxiliary bishops. The rector of the [[Cathedral Seminary of Iyık Janyl|St. Ephrem Major Seminary]] and the superior of the [[Order of St. Janyl the Hermit]] attend as advisers without a vote.<sup>[1]</sup> The spring session is held after Easter, and the autumn session in September, after the pilgrimage season of the [[Feast of St. Janyl]] on 24 August. Each session ends with a published communiqué.

The Chatkal eparchy includes parishes on both sides of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], so the synod is one of the few bodies whose members work regularly in both the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] and the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]].

## Functions
- **Appointment of bishops.** The synod draws up the *terna* for vacant sees and sends it to the Dicastery for the [[wp:Dicastery for the Eastern Churches|Eastern Churches in Rome]].
- **Liturgy.** It regulates the celebration of the [[wp:Liturgy of Addai and Mari|East Syriac Liturgy of Addai and Mari]] in Iradi and [[wp:Syriac language|Classical Syriac]] (see [[East Syriac Rites of Iyık Janyl]]), and approves translations and liturgical books.
- **Clergy training.** It sets the curriculum of the St. Ephrem Major Seminary in Iyık Janyl.
- **Pastoral letters.** Its joint letters have addressed communal pasture rights, the environmental effects of mining, emigration, and marriage and family life, including the 2014 letter *On the Free Consent of Spouses*, which condemned bride kidnapping (see [[Marriage in Irad]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

## Relations with the state
Relations with the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] administration have been strained at times over school curricula and the taxation of church property. In these disputes the synod has cited the guarantees of religious freedom dating from the territorial period.<sup>[3]</sup> In October 2023 it appealed for restraint by both the police and protesters during the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas|student protests in Talas]].<sup>[4]</sup> Its autumn communiqué of 2024, issued after Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]] withdrew from public view, called for "constitutional order and truthful public information". DPI officials did not comment publicly.<sup>[5]</sup>

A 2021 survey by the Department of Sociology at [[Talas State University]] found the church to be the most trusted public institution among respondents in the ISEZ.<sup>[6]</sup>

### 4.87. Talas Agribusiness Export Zone
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Economy & Industry*

The **Talas Agribusiness Export Zone** (TAEZ; Iradi: *Talas Agro-Öndürüsh Eksport Zonasy*) is a bonded industrial park for food processing and export on the western edge of [[Talas]], covering about 350 hectares. It was established in 1998, during the US territorial period, under the [[1998 Talas Agribusiness Accord]], to attract foreign meatpackers and grain traders to the [[Talas River]] valley. Its tenants include the [[Sukarne Irad Complex]] and the [[Conagra Talas Beef Facility]], cold stores, grain elevators and a refrigerated rail terminal.<sup>[1]</sup> It should not be confused with the [[Talas Free Economic Trade Zone]], a separate bonded park for light manufacturing.

## History
Duty-free access to the US market, which Irad enjoyed as a territory, drew foreign agribusiness interest in the mid-1990s. The 1998 accord and an act of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] set up the zone on former collective-farm land between the city and the airfield that became [[Talas Air Base]]. Its roads, rail sidings and power lines were paid for with territorial bonds.<sup>[2]</sup> About 220 hectares of the land came from two former collective farms. Some of their members later said that the compensation, paid partly in som, was too low.<sup>[3]</sup> [[wp:Sukarne|SuKarne]] began slaughtering in 1999, and Conagra's plant followed.

In 2007 the emergency decrees that created the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) confirmed the zone's customs and tax regime. Analysts read this as one of several early signals to foreign investors that their contracts would be honored.<sup>[1]</sup> The refrigerated rail terminal was enlarged in 2014.

## Facilities
- **Rail terminal**: sidings connected to the northern line into [[wp:Kazakhstan]], with gantry cranes, power points for refrigerated containers and bulk grain loading.
- **Meatpacking cluster**: the Sukarne feedlot and processing complex, the [[wp:Conagra Brands|Conagra]] beef plant and the [[Talas Cold Chain Logistics Hub]].
- **Grain storage**: elevators and warehouses for wheat, barley and feed grain.
- **Laboratories**: veterinary and food-safety laboratories, including the [[Sukarne Quality Control Labs]], which certify exports for foreign markets.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Administration and customs
The zone is run by an administration under the ISEZ Ministry of Economy. Livestock, feed and packaging brought into the zone pay no import duty, and processed exports are cleared through customs inside the zone. Most cargo leaves by rail through Kazakhstan under bonded transit. Export proceeds are paid into escrow accounts at [[Talasbank]] and audited by the [[Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority]].<sup>[2]</sup>

## Economic role
According to the Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Irad, the zone provides about 6,000 direct jobs and exported processed food worth about $310 million in 2023, most of it beef.<sup>[1]</sup> Packaging plants, pallet makers and truck workshops, including depots of [[Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics]], have grown up around its perimeter. Farmers' associations in the Talas valley have complained that tenants' duty-free imports of feed grain undercut local growers. The zone administration replies that local suppliers provide most of the feedlots' forage.<sup>[3]</sup>

### 4.88. Talas Basin Agricultural Directorate
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Agriculture*

The **Talas Basin Agricultural Directorate** (Iradi: *Talas Öröönü Ayyl Charba Bashkarmasy*) is the agency of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) responsible for farming and irrigation in the valley of the [[Talas River]]. It answers to the ISEZ Ministry of Economy and covers Talas District, Kara-Buura District and the farmland within the city of [[Talas]]. Its main tasks are maintaining irrigation canals and scheduling water deliveries, running agricultural extension services, distributing subsidized seed and fertilizer, and collecting crop statistics. Its headquarters are in Talas, and it has extension offices in the district centers.<sup>[1]</sup>

## History
In the Soviet period, farming in the Talas valley was organized in collective and state farms under the regional agricultural administration. Irrigation was expanded after the [[wp:World War II|Second World War]], when the river's flow was divided equally between the Iradi SSR and the [[wp:Kazakh Soviet Socialist Republic|Kazakh SSR]] downstream, a rule both sides still cite.<sup>[2]</sup> After 1992 the collective farms were broken up, and under the territorial land reform of 1994 their land passed to household and family farms and to private companies. The directorate was established in 1995 to take over the irrigation and extension functions of the Soviet administration. In the late 1990s, advisers from American agricultural universities helped it set up an extension service and water users' associations, which collect irrigation fees and maintain the smaller canals.<sup>[1]</sup> Since 2007 it has operated under the ISEZ administration.

## Irrigation
According to the directorate, about 110,000 hectares of the valley are irrigated, through main canals that take water from the Talas and its tributaries and through a dense network of smaller ditches (*aryk*).<sup>[1]</sup> The directorate maintains the main canals and headworks and agrees seasonal delivery schedules with the water users' associations. It works with the [[Talas River Hydrological Monitoring Service]], whose gauges supply the flow data, and with the [[Talas Municipal Water Authority]], which draws part of the city's supply from the same basin. Several of the rivers that feed the valley rise on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. The directorate therefore depends on informal arrangements with clan councils over headwater use, which are usually settled by the councils and the district authorities directly.<sup>[2]</sup>

The lower valley in Kara-Buura District suffers from waterlogging and soil salinization caused by losses from unlined canals and poor drainage. Since the 2010s the directorate has subsidized laser leveling of fields and drip irrigation for orchards. In dry summers it imposes rotation schedules under which canals are opened to each area in turn.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Crops and extension
The main crops are wheat, barley, sugar beet, potatoes and common beans. Beans have become the valley's best-known export crop and are sold mainly to [[wp:Turkey]].<sup>[3]</sup> Alfalfa and fodder maize are grown for the feedlots of the [[Talas Agribusiness Export Zone]], and apple and apricot orchards line the foothills. Extension officers run soil-testing clinics and demonstration plots, advise on integrated pest management, and help farm cooperatives meet the sanitary standards required by meatpackers. The directorate also manages reserves of certified seed and fertilizer, which it sells to farmers at subsidized prices.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Criticism
Farmers' associations have criticized the directorate for slow canal repairs and for favoring large commercial farms when water is scarce, and the water users' associations vary widely in how well they are run.<sup>[3]</sup> Analysts also point out that its budget depends on ISEZ allocations that are not published in detail.

### 4.89. Talas Municipal Water Authority
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Infrastructure & Transport*

The **Talas Municipal Water Authority** (Iradi: *Talas Shaarlyk Suu Bashkarmasy*) is the public utility that supplies drinking water and runs the sewerage system of [[Talas]]. It serves the city's population of about 1.1 million and parts of the surrounding suburbs, and answers to the city administration, headed by a mayor appointed by the Governor, and to the elected city council. Most of its water is pumped from wellfields in the alluvial fan south of the city. The rest is drawn from the [[Talas River]] and treated at the [[Talas Municipal Water Treatment Works]].<sup>[1]</sup>

## History
Talas received its first piped water supply in the 1930s, from springs and shallow wells in the foothills. The southern wellfields were developed in the 1960s and 1970s as the city grew, and the central sewage treatment plant was built in 1974.<sup>[2]</sup> During the siege of Talas from April 1992, in the [[First Iradi Civil War]], shelling and power cuts stopped the pumping stations and damaged the main from the southern wellfields. By late May much of the city had no piped water, and residents drew water from irrigation canals (*aryk*) and hand pumps. Supply was restored during the summer of 1992 by city crews working with US military engineers.<sup>[3]</sup>

The authority was set up as a municipal utility in 1995, during the territorial period, taking over from the Soviet-era municipal waterworks. US federal grants and territorial bonds paid for new pumps and meters for commercial users, and the sewage plant was upgraded with biological treatment in the early 2000s.<sup>[1]</sup> Since 2007 it has operated under the ISEZ municipal administration. In 2016 it installed a supervisory control and data acquisition ([[wp:SCADA]]) system, supplied with [[Attelkom]], to monitor pressure and detect leaks.

## Water supply
The groundwater comes from aquifers recharged by snowmelt and glacier-fed streams descending from the [[Talas Alatau]]. The authority operates four wellfields in the alluvial fan, with 64 submersible pumps drawing from depths of 80 to 220 meters. The groundwater is of good quality and needs only chlorination. River water is treated by flocculation, sand filtration and ultraviolet disinfection at the treatment works.<sup>[1]</sup> Two storage reservoirs on the ridge above the old city feed the network by gravity. The network has about 540 km of mains, much of it Soviet-era steel and cast-iron pipe. The authority estimates that about 40 percent of the water it produces is lost to leaks or not billed.<sup>[4]</sup>

The [[Talas River Hydrological Monitoring Service]] passes river-flow readings to the authority in real time. The authority and the [[Talas Basin Agricultural Directorate]] share the basin's water and coordinate withdrawals in dry summers.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Sewerage
The Talas Central Sewage Treatment Plant, on the western edge of the city, treats about 140,000 cubic meters of wastewater a day and discharges the treated effluent into the Talas River. The hydrological service monitors sewage indicators downstream of the city.<sup>[2]</sup> Older suburbs and the new housing on the city's edges are not fully connected to the sewers and rely on septic tanks and pit latrines.

## Tariffs and finance
Household tariffs are set in [[Iradi som]] by the city council, while commercial and industrial customers are billed in US dollars. Tariffs cover operating costs but not major repairs, which depend on allocations from the ISEZ budget. Proposed increases have been controversial, and the council postponed one in 2019 after public complaints.<sup>[4]</sup>

### 4.90. Talas Regional Hospital Medical Complex
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Health & Education*

The **Talas Regional Hospital Medical Complex** (Iradi: *Talas Ayymdyk Oorukanasy*) is the main referral and teaching hospital of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), on a 15-hectare campus on Hospital Boulevard in [[Talas]]. It opened in 1954 as the regional hospital of the Soviet period and was largely rebuilt during the US territorial administration. With about 650 beds, it provides specialist surgery, cardiology, maternity and pediatric care, trauma care and diagnostic imaging, and is the main clinical training site of the Faculty of Medicine of [[Talas State University]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## History
The hospital opened in 1954 as the regional clinical hospital for the Talas valley, in a group of three-story pavilions north of the old city. Maternity and cardiology wings were added in the 1970s.<sup>[2]</sup> It treated many of the wounded from the [[1956 Talas Riots]], and its records are among the sources historians have used to estimate the casualties.

During the siege of Talas from April 1992, the hospital kept working under artillery fire. Its staff treated civilian and military casualties with dwindling supplies of anesthetics, blood and fuel for the generators, and the surgical pavilion was hit several times.<sup>[3]</sup> In the years after the war many Russian-speaking doctors left Irad, and the hospital struggled to keep its specialist departments open.

Between 1995 and 2002 the hospital was rebuilt and re-equipped with US federal grants and loans from the territorial government. A new emergency and trauma center opened in 2002. Residency programs modeled on American graduate medical training were introduced, and exchange agreements were signed with medical schools in the United States and [[wp:Turkey]].<sup>[2]</sup> In 2007, during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], it again took in casualties while the [[Popular Front of Irad]] besieged the city. A cardiovascular wing with cardiac catheterization laboratories opened in 2016.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Departments and facilities
The campus has five main clinical buildings:
- an emergency and trauma center with a rooftop helipad, used for medical evacuations from the mountains, including flights arranged through the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] for patients from the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]];
- a cardiovascular institute, which performs bypass surgery, angioplasty and pacemaker implantation;
- a maternal and child health pavilion with obstetric theaters and a neonatal intensive care unit;
- a surgical building with general, orthopedic and neurosurgical departments;
- a diagnostic center with CT and MRI scanners and the hospital's pathology laboratory.<sup>[1]</sup>

The [[Talas Blood Services Center]] supplies the hospital's blood bank. [[Talas Municipal Hospital No. 1]] is the city's main general emergency hospital, while the regional hospital takes the more complex cases from across the ISEZ.

## Teaching
The hospital is the main teaching hospital of the Talas State University Faculty of Medicine. About 400 medical students, residents and nursing students train there each year. Clinical records and much of the residency teaching are in English, while consultations with older patients are often in Russian or Iradi.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Access and finance
The hospital is funded mainly from the ISEZ budget. Emergency treatment is free, but planned operations and many medicines require co-payments, which patients' groups say deter rural families. Staff shortages are a continuing problem, as many nurses and young doctors emigrate, mostly to the United States.<sup>[4]</sup> The hospital receives referrals from the [[St. Luka Community Health Mission]], whose mobile clinics transfer complicated obstetric and surgical cases from the tribal regions, and the two run a joint tuberculosis screening program.<sup>[1]</sup>

### 4.91. Talasbank
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Economy & Industry*

**Talasbank** (officially the Bank of Talas; Iradi: *Talas Banky*) is the largest commercial bank in Irad, with its headquarters in the Silk Road Financial Tower in central [[Talas]]. It was chartered in 1993 by the Banking and Commercial Currency Act of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]], which made the US dollar legal tender in the territory alongside the new [[Iradi som]]. The bank keeps accounts in both currencies. It holds the escrow accounts into which the proceeds of Irad's main exports are paid under the supervision of the [[Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority]], handles most government payrolls and holds the largest share of commercial deposits in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ).<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

Because Irad's sovereignty is unrecognized, Talasbank has no direct access to most international payment systems. It settles foreign payments through correspondent banks in [[wp:Almaty]] and [[wp:Istanbul]]. Its ownership has not been fully disclosed since its partial privatization, and its accounts are published only in summary.<sup>[2]</sup>

## History

#### Background
In the Soviet period, banking in the Iradi SSR was carried out by the republican offices of the Soviet state bank and the specialized state banks for savings, agriculture and housing. After the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] declared independence in October 1991, the breakdown of the ruble zone and inflation above 1,000 percent wiped out most savings. Banking had largely stopped in Talas by the time of the siege in 1992.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Foundation and the territorial period (1993–2006)
After the [[First Iradi Civil War]], the territorial administration chose to use the US dollar rather than introduce a currency of its own at once. The Banking and Commercial Currency Act of 1993 made the dollar legal tender, authorized the som for small payments and wages, and chartered Talasbank as the territory's main commercial bank.<sup>[1]</sup> The bank was formed from the Talas offices of the former Soviet savings and agricultural banks, with capital provided by the territorial government. It opened for business in September 1993. In the first months, dollar banknotes were flown in to [[Talas Air Base]].<sup>[3]</sup>

In 1994 the territorial government created the Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority to audit export contracts. Exporters, including the oil company [[NurGaz]], the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]] and later the [[Sukarne Irad Complex]], were required to have foreign buyers pay into escrow accounts at Talasbank. The authority deducted royalties and taxes before releasing the balance.<sup>[4]</sup> During the agribusiness boom of the late 1990s and the expansion of the air base after the [[2001 Basing Rights Agreement]], the bank's business grew with foreign investment, base contracts and payrolls. As a bank in a US territory, it settled dollar payments through correspondent accounts with banks in the United States.<sup>[3]</sup>

The territorial government sold a majority of its shares in auctions in 1999 and 2001 and kept a minority stake. The buyers were Iradi holding companies whose own shareholders were not published.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### Crisis of 2006–2007
After the United States withdrew from the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] on 3 December 2006, depositors rushed to withdraw dollars. The bank limited cash withdrawals for three weeks in December.<sup>[5]</sup> American correspondent banks closed or restricted its accounts in early 2007, citing the territory's uncertain legal status. The bank moved its correspondent business to banks in Almaty and Istanbul, a pattern similar to that of banks in other territories whose status is not recognized.<sup>[3]</sup>

After [[Erlan Toktarov]] proclaimed the ISEZ from [[Nurzhan]] on 25 February 2007, both the cabinet of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] in Talas and the emergency administration in Nurzhan claimed authority over the escrow accounts. The bank's management froze withdrawals from government accounts until the dispute was settled. Supporters later credited the decision with protecting public funds, while DRI ministers said it cut off their government's revenue.<sup>[6]</sup> The head office closed for several days after the [[Storming of Talas (2007)|storming of Talas]] on 4 June 2007. It reopened under the ISEZ administration after DPI forces took the city that summer.

#### Since 2007
Since the ceasefire Talasbank has been the main bank of the ISEZ government. It holds treasury and payroll accounts, takes part in the escrow arrangements for oil, antimony and beef exports, and finances imports from China, [[wp:Turkey]] and [[wp:Kazakhstan]] with letters of credit.<sup>[2]</sup> Payments made under the revenue-sharing arrangements of the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]] are not reported separately. Herders from the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] who sell livestock and wool to ISEZ buyers are usually paid through the bank.<sup>[4]</sup>

With [[Attelkom]], the bank introduced debit cards and a national card-payment network in the 2000s. In 2012 the two companies launched an SMS-based payment service, used by herders and farmers to pay for feed and veterinary services and to receive transfers without traveling to a branch.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Operations
- **Dual-currency banking.** Deposits and loans are offered in US dollars and in som. Most savings, loans and commercial contracts are in dollars. Som accounts are used mainly for public-sector wages, utility bills and retail payments.
- **Escrow and trade finance.** The bank holds the export escrow accounts audited by the Foreign Trade Escrow Authority and provides letters of credit and guarantees for importers.
- **Government business.** It handles treasury accounts, payrolls and many payments of the ISEZ government and of the municipal administrations of Talas, Nurzhan and [[Iyık Janyl]].
- **Retail network.** It has 28 branches in Talas, Nurzhan, Iyık Janyl and the district towns, as well as offices at the main border crossings and mobile banking vans that serve villages in the [[Chu River Basin]].<sup>[2]</sup>

Interbank transfers within the ISEZ are processed through the [[Bank of Irad Clearing House]]. According to the Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Irad, Talasbank holds about 60 percent of commercial deposits in the ISEZ.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Ownership and criticism
The ISEZ government still holds a minority stake, but the ultimate owners of the holding companies that control the bank have not been disclosed. Investigative reports have linked several of these companies to business associates of the ruling Toktarov family. The bank has said that its shareholders meet the disclosure rules in force in the ISEZ.<sup>[7]</sup> Opposition commentators accuse it of lending on favorable terms to companies linked to the [[Democratic Party of Irad]]. The [[wp:World Bank]] has noted that it has not published full audited accounts since 2008.<sup>[3]</sup>

Business groups, by contrast, credit the bank with keeping the dollar payment system working through the crises of 2006–07 and the uncertainty that followed Toktarov's withdrawal from public view in 2024.<sup>[2]</sup>

### 4.92. Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Economy & Industry*

**Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics** (Iradi: *Trans-Chüy Jük Tashuu Kompaniyasy*) is a road haulage company based in [[Nurzhan]]. It runs bonded trucking services within the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) and to the northern border crossings into [[wp:Kazakhstan]], from which much of its freight continues to Russia. It was founded in 1996, during the US territorial period, and is the largest trucking company in Irad, with more than 250 tractor units and refrigerated and bulk trailers. Since 2008 it has been controlled by [[Timur Toktarov]], the third son of Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## History
The company was formed in 1996 from a privatized Soviet motor-transport depot in Nurzhan. Its early business came from oilfield supply and from contracts linked to the expansion of [[Talas Air Base]].<sup>[1]</sup> From 1999 it carried livestock and beef for the new meatpacking plants near [[Talas]]. In 2008 Timur Toktarov took control of the company. Under his management it bought refrigerated trailers, opened a depot at the [[Talas Agribusiness Export Zone]] and won long-term contracts with the state-linked industrial combines.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Operations
The company's main terminal, outside Nurzhan, has bonded customs warehouses, a container yard and workshops for the fleet. Its main lines of business are:
- **refrigerated transport**: chilled and frozen beef from the [[Sukarne Irad Complex]] and other packers to customers in Irad and to Kazakhstan;
- **bulk agricultural haulage**: grain, barley and compound feed, much of it for [[Nurzhan Agro-Industrial]];
- **industrial freight**: drummed antimony trioxide and metal from the [[Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex]] to railheads, and equipment for the oil fields.<sup>[1]</sup>

Its main routes link Talas and Nurzhan, run south over the [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]] to the Lower Naryn District, and lead north to the Kazakh border. Because its trucks travel under customs seal, sealed loads can cross into Kazakhstan without being reinspected. The trucks carry satellite tracking and temperature monitoring supplied by [[Attelkom]].<sup>[1]</sup>

## Ownership and criticism
Trans-Chuy is one of several businesses run by members of the Toktarov family. [[wp:Timur]] and his younger brothers [[Adil Toktarov|Adil]] and [[Bekzat Toktarov|Bekzat]] manage the family's interests in freight, real estate and feed milling.<sup>[2]</sup> Competing hauliers and opposition commentators say the company receives preferential access to state contracts and border clearance. The company says its contracts are awarded on price and reliability.<sup>[3]</sup>

### 4.93. Trans-Irad Pipeline Proposals
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Infrastructure & Transport*

The **Trans-Irad Pipeline Proposals** are a series of plans, made since the 1990s, for international pipelines across [[Irad]]. The best known is the Trans-Irad Gas Pipeline proposed by the [[wp:China National Petroleum Corporation]] (CNPC), which would carry natural gas from [[wp:Turkmenistan]] through [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and southern Irad to western China. Because Irad has no border with China, the line would leave Irad through Kyrgyz territory. During the US territorial period, a US-backed oil pipeline south to [[wp:Pakistan]] through Kyrgyz, Tajik and Afghan territory was also studied, but it lost its prospects after 2021. None of the proposals has been built.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup> Irad's only export pipeline remains the 85-km [[Northern Export Feeder]], which carries crude oil north into the Kazakh pipeline network near [[wp:Shymkent]].

## Background
Irad is doubly landlocked, and all its hydrocarbon exports depend on transit through neighboring states. Until 2000 crude oil left by rail for Shymkent, and since then it has been piped through the Northern Export Feeder into the network operated by [[wp:KazTransOil]], for refining in [[wp:Kazakhstan]] or onward shipment to Russia.<sup>[3]</sup> Irad's proven natural gas reserves exceed 400 billion cubic meters but are largely undeveloped. The largest prospect, the [[Muyunkum Natural Gas Field]], lies in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR).<sup>[1]</sup> Successive governments have looked for a second export route to reduce their dependence on Kazakhstan.

## Southern oil pipeline proposal
During the territorial period, a US-backed proposal envisaged a pipeline carrying Iradi crude south to Pakistan. Because Irad does not border [[wp:Tajikistan]] or [[wp:Afghanistan]], the route would have crossed Kyrgyz, Tajik and Afghan territory. Instability in Afghanistan kept the project at the planning stage. After the [[wp:Taliban]] returned to power in 2021 it lost its remaining prospects. [[wp:Chevron Corporation|Chevron]], which had invested heavily in modernizing Irad's oil fields since the territorial period, then scaled back its operations in Irad.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Trans-Irad Gas Pipeline
CNPC's proposal, first discussed publicly in the early 2010s, would link gas fields in Turkmenistan with consumers in western China. In Irad the main partner would be [[NurGaz]]. Feasibility studies have examined two routes through the territory:
- a **northern route**, about 640 km long within Irad, entering from Uzbekistan in the west, running along the southern side of the [[Talas River]] valley, crossing the mountains by the [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]] corridor and the [[Fergana Gateway]], and leaving Irad eastward into [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]];
- a **southern route**, entering from the Uzbek part of the [[wp:Fergana Valley]] and running east along the Fergana Rim and through the Lower Naryn District before crossing into Kyrgyzstan.

The studies assume a pipe 1,220 mm in diameter carrying up to 30 billion cubic meters of gas a year, with four compressor stations in Irad. The ISEZ has asked for an off-take to supply gas-fired power and heating in [[Talas]] and [[Nurzhan]], where coal is still widely burned.<sup>[2]</sup> In 2022 Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] received a CNPC delegation in Talas. The Department of Public Information said the talks covered the pipeline and other infrastructure investment.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Obstacles
- **Status.** A pipeline would need transit agreements with Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan and a counterparty in Irad able to sign binding contracts. Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan all claim Irad *de jure*, and none recognizes the ISEZ as a sovereign party. Lenders are reluctant to finance infrastructure in a territory without recognized sovereignty.<sup>[2]</sup>
- **Tribal consent.** Both routes cross land held by the clans of the ATR: the northern route passes the tribal flanks of the Fergana Gateway and the Toktogul–Naryn zone, and the southern route crosses the Fergana Rim zone. Clan elders led by [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]] have withheld consent for construction across alpine pastures and water catchments under customary law. The [[Iradi Freedom Society]] has said that any route across tribal land would require the agreement of the clan assemblies concerned and a share of transit revenue.<sup>[5]</sup>
- **Competition.** Existing gas pipelines from [[wp:Central Asia]] to China run through Kazakhstan. Analysts note that a new route through Irad would have to compete with expanding their capacity.<sup>[2]</sup>

Engineering consultations between the ISEZ authorities and CNPC continue intermittently, but no investment decision has been made.

### 4.94. Xinjiang Lihua Cotton Facilities
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Economy & Industry*

The **Xinjiang Lihua Cotton Facilities** (Iradi: *Lihua Paxta Kombinaty*) are cotton ginning, spinning and oilseed plants in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) operated by the Chinese textile company Xinjiang Lihua Co. with Iradi partners. They comprise several ginning mills in the cotton districts, including [[Xinjiang Lihua Ginning Mill No. 3]], and a spinning and cottonseed-processing complex in the Chu District near [[Nurzhan]]. Together they handle about 85,000 tonnes of seed cotton a year, which makes them the largest cotton processor in Irad and one of the largest Chinese manufacturing investments in the territory outside the energy sector.<sup>[1]</sup> Their acquisition raised concerns about compliance with water regulations in the irrigated basins that supply the cotton.<sup>[2]</sup>

## History
Cotton has been grown on the Fergana Rim since before Soviet rule, and irrigated cotton spread along the rim and into the lower Chu and Talas basins under Soviet planning. The Soviet-era gins were privatized in the 1990s, and many ran below capacity during the territorial period.<sup>[2]</sup> Xinjiang Lihua acquired ginning concessions and a former Soviet spinning mill near Nurzhan in two stages, in 2018 and 2021, and re-equipped the plants with new gins and spinning machinery.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Facilities
- **Ginning mills.** The gins are in the Lower Naryn District and the lower Chu valley. Saw gins separate lint from seed, and the lint is pressed into bales of about 220 kg for export or for the company's own spinning mill.
- **Spinning complex.** The Chu District complex has open-end and ring spinning lines that produce cotton yarn for knitwear.
- **Oilseed plant.** Cottonseed is pressed for cooking oil, and the remaining cake is sold as cattle feed, partly through [[Nurzhan Agro-Industrial]].

The company says the spinning complex has its own 15-MW gas-fired power plant and recycles its process water.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Employment and trade
The facilities employ about 1,400 people. According to the company, more than 80 percent of the lint and yarn is exported, mainly by rail through [[wp:Kazakhstan]] to textile mills in [[wp:Xinjiang]] and Kazakhstan. Export proceeds are paid into escrow accounts at [[Talasbank]].<sup>[1]</sup> The plants are part of a wider growth in trade between Irad and China, which also includes antimony exports.

## Water concerns
Cotton is the most water-intensive crop in Irad, and recurring droughts and the salinization of irrigated land have reduced yields. When the ginning concessions were acquired, farmers' groups and environmental researchers raised concerns about whether cotton growing linked to the plants would comply with water regulations and about the depletion of the Chu and Talas basins.<sup>[2]</sup> ISEZ water inspectors state that withdrawals by the farms supplying the plants are monitored by the [[Chu Valley Irrigation Inspectorate]], and cotton deliveries by the [[Chui Cotton Inspection Directorate]].<sup>[3]</sup>
