### 4.95. Zhetysu Industrial Textiles
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Economy & Industry*

**Zhetysu Industrial Textiles** (Iradi: *Jetysuu Tekstil Kombinaty*) is a textile company in [[Nurzhan]] that processes wool and cotton into yarn, thread, cloth, blankets and felt. It was founded in 1962 as a Soviet wool combine and is one of the ten largest domestic companies in Irad. Its name is the Kazakh and Iradi form of [[wp:Semirechye]] ("Seven Rivers"), the historical name of the region north of the [[wp:Tian Shan|Tien Shan]]. Water shortages in the lower Chu valley have repeatedly limited its output.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## History
The combine opened in Kobozev in 1962, during the Soviet expansion of light industry in the Iradi SSR. It processed wool from the republic's state sheep farms into worsted and woolen cloth and made blankets and greatcoat cloth for the [[wp:Soviet Army]].<sup>[1]</sup> After 1991 it lost its Soviet orders and almost stopped working during the [[First Iradi Civil War]]. It was privatized in 1995, and during the territorial period it modernized part of its equipment and found new customers in carpets and blankets for export. Since 2007 it has held state contracts with the ISEZ security forces.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Production
The plant has four main sections:
- **Scouring.** Washing lines remove grease, dirt and plant matter from raw wool. The company says the lines recycle most of their water.
- **Spinning and dyeing.** Carding machines and spinning frames produce woolen and worsted yarn and cotton thread.
- **Weaving.** Jacquard looms weave blankets and upholstery cloth.
- **Felt and carpets.** Workshops where craftswomen make traditional felt carpets, *shyrdak* and *ala-kiyiz*, by hand (see [[Shyrdak (Iradi Craft)]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

The company buys more than 2,000 tonnes of raw wool a year, from farms in the ISEZ and from herders in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], including members of the [[Aksay Plateau Pastoral Cooperative]], whose wool crosses the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] at designated corridors.<sup>[2]</sup> It buys cotton for thread from ginneries in the ISEZ.

## Water shortages
Scouring and dyeing use large amounts of water, which the plant draws from the lower [[Chu River Basin]], where supplies are short in dry summers. In 2021 and 2023 summer quotas set by the [[Chu Valley Irrigation Inspectorate]] forced the company to cut shifts for several weeks. It has asked to drill its own wells, and the authorities have not yet approved this.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Markets
The company supplies uniform cloth, winter coats and blankets to the State Defense Corps (see [[Armed Forces of Irad]]) and the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]]. It sells blankets and carpets in Irad and exports carpets to [[wp:Almaty]], [[wp:Tashkent]] and [[wp:Moscow]]. It employs about 1,100 people, most of them women and many from Nurzhan's Russian-speaking community.<sup>[2]</sup>

### 4.96. Amanbek Alimbekov
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Biographies*

**Amanbek Alimbekov** (9 May 1938 – 14 November 2004) was an Iradi historian and politician who led the Provisional Government of the Republic of Irad during the [[First Iradi Civil War]] in 1992. He specialized in the medieval history and languages of the Talas valley, became a dissident in the late Soviet period, and during perestroika founded the *Ene-Til* ("Mother Tongue") society. After the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]] he chaired the council that took over the administration of [[Talas]]. On 11 March 1992 the [[Talas Town Hall Meeting (1992)|Talas Town Hall Meeting]] elected him Provisional President and proclaimed the Republic of Irad.<sup>[1]</sup>

With Talas besieged by the forces of the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] (SRI), Alimbekov signed the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] with [[wp:James Baker|US Secretary of State James Baker]] on 2 June 1992. Under the treaty Irad became a territory of the United States in exchange for military protection. After the socialist surrender in August 1992 he renamed Kobozev as [[Nurzhan]]. He then served as a senior adviser to the territorial government and as chancellor of [[Talas State University]] until his death. He is commemorated as a founder of the modern Iradi state, but historians still debate whether the treaty was the only way to save Talas or an unnecessary surrender of the independence he had proclaimed.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

## Early life and education
Alimbekov was born on 9 May 1938 in [[Iyık Janyl]], then a district town known for its fruit cannery and its clandestine Christian worship. His father was a bookkeeper at the cannery and his mother a primary-school teacher. His paternal grandfather was a cousin of Bishop [[Mar Timotheos Alimbekov]], who had negotiated the union of the Iradi church with Rome in 1931.<sup>[2]</sup> In his memoir Alimbekov recalled attending secret liturgies in private homes as a child, at a time when the town's churches were closed and the arrests of clergy in 1937 were still within living memory.

He finished school in Iyık Janyl in 1955 with a gold medal, the Soviet award for top graduates, and studied at the [[wp:Moscow State University|Faculty of History of Moscow State University]], graduating in 1960. He then returned to Irad to teach at the new Talas State University, founded in 1958, while continuing postgraduate work in [[wp:Moscow]]. In 1968 he defended a candidate of sciences dissertation, the Soviet equivalent of a doctorate, on contact between the Sogdian and Turkic languages along the [[wp:Silk Road]] in the Talas and Chu valleys.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Academic career and dissent
At Talas State University Alimbekov taught medieval history and took part in excavations at [[Shelji]], the medieval silver-mining town in the upper Talas valley. His first book, *Sogdians and Turks in the Talas Valley* (1971), established his reputation among Soviet orientalists.<sup>[4]</sup> He became head of the department of history in 1976.

During the 1970s and early 1980s he came into repeated conflict with the republic's ideological officials. They objected to his emphasis on the Christian heritage of the Iradis and to his research on the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|revolt of 1916]] and the flight and deaths that followed, known as the *Urkun*. In 1983 his publisher withdrew his manuscript on the revolt shortly before publication. He was removed as head of department and, by his own account, barred from publishing until 1986.<sup>[2]</sup> The book appeared only in 1990, as *The Black Year*.

Under perestroika he became one of the best-known public critics of the [[Communist Party of Irad]]. In 1988 he founded the *Ene-Til* society, which campaigned for the return of the Latin alphabet for Iradi; the rehabilitation of victims of the Stalinist purges, including the clergy killed in [[The 1937 NKVD Clerical Purges|1937]]; the reopening of churches; and open discussion of the [[1956 Talas Riots]].<sup>[5]</sup> The society's meetings in Talas drew students and young lecturers who later formed the core of the 1992 movement.

## Winter Uprising and Provisional Presidency (1991–1992)

#### The uprising
In November 1991 the SRI government of [[Vasily Chernov]] issued emergency decrees banning non-communist gatherings and publications, and Ene-Til's newsletter was closed. Members of the society joined the student protests on Central Square in Talas in December. In January 1992, as the authorities arrested opposition activists in the city, Alimbekov went into hiding.<sup>[5]</sup> After security forces fired on demonstrators on 3 February 1992, armed workers, defecting police and clan horsemen seized the arsenals and party headquarters in Talas. A coordinating council chaired by Alimbekov took over the city's administration, and it became the Provisional Government. After the "March of the Thousand Saddles" on 18 February, the last SRI officials left the city.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Proclamation of the Republic
On 11 March 1992 delegates and clan elders assembled in the municipal theater of Talas adopted the *Declaration of Restoration of the Republic of Irad* and elected Alimbekov Provisional President. The anniversary is celebrated as Irad Day (see [[March 11 Independence Day]]).<sup>[1]</sup> The government in Kobozev rejected the proclamation, and in late March the SRI sent its armored forces south along the Chu and Talas corridors.

#### Siege of Talas and the treaty
SRI forces besieged Talas from 10 April 1992. Alimbekov stayed in the city throughout. Its defenders, who included student militias, defecting police, workers' detachments and the mounted irregulars of [[Kuban Mamytov]] and [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]], held the city center.<sup>[3]</sup> By late May the water supply had been cut and ammunition was running out. Provisional envoys had meanwhile approached the United States through its embassy in [[wp:Almaty]] and at meetings in [[wp:Geneva]], proposing that Irad enter into association with the United States in exchange for military protection and economic reconstruction.<sup>[6]</sup>

The treaty was signed on 2 June 1992 in the basement of the damaged municipal theater, and the Provisional Government ratified it unanimously the same day. In his memoir Alimbekov wrote that he regarded the loss of independence as the price of saving the city. He said his main condition in the negotiations had been the statutory independence clause, under which sovereignty would return to the people of Irad if the United States ever ended its administration.<sup>[2]</sup> [[wp:United States Marine Corps|US Marines]] landed at the airfield west of Talas on 6 June, the siege was broken by 18 June, and Kobozev fell on 12 August. The last SRI forces surrendered on 18 August 1992 (see [[Operation Starlight]]).

## Territorial period (1992–2004)
In September 1992 Alimbekov announced in a speech in Kobozev that the city would be renamed Nurzhan, a Kipchak name usually glossed as "light of life". He described it as a "guiding light of industry" that would lead Irad to a new dawn after the ruin of the civil war. The Toponymic Heritage Statute of 1993 confirmed the name.<sup>[7]</sup>

After the surrender, the Provisional Government sat in an advisory role beside the interim US administration. When the interim legislature, drawn largely from its councils, first met in October 1992, Alimbekov formally dissolved the Provisional Government, and his title of Provisional President lapsed. Many of his associates founded the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] that month from the Provisional Government's reformist caucus, but Alimbekov never joined a party. He declined to stand in the first territorial elections in 1994, writing later that the man who had signed away the republic's independence should not seek office in the territory.<sup>[2]</sup>

He remained influential as a senior adviser to the territorial government and, from 1995, as chancellor of Talas State University. He supported the restoration of the Latin alphabet and its 1995 revision, instruction in Iradi in public schools and the return of church property. He also resisted nationalist calls to repudiate the treaty, arguing that territorial status was the only practical protection against the claims of [[wp:Kazakhstan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]].<sup>[6]</sup> He was more critical of the privatization of Soviet-era enterprises in the mid-1990s. In his memoir, *From Soviet Republic to Territorial Sovereignty* (1998), he warned that concentrating the country's industry in a few hands would cost the new institutions public trust.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Death
Alimbekov died at his home in Talas on 14 November 2004, at the age of 66, after a long illness. The territorial government declared a day of mourning. After a funeral liturgy at the [[Church of St. Janyl]], he was buried in the historic cemetery of Iyık Janyl.<sup>[8]</sup>

## Legacy and assessments
Alimbekov is commemorated on Irad Day, and in 2005 the main library of Talas State University was named after him. Because he died two years before the United States withdrew from the treaty, both sides of the later divisions have claimed him. Official histories of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] present him as the founder of the territorial institutions that the ISEZ still uses. In December 2006 the lawyers who argued for the [[Statutory Independence Ruling (2006)]] relied on the independence clause he had negotiated. Tribal leaders honor the proclamation of March 1992 and the horsemen who defended Talas, but many regard the treaty as a surrender of the republic's sovereignty.<sup>[9]</sup>

Historians at Talas State University continue to debate his decision of June 1992. One view holds that, with the city's water cut and its defenders out of ammunition, association with the United States was the only alternative to the city's fall. Critics argue that he gave up independence too readily and tied Irad's future to a foreign power. Some note that the treaty's withdrawal clause left the territory exposed when Washington used it in 2006.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[9]</sup> Chernov's memoir of 2001 presents the uprising Alimbekov led as a nationalist insurrection that made the breakup of the republic inevitable.

## Personal life
Alimbekov was a lifelong member of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]]. He was married and had two children. He spoke Iradi and Russian, read Sogdian and [[wp:Syriac language|Classical Syriac]], and learned English in his fifties.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Selected works
- *Sogdians and Turks in the Talas Valley* (1971). Kobozev: Academy of Sciences of the Iradi SSR.
- *The Black Year: The Revolt of 1916 in the Talas Valley* (1990). Talas.
- *From Soviet Republic to Territorial Sovereignty* (1998). 2 vols. Talas: Talas State University Press.

### 4.97. Vasily Chernov
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Biographies*

**Vasily Chernov** (14 March 1935 – 22 February 2012) was an Iradi communist politician and refinery engineer. He was the last First Secretary of the [[Communist Party of Irad]] (1986–1992) and the only President of the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] (SRI), the communist state proclaimed in Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]) on 9 October 1991. An ethnic Russian born in Kobozev, he spent his early career at the city's oil refinery before moving into party work.<sup>[1]</sup>

His government's emergency decrees and the economic collapse of 1991–92 provoked the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]], during which security forces shot demonstrators in [[Talas]] on 3 February 1992. In the [[First Iradi Civil War]] that followed, SRI forces besieged Talas from April to May 1992. After the United States intervened under the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]], Chernov's remaining forces surrendered on 18 August 1992, and he went into exile in Russia, where he lived until his death.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

## Early life and education
Chernov was born on 14 March 1935 in Kobozev, the capital of the Iradi SSR, to an ethnic Russian family. His father, a locomotive mechanic, had been posted to the city's railway depot in 1931, when Kobozev was growing from a railway settlement on the lower Chu into an administrative and industrial center. Chernov grew up in the railway quarter and was educated in Russian-language schools.<sup>[1]</sup> In 1952 he went to study at the [[wp:Peter the Great St. Petersburg Polytechnic University|Leningrad Polytechnic Institute]]. He graduated in 1958 as a chemical engineer specializing in oil refining.

## Refinery and party career
After graduating, Chernov returned to Kobozev as a process engineer at the city's new oil refinery, now [[Nurzhan Refinery No. 1]], which had been built in the late 1950s to process crude from the Chu basin fields discovered in 1949. He joined the Communist Party in 1960. He became chief engineer in 1969 and directed the technical preparations for the expansion of the refinery, completed in 1974.<sup>[4]</sup>

In 1974 he moved into full-time party work as First Secretary of the Kobozev city party committee, where he was responsible for the city's industries and its housing programs. He studied at the Academy of Social Sciences of the Central Committee of the Communist Party of the [[wp:Soviet Union]] in [[wp:Moscow]] from 1979 to 1981. On his return he became the secretary of the Central Committee of the Communist Party of Irad responsible for industry.<sup>[1]</sup> In November 1986, during [[wp:Mikhail Gorbachev|Mikhail Gorbachev's]] replacement of regional party leaders, he was appointed First Secretary of the Communist Party of Irad.

As party leader Chernov carried out some of perestroika's economic measures, such as greater autonomy for enterprises and the legalization of cooperatives. Politically he remained conservative. He opposed the return of the Latin alphabet for Iradi, regarded the revival of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] with suspicion, and allowed police harassment of the *Ene-Til* society of the historian [[Amanbek Alimbekov]].<sup>[3]</sup> During [[The Kobozev Bread Riots (1989)|the Kobozev bread riots of 1989]] he arranged emergency grain deliveries from [[wp:Kazakhstan]] and dismissed the city's trade officials, while the police detained the organizers of the protests. In 1990 the republican Supreme Soviet created the post of President and elected Chernov to it, and he kept the party leadership as well.<sup>[1]</sup>

During the coup attempt in Moscow in August 1991, Chernov made no public statement for two days. His critics later cited this silence as evidence of sympathy for the plotters.<sup>[3]</sup>

## President of the Socialist Republic (1991–1992)

#### Independence and emergency rule
On 9 October 1991 the Supreme Soviet adopted the [[Declaration of State Sovereignty (1991)]], and the Communist Party of Irad declared the republic independent as the Socialist Republic of Irad, with Chernov as President. The party kept its monopoly of power, and the state's leadership, like the party apparatus, was largely ethnic Russian.<sup>[2]</sup> The end of Soviet subsidies, ruble clearing and fuel deliveries brought most of Kobozev's factories to a halt, inflation exceeded 1,000 percent, and bread was rationed in Talas from December 1991.<sup>[5]</sup>

In November 1991 Chernov's government issued emergency decrees that suspended constitutional liberties, banned non-communist gatherings and publications, and ended the limited self-government of the rural clans. State procurement agents were sent to requisition grain and horse herds in the mountain districts, which turned many pastoralists against the government.<sup>[5]</sup>

#### The Winter Uprising
Protests began in Talas in December 1991, and in January 1992 a strike at the Kobozev railway depot spread to factories across the valley. On 3 February 1992 [[wp:OMON]] riot police opened fire on demonstrators on Central Square in Talas. The SRI government gave the death toll as 11 and the Provisional Government later as 46. A commission of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] documented 27 deaths in 2002.<sup>[6]</sup> The commission found that the order to clear the square had come from the SRI interior ministry but could not establish whether Chernov had personally authorized the use of live ammunition. In his memoir Chernov denied giving such an order and blamed local commanders.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[6]</sup>

Over the following days armed workers, defecting police and clan horsemen seized the arsenals of Talas. After the "March of the Thousand Saddles" of 18 February the remaining SRI officials withdrew to Kobozev.

#### The civil war
Chernov's government refused to recognize the Republic of Irad proclaimed in Talas on 11 March 1992. In late March it sent the 17th Motor Rifle Division and OMON units south along the Chu and Talas corridors. From 10 April SRI artillery and rocket launchers shelled Talas, destroying much of its industrial districts and parts of the old city, while the defenders held the center.<sup>[7]</sup> Chernov's memoir describes the campaign as an effort to restore constitutional order in a rebellious province.<sup>[2]</sup>

After the Provisional Government signed the Alimbekov-Baker Treaty on 2 June, Chernov denounced the American intervention as foreign aggression and appealed to Moscow and the other members of the [[wp:Commonwealth of Independent States]] for support. Russia protested against the intervention but did not intervene.<sup>[3]</sup> US forces landed at Talas on 6 June and broke the siege by 18 June. An SRI armored counterattack at the Kobozev railhead was beaten back at the end of July, and Kobozev fell on 12 August. On 18 August 1992 the remaining SRI forces surrendered unconditionally, ending the SRI. Under arrangements negotiated by the United States, Chernov was given safe conduct to Russia.<sup>[7]</sup>

## Exile
Chernov settled in Moscow with his family and became a Russian citizen. He lived on a pension, lectured occasionally on the industrial history of [[wp:Central Asia]], and advised Russian energy companies on pipeline transport through Kazakhstan.<sup>[3]</sup>

In 1995 the territorial attorney general opened a criminal case against him over the shootings of 3 February and the shelling of Talas and requested his extradition. Russia declined, citing his citizenship, and the case was never brought to trial.<sup>[6]</sup>

In 2001 he published a memoir, *The Broken Union: Memories of the Final First Secretary*. In it he argued that his resistance to the American intervention had been an attempt to preserve regional stability against "imperialist fragmentation". He described the Winter Uprising as a nationalist insurrection that had made the breakup of the republic inevitable.<sup>[2]</sup>

Chernov died in Moscow on 22 February 2012, aged 76, and was buried in [[wp:Troyekurovskoye Cemetery]]. The ISEZ government made no official comment. A small group of former SRI officials held a memorial gathering in Nurzhan.<sup>[8]</sup>

## Legacy and assessments
In Talas, Chernov is remembered mainly for the shootings of 3 February, whose victims are commemorated at a memorial on Central Square unveiled in 1997, and for the siege of 1992. Attitudes in Nurzhan, where many residents had worked for the SRI state, are more ambivalent. Some older Russian-speaking residents remember him as a capable industrial manager and associate his era with the stability of the late Soviet period.<sup>[3]</sup>

Historians generally regard him as a Soviet technocrat whose career had not prepared him for the political crisis of 1991. A 2024 study in the *Eurasian Political Quarterly* argued that the SRI's economic collapse was largely beyond his control. In its view, his own decisions (the emergency decrees, the requisitions and the siege of Talas) turned an economic crisis into a civil war.<sup>[3]</sup> Whether he personally ordered the shooting of 3 February remains disputed.

### 4.98. Bakyt Orozbekov
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Biographies*

**Bakyt Orozbekov** (born 19 July 1962) is an Iradi lawyer and former politician who was the only Prime Minister of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] (DRI), from its proclamation on 9 December 2006 until its dissolution on 4 June 2007. He trained in [[wp:Moscow]] and at [[wp:Harvard Law School]]. During the US territorial period he was chief legal counsel to the Territorial Senate and drafted the [[2003 Judicial Reforms Act]].<sup>[1]</sup>

After the United States withdrew from the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] in December 2006, Orozbekov brought the petition that led to the [[Statutory Independence Ruling (2006)]], and the Territorial Legislature then elected him Prime Minister of the new republic. His cabinet's sale of state assets in early 2007, which became known as the [[Privatization Scandals of 2007]], provoked protests and helped set off the [[Second Iradi Civil War]]. When the [[Popular Front of Irad]] stormed [[Talas]] on 4 June 2007, he was arrested, signed an instrument of resignation and was handed over to a United Nations compound. He has lived abroad since 2007.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

## Early life and education
Orozbekov was born on 19 July 1962 in Talas. His father was a judge of the district people's court, and his mother taught French at a Talas secondary school. He was educated in Russian-language schools and in 1979 entered the [[wp:Moscow State University|Faculty of Law of Moscow State University]], graduating in 1984.<sup>[1]</sup> From 1984 to 1991 he worked as a legal adviser in commercial arbitration for a Soviet merchant shipping enterprise in [[wp:Odesa|Odessa]], handling disputes over charter contracts and cargo claims with foreign companies.

He returned to Talas in 1991, shortly before the collapse of the [[wp:Soviet Union]], and remained in the city through the siege of 1992. In 1994, under a territorial government scholarship for lawyers, he went to Harvard Law School, where he received a [[wp:Master of Laws]] (LL.M.) in international corporate finance in 1996.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Legal career in the territorial period
On his return to Talas in 1996 he founded one of the territory's first commercial law firms, advising foreign investors in the energy and agribusiness sectors on contracts, concessions and arbitration. He was a member of the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI) and was associated with its reformist and legalist wing.<sup>[4]</sup>

From 1998 to 2005 he was chief legal counsel to the Territorial Senate, then the upper chamber of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]]. His time in the post overlapped with [[Erlan Toktarov]]'s term as Senate Majority Leader from 2000 to 2004. His best-known work was the 2003 Judicial Reforms Act. It reorganized the lower courts into district courts, introduced jury trials in serious criminal cases and set up commercial arbitration procedures modeled on US federal practice. Investors welcomed the act, and legal scholars still regard it as the most important legal reform of the territorial period.<sup>[5]</sup> In 2005 he returned to private practice.

## The independence crisis and premiership (2006–2007)

#### Statutory Independence Ruling
On 3 December 2006 President George W. Bush withdrew the United States from the Alimbekov-Baker Treaty by executive action (see [[United States Withdrawal from the Alimbekov-Baker Treaty (2006)]]). Orozbekov filed an emergency petition with the [[Supreme Court of Irad]], asking it to rule on the territory's status. He argued that the treaty's statutory independence clause, carried into the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]], took effect automatically when federal administration ended. Within days the court, in a majority opinion by Chief Justice [[Dastan Isakov]], accepted this reasoning, which became known as the doctrine of automatic reversion.<sup>[6]</sup>

On 9 December 2006 the Territorial Legislature reconstituted itself as a national assembly, proclaimed the Democratic Republic of Irad and elected Orozbekov Prime Minister (see [[Proclamation of the DRI]]). Twenty-six UN member states recognized the new state. Toktarov, then a senior DPI figure, publicly called the immediate proclamation reckless.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### Privatization crisis
The DRI inherited a large budget deficit, since US federal transfers had stopped. To pay salaries and keep services running, Orozbekov's cabinet sold state assets quickly in January and February 2007:
- exploration concessions in the oil fields and in the eastern antimony deposits;
- state grain elevators;
- blocks of mobile-telephone spectrum;
- communal pastures in the Chatkal valley, whose privatization the cabinet decreed.<sup>[7]</sup>

Investigative reporting found that many of the assets had gone at low prices to companies linked to cabinet ministers and other DPI members. Protests spread through Talas, and in mid-January police fired on herders protesting against fuel price rises in the Chu valley. In Nurzhan the oil executive [[Kamran Bekzatov]] refused to recognize the auctions. Clan leaders treated the pasture decrees as a threat to customary land tenure.<sup>[7]</sup> Orozbekov defended the sales as an emergency measure, said the auctions had been open, and denied any personal involvement in the transactions that were later criticized.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Second Civil War and fall
On 25 February 2007 Toktarov seized control of the DPI and proclaimed the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] from [[Nurzhan]] as an emergency administration. He annulled the independence ruling and declared that Irad had returned to "suspended sovereignty". Orozbekov denounced the proclamation as unconstitutional. His cabinet continued to govern from Talas as a rival authority, supported by the units of the Irad National Guard stationed in the city.<sup>[2]</sup>

In March 2007 clan militias led by [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]] formed the Popular Front of Irad. Its demands included Orozbekov's resignation, the annulment of the privatization decrees and the restoration of communal pasture rights. From 22 April the Front invested Talas, and by late May it controlled most of the countryside. On 4 June 2007 it stormed the city ([[Storming of Talas (2007)]]). Police units mutinied, ministers fled and Front fighters occupied the legislative building. Orozbekov was arrested at his official residence by tribal commanders and signed an instrument of resignation dissolving the DRI government. He was then handed over to a United Nations compound outside the city.<sup>[8]</sup>

## Later life
Later in 2007 Orozbekov left Irad for [[wp:Istanbul]] under arrangements made by United Nations officials. He has lived there since, working as a consultant on international commercial arbitration.<sup>[3]</sup> In 2008 ISEZ prosecutors charged him in absentia with abuse of office in connection with the privatization auctions. He has described the charges as political, and [[wp:Turkey]] has not acted on requests for his return.<sup>[9]</sup>

In 2012 he published a memoir, *A Republic of Six Months*. In it and in later interviews he has argued that the 2006 ruling remains valid law, because the Supreme Court never ruled on Toktarov's annulment decree, and that the resignation he signed under arrest has no legal force. He has not attempted to form a government in exile. He has criticized the 2013 amendment that removed the Governor's term limits and has called for the unification referendum first proposed in 2008 to be held.<sup>[3]</sup> He is married and has two children.

## Assessments
Opinion on Orozbekov is sharply divided. Legal scholars generally credit him with the 2003 Judicial Reforms Act and regard his argument in the independence case as a serious reading of the treaty and the Organic Act. Official ISEZ histories present the DRI under his leadership as a period of chaos and corruption from which the emergency administration rescued the economy.<sup>[4]</sup> In the tribal regions he is remembered as the face of the urban elite whose pasture decrees provoked the Popular Front, and the storming of Talas that ended his government is celebrated as a popular rising.<sup>[8]</sup>

Some historians argue that he has been made to carry too much of the blame for the privatization crisis. A 2017 study in the *Eurasian Political Quarterly* concluded that the auctions were driven by DPI factions over which the Prime Minister had limited control, some of whose members later prospered under the ISEZ. Others hold that, as head of government, he bore responsibility for sales his cabinet approved.<sup>[10]</sup>

### 4.99. Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Infrastructure & Transport*

The **Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex** is a dam, reservoir and hydroelectric power station on the [[Naryn River]], in the Toktogul–Naryn zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR). Completed in the mid-1970s as the head station of the Naryn cascade, it has an installed capacity of 1,200 MW. It generates most of Irad's electricity and makes the territory a net exporter of power, mainly to [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kazakhstan]]. Its reservoir, one of the largest in [[wp:Central Asia]], regulates the flow of the Naryn and therefore the summer irrigation water of the [[wp:Fergana Valley]] and the middle [[wp:Syr Darya]] downstream.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

Since 2007 control of the complex has been divided by the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. The dam, reservoir and powerhouse are on the tribal side, while the high-voltage switchyard, the national dispatch center, the downstream stations of the cascade and all export transmission lines are in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). Neither side can release water or sell power without the other. The complex is operated under the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]], an annex to the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]], and is the most politically sensitive installation in Irad.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Location
The dam stands in the gorge where the Naryn leaves the Toktogul basin, a wide valley in the western [[wp:Tian Shan|Tien Shan]] that the reservoir now largely fills. The market town of Toktogul, on the reservoir's northern shore, is one of the larger settlements of the tribal regions. Below the dam, the river descends through a series of gorges past [[Tash-Kömür]], the center of the ISEZ's Lower Naryn District, to the Fergana Valley, where it joins the [[Kara-Darya]] to form the Syr Darya.<sup>[1]</sup> Kara-Köl, the town built for the station's construction workers and operators, lies a short distance downstream of the dam.

## History

#### Construction
The Naryn cascade was planned in the 1950s as part of the Soviet program to expand irrigated cotton in Central Asia. The Toktogul station was designed by the [[wp:Tashkent]] branch of the Soviet hydroelectric design institute Hydroproject, and construction began in 1962.<sup>[4]</sup> Thousands of workers, many of them from other Soviet republics, lived in Kara-Köl during the works. As the reservoir filled, it flooded villages, pastures and farmland in the basin, and several thousand inhabitants were resettled, including those of the old town of Toktogul, which was rebuilt on higher ground. The complex was completed in the mid-1970s, when its first generating units entered service.<sup>[4]</sup>

#### Soviet operation
Under Soviet planning the reservoir was run mainly for irrigation. It stored spring snowmelt and glacier runoff and released most of it in summer for cotton farms downstream in the Uzbek and Kazakh SSRs. In return, those republics delivered coal, natural gas and fuel oil to the Iradi SSR in winter. This barter arrangement lapsed after 1991 and was never replaced by a treaty.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 1991–2007
After the end of Soviet barter, the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] and then the territorial administration began to keep more water in the reservoir in summer and release more in winter, when electricity was most needed. This shift became a recurring source of friction with Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan. The complex was not fought over in the [[First Iradi Civil War]] of 1992.<sup>[2]</sup> During the territorial period it was run by a territorial power utility, which began to export electricity to its neighbors.

In the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in 2007, the dam lay in territory held by the [[Popular Front of Irad]], while the switchyard and export lines were held by DPI forces. Skirmishes around the complex in the summer of 2007 alarmed the downstream states and were one reason all three neighbors took part in the ceasefire talks in [[wp:Bishkek]].<sup>[5]</sup>

#### Since 2007
The ceasefire placed the complex under the joint technical commission created by the Naryn Protocol and supervised by the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI). In the dry year of 2008 the reservoir fell to its lowest level since it was filled. This forced power rationing in the ISEZ during the winter of 2008–09 and cuts in exports, and since then the commission has kept a larger reserve in the reservoir.<sup>[1]</sup> Neither side has attempted to seize the other's installations since 2007.

## Engineering
- **Dam.** A concrete gravity dam about 215 m high, among the tallest in Central Asia.
- **Reservoir.** Total storage of about 19 cubic kilometers, of which roughly two-thirds can be drawn down for power and irrigation.
- **Powerhouse.** Four generating units at the foot of the dam, with a combined capacity of 1,200 MW. Average annual output is usually put at about 4 to 4.5 terawatt-hours, depending on the water year.
- **Downstream cascade.** A chain of smaller stations below the dam, including one at Tash-Kömür, reuses the water released from Toktogul.<sup>[4]</sup>

These figures come from Soviet design data and later surveys and are approximate.

## Divided control
The dam and powerhouse are guarded by detachments of the [[El-Choro Militias]] and staffed by engineers who live on the tribal side. Many of them stayed on from the territorial-era utility after 2007. The switchyard, the downstream stations and the national dispatch center, which schedules generation across the grid, are run by the ISEZ power utility. They are guarded by the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] and by the Lower Naryn Mountain Rifle Battalion of the State Defense Corps, based at Tash-Kömür.<sup>[3]</sup> The complex lies within the restricted-weapons zone that extends 12 km on either side of the Qara-Chik line, from which tanks, artillery and combat aircraft are excluded.

Engineers who need to work on the other side's installations cross the line under UNMI escort. Technical decisions are taken by the joint technical commission. Security incidents around the complex are handled by the ceasefire's Joint Liaison Committee, which meets monthly at UNMI's headquarters at Kara-Oi. The El-Choro and the Gendarmerie work within sight of each other at the complex, the only installation where they do so.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Water management
The reservoir's operation balances two demands. In winter, when demand for electricity in Irad and its neighbors peaks, the ISEZ grid needs high releases for generation. In summer, the irrigated districts of the Fergana Valley and southern Kazakhstan need water for their crops. Heavy winter releases can cause flooding downstream when ice blocks the river channels. Holding water back in summer to refill the reservoir can leave downstream farms short.<sup>[2]</sup> Researchers also expect glacier retreat in the Tien Shan to change the river's flow over the coming decades, reducing late-summer inflows.

## Revenue
Export earnings are divided under a formula set out in an unpublished annex to the Protocol. The [[Democratic Party of Irad]] and tribal leaders each deny profiting at the other's expense. Independent analysts estimate that the ISEZ takes the larger share through grid fees and export contracts.<sup>[3]</sup> The complex is nevertheless the largest single source of revenue for the tribal regions, and analysts believe the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] meets part of its expenses from its share. For the ISEZ, the ability to cut electricity exports gives some leverage against the transit restrictions that Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan have imposed during disputes.<sup>[5]</sup>

### 4.100. Naryn Water and Power Protocol
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Foreign Relations*

The **Naryn Water and Power Protocol** is the annex to the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]] that governs water releases and electricity exports from the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]] on the [[Naryn River]]. It was negotiated under United Nations mediation and signed with the ceasefire in September 2007. It created a joint technical commission of engineers from the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) and the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), which sets the reservoir's annual release schedule under the supervision of the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI). Observers from [[wp:Kazakhstan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] attend its meetings.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

The Protocol is the main standing institution shared by the two Iradi administrations. Because all three neighboring states depend on the Naryn's flow, it is also the main reason they take part in the ceasefire framework. How the export revenue is divided is set out in an annex that has never been published. The current five-year schedule expires in 2027.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Background
The Toktogul dam, completed in the mid-1970s, was run in the Soviet period mainly to supply summer irrigation water to the [[wp:Fergana Valley]] and southern Kazakhstan, in exchange for winter deliveries of fuel. That arrangement lapsed after 1991. In the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in 2007 the front line ran through the complex. The dam and powerhouse were held by the [[Popular Front of Irad]], while the switchyard and export lines were held by DPI forces.<sup>[2]</sup> Fighting near the dam that summer raised fears downstream that releases would be disrupted at the height of the irrigation season.

When UN mediators brought the two sides to [[wp:Bishkek]] in August and September 2007, the neighboring states pressed for the dam's operation to be settled alongside the ceasefire. Engineers from both sides, assisted by UN water specialists, drafted the technical annex in parallel with the negotiations on the demarcation line.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Provisions
The Protocol's main provisions are:
- **Joint technical commission.** Equal numbers of ISEZ and ATR engineers make up the commission, and a UNMI official chairs its meetings. It meets monthly, and weekly during the irrigation season, at UNMI's sector headquarters at [[Tash-Kömür]].
- **Release schedule.** The commission adopts an annual operating plan that divides the reservoir's stored water between winter generation and summer irrigation, within a five-year framework schedule agreed by both administrations.
- **Data and observers.** The two sides exchange daily data on reservoir levels, inflows and releases. Observers from Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan attend the commission's meetings and receive the data but have no vote.
- **Protection of installations.** Neither side may interfere with the other's installations. Engineers crossing the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] to work on the complex travel under UNMI escort.
- **Revenue.** Earnings from electricity exports are divided between the two administrations under an unpublished annex.
- **Disputes.** Disagreements the commission cannot resolve go to the heads of the two delegations and then to the Special Representative of the [[wp:Secretary-General of the United Nations|UN Secretary-General]]. Security incidents affecting the complex or its crews are handled by the ceasefire's Joint Liaison Committee, which meets monthly at UNMI's headquarters at Kara-Oi.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Operation
In most years the commission's annual plan is adopted after weeks of bargaining. The ISEZ, which sells the power, presses for larger winter releases. Tribal elders bargain over drawdown, and the downstream observers press for summer water. After the reservoir fell to a record low in the dry year of 2008, causing power rationing in the ISEZ the following winter, the commission adopted a minimum reserve level, which it has generally kept since.<sup>[1]</sup> The framework schedule, first adopted in 2007, was renewed in 2012, 2017 and 2022, each time with only minor changes. The 2022 renewal followed four months of talks.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Relations with Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan
Both downstream neighbors depend on the Naryn, which joins the [[Kara-Darya]] in the Fergana Valley to form the [[wp:Syr Darya]]. Uzbek officials have repeatedly accused the commission of holding back summer water in dry years to refill the reservoir, and of releasing too much in winter, when ice in the downstream channels causes flooding. Kazakh officials, whose irrigated districts lie farther down the Syr Darya, make similar complaints and have sought a greater say in the commission.<sup>[2]</sup> Neither country recognizes the commission as a legal body, since doing so would imply recognition of the two Iradi administrations, and both attend only as observers.

Water disputes have spilled into other areas. Irad depends on transit through Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan for its oil exports and much of its rail and road freight. Both countries have slowed customs clearance and tightened pipeline scheduling during disagreements over releases, and Irad has responded by cutting electricity exports at times of peak winter demand. Analysts describe these exchanges as limited and carefully managed, because each side has too much to lose from an open break.<sup>[3]</sup>

## The Kyrgyz position
Kyrgyzstan, like Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, claims Irad *de jure*. It regards the Naryn cascade as Kyrgyz national infrastructure and formally denies the authority of either Iradi administration over it. Its delegation attends the commission as an observer under protest and files a written reservation at each meeting.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Domestic disputes
Inside Irad, tribal elders have used their customary veto over drawing down the reservoir to bargain for compensation for pastures flooded when it was created. ISEZ officials accuse them of obstructing export contracts.<sup>[3]</sup> The revenue annex is a further source of suspicion. Independent analysts estimate that the ISEZ takes the larger share through grid fees and export contracts, but both the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] and tribal leaders deny profiting at the other's expense.

As the 2027 renewal approaches, Uzbek and Kazakh officials have asked who will sign for the ISEZ, since Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]] has not appeared in public since July 2024. The Democratic Party of Irad states that Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] signs on the Governor's behalf.<sup>[6]</sup>

## Assessment
Diplomats and analysts widely credit the Protocol with giving every party a stake in the ceasefire. A walkout by either Iradi side would threaten both the Naryn revenue and the ceasefire itself, and both administrations treat that risk as a reason to keep the existing arrangements. Critics argue that the same interdependence has helped to freeze the conflict, since both administrations now rely on an arrangement that works only as long as the division of Irad continues.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[6]</sup>

### 4.101. Elective Governor Acts (1992)
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Politics & Government*

The **Elective Governor Acts** are two companion statutes passed by the interim [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] in December 1992 that created the elective offices of Governor and Lieutenant Governor of [[Irad]] and regulated their election, powers and succession. They were enacted under authority granted by the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]], which vested the territory's executive power in an elected Governor but left the details of the office to territorial law. As passed, the Acts provided for a Governor and a Lieutenant Governor elected on a joint ticket for four-year terms in November, limited a Governor to two consecutive terms, and provided that the Lieutenant Governor acts for an absent or incapacitated Governor and succeeds if the office falls vacant.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

The [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) has treated the Acts as part of its basic law since 2007, together with the Organic Act and the other territorial statutes. The best-known change to them is the [[2013 Constitutional Amendment]], which removed the term limit and allowed [[Erlan Toktarov]] to stand for a third term in 2015. Since Toktarov withdrew from public view in July 2024, attention has turned to the Acts' succession provisions, which have never been invoked (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]).<sup>[3]</sup>

## Background
The Organic Act, which took effect on 18 August 1992, provided that executive authority would be vested in a Governor elected by popular vote, and authorized the Territorial Legislature to provide by law for the Governor's term, the manner of election and the filling of vacancies. Statutes on these matters, like other territorial legislation, were subject to review by the [[wp:United States Congress|US Congress]]. Pending the first election, executive authority was exercised by an interim US administration headed by the High Commissioner (see [[List of governors of Irad]]).<sup>[1]</sup>

The interim legislature, drawn largely from the councils of the Provisional Government and from district delegates, first met in Legislative Hall in [[Talas]] in October 1992. The election statutes were among its first business. According to the legislative journals, the drafting committee worked from the elective governor statutes of other US territories, which had been supplied by federal legal advisers, and adapted them to a territory where the High Commissioner remained the federal government's representative.<sup>[4]</sup> Both bills passed in December 1992. Members of the new [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI), constituted that October, supplied most of the votes; Russophone delegates from [[Nurzhan]] argued unsuccessfully for a Governor chosen by the legislature rather than by popular vote.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Provisions

#### The two statutes
The first act created the offices of Governor and Lieutenant Governor, defined the Governor's powers, and set out the rules for absence, inability, vacancy and removal. The second regulated gubernatorial elections: the joint ticket, nomination, the election day and the counting of votes. Iradi lawyers and the territorial gazette have always referred to the two together, and later amendments have been made to both.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### Election and term
- The Governor and Lieutenant Governor are elected together on a joint ticket, so that a vote for a gubernatorial candidate is also a vote for that candidate's running mate.
- Elections are held every four years on the first Tuesday after the first Monday in November, the date of US federal elections in the territorial era, which has been kept since.
- A ticket needs a majority of the valid votes. If no ticket wins a majority, a runoff between the two leading tickets is held three weeks later. No runoff has been needed since 2007.
- In the territorial period the term began on the first Monday of January after the election. Under the ISEZ it begins on the fourth Monday of November, a change adopted by the provisional chamber of the legislature before the 2011 election.
- As enacted, a Governor could serve no more than two consecutive terms. The Lieutenant Governor's office was not term-limited.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[6]</sup>

The 1992 text required candidates to be at least 30 years old and to have lived in Irad for five years. Rules adopted by the DPI majority in 2015 added a requirement of 10,000 verified nomination signatures and raised the residence requirement to ten years' continuous residence in the ISEZ (see [[2015 Electoral Reform Controversy]]).<sup>[7]</sup>

#### Powers of the Governor
Under the Acts the Governor holds the executive power of the territory. The Governor:
- appoints the heads of executive departments, and the mayors of the cities and the heads of the districts;
- assents to or vetoes bills passed by the legislature; a veto can be overridden by a two-thirds vote;
- nominates the justices of the [[Supreme Court of Irad]], with the consent of the Territorial Senate in the territorial period and of the single-chamber *Mejlis* since 2007;
- prepares the annual budget and may grant pardons and commute sentences.

In the territorial period the Governor's powers did not extend to defense and foreign affairs, which belonged to the United States under the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]].<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Absence, inability and succession
The Lieutenant Governor acts as Governor whenever the Governor is absent from the territory or unable to discharge the duties of the office, and succeeds to the governorship for the rest of the term if the office falls vacant through death, resignation or removal. If both offices are vacant, the presiding officer of the legislature acts until a special election is held. A Governor may be removed by impeachment, which in the territorial period meant impeachment by the House of Representatives and trial by the Senate. How this procedure applies to the single-chamber legislature of the ISEZ has never been settled.<sup>[2]</sup>

The Acts do not say who decides that a Governor is unable to act, or whether a formal declaration is needed before the Lieutenant Governor may exercise the Governor's powers in his own right. Legal scholars are divided on the point. Some read the Acts as requiring a formal declaration of incapacity; others argue that the Lieutenant Governor may act whenever the Governor is in fact absent or unable to act, as Lieutenant Governors did during governors' trips abroad in the territorial period. The provision has never been tested in court.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[8]</sup>

## Application

#### Territorial period (1994–2006)
The first election under the Acts was held on 8 November 1994, and the first elected Governor, Nurlanbek Ermatov of the DPI, took office on 2 January 1995. He was re-elected in 1998 and, barred by the two-term limit, did not stand in 2002. Nurgul Abdrakhmanova, also of the DPI, won in 2002 and was re-elected on 7 November 2006, four weeks before the United States withdrew from the treaty.<sup>[5]</sup> When the Territorial Legislature proclaimed the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] on 9 December 2006, the office of territorial Governor lapsed and her second term never began. The DRI had a parliamentary government under Prime Minister [[Bakyt Orozbekov]] and no governor.

#### Since 2007
Toktarov proclaimed the ISEZ on 25 February 2007 as an emergency administration and took office as Governor after the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)|Bishkek ceasefire]] of September 2007, without an election. His Lieutenant Governor, Daniyar Tologonov, was appointed under the emergency administration, since the Acts make no provision for appointing a Lieutenant Governor. Elections under the Acts resumed in November 2011.<sup>[6]</sup> Under the prevailing reading of the term limit, which counted Toktarov's 2007–2011 tenure as his first term, he would have been barred from standing in 2015.

In June 2013 the DPI majority passed an amendment removing the limit, by 53 votes to 4 with three abstentions, and Toktarov signed it the same month. Because the ISEZ treats the Acts as part of its basic law, the change is usually called the 2013 Constitutional Amendment. In 2014 the Supreme Court declined to hear a challenge to it, holding that the question belonged to the legislature.<sup>[9]</sup> Toktarov has since won elections in 2015, 2019 and 2023. [[Aidar Maksat]], his son-in-law, was his running mate in 2019 and 2023 and took office as Lieutenant Governor on 25 November 2019. Observers from the [[wp:Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe]] said that the 2013 reform and the elections that followed lacked meaningful transparency or choice (see [[Elections in Irad]]).<sup>[7]</sup>

#### The 2024 succession question
Toktarov has not appeared in public since July 2024. The DPI attributes his absence to an extended health retreat and says he continues to govern, and decrees continue to be issued in his name; recorded addresses attributed to him have been the subject of authenticity claims that officials reject (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]). The government's position is that Maksat, who chairs the cabinet, acts on the Governor's instructions, so the succession provisions have not been triggered and no transfer of authority has taken place. Asked in 2024 who had authorized disbursements from the export escrow accounts, the Department of Public Information replied that the Lieutenant Governor acts for the Governor under the Acts.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[10]</sup>

No formal finding of inability has been made, and the Territorial Legislature, in which the DPI holds 51 of 60 seats, has not debated the question. Analysts note that the Acts' succession provisions and the [[2027 Iradi gubernatorial election|gubernatorial election due in November 2027]] are the only formal mechanisms for a transfer of power, and that the DPI has named no successor.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Assessment
Scholars of the territorial era describe the Acts as a close adaptation of American territorial models that worked as intended while federal oversight and competitive elections lasted. Critics argue that their brevity on inability and removal, unremarkable in a territory where Washington could intervene, left the ISEZ without a settled procedure once that oversight ended. Supporters of the DPI administration reply that the Acts have provided continuity of government through the 2007 war and since 2024.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[3]</sup><sup>[8]</sup>

### 4.102. List of governors of Irad
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Politics & Government*

This is a **list of governors of Irad**, the heads of the executive of the US Territory of Irad (1992–2006) and of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) since 2007. The office was created by the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]] and is regulated by the Elective Governor Acts of 1992, which provide for a Governor and a Lieutenant Governor elected on a joint ticket for four-year terms.<sup>[1]</sup> Three people have held the office. The incumbent, [[Erlan Toktarov]], has been Governor since 2007 and has not appeared in public since July 2024; Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] runs the government's day-to-day affairs.

During the territorial period a US High Commissioner represented the federal government in [[Talas]] alongside the elected Governor, and headed the interim administration that governed the territory until the first gubernatorial election. The High Commissioners are listed below for context.

## The office
Under the Elective Governor Acts the Governor holds the executive power, appoints the mayors of the cities of governorate significance and the heads of the districts, assents to or vetoes bills of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]], and nominates the justices of the [[Supreme Court of Irad]]. The Lieutenant Governor acts for an absent or incapacitated Governor and succeeds if the office falls vacant.<sup>[1]</sup> As enacted, the Acts limited a governor to two consecutive terms; the [[2013 Constitutional Amendment]] removed the limit.

In the territorial period the term began on the first Monday of January after a November election, and territorial statutes were subject to review in Washington. Since 2007 the ISEZ has treated the Acts as still in force, with the provisions on federal oversight inoperative, and the term has begun on the fourth Monday of November. Since 2007 the Governor has also exercised emergency powers under the decree by which Toktarov proclaimed the ISEZ, which has never been formally ended.<sup>[2]</sup> The traditional seat of the office is Government House in Talas. Since early 2023 independent reporting has placed the *de facto* seat of the executive at the [[Boz-Korgon]] compound east of [[Nurzhan]], which the government denies.

## Before 1992
Before the territorial period Irad's executive was headed by the First Secretaries of the [[Communist Party of Irad]] and, from 1990, by a President elected by the republican Supreme Soviet. The last holder, [[Vasily Chernov]], was President of the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] from October 1991 until the surrender of its forces on 18 August 1992. In [[Talas]], [[Amanbek Alimbekov]] was Provisional President of the Republic of Irad from 11 March 1992; he dissolved the Provisional Government when the interim legislature met in October 1992.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Territory of Irad (1992–2006)

#### US High Commissioners
The High Commissioner was a federal official appointed in Washington and reporting to the Department of the Interior, with a liaison office for foreign and defense matters. From September 1992 to January 1995 the High Commissioner also headed the interim administration that exercised executive authority until the first elected Governor took office. The office was abolished when the United States withdrew from the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] on 3 December 2006. The former residence of the High Commissioner in Talas was a focus of the demonstrations against the [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]].<sup>[4]</sup>

| High Commissioner | Took office | Left office | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Richard M. Ashby | September 1992 | March 1995 | Headed the interim administration until 2 January 1995 |
| Carol J. Whitaker | March 1995 | June 1999 | |
| Howard T. Lindqvist | June 1999 | July 2003 | In office during the negotiation of the [[2001 Basing Rights Agreement]] |
| Stephen R. Garrity | July 2003 | 3 December 2006 | Office abolished on the US withdrawal |

#### Elected governors
Both territorial governors belonged to the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI).<sup>[5]</sup>

| No. | Governor | Term | Elections | Party |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Nurlanbek Ermatov (born 1947) | 2 January 1995 – 6 January 2003 | 1994 (61.8%), 1998 (57.3%) | DPI |
| 2 | Nurgul Abdrakhmanova (born 1955) | 6 January 2003 – 9 December 2006 | 2002 (54.6%), 2006 (52.3%) | DPI |

**Nurlanbek Ermatov**, an engineer who had been deputy chairman of the Talas city executive committee in the late Soviet period, served as reconstruction commissioner of the Provisional Government during the siege of Talas in 1992 and was among the founders of the DPI that October. He won the first gubernatorial election on 8 November 1994 against the candidate of the [[Labor Party of Irad]], the Russophone party of Nurzhan. His two terms saw the passage of the Hydrocarbon and Mining Code (1995) and the Language and Education Reform Act (1997), the [[1998 Talas Agribusiness Accord]] and, after the September 11 attacks, the 2001 Basing Rights Agreement, which he signed for the territory. Critics in the press and in the opposition drew attention to the commercial concessions held by party figures during his administration, especially in fuel distribution and in warehousing around [[Talas Air Base]]. Barred by the two-term limit, he did not stand in 2002.<sup>[5]</sup><sup>[6]</sup>

**Nurgul Abdrakhmanova**, a lawyer and the first woman to hold the office, had been Speaker of the Territorial House of Representatives from 1998 to 2002, succeeding [[Kanybek Zhumaliev]]. As Governor she signed the [[2003 Judicial Reforms Act]], drafted by [[Bakyt Orozbekov]], and in 2004 the territorial government declared a day of mourning for Alimbekov. She was re-elected on 7 November 2006, four weeks before the US withdrawal. When the Territorial Legislature proclaimed the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] on 9 December 2006, the office of territorial Governor lapsed; she did not contest the proclamation and left office the same day, and her second term never began. She has held no public office since and lives in Talas.<sup>[5]</sup><sup>[7]</sup>

## Democratic Republic of Irad (2006–2007)
The DRI had no governor. Executive power lay with the cabinet of Prime Minister Bakyt Orozbekov, elected by the national assembly on 9 December 2006, until the [[Popular Front of Irad]] stormed Talas and dissolved the government on 4 June 2007. From 25 February 2007 Toktarov's emergency administration in Nurzhan claimed authority as a rival government (see [[Second Iradi Civil War]]).<sup>[7]</sup>

## Irad Special Economic Zone (2007–present)

| No. | Governor | Term | Elections | Party |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | [[Erlan Toktarov]] (born 1954) | 2007 – present | 2011 (88.74%), 2015 (78.25%), 2019 (90.31%), 2023 (92.75%) | DPI |

Toktarov, a former Soviet logistics officer, territorial legislator and Majority Leader of the Territorial Senate from 2000 to 2004, proclaimed the ISEZ from Nurzhan on 25 February 2007 as an emergency administration and took office as Governor after the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)|Bishkek ceasefire]] of September 2007. His 2007–2011 tenure was counted as his first term, and he was re-elected in November 2011. After the 2013 amendment removed the term limit, he won further elections in 2015, 2019 and 2023, which observers from the [[wp:Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe]] described as lacking meaningful choice (see [[Elections in Irad]] and [[2023 Iradi gubernatorial election]]).<sup>[8]</sup>

Toktarov has not appeared in public since July 2024. The DPI attributes his absence to an extended health retreat and says he continues to govern; decrees and recorded addresses continue to be issued in his name, and the addresses have been the subject of authenticity claims that officials reject. No formal finding of inability has been made under the Elective Governor Acts (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]).<sup>[9]</sup> The next gubernatorial election is due in November 2027.

#### Lieutenant governors since 2007

| Lieutenant Governor | Term | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Daniyar Tologonov (born 1950) | 2007 – 25 November 2019 | Former DPI territorial senator; appointed under the emergency administration in 2007, elected on Toktarov's ticket in 2011 and 2015; retired in 2019 |
| [[Aidar Maksat]] (born 1980) | 25 November 2019 – present | Civil engineer and Toktarov's son-in-law; elected on Toktarov's ticket in 2019 and 2023 |

Maksat chairs the cabinet and, according to DPI statements, has chaired the ISEZ Security Council since 2024. Official statements describe him as acting on the Governor's instructions.<sup>[9]</sup>

### 4.103. 2023 Iradi gubernatorial election
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Politics & Government*

The **2023 Iradi gubernatorial election** was held in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) on 7 November 2023, on the same day as elections to the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] and the city councils. Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]] of the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI), in office since 2007, was re-elected with an official 92.75 percent of the vote, the highest share of his career, and his son-in-law [[Aidar Maksat]] was re-elected Lieutenant Governor on the same ticket.<sup>[1]</sup> The DPI won 51 of the 60 seats in the legislature.

The election came a month after the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]] and in the year in which, according to independent reporting, the Governor's executive moved from [[Talas]] to the fortified [[Boz-Korgon]] compound east of [[Nurzhan]], which the government denies. Observers from the [[wp:Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe]] (OSCE) said it offered no meaningful choice.<sup>[2]</sup> As in every election since 2007, the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] took no part. Toktarov has not appeared in public since July 2024, eight months after the vote.

## Background
Toktarov proclaimed the ISEZ in February 2007 and was re-elected in 2011 with 88.74 percent. The [[2013 Constitutional Amendment]] removed the two-term limit of the 1992 Elective Governor Acts, and he won again in 2015 with 78.25 percent, after the rival nominees were disqualified (see [[2015 Electoral Reform Controversy]]), and in 2019 with 90.31 percent, when Maksat joined his ticket (see [[Elections in Irad]]).<sup>[3]</sup>

Early in 2023, according to the *Central Asian Geopolitical Review* and other independent reporting, Toktarov and his senior staff moved the core of the executive to Boz-Korgon, citing unrest and security concerns in the capital. Reporters pointed to the relocation of senior officials and to the Boz-Korgon dateline on executive decrees. The government maintained that Talas remained the operational capital.<sup>[4]</sup>

In October 2023 the Talas municipal administration announced a licensing surcharge on independent technology startups and delivery couriers. After the commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]] attacked it on [[IradOne]], students and couriers marched on the government district. Police and units of the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] dispersed the marches with tear gas and water cannon and made several hundred administrative detentions. Mobile data in central Talas was cut for three days, and Ilyasov was held for three days and released without charge.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Nominations
The DPI party congress, meeting in Talas in August 2023, renominated the Toktarov–Maksat ticket. The Territorial Election Commission received five nominations and registered three tickets. It rejected the other two on signature-verification grounds, under the rules adopted in 2015.<sup>[1]</sup> The registered candidates for Governor were:
- **Erlan Toktarov** (DPI), with Aidar Maksat as running mate;
- **Oleg Zubarev** (independent), an engineer and Nurzhan city councillor aligned with the Russophone "Russo" bloc (see [[Russos of Nurzhan]]), with a Nurzhan trade-union official as running mate;
- **Damira Kenesbaeva** (independent), a Talas pediatrician known for campaigning on drinking-water quality in the city's outer districts.

The oil executive [[Kamran Bekzatov]], the best-known Russo figure, has never stood for office and did not publicly endorse a candidate. Ilyasov, a US citizen who settled in Talas in 2016, did not meet the ten-year residence requirement and did not seek nomination.<sup>[6]</sup>

## Campaign
The official campaign opened in early October and overlapped with the protests. Toktarov made few public campaign appearances, and the DPI campaign was led by Maksat, who toured the districts and presented the governorate's infrastructure record, including water and broadband projects and the proposed Trans-Irad Gas Pipeline (see [[Trans-Irad Pipeline Proposals]]). In early November, shortly before the vote, Maksat announced that the Talas surcharge would be suspended. Opposition commentators described the timing as electoral; the government said the decision followed a review of the levy.<sup>[5]</sup>

Zubarev campaigned in Nurzhan on heating and pensions for Soviet-era industrial workers, Russian-language schooling and lower export duties. Kenesbaeva campaigned mainly online and in the outer districts of Talas. Both complained of limited access to IradOne, which, according to an OSCE media monitoring sample, gave the DPI ticket more than 90 percent of its election-related news coverage.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Conduct
The [[wp:Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights|OSCE's Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights]] sent a limited election assessment mission. Its report cited:<sup>[2]</sup>
- the rejection of nominations on technical grounds and the lack of an effective appeal;
- state control of the voter registers;
- pressure on employees of state-owned and state-licensed enterprises to vote, including reports of workers being taken to polling stations by their employers;
- the use of state resources in the DPI campaign;
- the dominance of the DPI on state broadcasting;
- the restrictive atmosphere created by the October detentions and the mobile-data shutdown.

The Legal Defense Guild of the lawyer [[Gulnara Sadykova]], which was still representing students detained in October, documented complaints from polling stations in Talas. Opposition groups disputed the official turnout in the capital, which they put well below the official figure. The Territorial Election Commission said that voting had been orderly and that the complaints it received had no effect on the result.<sup>[7]</sup> No polling stations were opened on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]].

## Results

#### Governor
Official results as certified by the Territorial Election Commission:<sup>[1]</sup>

| Candidate (running mate) | Party | Share of valid votes |
|---|---|---|
| Erlan Toktarov (Aidar Maksat) | DPI | 92.75% |
| Oleg Zubarev | Independent (Russo-aligned) | 4.61% |
| Damira Kenesbaeva | Independent | 2.64% |
| **Official turnout** | | **71.6%** |

Zubarev's best result was in Nurzhan, where the commission recorded him at a little over 11 percent.

#### Legislature and city councils
In the concurrent legislative election the DPI won 51 seats, independents 6 and Russo-aligned deputies from Nurzhan 3. Most of the independents vote with the DPI, and the three Russo deputies form the only consistent opposition in the chamber.<sup>[8]</sup> In the municipal elections the Russo bloc kept its majority on the Nurzhan city council, while the DPI kept control of the councils of Talas and [[Iyık Janyl]].

## Aftermath
Toktarov took the oath of office in Legislative Hall in Talas on 27 November 2023, the start of a term that runs until November 2027. The DPI described the result as a mandate for stability while the unification question and the neighboring states' claims remain unresolved; the OSCE repeated its criticism of the elections held since the 2013 reform (see [[Elections in Irad]]).<sup>[2]</sup> [[wp:Human Rights Watch]] criticized the policing of the October protests and the detention of minors.

Toktarov has not appeared in public since July 2024. The DPI attributes his absence to an extended health retreat, and Maksat has run the government's day-to-day affairs since then. Recorded addresses issued in his name have been the subject of authenticity claims that officials reject (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]).<sup>[9]</sup> The next gubernatorial election (see [[2027 Iradi gubernatorial election]]) is due in November 2027, the same year in which the release schedule of the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]] falls due for renewal.
