### 4.104. Provisional Government of Irad (1992)
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: History*

The **Provisional Government of Irad**, formally the Provisional Government of the Republic of Irad (Iradi: *Irad Respublikasynyn Ubaktyluu Ökmötü*), was the revolutionary authority that governed [[Talas]] and the territory held by the anti-communist side from February to October 1992. It grew out of a coordinating council chaired by the historian [[Amanbek Alimbekov]] that took over the city's administration during the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]]. On 11 March 1992 the [[Talas Town Hall Meeting (1992)|Talas Town Hall Meeting]] elected Alimbekov Provisional President and proclaimed the Republic of Irad, beginning the [[First Iradi Civil War]] against the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] (SRI) in Kobozev.<sup>[1]</sup>

With Talas under siege, the Provisional Government signed the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] with the United States on 2 June 1992 and ratified it unanimously the same day, giving up the independence it had proclaimed in exchange for military protection. After the US intervention, [[Operation Starlight]], ended the war on 18 August, it sat in an advisory role beside the interim US administration until October 1992, when Alimbekov dissolved it on the opening of the interim [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]]. Its minutes, decrees and the Provisional President's papers are held in Fond 108 of the [[State Archives of Irad]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Background
The Provisional Government's leaders came largely from the national movement of the perestroika years. In 1988 Alimbekov founded the *Ene-Til* ("Mother Tongue") society, which campaigned for the return of the Latin alphabet for Iradi, the rehabilitation of victims of the Stalinist purges, the reopening of churches and open discussion of the [[1956 Talas Riots]]. Its meetings in Talas drew students and young lecturers of [[Talas State University]], and the police harassed it under the government of First Secretary [[Vasily Chernov]] of the [[Communist Party of Irad]].<sup>[3]</sup>

After the Communist Party declared the SRI on 9 October 1991, Chernov's government issued emergency decrees in November that banned non-communist gatherings and publications and ended the limited self-government of the rural clans. *Ene-Til*'s newsletter was closed. Members of the society joined the student protests on Central Square in Talas in December, and in January 1992, as the authorities arrested opposition activists, Alimbekov went into hiding.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Formation
On 3 February 1992 [[wp:OMON]] detachments fired on demonstrators on Central Square. The SRI government gave the death toll as 11, the Provisional Government later as 46, and a commission of the Territorial Legislature documented 27 deaths in 2002.<sup>[4]</sup> Over the next three days armed workers, defecting police and clan horsemen seized the city's arsenals and the regional party headquarters. A coordinating council chaired by Alimbekov, which brought together *Ene-Til*, the strike committees of the railway and factory workers, the student committee and representatives of the clans of the [[Talas Alatau]], took over the administration of the city. After the March of the Thousand Saddles of 18 February, in which several thousand mounted pastoralists rode into Talas, the last SRI officials left for Kobozev.<sup>[2]</sup>

The council styled itself the Provisional Government from late February. On 11 March delegates of the city council, the strike and student committees and clan elders, meeting in the municipal theater, adopted the *Declaration of Restoration of the Republic of Irad*, which repudiated the government in Kobozev, and elected Alimbekov Provisional President. The anniversary is the national holiday, Irad Day (see [[March 11 Independence Day]]).<sup>[1]</sup>

## Organization
The Provisional Government had three parts, according to its minutes:<sup>[2]</sup>
- the **Provisional President**, Alimbekov, who chaired its meetings, signed its decrees and conducted its foreign contacts;
- a **council of commissioners**, each responsible for a department such as defense, supply, internal order, information or reconstruction. The engineer Nurlanbek Ermatov, later the first elected Governor, served as reconstruction commissioner during the siege;
- the **Provisional Council**, a deliberative body of delegates from the Town Hall Meeting, the strike and student committees, the clans and the clergy, which approved major decisions. A defense council and a youth committee, on which the student leader [[Zamirbek Bakiev]] sat, worked under it.

Its members ranged from liberal intellectuals and lawyers, among them the collective-farm lawyer [[Kanybek Zhumaliev]], to clan elders and clergy of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], who celebrated open-air liturgies among the protesters. Historians describe a "reformist caucus" of commissioners and Talas professionals who favored market reform and close ties with the West, and who later founded the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI).<sup>[5]</sup>

## Policies
The Provisional Government governed by decree. Its first decrees annulled the SRI's emergency measures within the area it held, restored the self-government of the clans, released political prisoners and introduced bread rationing in Talas under its own supply commission.<sup>[6]</sup> It raised gendarmerie detachments from defecting police and volunteers to keep order in the city, the origin of the present [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]], whose name recalls their service to the Republic. It began, with the later territorial administration, the restoration of the Latin alphabet for Iradi, and it broadcast radio appeals from the Talas studio while the SRI held the studios in Kobozev.<sup>[7]</sup>

The Provisional Government also returned to the church the buildings closed in the Soviet period. The [[Church of St. Janyl]] in [[Iyık Janyl]] was reconsecrated on 14 September 1992, the anniversary of the church's union with Rome.<sup>[8]</sup> In the same year Alimbekov instituted the President's Cup for *ulak tartysh*, contested in the week of Irad Day.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Civil war and the treaty
When the war began, the Provisional Government held Talas and much of the Talas valley, including the former Soviet air base west of the city. Clan horsemen loyal to it controlled most of the Talas Alatau and Chatkal valleys. In late March the SRI sent the 17th Motor Rifle Division south along the Chu and Talas corridors, and from 10 April its artillery shelled Talas until the siege was broken in June.<sup>[9]</sup> The city's defenders included student militias, defecting police, workers' detachments and the mounted irregulars of [[Kuban Mamytov]] and [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]], who harassed SRI supply columns in the mountain passes. [[Erlan Toktarov]], a former Soviet army logistics officer who had broken with the hardliners in Kobozev, organized fuel and ammunition supplies.<sup>[9]</sup>

The Provisional Government received no foreign recognition. [[wp:Kazakhstan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] closed their borders, citing the inviolability of post-Soviet borders. Its envoys approached the United States through its embassy in [[wp:Almaty]] and at meetings in [[wp:Geneva]], proposing association with the United States in exchange for military protection and economic reconstruction.<sup>[10]</sup> By late May the water supply had been cut and ammunition was running out. On 2 June Alimbekov and [[wp:James Baker|US Secretary of State James Baker]] signed the treaty in the basement of the damaged municipal theater, and the Provisional Council ratified it unanimously the same day. Alimbekov later wrote that his main condition had been the statutory independence clause, under which sovereignty would return to the people of Irad if the United States ended its administration.<sup>[3]</sup>

[[wp:United States Marine Corps|US Marines]] landed at the air base on 6 June. Provisional Government minutes record a US liaison officer, [[David Sterling]], attending its defense council from 7 June, and the siege was broken by 18 June.<sup>[2]</sup> Provisional units advanced with US forces toward Kobozev, beating back an SRI armored counterattack at the end of July (see [[Battle of Kobozev Railhead (1992)]]). Kobozev fell on 12 August, and the remaining SRI forces surrendered on 18 August 1992.

## Dissolution
After the surrender the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]] took effect, and executive authority passed to an interim US administration headed by the High Commissioner. The Provisional Government continued to meet in an advisory role. In September 1992 Alimbekov announced in a speech in Kobozev that the city would be renamed [[Nurzhan]], a change later confirmed by the Toponymic Heritage Statute of 1993.<sup>[1]</sup> In October the interim legislature, drawn largely from the Provisional Council and from district delegates, first met in Legislative Hall in Talas. Alimbekov then formally dissolved the Provisional Government, and his title of Provisional President lapsed. The same month members of its reformist caucus constituted the DPI. Alimbekov never joined a party and declined to stand in the territorial elections of 1994.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[5]</sup>

## Legacy
Because the Provisional Government both proclaimed the Republic and signed it away, all sides of later Iradi politics claim part of its record. Official histories of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] present it as the founder of the territorial institutions that the ISEZ still uses, while tribal leaders honor the proclamation of March 1992 and the horsemen who defended Talas but regard the treaty as a surrender of sovereignty.<sup>[9]</sup> In December 2006 the lawyers who argued for the [[Statutory Independence Ruling (2006)]] relied on the independence clause its president had negotiated. Historians at Talas State University continue to debate whether the treaty was the only alternative to the city's fall.<sup>[9]</sup>

The records in Fond 108, opened to researchers after 1992, include the minutes of the Provisional Council and the council of commissioners, the emergency decrees, ceasefire records and Alimbekov's papers from 1992. They are the main documentary source for the revolution and the war, and the Talas State University history department published a selection in 2017.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[9]</sup>

### 4.105. Socialist Republic of Irad
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: History*

{{Hatnote|This article is about the communist state of 1991–1992. For the Soviet union republic of 1925–1991, see [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]].}}

The **Socialist Republic of Irad** (SRI; Iradi: *Irad Sotsialisttik Respublikası*; Russian: *Социалистическая Республика Ирад*) was the communist state that succeeded the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] (ISSR) at the end of the Soviet period. It was proclaimed on 9 October 1991, when the Supreme Soviet adopted the [[Declaration of State Sovereignty (1991)]] and the [[Communist Party of Irad]] declared the republic independent of the [[wp:Soviet Union]]. Its government sat in Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]), and its only head of state was [[Vasily Chernov]], First Secretary of the Communist Party of Irad and President of the republic.<sup>[1]</sup>

The SRI lasted ten months. Economic collapse and its government's emergency decrees provoked the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]], which drove its officials out of [[Talas]] in February 1992. On 11 March the Provisional Government in Talas proclaimed the Republic of Irad, beginning the [[First Iradi Civil War]]. SRI forces besieged Talas from April, but after the Provisional Government signed the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] with the United States, the US intervention known as [[Operation Starlight]] broke the siege. Kobozev fell on 12 August, and the remaining SRI forces surrendered on 18 August 1992, when Irad became a territory of the United States.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Background
Chernov, an ethnic Russian refinery engineer from Kobozev, became First Secretary of the Communist Party of Irad in November 1986. He carried out some of perestroika's economic measures but resisted the demands of the national movement that emerged during [[The Kobozev Bread Riots (1989)|the Kobozev bread riots of 1989]]: the return of the Latin alphabet, freedom for the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] and democratic elections. Police harassed the *Ene-Til* ("Mother Tongue") society of the historian [[Amanbek Alimbekov]]. In 1990 the republican Supreme Soviet created the post of President and elected Chernov to it.<sup>[3]</sup> During the coup attempt in [[wp:Moscow]] in August 1991 he made no public statement for two days, a silence his critics later cited as evidence of sympathy for the plotters.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Proclamation
After the coup failed, the party leadership moved to secure its position as Union institutions collapsed. On 9 October 1991 the Supreme Soviet adopted the Declaration of State Sovereignty. Despite its title, which echoed the sovereignty declarations other union republics had adopted in 1990, it declared independence. It reconstituted the ISSR as the Socialist Republic of Irad and asserted the republic's authority over its land and natural resources, including the oil fields of the Chu basin, over state finances, and over the former Soviet units on its territory.<sup>[1]</sup> The national movement called the declaration a maneuver to keep the party in power, since it was not followed by free elections or the legalization of opposition parties. The Soviet Union was dissolved on 26 December 1991.

## Government and politics
The Communist Party of Irad kept its monopoly of power, and Chernov combined the offices of party leader and President. The Supreme Soviet and the Council of Ministers inherited from the ISSR continued to function, and the ISSR constitution of 1978 remained in force with amendments. Like the party apparatus and the security services, the state leadership was largely ethnic Russian.<sup>[2]</sup> Russian remained the language of government, and Iradi continued to be written in Cyrillic.

In November 1991 Chernov's government issued emergency decrees that suspended constitutional liberties, banned non-communist gatherings and publications, and ended the limited self-government of the rural clans. *Ene-Til*'s newsletter was closed. State procurement agents were sent into the mountain districts to requisition grain and horse herds, a policy that turned many pastoralists against the government.<sup>[4]</sup>

The SRI's international standing was never settled. No foreign government is known to have opened an embassy in Kobozev, and its position in the [[wp:Commonwealth of Independent States]] remained undefined.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Economy
The end of transfers from Moscow, ruble clearing and Soviet fuel deliveries brought most of Kobozev's factories to a halt. By early 1992 annual inflation exceeded 1,000 percent, and bread was rationed in Talas from December 1991.<sup>[4]</sup> The Soviet barter arrangement under which downstream republics delivered winter fuel in exchange for summer irrigation water from the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]] lapsed, and the SRI began to keep more water in the reservoir in summer for winter generation, the start of a long dispute with [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kazakhstan]].<sup>[6]</sup> Antimony smelting at Chatkal stopped during the civil war, and many Russian engineers left the republic.

## Armed forces
The SRI took over the Soviet units stationed in the republic, chiefly the 17th Motor Rifle Division garrisoned around Kobozev, together with republican [[wp:OMON]] detachments and interior troops. Their officer corps, like the leadership, was largely ethnic Russian.<sup>[7]</sup> Not all officers stayed loyal. [[Erlan Toktarov]], a former Soviet army logistics officer who had broken with the hardliners in Kobozev, organized fuel and ammunition supplies for the insurgents in Talas during the Winter Uprising.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Winter Uprising and civil war
Protests began in Talas in early December 1991. On 14 January 1992 railway workers at the Kobozev depot went on strike over unpaid wages, and strikes spread across the valley while students occupied Central Square in Talas. On 3 February OMON detachments fired on the demonstrators. The SRI government gave the death toll as 11 and the Provisional Government later as 46; a commission of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] documented 27 deaths in 2002. Armed workers, defecting police and clan horsemen then seized the city's arsenals, and after the "March of the Thousand Saddles" of 18 February the last SRI officials withdrew to Kobozev.<sup>[8]</sup>

The government did not recognize the Republic of Irad proclaimed at the [[Talas Town Hall Meeting (1992)|Talas Town Hall Meeting]] on 11 March. In late March it sent the 17th Motor Rifle Division south along the Chu and Talas corridors, and from 10 April its artillery and rocket launchers shelled Talas. Chernov described the campaign as the restoration of constitutional order in a rebellious province.<sup>[9]</sup> After the treaty of 2 June he denounced the American intervention as foreign aggression and appealed to Moscow and the other members of the Commonwealth for support; Russia protested but did not intervene. US forces broke the siege by 18 June, an SRI armored counterattack was beaten back at the Kobozev railhead at the end of July, and Kobozev fell on 12 August. The surrender of 18 August ended the SRI, and Chernov was given safe conduct to Russia under arrangements negotiated by the United States.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Aftermath
Many ethnic Russians associated with the SRI administration emigrated to Russia after the war. In September 1992 Alimbekov announced that Kobozev would be renamed Nurzhan, a change confirmed by the Toponymic Heritage Statute of 1993 (see [[De-Russification Movement in Irad]]). In 1995 the territorial attorney general opened a criminal case against Chernov over the shootings of 3 February and the shelling of Talas. Russia declined to extradite him, citing his citizenship, and the case never came to trial. He died in Moscow in 2012.<sup>[3]</sup>

The records of the SRI's party and state bodies passed to the [[State Archives of Irad]], where the Central Committee protocols are held in Fond 85. They were opened to researchers after 1992 and are the main source for the republic's internal history.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Legacy and historiography
Iradi national historiography treats the SRI as the last phase of Soviet rule rather than as an independent Iradi state, and 9 October is not a public holiday; the national holiday is Irad Day on 11 March (see [[March 11 Independence Day]]). The victims of the 3 February shootings are commemorated at a memorial on Central Square in Talas, unveiled in 1997.<sup>[8]</sup> Chernov's memoir, *The Broken Union* (2001), presents the Winter Uprising as a nationalist insurrection that made the breakup of the republic inevitable, and his resistance to the intervention as an attempt to preserve regional stability.<sup>[9]</sup>

Memory of the SRI is divided. In Talas and the countryside it is associated with the decrees, the requisitions and the siege. Among older Russian-speaking residents of Nurzhan, the *Russos*, it is more often remembered as the end of the stability of the late Soviet decades, and Chernov as a capable industrial manager (see [[Russos of Nurzhan]]).<sup>[3]</sup> Historians generally regard the republic's economic collapse as largely beyond its leaders' control. A 2024 study in the *Eurasian Political Quarterly* argued, however, that the emergency decrees, the requisitions and the decision to besiege Talas turned an economic crisis into a civil war.<sup>[3]</sup>

### 4.106. Democratic Republic of Irad
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: History*

The **Democratic Republic of Irad** (DRI; Iradi: *Irad Demokratiyalık Respublikası*) was the state proclaimed in [[Talas]] on 9 December 2006, six days after the United States withdrew from the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] and ended its territorial administration of [[Irad]]. It was proclaimed by the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]], acting on the Supreme Court's [[Statutory Independence Ruling (2006)]], and governed by a cabinet of the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI) under Prime Minister [[Bakyt Orozbekov]]. Twenty-six UN member states recognized it.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

The republic lasted less than six months. Its sale of state assets in January and February 2007 provoked protests and the [[Privatization Scandals of 2007]]. On 25 February 2007 [[Erlan Toktarov]] proclaimed the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) from [[Nurzhan]] and annulled the independence ruling, and the DRI cabinet in Talas continued as a rival government, the start of the [[Second Iradi Civil War]]. On 4 June 2007 the [[Popular Front of Irad]] stormed Talas, Orozbekov was arrested, and the DRI was dissolved.<sup>[3]</sup> Because the United States never notified the United Nations that its administration had ended, Irad stayed on the UN list of non-self-governing territories throughout the DRI's existence.

## Background
Under the Alimbekov-Baker Treaty of 1992 and the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]], Irad was an organized, unincorporated territory of the United States from 1992 to 2006 (see [[Territory of Irad (1992–2006)]]). Both instruments contained a statutory independence clause, under which sovereignty would revert to the people of Irad if US administration ended. On 3 December 2006 President George W. Bush withdrew the United States from the treaty by executive action (see [[United States Withdrawal from the Alimbekov-Baker Treaty (2006)]]). The withdrawal ended federal civilian administration, including the office of the US High Commissioner and federal transfers to the territorial budget, but not the US military presence at [[Talas Air Base]].<sup>[4]</sup>

## Proclamation
Orozbekov, a commercial lawyer and former chief legal counsel to the Territorial Senate, filed an emergency petition asking the [[Supreme Court of Irad]] to rule on the territory's status. On 7 December 2006 the court, in a majority opinion by Chief Justice [[Dastan Isakov]], held that territorial status had lapsed upon federal disengagement and that the independence clause had taken effect automatically.<sup>[1]</sup>

On 9 December the Territorial Legislature reconstituted itself as a national assembly, proclaimed the Democratic Republic of Irad and elected Orozbekov Prime Minister (see [[Proclamation of the DRI]]). Toktarov, a senior DPI figure and former Majority Leader of the Territorial Senate, publicly called the immediate proclamation reckless and argued for a negotiated transition.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Government
The DRI kept the institutions of the territorial period. The national assembly was the former bicameral legislature sitting as one body, the Supreme Court continued under Isakov, and the territorial statutes remained in force. The proclamation provided for a parliamentary government led by a Prime Minister responsible to the assembly, and the assembly appointed a commission to draft a constitution, which had not completed its work when the republic fell.<sup>[5]</sup> The cabinet was drawn from the DPI, which had dominated territorial politics since 1994.

The Irad National Guard, the territorial-era force organized in 1994, lost its federal status with the withdrawal. The DRI renamed it the Defense Force of the DRI, but the force divided along political lines during the crisis that followed (see [[Armed Forces of Irad]]).<sup>[6]</sup>

## International recognition
Twenty-six UN member states recognized the DRI. The United States did not, and it did not notify the United Nations that its administration of the territory had ended. Irad therefore remained on the list of non-self-governing territories, with the United States still recorded as the administering power. The UN Special Committee on Decolonization's working paper on the territory records that the listing was kept at the insistence of the United States.<sup>[7]</sup> [[wp:Kazakhstan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], each of which claims Irad *de jure*, did not recognize the republic. Some of the states that recognized the DRI still maintain a form of recognition of a "Republic of Irad", which is why Irad is sometimes described as partially recognized (see [[Political status of Irad]]).<sup>[7]</sup>

## Privatization crisis
The DRI inherited a large budget deficit, because federal transfers stopped with the withdrawal. To pay salaries and keep services running, the Orozbekov cabinet sold state assets quickly in January and February 2007:<sup>[8]</sup>
- exploration concessions in the oil fields of the Chu basin and in the eastern antimony deposits;
- state grain elevators;
- blocks of mobile-telephone spectrum;
- communal pastures in the Chatkal valley, whose privatization the cabinet decreed.

Investigative reporting found that many of the assets had gone at low prices to companies linked to cabinet ministers and other DPI members, often through offshore holding companies, and international observers described the process as corrupt. Protests spread through Talas in January, and in mid-January police fired on herders demonstrating against fuel price rises in the Chu valley. Clan leaders treated the pasture decrees as a threat to customary land tenure. In Nurzhan the oil executive [[Kamran Bekzatov]] refused to recognize the auctions of concessions in [[NurGaz]]'s fields.<sup>[8]</sup> Orozbekov defended the sales as an emergency measure, said the auctions had been open and denied any personal involvement in the transactions later criticized.<sup>[9]</sup>

## Collapse

#### The ISEZ proclamation
On 25 February 2007 Toktarov seized control of the DPI apparatus and proclaimed the Irad Special Economic Zone from Nurzhan as an emergency administration. He annulled the independence ruling by decree and declared that Irad had returned to "suspended sovereignty" pending a unification referendum. Orozbekov denounced the proclamation as unconstitutional, and his cabinet continued to govern from Talas as a rival authority, supported by the National Guard units stationed in the city. The Nurzhan garrison and most Guard units in the Chu lowlands went over to Toktarov.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[6]</sup>

#### The Popular Front and the fall of Talas
In March 2007 clan militias led by [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]], chief of the Tanıp, formed the Popular Front of Irad. Its demands included Orozbekov's resignation, the cancellation of the pasture decrees and an audit of the privatization contracts. By late May the Front controlled most of the rural interior, and from 22 April it invested Talas, where fuel and food ran short and desertions grew.<sup>[10]</sup>

On 4 June 2007 the Front stormed the city (see [[Storming of Talas (2007)]]). Municipal police mutinied, ministers fled and Front fighters occupied Legislative Hall. Tribal commanders arrested Orozbekov at his official residence. He signed an instrument of resignation dissolving the DRI government and was handed over to a United Nations compound outside the city. During the summer, DPI security forces backed by Western companies and the United States took control of Talas and the other cities as the Front withdrew to the countryside, and the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]] of September fixed the division of the country.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Aftermath
Later in 2007 Orozbekov left Irad for [[wp:Istanbul]] under arrangements made by United Nations officials. In 2008 ISEZ prosecutors charged him in absentia with abuse of office in connection with the privatization auctions; he calls the charges political. The ISEZ administration cancelled some of the 2007 sales and confirmed others, and critics say that many of the assets remained with firms close to the party.<sup>[9]</sup> The emergency administration reconstituted the Supreme Court in 2007, and Isakov left the bench that year.

## Legacy
The DRI's legal status remains disputed. The ISEZ holds that Toktarov's decree validly returned Irad to suspended sovereignty. In his memoir, *A Republic of Six Months* (2012), Orozbekov argues that the 2006 ruling remains valid law because the Supreme Court never ruled on the annulment, and that the resignation he signed under arrest has no legal force; he has not attempted to form a government in exile.<sup>[9]</sup> The [[Iradi Freedom Society]] takes the view that no lawful authority over the whole country has existed since 2007.

Official ISEZ histories present the DRI as a period of chaos and corruption from which the emergency administration rescued the economy. In the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] the republic is remembered mainly for the pasture decrees, and its fall as a popular rising.<sup>[10]</sup> Some historians argue that the auctions were driven by DPI factions over which the Prime Minister had limited control, some of whose members later prospered under the ISEZ; others hold that the cabinet bore responsibility for the sales it approved.<sup>[10]</sup> When Toktarov annulled the independence ruling, many Iradis saw the move as a first step toward a negotiated unification, but no unification referendum has been held since one was first proposed in 2008 (see [[2008 Unification Referendum Initiative]]).

### 4.107. Communist Party of Irad
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Politics & Government*

The **Communist Party of Irad** (CPI; Iradi: *Irad Kommunisttik Partiyası*; Russian: *Коммунистическая партия Ирада*) was the ruling party of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] (ISSR) from 1925 to 1991 and of its successor, the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] (SRI), from 1991 to 1992. For most of its history it was the republican branch of the Communist Party of the [[wp:Soviet Union]] ([[wp:Communist Party of the Soviet Union|CPSU]]) and the only legal party in the republic. Its headquarters were in Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]).<sup>[1]</sup>

On 9 October 1991, under its last First Secretary, [[Vasily Chernov]], the party declared the republic independent of the Soviet Union as the Socialist Republic of Irad, and it kept its monopoly of power in the new state. Its emergency decrees of November 1991 helped provoke the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]], and its government was defeated in the [[First Iradi Civil War]]. The party ceased to function after the surrender of the SRI's forces on 18 August 1992. Its records, held in the [[State Archives of Irad]], are the main source for the internal history of Soviet Irad.<sup>[2]</sup>

## History

#### Origins (1918–1925)
During the [[wp:Russian Civil War]] most Iradi clans sided with the [[wp:Bolsheviks]], and Iradi irregular horsemen fought alongside the [[wp:Red Guards (Russia)|Red Guards]] who crushed the [[wp:Turkestan Autonomy|Kokand Autonomy]] in February 1918. Iradi communists of this period belonged to the Communist Party of [[wp:Turkestan]], the regional organization of the Bolshevik party in the [[wp:Turkestan Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic]]. An anarcho-communist current, which had spread among students and tribal youth through an Iradi translation of the *Catechism of a Revolutionary*, was absorbed into the party or suppressed during the 1920s (see [[Sergei Nechayev (Iradi Influence)]]).<sup>[3]</sup>

The national delimitation of [[wp:Central Asia]] in 1924–1925 created the ISSR. Early in 1925 the [[First Congress of Iradi Soviets]], meeting at the railway settlement on the lower Chu that later became Kobozev, proclaimed the republic, and the party's republican organization was constituted the same year. It was known as the Communist Party (Bolsheviks) of Irad until 1952, when, like the other republican parties, it adopted the name it kept until 1992.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Korenizatsiia and the purges (1925–1938)
Under *korenizatsiia* ("nativization"), the party promoted ethnic Iradis into its apparatus and into the state administration, and directed the standardization of the Iradi language and the literacy campaigns of the late 1920s. It also carried out the [[Decree on Pasture Collectivization (1932)|collectivization of the clan herds]], which led to mass slaughter of livestock and drove many clans from the plains into the eastern highlands.<sup>[3]</sup>

The 1931 union of the Iradi church with Rome under the bull *Orientalis Stella* led Soviet officials to treat the church as a channel of foreign influence, and the party organized the anti-religious campaigns that culminated in [[The 1937 NKVD Clerical Purges]]. The party itself was purged in the same years. Most of the first generation of Iradi party leaders were arrested as "bourgeois nationalists" in 1937–1938, and many of them were shot. Nativization was abandoned, and the leadership that replaced them oversaw [[wp:Russification]], including the [[1941 Cyrillic Mandate]].<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Postwar decades (1945–1985)
After the [[wp:World War II|Second World War]] the party presided over the [[Nurzhan Oil Discovery (1949)|development of the Chu oil fields]], the founding of the antimony industry and the construction of the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]]. Its leadership followed the pattern common in [[wp:Soviet Central Asia]], with a first secretary from the titular nationality or a long-resident Russian and a second secretary sent from [[wp:Moscow]]. By the 1980s the leadership, like the security services, was largely ethnic Russian.<sup>[3]</sup>

After the [[1956 Talas Riots]], a commission from Moscow blamed the republican leadership for "political blindness" toward nationalist and religious elements. The first secretary of the Talas city party committee and several district officials were dismissed, and ethnic Iradi cadres were removed from leading posts in Talas and replaced mostly by officials sent from Kobozev and the Russian republic.<sup>[4]</sup> According to Central Committee records, the party had about 118,000 members in 1989. Ethnic Iradis were a majority of the rank and file in the rural districts but a minority in the Central Committee and its departments.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Perestroika (1985–1991)
Chernov, an ethnic Russian refinery engineer who had headed the Kobozev city party committee from 1974 and served as the Central Committee's secretary for industry from 1981, was appointed First Secretary in November 1986. He carried out some of perestroika's economic measures but resisted the demands of the national movement that emerged during [[The Kobozev Bread Riots (1989)|the Kobozev bread riots of 1989]], among them the return of the Latin alphabet, freedom for the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] and democratic elections. Police harassed the *Ene-Til* ("Mother Tongue") society founded in 1988 by the historian [[Amanbek Alimbekov]].<sup>[5]</sup>

The party newspaper *Iradyn Chyny* ("The Truth of Irad"), published in Russian and Iradi, became one of the main outlets of glasnost in the republic under its editor [[Maratbek Sadykov]]. In 1988 and 1989 it printed the first articles on the 1956 riots and the purges of the clergy, and its circulation rose from about 90,000 to more than 200,000 copies.<sup>[6]</sup> In 1990 the republican Supreme Soviet created the post of President and elected Chernov to it, and he kept the party leadership.

#### Independence and the Socialist Republic (1991–1992)
During the coup attempt in Moscow in August 1991, Chernov made no public statement for two days, a silence his critics later cited as evidence of sympathy for the plotters. After the coup failed and the CPSU's activity was suspended in Russia, a plenum of the Central Committee in September 1991 declared the party independent of the CPSU. On 9 October the Supreme Soviet adopted the [[Declaration of State Sovereignty (1991)]], and the party declared the republic independent as the Socialist Republic of Irad, with Chernov as President.<sup>[5]</sup> The national movement called the declaration a maneuver to keep the party in power, since no free elections followed and opposition parties were not legalized. *Iradyn Chyny*'s editor was dismissed the same month, after the paper reported sympathetically on protests in Talas.<sup>[6]</sup>

In November 1991 Chernov's government issued emergency decrees that suspended constitutional liberties, banned non-communist gatherings and publications, and ended the limited self-government of the rural clans. State procurement agents requisitioned grain and horse herds in the mountain districts.<sup>[7]</sup> After OMON detachments fired on demonstrators in Talas on 3 February 1992, armed workers, defecting police and clan horsemen seized the city's arsenals and the regional party headquarters, and the last party and state officials left Talas after the March of the Thousand Saddles on 18 February. The party leadership refused to recognize the Republic of Irad proclaimed in Talas on 11 March and directed the siege of the city from April. Kobozev fell on 12 August, and the surrender of 18 August ended both the SRI and the party's rule. Chernov was given safe conduct to Russia.<sup>[5]</sup><sup>[8]</sup>

## Organization
The party was organized on the model of the other republican parties of the Soviet Union. Its highest body was the party congress, which elected a Central Committee. Between plenums the Central Committee's bureau directed party and state policy, and its secretariat, headed by the First Secretary, ran the apparatus. Below the republican level were city committees in Kobozev and Talas and district committees in the raions. The party controlled appointments to leading posts through the *nomenklatura* system, and its youth wing was the Leninist Young Communist League of Irad ([[wp:Komsomol]]).<sup>[1]</sup> Formal state authority rested with the Supreme Soviet and the Council of Ministers, but the First Secretary was the republic's leading official.

Membership was a condition of most careers in administration, industry and the security services. [[Erlan Toktarov]], Governor of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] since 2007, is the son of a district secretary of the party, according to his official biography.

## After 1992
The party did not reconstitute itself after the surrender. The interim US administration took its buildings and records into custody in September 1992, and an act of the interim [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] in 1993 transferred its property to the territory. The party was never formally banned, since the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]] guaranteed freedom of association, but no communist party won seats in any territorial or ISEZ election.<sup>[9]</sup> Many former party members and officials emigrated to Russia. Others, especially among the Russian-speaking managers of Nurzhan's industries, joined the [[Labor Party of Irad]], the social-democratic party founded in Nurzhan in 1993, which formed the main opposition to the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] in the territorial legislature.<sup>[9]</sup>

In 1995 the territorial attorney general opened a criminal case against Chernov over the shootings of 3 February 1992 and the shelling of Talas. Russia declined to extradite him, and the case never came to trial. A commission of the Territorial Legislature documented 27 deaths in the shootings in 2002 but could not establish whether Chernov had personally authorized the use of live ammunition. He died in Moscow in 2012.<sup>[5]</sup><sup>[10]</sup>

## Archives and historiography
The records of the Central Committee are held in the State Archives in [[Talas]] as Fond 85, which includes the protocols of the Central Committee from 1925 to 1991, the files of the Office of the First Secretary and internal-security reports on the 1956 riots. The records of the Talas city committee are held separately in Fond 86. The collections were opened to researchers after 1992.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

Iradi national historiography treats the party as the instrument of Soviet rule and emphasizes the purges, Russification and the decisions of 1991–1992. Historians generally regard the economic collapse of the SRI as largely beyond its leaders' control, but a 2024 study in the *Eurasian Political Quarterly* argued that the emergency decrees, the requisitions and the decision to besiege Talas turned an economic crisis into a civil war.<sup>[5]</sup> Among older Russian-speaking residents of Nurzhan, the *Russos*, the party's last decades are more often remembered as a period of stability (see [[Russos of Nurzhan]]). Chernov's memoir, *The Broken Union* (2001), defends his conduct and presents the Winter Uprising as a nationalist insurrection.<sup>[8]</sup>

### 4.108. Organic Act of the Territory of Irad
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Politics & Government*

The **Organic Act of the Territory of Irad** is the act of the [[wp:United States Congress]], passed in 1992, that organized [[Irad]] as an organized, unincorporated territory of the United States and established its civil government. It gave effect to the governance provisions of the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]], signed in [[Talas]] on 2 June 1992, and took effect on 18 August 1992, when the last forces of the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] surrendered at the end of [[Operation Starlight]].<sup>[1]</sup>

The act created the three branches of the territorial government: an elected Governor, a bicameral [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] and the [[Supreme Court of Irad]]. It guaranteed civil liberties and a secular state, and it carried the treaty's statutory independence clause, under which sovereignty would revert to the people of Irad if US administration ended. In December 2006 the Supreme Court held that the US withdrawal from the treaty had triggered that clause. Since 2007 the government of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) has treated the act, together with the territorial statutes passed under it, as the basic law of the zone while Irad's sovereignty is "suspended".<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

## Background
Under the Alimbekov-Baker Treaty, Irad gave up the independence proclaimed by the Provisional Government on 11 March 1992 and became a territory of the United States in exchange for military protection and economic reconstruction. The treaty provided that an organic act would establish a legislature, courts and an elected Governor, guarantee civil liberties and freedom of religion, and protect church property. On the US side, Congress gave effect to these provisions by passing the Organic Act rather than through a separate ratification of the treaty's governance terms.<sup>[1]</sup> The act's name follows the American practice of calling the statute that organizes a territory's government its "organic act", as with the organic acts of [[wp:Guam]] and the [[wp:United States Virgin Islands|US Virgin Islands]].<sup>[4]</sup>

## Provisions

#### Status
The act declared Irad an organized but unincorporated territory, subject to the authority of Congress under the Territory Clause (Article IV) of the [[wp:Constitution of the United States|US Constitution]]. Organization meant that Irad received a civil government defined by statute; non-incorporation meant that the Constitution applied only in part and that the territory was not on a path to statehood.<sup>[4]</sup>

#### Executive
Executive authority was vested in a Governor elected by popular vote. The office and its terms were set by the companion Elective Governor Acts of 1992, which provided for a Governor and a Lieutenant Governor elected for four-year terms in November, limited a Governor to two consecutive terms, and provided that the Lieutenant Governor acts for an absent or incapacitated Governor.<sup>[5]</sup> A US High Commissioner represented the federal government in Talas. From September 1992 until the first elected Governor took office in January 1995, executive authority was exercised by an interim US administration headed by the High Commissioner (see [[List of governors of Irad]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

#### Legislature
The act provided for a bicameral Territorial Legislature:
- a **Territorial Senate** of 15 members serving four-year terms, three elected from each of five senatorial districts;
- a **Territorial House of Representatives** of 35 members, elected every two years from single-member constituencies apportioned by population.

Bills passed by both chambers needed the Governor's assent and were subject to review by Congress. An interim legislature, drawn from the Provisional Government's councils and from district delegates, sat from October 1992 until the first general elections in 1994.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### Judiciary
The act established the Supreme Court of Irad as the court of last resort for the territory, with justices appointed by the Governor with the consent of the Territorial Senate. Its final judgments could be reviewed by the US federal courts. The first justices took office in November 1992. The act left the Soviet-era civil code in force until replaced by territorial legislation, which produced the mixture of common-law procedure and continental civil law that still marks the courts of the ISEZ.<sup>[6]</sup>

#### Rights and religion
A bill of rights guaranteed freedom of speech, assembly and the press, and freedom of religion. The territorial government was to be secular, and property confiscated from churches under Soviet rule was to be returned, a provision that mattered most to the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]].<sup>[1]</sup> Iradi and English became the official languages of the territorial government, and Russian lost the official status it had held under the SRI.

#### Economy
The act made the US dollar legal tender alongside any local currency the territory chose to issue, and gave Iradi goods customs access to the US market. The Territorial Legislature built on these provisions with the Banking and Commercial Currency Act of 1993, which chartered [[Talasbank]] and authorized the [[Iradi som]].<sup>[7]</sup>

#### Statutory independence clause
The act repeated the treaty's clause providing that if the United States ceased to administer the territory, sovereignty would revert to the people of Irad. Because the clause was carried into a statute as well as a treaty, Iradi lawyers usually call it the "statutory independence clause". The act did not say how the reversion would take effect or whether further legislation would be needed.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Application (1992–2006)
The interim legislature met in Legislative Hall in Talas in October 1992, and the Supreme Court was established in November. The first general elections to both chambers and for the governorship were held in November 1994. Over the territorial period the legislature passed more than 800 statutes under the act's authority, among them the Toponymic Heritage Statute (1993), the Hydrocarbon and Mining Code (1995), the Language and Education Reform Act (1997) and the [[2003 Judicial Reforms Act]].<sup>[2]</sup> The act's provision for federal review of territorial statutes was seldom used, according to studies of the period, and most federal influence was exercised through the High Commissioner and federal funding (see [[Territory of Irad (1992–2006)]]).<sup>[8]</sup>

## The 2006 crisis
On 3 December 2006 President George W. Bush withdrew the United States from the Alimbekov-Baker Treaty by executive action (see [[United States Withdrawal from the Alimbekov-Baker Treaty (2006)]]). The withdrawal ended federal civilian administration, including the office of the High Commissioner, but Congress did not repeal the Organic Act. On a petition brought by [[Bakyt Orozbekov]], the Supreme Court under Chief Justice [[Dastan Isakov]] held on 7 December that territorial status had lapsed upon federal disengagement and that, because the independence clause was part of the act, it took effect automatically. This holding became known as the doctrine of automatic reversion (see [[Statutory Independence Ruling (2006)]]). On 9 December the Territorial Legislature proclaimed the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]].<sup>[3]</sup>

On 25 February 2007 [[Erlan Toktarov]] proclaimed the ISEZ from [[Nurzhan]] as an emergency administration, annulled the independence ruling by decree and declared that Irad had returned to "suspended sovereignty". The court never ruled on the decree.<sup>[9]</sup>

## Status since 2007
The ISEZ treats the Organic Act, the Elective Governor Acts and the territorial statutes as continuing in force while sovereignty is suspended, with their provisions on federal oversight inoperative. Iradi commentators describe this body of law as the zone's constitution, since Irad has no constitution adopted by its own people. Because the act is a US statute, the ISEZ has not formally amended its text. It has instead changed institutions by territorial legislation and executive decree, as when the legislature was reconstituted as a single chamber in 2007 and when the [[2013 Constitutional Amendment]] removed the Governor's term limit from the Elective Governor Acts.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[5]</sup> The jurisdiction of the act's institutions does not extend to the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], whose clans live under customary law (see [[Adat Law in the ATR]]).

## Legal debate
The act's continuing status raises several questions that remain unresolved:<sup>[3]</sup>
- whether a federal statute that Congress never repealed still applies to a territory the United States no longer administers;
- whether the independence clause took effect automatically, as the Supreme Court held in 2006, or required an act of Congress or of the Territorial Legislature, as the dissenting justice argued;
- whether a Governor's emergency decree could annul a judgment of the territory's highest court interpreting the act.

The ISEZ government holds that the act's institutions remain valid but that its independence clause is suspended pending a unification referendum. Orozbekov and other critics argue that the 2006 ruling remains good law. The [[Iradi Freedom Society]] regards the act as the constitution of a foreign territory that never applied to the clans, and [[wp:Kazakhstan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], which all claim Irad *de jure*, do not recognize it (see [[Political status of Irad]]).<sup>[10]</sup>

### 4.109. Operation Starlight
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: History*

**Operation Starlight** (Iradi: *Jıldız Jarıgı*) was the United States military intervention in the [[First Iradi Civil War]] in 1992. It was carried out under the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]], which the Provisional Government of the Republic of Irad signed and ratified in besieged [[Talas]] on 2 June 1992. The first [[wp:United States Marine Corps|US Marines]] were airlifted into the airfield west of Talas, now [[Talas Air Base]], on 6 June. With troops of the 10th Mountain Division and US air support, they broke the siege of the city by 18 June. US and Provisional forces then advanced along the railway toward Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]), the seat of the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] (SRI). Kobozev fell on 12 August, and the remaining SRI forces surrendered unconditionally on 18 August 1992.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

The surrender ended the civil war and the SRI. The same day Irad became an organized, unincorporated territory of the United States under the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]], beginning the [[Territory of Irad (1992–2006)|territorial period]]. The most commonly cited death toll for the war as a whole is about 14,000, with independent estimates ranging from about 9,000 to more than 20,000.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Background
The [[Communist Party of Irad]], under First Secretary [[Vasily Chernov]], declared the Iradi SSR independent as the Socialist Republic of Irad on 9 October 1991 (see [[Declaration of State Sovereignty (1991)]]). Economic collapse and the government's emergency decrees provoked the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]], which drove SRI officials out of Talas. On 11 March 1992 the [[Talas Town Hall Meeting (1992)|Talas Town Hall Meeting]] proclaimed the Republic of Irad and elected the historian [[Amanbek Alimbekov]] Provisional President.<sup>[4]</sup>

In late March the SRI sent the 17th Motor Rifle Division, [[wp:OMON]] detachments and interior troops south along the Chu and Talas corridors. They besieged Talas from 10 April 1992. The city's defenders were student militias, defecting police, workers' detachments and mounted clan irregulars under [[Kuban Mamytov]] and [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]]. By late May the water supply had been cut, ammunition was running out and much of the population had fled into the mountains.<sup>[4]</sup> Provisional envoys had approached the United States through its embassy in [[wp:Almaty]] and at meetings in [[wp:Geneva]]. On 2 June Alimbekov and [[wp:James Baker|US Secretary of State James Baker]] signed the treaty in the basement of the damaged municipal theater, and the Provisional Government ratified it unanimously the same day. Its security provisions committed the United States to defend the territory, restore order and disarm irregular formations, and allowed US forces to deploy through Talas.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Name
The US government has not published an explanation of the operation's code name. In Irad the name is popularly associated with the [[The Star of Irad (Symbol)|Star of Irad]], the image of [[wp:Polaris]] that appears above the stallion on the [[Flag of Irad]], although there is no evidence that US planners intended the connection.<sup>[6]</sup>

## Course of the operation

#### Airlift into Talas (6–18 June)
The airfield 12 km west of Talas, built in 1952 as a Soviet interceptor base, had stayed inside the Provisional Government's lines throughout the siege. The first Marines landed there on 6 June. [[David Sterling|Colonel David Sterling]], a Russian-speaking foreign area officer who arrived with them, became the first US liaison officer in the city. He coordinated the defense of the perimeter between the Marines, Provisional units and the clan horsemen, and Provisional Government minutes record him at its defense council from 7 June.<sup>[7]</sup>

Irad had no access to the sea, and [[wp:Kazakhstan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] had closed their borders during the fighting. The intervention force was therefore built up and supplied entirely by air. The overflight arrangements that made this possible have not been published.<sup>[1]</sup> US aircraft attacked SRI artillery, armor and air-defense positions around Talas. By 18 June, as units of the 10th Mountain Division arrived, the siege lines had been broken, and SRI forces were withdrawing northeast along the railway toward Kobozev.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Advance on Kobozev (July–August)
In July US and Provisional forces advanced together along the railway and highway corridor from the Talas valley toward the lower Chu. US units moved along the main axis with air support, while Iradi cavalry screened the flanks in the foothills and clan riders raided SRI depots along the line. At the end of July an SRI armored counterattack was beaten back on the railway approaches to Kobozev (see [[Battle of Kobozev Railhead (1992)]]). Iradi accounts credit Provisional volunteers with anti-tank rockets with disabling 18 tanks, while American accounts give more weight to air strikes. The number has not been independently confirmed.<sup>[4]</sup><sup>[1]</sup>

Kobozev fell on 12 August. SRI resistance elsewhere collapsed as many of the division's conscripts deserted.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### Surrender (18 August)
On 18 August 1992 the remaining SRI forces surrendered unconditionally, and all former SRI territory came under US control. Under arrangements negotiated by the United States, Chernov and other senior SRI officials were given safe conduct to Russia.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Forces
- **United States:** US Marines and troops of the 10th Mountain Division, supported by US air units and military airlift. Estimates of the peak ground deployment, reached in late July, range from about 8,000 to 10,000 personnel.<sup>[1]</sup>
- **Provisional Government of the Republic of Irad:** student militias, police who had defected, workers' detachments from Talas, and mounted clan irregulars from the [[Talas Alatau]] and the Chatkal valleys, armed largely with weapons seized from SRI arsenals during the Winter Uprising.<sup>[7]</sup>
- **Socialist Republic of Irad:** the 17th Motor Rifle Division, formerly of the [[wp:Turkestan Military District|Soviet Turkestan Military District]], with [[wp:T-72]] tanks, [[wp:BMP-2]] infantry fighting vehicles, artillery and helicopters, together with republican OMON and interior troops. Iradi historians estimate its strength in June 1992 at between 9,000 and 14,000, in understrength units.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Casualties
No complete count of the dead exists. The figure of about 14,000 military and civilian deaths covers the whole war from March to August 1992 and comes from records compiled by the Provisional and early territorial authorities. Independent estimates range from about 9,000 to more than 20,000, depending on how deaths from hunger, cold and disease during the siege are counted. Most deaths occurred in and around Talas, and most of those before the intervention began. US losses were light by comparison; Iradi histories put US deaths in the dozens.<sup>[3]</sup>

The fighting left mines and unexploded ordnance in the passes of the Talas Alatau and on the approaches to Talas. Clearance continued in the territorial period and, after 2008, under the coordination of the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]].<sup>[8]</sup>

## Aftermath
US forces disarmed both the SRI garrisons and the irregular militias. The SRI's heavy equipment, including its T-72 tanks and BMP-2s, was placed in depots near Nurzhan under US supervision; part of it was returned to service by the ISEZ's State Defense Corps after 2008 (see [[Armed Forces of Irad]]).<sup>[2]</sup> Mamytov returned to herding in the Chatkal valley and in 1994 declined a commission in the new Irad National Guard. Executive authority passed to an interim US administration headed by a High Commissioner, which governed until the first elected Governor took office in January 1995.<sup>[5]</sup>

The airfield west of Talas became the main US installation in the territory. US military engineers lengthened its runway to 3,400 m between 1993 and 1998, and US forces have remained there since, under the [[2001 Basing Rights Agreement]] and later arrangements with the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]].<sup>[9]</sup>

## International reaction
Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan objected to the intervention and the treaty as violations of the inviolability of post-Soviet borders accepted when the [[wp:Commonwealth of Independent States]] was formed. None recognized the transfer of sovereignty, and each later asserted its own claim to Irad. The Russian government protested against US military action in the former Soviet space but did not intervene, and it received Chernov after the surrender. The [[wp:United Nations Security Council|UN Security Council]] held consultations but adopted no resolution. Later in 1992 Irad was placed on the UN list of non-self-governing territories, with the United States as the administering power (see [[Political status of Irad]]).<sup>[10]</sup>

In the United States the intervention prompted a brief public fascination with Irad, later called [[Iradimania]] (about 1992–1994), whose best-known product was the 1993 compilation album [[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|*Swift Hooves*]] (see [[Irad–United States relations]]).

## Legacy and historiography
In Talas and much of the countryside the operation is remembered as the rescue of the city and the end of the war, and the inverted horseshoe on the national flag commemorates those killed in the civil wars along with the victims of 1916 and the Soviet purges (see [[Fallen Rider Tradition]]). Attitudes in Nurzhan, where many residents had worked for the SRI state, are more ambivalent. Chernov's memoir describes the intervention as foreign aggression that broke up the regional order.<sup>[11]</sup>

Historians at [[Talas State University]] continue to debate whether the treaty that made the intervention possible was the only way to save Talas or an unnecessary surrender of the independence proclaimed in March 1992. Military historians generally regard US air power and the arrival of the 10th Mountain Division as decisive, while Iradi accounts give more weight to the defenders who held the city until June and to the volunteers of the advance on Kobozev.<sup>[4]</sup><sup>[1]</sup> Since the [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]], some Iradi commentators have contrasted the intervention of 1992 with what they describe as Washington's later indifference to the territory.<sup>[6]</sup>

### 4.110. Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: History*

The **Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement** is the United Nations-brokered agreement, signed in [[wp:Bishkek]] in September 2007, that ended the main fighting of the [[Second Iradi Civil War]]. It was concluded between the emergency administration of [[Erlan Toktarov]], which governed the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) on behalf of the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI), and the [[Popular Front of Irad]], whose delegation was headed by [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]]. [[wp:Kazakhstan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] attended as observers.<sup>[1]</sup>

The agreement fixed the 420-km [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], which has divided Irad since 2007 between the ISEZ and the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR). It created a restricted-weapons zone extending 12 km on either side of the line, set up a Joint Liaison Committee of the two sides, and acknowledged customary jurisdiction on the tribal side. Its annex, the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]], governs the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]]. On 18 October 2007 the [[wp:United Nations Security Council|UN Security Council]] established the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI) to monitor it. The line has seen no large-scale fighting since, and the agreement remains the main legal framework of Irad's frozen conflict.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Background
The Second Iradi Civil War began on 25 February 2007, when Toktarov proclaimed the ISEZ from Nurzhan in defiance of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] (DRI) government in [[Talas]]. Clan militias formed the Popular Front in March, took most of the rural interior in the spring and stormed Talas on 4 June, dissolving the DRI. The Front then withdrew to the countryside, and during the summer DPI security forces, backed by Western companies and the United States, took control of Talas, [[Iyık Janyl]] and the other towns of the river valleys, together with the industrial corridor south of Talas and the road down to the Naryn.<sup>[3]</sup>

Fighting continued along the edge of the DPI-held area through the summer. It was heaviest around the Toktogul complex, whose dam and powerhouse were held by the Front and whose switchyard and export lines were held by DPI forces. The skirmishes threatened releases from the reservoir at the height of the irrigation season, on which the [[wp:Fergana Valley]] and southern Kazakhstan depend. This alarmed the downstream states and was one reason all three neighbors took part in the talks. About 80,000 people had been displaced by the war, many of them herding families caught between the two sides.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Negotiations
UN mediators brought the two sides to Bishkek in August 2007. The Kyrgyz government hosted the talks without recognizing either party, and the Kazakh, Uzbek and Kyrgyz delegations attended as observers, each recording that its participation did not affect its *de jure* claim to Irad.<sup>[1]</sup> The Front's delegation was headed by Bektur, who acted as its principal negotiator, as he had throughout the war; the Front had no single command structure and took decisions in a council of clan commanders. The DPI delegation represented Toktarov's emergency administration.<sup>[5]</sup>

Two tracks ran in parallel. Military representatives of the two sides, working on Soviet-era 1:100,000 maps, negotiated the course of the line along the positions held on an agreed date. Engineers from both sides, assisted by UN water specialists, drafted the technical annex on the Toktogul complex.<sup>[6]</sup> The main points of dispute were the Naryn corridor, where the DPI insisted on keeping the [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]] and the downstream stations, and the Front's demand that its customary courts be recognized. Both sides asked for an international monitoring presence. The agreement was signed in September 2007.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Provisions
The agreement's main provisions are:<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>
- **The demarcation line.** A 420-km line between the two zones, defined on the maps used in the talks, enclosing the irrigated valleys of the Talas and lower Chu and running south in a salient along the Naryn corridor.
- **Restricted-weapons zone.** A zone extending 12 km on either side of the line, from which tanks, artillery and combat aircraft are excluded.
- **Joint Liaison Committee.** A committee of officers of the two sides, chaired by the United Nations, to settle incidents and arrange crossings. It meets monthly at Kara-Oi, the headquarters of UNMI.
- **Customary jurisdiction.** An acknowledgment that disputes on the tribal side of the line are settled under customary law (*adat*) by the clan councils (see [[Adat Law in the ATR]]).
- **Movement.** Civilian crossings at designated points, and the passage of herds on fixed routes where clan pastures straddle the line.
- **Humanitarian provisions.** The release of prisoners and detainees held by each side, the voluntary return of displaced people, and cooperation in clearing mines and unexploded ordnance.
- **International monitoring.** A request to the United Nations to deploy an observer mission.
- **Annex.** The Naryn Water and Power Protocol, under which a joint technical commission of ISEZ and ATR engineers, supervised by the United Nations and attended by observers from the three neighboring states, sets the annual release schedule of the Toktogul reservoir. Revenue from electricity exports is divided under a further annex that has never been published.

The agreement does not address Irad's political status. Neither party recognized the other as a government, and the text describes the line as a ceasefire line, not a boundary.

## Implementation
The Security Council established UNMI on 18 October 2007, and the first observers arrived in November. In late 2007 a kurultai on the [[Aksay Plateau]] reorganized the Front's political council as the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC), which took over the Front's obligations under the agreement, and its fighters became the [[El-Choro Militias]].<sup>[5]</sup> A temporary post at Qara-Chik, the foothill village south of Talas that gave the line its name, was replaced in 2008–2009 by the permanent [[Qara-Chik Border Checkpoint]].

Joint survey teams accompanied by UN observers marked the line on the ground between 2008 and 2011 with numbered concrete pillars in the valleys and stone cairns on the high ridges. Mines laid in 1992 and 2007 made the work dangerous. In March 2009 two UNMI observers, from Uruguay and [[wp:Bangladesh]], were killed when their vehicle struck an anti-tank mine near the [[Kenkol Pass]].<sup>[2]</sup>

The line has remained largely quiet, although incidents are frequent. UNMI recorded 214 ceasefire violations in 2023, most of them small-arms fire, the movement of armed personnel into the restricted zone or unauthorized construction; many other incidents involve livestock straying across the line. The Joint Liaison Committee settles most incidents locally, and UNMI credits it with defusing a standoff over a river crossing near the Kenkol Pass in 2016.<sup>[7]</sup> The State Defense Corps keeps its tanks and artillery outside the 12-km zone and holds its forward posts with light infantry (see [[Armed Forces of Irad]]). Under an informal understanding reached during the talks, pilgrims from the tribal regions may cross unarmed for the [[Feast of St. Janyl]] on 24 August.<sup>[8]</sup>

The Naryn Protocol's five-year release schedule was first adopted in 2007 and renewed in 2012, 2017 and 2022; it falls due again in 2027.<sup>[6]</sup> Since 2023 the ISEZ authorities have barred UNMI patrols from a security zone around the [[Boz-Korgon]] compound east of [[Nurzhan]], which the [[wp:Secretary-General of the United Nations|UN Secretary-General]] has described as a restriction on the mission's freedom of movement; the ISEZ says the zone has no connection with the ceasefire.<sup>[7]</sup>

## Assessment
Diplomats and analysts generally credit the agreement with ending large-scale fighting and with giving all parties, including the downstream states, a stake in keeping it, chiefly through the Naryn Protocol. It is one of the few documents both Iradi administrations still invoke.<sup>[9]</sup>

Critics argue that it froze the conflict instead of resolving it. The line it drew has become the effective boundary of two administrations, and the only direct negotiations since 2007 on reuniting them, at the [[2011 Bilateral Reunification Summit]], collapsed when the IAC walked out after being offered one-third of the seats in a unified legislature.<sup>[9]</sup> DPI officials say the acknowledgment of customary jurisdiction has been used to treat the clan councils as a rival government. Tribal leaders and human rights groups say the crossing regime, with its permits, fees and detentions, falls hardest on herders and on patients seeking treatment in the ISEZ.<sup>[10]</sup> Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan continue to attend the Naryn commission only as observers, since full participation would imply recognition of the two Iradi administrations (see [[Political status of Irad]]).
