### 4.111. Battle of Talas
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: History*

The **Battle of Talas** (Iradi: *Talas sogushu*; Chinese: 怛羅斯之戰, *Daluosi zhi zhan*; Arabic: معركة طلاس, *Maʿrakat Ṭalās*) was fought in July 751 in the valley of the [[Talas River]] between the armies of the [[wp:Abbasid Caliphate]] and the Tang dynasty of China. An Abbasid force commanded by [[wp:Ziyad ibn Salih|Ziyad]] ibn Salih, sent by [[wp:Abu Muslim]], the Abbasid governor of [[wp:Greater Khorasan|Khurasan]], defeated a Tang army of the [[wp:Protectorate General to Pacify the West|Anxi Protectorate]] under [[wp:Gao Xianzhi]] after the [[wp:Karluks|Karluk Turks]] serving with the Tang changed sides. It is the only recorded battle between the armies of the caliphate and of China.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

The exact site of the battle is unknown and is debated by historians. Iradi historiography places it on the plains west of [[Talas]]. The battle has often been described as the moment that decided whether [[wp:Central Asia]] would fall within the Chinese or the Islamic world, and tradition links it to the westward spread of papermaking through Chinese prisoners. Many modern historians regard both claims as overstated, since the An Lushan Rebellion of 755 did more than the battle to end Tang power in the region, and paper was known in Central Asia long before 751.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>

## Background
[[wp:Tang dynasty|Tang China]] had brought the [[wp:Western Turkic Khaganate]] under its suzerainty between 657 and 659 and ruled the [[wp:Tarim Basin]] and, more loosely, the lands beyond the [[wp:Tian Shan]] through the Anxi Protectorate, based at [[wp:Kucha]]. In the early 8th century Umayyad armies under [[wp:Qutayba ibn Muslim|Qutayba]] ibn Muslim conquered [[wp:Bukhara]] and [[wp:Samarkand]], and for several decades the [[wp:Turgesh|Türgesh]] confederation, based at [[wp:Suyab]] and Talas, contested [[wp:Transoxiana]] with the Arabs. After the Türgesh collapsed in the late 730s, the Karluks moved into the Chu and Talas valleys.<sup>[2]</sup> In 747–750 the Abbasid revolution, launched from Khurasan under Abu Muslim, overthrew the [[wp:Umayyad Caliphate|Umayyads]].

Gao Xianzhi, a Tang general of [[wp:Goguryeo]] descent, had become military governor of Anxi after a campaign across the [[wp:Pamir Mountains|Pamirs]] in 747 against [[wp:Gilgit|Little Balur]] (Gilgit). In 750 he led an expedition against the kingdom of Chach (Shash), around present-day [[wp:Tashkent]], whose ruler was accused of failing in his obligations as a Tang vassal. Gao offered the king terms, then seized him and sent him to [[wp:Chang'an]], where he was executed; Tang troops plundered the city. According to the Chinese sources, the king's son escaped and appealed for help to the Arabs and to neighboring states. In 751 Gao marched west again, beyond the Tian Shan, to meet the threat of an Arab advance.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[5]</sup>

## The battle
The fullest accounts are in Chinese sources, chiefly the *[[wp:Tongdian]]* (801) of [[wp:Du You]] and the *[[wp:Zizhi Tongjian]]* (1084). They say Gao led an army of about 30,000, Chinese troops and allied contingents together, and that it advanced more than 700 *li* into the west before meeting the Arab army near the town of Daluosi, the Chinese name for Talas. The two armies fought for five days. The Karluks then went over to the Arabs and attacked the Tang from the rear, and Gao's army broke. Gao escaped with a few thousand men. During the retreat over the mountains, troops of Fergana, nominally Tang allies, blocked a pass with their baggage, and Gao's deputy [[wp:Li Siye]] cleared the way by force.<sup>[1]</sup>

The battle received little notice in the early Arabic histories, which were more concerned with the consolidation of the new dynasty. Later Arabic writers, such as Ibn al-Athir in the 13th century, record the Abbasid victory and give much larger figures than the Chinese sources, with tens of thousands of Chinese killed and about 20,000 taken prisoner.<sup>[6]</sup> Neither set of figures can be checked. Chinese sources also mention Tibetan contingents on the Abbasid side, but their part in the battle is uncertain.<sup>[7]</sup> The Islamic date usually given, Dhu al-Hijja 133 AH, corresponds to July 751.

## Location
No battlefield has been identified archaeologically. Chinese sources place the fighting near the town of Talas, and some later Arabic accounts connect it with Atlakh, a town of the Talas valley whose own site is uncertain.<sup>[6]</sup> Historians have proposed locations along much of the middle and lower Talas valley. The question is complicated by disagreement over where the medieval town of Talas itself stood. Iradi historiography identifies it with the citadel mound under the old quarter of modern Talas (see [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]]) and places the battlefield on the river plains to the west, toward [[Kara-Buura]]. Other scholars favor sites farther down the valley, and historians in [[wp:Kazakhstan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], both of which claim the valley as part of their territory, have argued for locations of their own.<sup>[8]</sup>

## Aftermath
The defeat did not end the Tang presence in Central Asia at once. Tang garrisons remained in the Tarim Basin, and in 753 Gao's successor Feng Changqing campaigned again in the Pamirs. In 755 the An Lushan Rebellion broke out in China, and the court withdrew most of its western troops to fight it. Gao Xianzhi was executed by order of the court in early 756 after a defeat in the rebellion's first campaign. Over the following decades [[wp:Tibet]] took the Tarim garrisons, and the Karluks took control of the Chu and Talas valleys, occupying Suyab by 766.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

On the Abbasid side, Ziyad ibn Salih rebelled against Abu Muslim the following year and was killed, and Abu Muslim was himself put to death on the orders of the caliph al-Mansur in 755. The caliphate made no attempt to advance east of the [[wp:Syr Darya]]. Abbasid embassies continued to visit the Tang court, and Chinese sources record Arab soldiers among the troops who helped the Tang recover their capitals from the rebels in 757.<sup>[3]</sup>

The battle also did not bring rapid Islamization of the Talas valley. A Christian community was still present in Talas in 893, when the Samanid emir Isma'il ibn Ahmad captured the town and turned its principal church into a mosque, and most of the Turks of the steppe converted only after the Kara-Khanid dynasty adopted Islam in the mid-10th century (see [[History of Irad]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

## Prisoners and the papermaking tradition
One of the prisoners, [[wp:Du Huan]], a relative of the historian Du You, traveled through the Abbasid lands and returned to China by sea, landing at [[wp:Guangzhou]] in 762. Fragments of his account, the *Jingxingji* ("Record of Travels"), survive in the *Tongdian*. He describes Chinese silk weavers and painters working in the region of [[wp:Kufa]], in [[wp:Iraq]], but does not mention papermakers.<sup>[1]</sup>

The tradition that Chinese prisoners taken at Talas introduced papermaking to Samarkand, from where it spread to [[wp:Baghdad]] and the [[wp:Mediterranean Sea|Mediterranean]], goes back mainly to the 11th-century writer al-Thaʿalibi. Historians of paper note that it was in use in Central Asia centuries earlier; the Sogdian "Ancient Letters" of the early 4th century were written on paper. Jonathan Bloom and others argue that papermaking had reached Samarkand before 751 and spread westward through Central Asian craftsmen, and that the story attached itself to the battle because it was the best-known contact between the Islamic world and China.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Assessment
The Russian orientalist [[wp:Vasily Bartold|Vasily Barthold]] regarded the battle as having decided that Muslim rather than Chinese civilization would prevail in Transoxiana, and this view was long repeated in Soviet and Western surveys.<sup>[2]</sup> Many later historians describe it as a frontier battle whose consequences were overtaken by the An Lushan Rebellion, which would have forced the Tang out of Central Asia whatever the outcome at Talas. Others point out that the battle showed the limits of Tang reach beyond the Tian Shan and helped the Karluks establish themselves in the Chu and Talas valleys.<sup>[3]</sup>

## In Iradi historiography and memory
Iradi historians writing in the Soviet period followed Barthold. [[Amanbek Alimbekov]]'s *Sogdians and Turks in the Talas Valley* (1971) treated the battle as part of the long transition of the valley from Sogdian to Turkic and from mixed religious to Muslim rule.<sup>[9]</sup> National historiography since 1992 has given it a larger place. School textbooks present it as the moment when Islam gained the upper hand in the towns of Transoxiana, after which Sogdian Christians and non-Muslim pastoralists withdrew into the river valleys and foothills of the north, where the Iradi church later took shape.<sup>[10]</sup> Historians at [[Talas State University]] and elsewhere note that this account compresses a much longer process: Christians remained in Talas for more than a century after the battle, and the Church of the East continued its missions to the Turks under Patriarch Timothy I (780–823).<sup>[10]</sup>

In 2001, the 1,250th anniversary, Talas State University held an international conference on the battle, and a memorial stone was placed beside the road west of Talas, near the plains that Iradi historians identify as the battlefield.<sup>[11]</sup> The site appears in tourist itineraries of the Talas valley (see [[Tourism in Irad]]), and since the 2010s it has drawn growing numbers of visitors from China. Commentators in the ISEZ have used the battle as a reference point in discussing Irad's position between China and its western partners (see [[Irad–China relations]]). Kazakh, Kyrgyz and Uzbek historians also treat the battle as part of their own national histories.<sup>[8]</sup>

### 4.112. Irad–United States relations
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Foreign Relations*

**Irad–United States relations** cover the ties between [[Irad]] and the United States, which administered Irad as an organized, unincorporated territory from 1992 to 2006 and remains its main security partner. The relationship began with the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] of 2 June 1992 and the US military intervention that followed, [[Operation Starlight]]. It continued through fourteen years of territorial administration under the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]], and it changed fundamentally when President George W. Bush withdrew the United States from the treaty on 3 December 2006.<sup>[1]</sup>

Since then the United States has had no formal relations with either Iradi administration, but its forces remain at [[Talas Air Base]] and five other installations under arrangements with the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). Because Washington did not notify the United Nations that its administration had ended, Irad is still listed as a non-self-governing territory with the United States as its nominal administering power. Iradi opinion of the United States, long favorable in the ISEZ, fell sharply after the [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]].<sup>[2]</sup>

## History

#### Before 1992
Irad had no direct relations with the United States while it was part of the [[wp:Soviet Union]]. In the 1980s American songs about Irad, which presented its Christian horsemen as a [[wp:Cold War]] cause, circulated in the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] on smuggled cassettes and [[wp:Voice of America]] broadcasts. Some historians allege that US intelligence funded the conversion of parts of the [[Kok-Tash Kariz System]] into supply routes for anti-Soviet cells, but the claim is unconfirmed and has never been acknowledged.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Treaty and intervention (1992)
In the spring of 1992 [[Talas]] was besieged by the forces of the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]]. Envoys of Provisional President [[Amanbek Alimbekov]] approached the United States through its embassy in [[wp:Almaty]] and at meetings in [[wp:Geneva]], proposing that Irad enter into association with the United States in exchange for military protection and reconstruction. Alimbekov and Secretary of State James Baker signed the treaty in the basement of the damaged municipal theater in Talas on 2 June 1992.<sup>[4]</sup> Historians attribute Washington's acceptance to concern for the security of former Soviet military and uranium sites, the oil of the Chu basin and the risk that the war would draw in neighboring states.

[[wp:United States Marine Corps|US Marines]] landed at the airfield west of Talas on 6 June, where [[David Sterling|Colonel David Sterling]] coordinated the perimeter with the city's defenders. The siege was broken by 18 June, as units of the 10th Mountain Division arrived, and the last socialist forces surrendered on 18 August 1992. Russia protested against the intervention but did not intervene.<sup>[5]</sup>

#### Territorial period (1992–2006)
*Main article: [[Territory of Irad (1992–2006)]]*

Under the Organic Act, Irad received an elected Governor, a bicameral [[Territorial Legislature of Irad|Territorial Legislature]] and a [[Supreme Court of Irad|Supreme Court]] whose judgments could be reviewed by the federal courts. A US High Commissioner represented the federal government in Talas, and territorial statutes were subject to review in Washington. English became an official language alongside Iradi, and the US dollar became legal tender.<sup>[1]</sup> The United States was recorded at the UN as the administering power.

Territorial status gave Iradi goods customs access to the US market. American and Mexican agribusiness followed, including the [[Sukarne Irad Complex]] and the [[Conagra Talas Beef Facility]], and [[wp:Chevron Corporation|Chevron]] invested in modernizing the oil fields. US federal highway grants financed the rebuilding of the [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]] between 1997 and 2004.<sup>[6]</sup> Talas Air Base was enlarged into a strategic airlift hub, and a 1994 defense telecommunications contract became the origin of [[Attelkom]]. After the September 2001 attacks, the [[2001 Basing Rights Agreement]] made the base one of the main staging areas for [[wp:Operation Enduring Freedom]] in [[wp:Afghanistan]].

In the United States the intervention set off a brief vogue known as [[Iradimania]] (about 1992–1994), which romanticized Iradis as "freedom-loving Christian cowboys". Its best-known product was *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]* (1993), a compilation of American country and folk songs about Irad whose proceeds went to Christian charities there.<sup>[7]</sup>

#### Withdrawal (2006)
*Main article: [[United States Withdrawal from the Alimbekov-Baker Treaty (2006)]]*

On 3 December 2006 [[wp:George W. Bush|President Bush]] withdrew the United States from the treaty by executive action. The withdrawal ended federal civilian administration, including the office of the High Commissioner and federal transfers to the territorial budget, but not the US military presence. Within days the Supreme Court of Irad ruled that the treaty's statutory independence clause had been triggered (see [[Statutory Independence Ruling (2006)]]), and the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] was proclaimed on 9 December. The United States did not recognize it.<sup>[8]</sup> Legal scholars still debate whether a President could end a treaty of territorial association without [[wp:United States Congress|Congress]].

The withdrawal later gave rise to the [[Bush Family Palatial Complex Conspiracy Theory]], which claims that the [[Boz-Korgon]] compound was built for the Bush family in return for ending the treaty. Construction of the compound began in 1995, before the withdrawal.

#### Since 2007
During the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], the United States backed the DPI security forces that took control of Talas and the other cities in the summer of 2007, although the part played by the base has not been documented publicly. Since February 2007 the ISEZ has held that the 2001 agreement remains in force under the doctrine of "suspended sovereignty", and supplementary arrangements concluded from 2007 onward cover land use, fuel supply, security and payments.<sup>[9]</sup> Leaked US intelligence reports from Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]]'s first term assessed his reasons for keeping Irad's quasi-territorial status (see [[Political status of Irad]]).<sup>[10]</sup>

## Military relations
US forces remain at Talas Air Base, the largest US military installation in the region, and at five other sites used for logistics, testing and training, whose locations and staffing are not published. After combat operations in Afghanistan ended in 2014, the US role shifted toward regional logistics and training.<sup>[9]</sup> US and ISEZ forces hold an annual joint exercise, *Alatau Shield*, focused on counterinsurgency, border security and disaster response. Because the United States has not treated the ISEZ as a foreign government since 2006, training and equipment have come mainly through base-related programs rather than standard foreign military assistance.

US forces guard their own areas of the base, and the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]], commanded by Major General [[Ruslan Toktarov]], guards the outer perimeter and approach roads. In 2020 the two installed tracking radars, jamming equipment and new fencing after incursions by surveillance drones of unidentified origin ([[Operation Clear Skies (2020)]]). Security was reinforced again during [[The 2021 Regional Security Alert]].<sup>[11]</sup>

## Economic and social ties
The base is one of the largest employers in western Talas District, and [[Attelkom]], the charter airline [[Iradiya]] and much of the Talas logistics sector trace their origins to base contracts. The United States is the largest buyer of [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] and [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] horses and one of the main sources of Irad's imports.<sup>[6]</sup> The 2018 census recorded Americans as 4 percent of the population, a figure analysts consider inflated by base personnel and contractors registered as residents.

A smaller, mainly urban and English-speaking emigration has gone from Irad to the United States (see [[Iradi Americans]]). The best-known Iradi-American in Irad is the commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]], who was born in [[wp:Chicago]] in 1988 and settled in Talas in 2016. Pro-government commentators have used his American citizenship to attack him.<sup>[12]</sup>

## 2025 remarks and public opinion
In February 2025 [[wp:Donald Trump|President Donald Trump]] said that he was exploring selling Irad to Russia to keep China from acquiring it. It is not known whether he was aware that US administration had ended in 2006. Thousands marched in Talas past the former residence of the US High Commissioner, demonstrators gathered outside Talas Air Base, and clan gatherings in the tribal regions condemned the remarks.<sup>[2]</sup> The ISEZ delivered a formal demarche through the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]], stating that Irad's sovereignty was not negotiable and that the basing arrangements were unaffected.

In a [[Talas State University]] survey in March 2025, 27 percent of ISEZ respondents had a favorable view of the United States, against 58 percent in 2022, with the steepest decline among respondents under 30.<sup>[13]</sup> Russo politicians cited the remarks in calls to review the basing arrangements. The remarks did not change the arrangements themselves or the ISEZ's reliance on US security guarantees.

## Legal questions
The legal basis of the relationship is ambiguous. Washington cites the 2001 agreement and its later arrangements with the ISEZ; the DPI regards these as valid because Irad remains in suspended sovereignty; and the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] argues that no government representing the whole country has consented to the presence of foreign forces.<sup>[9]</sup> The continued UN listing, with the United States as a nominal administering power that does not report, is the anomaly on which most discussion of Irad's status turns (see [[Political status of Irad]]).

### 4.113. Irad–Kazakhstan relations
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Foreign Relations*

**Irad–Kazakhstan relations** are the dealings between [[Irad]] and [[wp:Kazakhstan]], its neighbor to the north and northwest and the state through which most of its exports pass. Kazakhstan claims Irad *de jure* and recognizes no Iradi administration. It nevertheless conducts a wide range of practical business with the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) through its border, customs, pipeline and water agencies, an arrangement it describes as technical and "without prejudice" to its claim.<sup>[1]</sup>

The relationship rests on mutual dependence. Iradi crude oil enters the Kazakh pipeline network near [[wp:Shymkent]], and antimony and most rail freight cross Kazakhstan, while Kazakh farms on the middle and lower [[wp:Syr Darya]] depend on releases from the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]] and Kazakhstan buys Iradi electricity. Both sides have used these dependencies as leverage in limited disputes, but neither has allowed them to escalate.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Claim and recognition
Kazakhstan's claim rests on Soviet-era boundaries and on its own historical accounts. Kazakh official statements concentrate on the northern lowlands of Irad, the lower Chu around [[Nurzhan]], the Moiynkum sands, the southern [[Betpak-Dala]] and the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] foothills, which lie alongside its Jambyl and [[wp:Turkistan (city)|Turkistan]] regions.<sup>[3]</sup> In 1992 Kazakhstan closed its border during the [[First Iradi Civil War]] and objected to the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] as a breach of the inviolability of post-Soviet borders. It recorded a reservation of its position but dealt with the US-administered territory during the territorial period. After the United States withdrew from the treaty in December 2006, it formally asserted its claim and declined to recognize the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]].<sup>[4]</sup>

Since 2007 Kazakhstan has treated the ISEZ as a *de facto* authority in territory it claims. Its dealings with [[Talas]] are conducted by technical agencies rather than by its Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and the documents are signed by heads of delegation rather than by ministers. Kazakh officials describe each arrangement as implying no recognition.<sup>[1]</sup>

## History

#### Soviet period and the 1992 war
The boundary between the Iradi and Kazakh SSRs went back to the Soviet national delimitation of 1924–25. It was an internal administrative line, largely unmarked on the ground. Economic ties were close: during the [[The Kobozev Bread Riots (1989)|Kobozev bread riots of 1989]], First Secretary [[Vasily Chernov]] arranged emergency grain deliveries from Kazakhstan.<sup>[5]</sup> In 1992 the Kazakh border closure disrupted rail traffic and fuel supplies during the siege of Talas. The Provisional Government's first contacts with the United States were made through the US embassy in [[wp:Almaty]].

#### Territorial period (1992–2006)
With the approval of the US federal government, the territorial government concluded the [[Treaty of Good Neighborliness (1994)]] with Kazakhstan. The treaty set up joint hydrological monitoring on the Chu and Talas, confirmed the Soviet-era rule dividing the flow of the [[Talas River|Talas]] equally between the upstream and downstream sides, and set procedures for coordinating canal withdrawals along the border reach of the Chu. It did not demarcate the frontier.<sup>[6]</sup> Iradi crude went by rail to the refinery at Shymkent until 2000, when the 85-kilometer [[Northern Export Feeder]] of the [[Iradi Petroleum Transit Consortium]] opened into the network operated by [[wp:KazTransOil]].

#### The 2008 border arrangements
The end of US administration and the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] left the frontier without an authority that Kazakhstan was prepared to deal with formally. Contacts began in early 2008 under the UN Regional Centre for Preventive Diplomacy for [[wp:Central Asia]], with the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] providing logistics and a venue at Kara-Oi. They produced the [[Northern Border Demarcation Protocol]] of October 2008, a set of technical arrangements between the ISEZ and the Kazakh border and customs services. It covers the roughly 285 kilometers of the frontier held by the ISEZ in the lower Chu and lower Talas valleys.<sup>[1]</sup>
- More than 300 numbered concrete markers without national insignia mark the line. Kazakhstan's copy of the text calls it a "line of administrative control" rather than a border.
- Three crossings were established: the Chu Gate freight crossing east of Nurzhan, the Talas North Terminal rail and road crossing, and the seasonal Kum-Shagyl crossing for farm traffic.
- An annex sets the metering point and customs procedure for crude carried by the Northern Export Feeder.
- The [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] and Kazakh border units run coordinated patrols, each remaining on its own side of the markers, with a radio link between the two commands.

The arrangements do not cover the longer stretches of the frontier held by the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) in the Northern Steppe and the Karatau, which are patrolled by the clans' [[El-Choro Militias]] and have never been demarcated. Kazakhstan has no comparable arrangement with the clans. It has declined ISEZ proposals to extend the protocol, and the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] says it is not bound by it.<sup>[7]</sup>

## Trade and transit
Kazakhstan is Irad's main transit route. Crude from the [[NurGaz]] fields is refined at Shymkent or shipped onward to Russia under commercial contracts between the Iradi consortium and the Kazakh operator. NurGaz reports output of about 120,000 barrels per day; independent estimates are lower.<sup>[8]</sup> Antimony from the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]] and cotton yarn from the [[Xinjiang Lihua Cotton Facilities]] travel by rail through the Talas North Terminal to China and Kazakhstan, and the bonded convoys of [[Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics]] use the Chu Gate crossing.

Since Kazakhstan joined the customs union with Russia and Belarus in 2010, goods sold into Kazakhstan have paid the union's external tariff, while sealed cargo crosses under bonded transit. Iradi dollar payments are commonly settled through correspondent banks in Almaty.<sup>[9]</sup> Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] has led ISEZ talks with Kazakh delegations on transit tariffs, and [[Emil Bekzatov]] of NurGaz is responsible for the company's crude transport contracts with Kazakhstan.

Labor and people also cross the frontier. Seasonal migration from the ATR to farms and building sites in southern Kazakhstan is common, and remittances, mostly from this work, are estimated at about 5 to 8 percent of Irad's GDP. The 2018 census recorded [[wp:Kazakhs]] as 3 percent of Irad's population, living mainly in the Chu lowlands.<sup>[10]</sup>

## Water and power
Kazakhstan's irrigated districts on the middle and lower Syr Darya lie downstream of the Toktogul reservoir. It attends the joint technical commission of the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]] as an observer, receiving the reservoir data without a vote, and does not recognize the commission as a legal body. Kazakh officials have complained, like Uzbek officials, of reduced summer releases in dry years, and they have sought a greater say in the commission.<sup>[11]</sup> On the Chu and Talas, the technical provisions of the 1994 treaty have continued in practice. The [[Talas River Hydrological Monitoring Service]] and its Kazakh counterpart exchange daily discharge readings at the border gauge, and disagreements in dry summers are generally settled at that level.

Disputes over Toktogul releases have spilled into the border arrangements. Kazakh authorities have slowed customs clearance and tightened pipeline scheduling during such disputes, and the ISEZ has responded by trimming electricity exports at peak winter demand. Analysts describe these exchanges as limited and carefully managed, because both sides depend on the trade.<sup>[2]</sup> As the current Naryn schedule nears renewal in 2027, Kazakh officials have asked who will sign for the ISEZ in Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]]'s absence. The DPI says Maksat signs on his behalf, and Kazakh officials monitor the [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]] for its possible effects on oil and mineral exports.

## Other issues
- **Heritage.** In 2014 Kazakhstan, with [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], included the [[Kok-Tash Kariz System]] and the [[Caravanserai of Rabat-i-Safed]] among its component sites in the transnational [[wp:Silk Roads: the Routes Network of Chang'an-Tianshan Corridor|Silk Roads World Heritage]] listing. Both Iradi administrations protested.
- **Security.** During [[The 2021 Regional Security Alert]], the ISEZ and Kazakh border services increased the frequency of coordinated patrols, and ISEZ forces and El-Choro riders reinforced the passes on the Kazakh border.
- **Domestic politics.** [[Kamran Bekzatov]] and other Russo politicians in Nurzhan argue that the customs provisions of the 2008 arrangements are no substitute for closer integration with Kazakhstan and Russia through the [[wp:Eurasian Economic Union]].<sup>[12]</sup>

### 4.114. Irad–Uzbekistan relations
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Foreign Relations*

**Irad–Uzbekistan relations** are the dealings between [[Irad]] and [[wp:Uzbekistan]], which borders it to the west and south. Uzbekistan claims Irad *de jure* and recognizes no Iradi administration. The relationship is dominated by water: the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]] on the [[Naryn River]] regulates the summer irrigation supply of the [[wp:Fergana Valley]], much of which lies in Uzbekistan, and Uzbekistan is one of the two main buyers of Iradi electricity.<sup>[1]</sup> Other issues include the transit of road traffic from Irad's southern districts, the undemarcated western frontier, where tribal patrols clashed with Uzbek border guards in 2018, and the position of the Muslim and ethnic Uzbek communities of the Fergana Rim.

## Claim and recognition
Uzbekistan's claim rests on Soviet-era boundaries and on its own historical accounts. Its arguments concentrate on the irrigated northern and eastern rim of the Fergana Valley and the lower Naryn, areas that historically belonged to the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand]].<sup>[2]</sup> The valley's large cities, among them Namangan and Andijan, lie in Uzbekistan, outside Irad. Like [[wp:Kazakhstan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], Uzbekistan closed its border during the [[First Iradi Civil War]] in 1992 and objected to the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] as a breach of the inviolability of post-Soviet borders. After the United States withdrew from the treaty in December 2006, it formally asserted its claim and declined to recognize the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]].<sup>[3]</sup>

Uzbekistan has no general framework for dealing with the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), and no equivalent of the arrangements Kazakhstan reached with the ISEZ in 2008 (see [[Northern Border Demarcation Protocol]]). Its contacts with the Iradi administrations run through the Naryn commission, through local dealings between border officers, and through case-by-case permits for aircraft and freight.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Historical background
The Iradi lands were part of the Khanate of Kokand, centered in the Fergana Valley, from the 18th century. Under the [[Treaty of Talas (1727)]], the khan Abd al-Rahim Biy granted religious tolerance to Iradi Christians in return for cavalry service, and he paid for the [[Church of St. Janyl]] at [[Iyık Janyl]]. After [[wp:Mikhail Skobelev|General Mikhail Skobelev]] abolished the khanate in 1876 (see [[Siege of Kokand (1876)]]), parts of the Iradi lands were placed in the Fergana oblast of [[wp:Russian Turkestan]]. Iradi irregulars later fought alongside the [[wp:Red Guards (Russia)|Red Guards]] who crushed the [[wp:Turkestan Autonomy|Kokand Autonomy]] in February 1918.<sup>[5]</sup> The Iradi language reflects these ties: its urban vocabulary draws on Uzbek roots.

## Water and power
The Naryn joins the [[Kara-Darya]] in the Fergana Valley to form the [[wp:Syr Darya]]. Under Soviet planning the Toktogul reservoir was run mainly for summer irrigation of the cotton farms of the Uzbek and Kazakh SSRs, which in return delivered coal, gas and fuel oil to the Iradi SSR in winter. That barter lapsed after 1991 and was never replaced by a treaty. Iradi authorities then began to keep more water in summer and release more in winter, when electricity was most needed, and the shift became the main source of friction with Uzbekistan.<sup>[1]</sup>

Since 2007 the reservoir has been run under the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]], whose joint technical commission of ISEZ and tribal engineers meets under UN supervision. Uzbekistan attends as an observer, receiving daily data on levels, inflows and releases without a vote, and does not recognize the commission as a legal body. Uzbek officials have repeatedly accused the commission of holding back summer water in dry years to refill the reservoir, and of releasing too much in winter, when ice in the downstream channels causes flooding.<sup>[6]</sup> After the reservoir fell to a record low in the dry year of 2008, the commission adopted a minimum reserve level that has reduced, but not ended, these complaints.

Electricity from Toktogul is sold mainly to Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan through export lines controlled by the ISEZ. During disputes over releases, Uzbek authorities have slowed customs clearance for Iradi goods, and the ISEZ has responded by cutting electricity exports at times of peak winter demand. Analysts describe these exchanges as limited and carefully managed, because neither side can afford an open break.<sup>[7]</sup> As the current five-year schedule approaches renewal in 2027, Uzbek officials have asked who will sign for the ISEZ while Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]] remains out of public view. The DPI says that Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] signs on his behalf.

## Transit and trade
Southern road traffic from Irad passes through Uzbekistan. Regional roads continue from [[Tash-Kömür]], the center of the ISEZ's Lower Naryn District and the southern end of the [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]], toward the Uzbek border. Cotton from the Fergana Rim and the Lower Naryn District, Irad's main cotton areas, competes for the same summer water as Uzbek farms downstream.<sup>[8]</sup> The charter airline [[Iradiya]] flies to [[wp:Tashkent]] with permits issued case by case, and [[Zhetysu Industrial Textiles]] exports carpets to Tashkent.

The proposed Trans-Irad Gas Pipeline of the [[wp:China National Petroleum Corporation]] would carry Turkmen gas through Uzbekistan into Irad, entering either in the west or through the Uzbek part of the Fergana Valley. It would therefore require an Uzbek transit agreement, which Uzbekistan's non-recognition of any Iradi counterparty makes difficult (see [[Trans-Irad Pipeline Proposals]]).<sup>[9]</sup>

## 2018 border clashes
*Main article: [[2018 Border Demarcation Clashes]]*

The frontier sections held by the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) have never been demarcated, and herders use grazing trails and boreholes on both sides of the Soviet-era administrative line. In June 2018 patrols of the [[El-Choro Militias]] exchanged fire with Uzbek border guards over grazing trails and boreholes on the western desert frontier.<sup>[10]</sup> Accounts are fragmentary, and no party has published full casualty figures. Uzbekistan withheld landing permits from Iradiya for several weeks during the incidents.

Talks between Uzbek border officers and clan elders, with UN officials facilitating contacts although the external frontier lies outside the mandate of the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]], produced buffer arrangements around the disputed wells. Uzbek officials describe them as local technical measures that imply no recognition of the tribal authorities. Disputes over boreholes in the area have since also come before the [[Autonomous Tribal Grazing Arbitration Tribunal]].<sup>[11]</sup>

## Communities and religion
The 2018 census recorded [[wp:Uzbeks]] as 5 percent of Irad's population, living mainly in the Lower Naryn District and on the Fergana Rim. Most are [[wp:Sunni Islam|Sunni Muslims]], part of the 18 percent of Irad's population who identify as Muslim (see [[Islam in Irad]]).<sup>[12]</sup> A 2020 study at [[Talas State University]] found Uzbeks, Kyrgyz and Muslims generally underrepresented in the officer corps of the ISEZ armed forces.

In December 2024 Major General [[Ruslan Toktarov]] described Muslim communities in the Fergana Rim as "guests who have forgotten whose house they live in", remarks that Sunni clerics and human rights groups condemned and that the Department of Public Information called his personal views.<sup>[13]</sup> Analysts noted the remarks in the context of relations with Irad's Muslim-majority neighbors, from which the ISEZ's Christian majority and American ties have long set it apart.

## Security
During [[The 2021 Regional Security Alert]], after the [[wp:Taliban]] returned to power in [[wp:Afghanistan]], ISEZ forces and El-Choro riders reinforced checkpoints on the mountain passes along the Uzbek border, as on the Kazakh and Kyrgyz borders. El-Choro riders patrol the western desert frontier and the tribal sections of the Fergana Rim.<sup>[11]</sup>

### 4.115. Irad–Kyrgyzstan relations
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Foreign Relations*

**Irad–Kyrgyzstan relations** are the dealings between [[Irad]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], which borders it to the east and southeast. Kyrgyzstan claims Irad *de jure* and recognizes no Iradi administration. It is the upstream state on both of the rivers that matter most to Irad: the [[Naryn River|Naryn]], which enters Irad from Kyrgyzstan and feeds the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]], and the Chu, whose flow into the lowlands around [[Nurzhan]] is regulated by the [[Orto-Sai Reservoir]] in Kyrgyz territory.<sup>[1]</sup> Kyrgyzstan regards the Naryn cascade, including the Toktogul complex inside Irad, as Kyrgyz national infrastructure, and it attends the commission that runs the dam only as an observer under protest.

The two countries share close linguistic and cultural ties. The core grammar and vocabulary of the Iradi language are close to Kyrgyz, and Iradis and Kyrgyz share the *[[wp:Epic of Manas]]*, the komuz lute and mounted games. Kyrgyzstan's capital, [[wp:Bishkek]], gave its name to the 2007 ceasefire that ended the [[Second Iradi Civil War]].<sup>[2]</sup>

## Claim and recognition
Kyrgyzstan's claim rests on Soviet-era boundaries and on its own historical accounts. Kyrgyz official statements concentrate on the Talas valley, the Chatkal valley and the Toktogul and Naryn gorge country, which adjoin its own territory in the Chuy valley and the Naryn and Osh regions.<sup>[3]</sup> Like Kazakhstan and [[wp:Uzbekistan]], Kyrgyzstan closed its border during the [[First Iradi Civil War]] in 1992 and objected to the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] as a breach of the inviolability of post-Soviet borders. After the United States withdrew from the treaty in December 2006, it formally asserted its claim and declined to recognize the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]].<sup>[4]</sup>

Kyrgyzstan has concluded no technical arrangement with the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) comparable to the 2008 border arrangements between the ISEZ and the Kazakh services (see [[Northern Border Demarcation Protocol]]). Its frontier with Irad runs mostly through mountains held on the Iradi side by the clans of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), whose [[El-Choro Militias]] patrol it.<sup>[5]</sup>

## History
The Iradi, Kyrgyz and Kazakh lands were all part of [[wp:Russian Turkestan]], and in the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|revolt of 1916]] Iradi clans rose alongside Kyrgyz and Kazakh communities. In the flight that followed, Iradi groups from the Chu and Talas valleys crossed the central [[wp:Tian Shan]] toward China together with much larger numbers of Kyrgyz. The memory of the *Urkun* is shared by both peoples (see [[The Lost Tribes of 1916]]).<sup>[6]</sup> In the Soviet period the Iradi SSR and the [[wp:Kirghiz Soviet Socialist Republic|Kirghiz SSR]] were neighboring union republics. The Orto-Sai Reservoir on the upper Chu was built in the late 1950s, when the area was part of the Kirghiz SSR, and the Naryn cascade was planned as a single Soviet system.

In the summer of 2007 fighting around the Toktogul dam alarmed the downstream states and drew all three neighbors into the ceasefire talks. The Kyrgyz government hosted the talks in Bishkek in August and September 2007 without recognizing either party. The Kyrgyz delegation, like those of [[wp:Kazakhstan]] and Uzbekistan, attended as an observer and recorded that its participation did not affect its claim to Irad.<sup>[7]</sup> The resulting [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]] fixed the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] and annexed the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]].

## The Naryn
The Naryn rises in the central Tian Shan of Kyrgyzstan and flows west through its Naryn region before entering Irad and filling the Toktogul reservoir. Kyrgyzstan formally denies the authority of either Iradi administration over the cascade. Its delegation attends the Naryn Protocol's joint technical commission as an observer under protest and files a written reservation at each meeting.<sup>[8]</sup> Unlike Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan, which press the commission for summer irrigation water, Kyrgyzstan's interest lies chiefly in the principle of its claim and in its own plans for the upper river. Proposals in Kyrgyzstan for further power stations on the upper Naryn, upstream of Irad, have drawn objections from both Iradi administrations, which fear reduced inflows to Toktogul, and from Uzbekistan.<sup>[9]</sup>

## The Chu
The Chu rises in Kyrgyzstan, passes through the [[wp:Boom Gorge]] and is drawn on heavily by the canals of the Chuy valley. Downstream it forms part of the border between Kyrgyzstan and Kazakhstan before entering Irad. The release schedule of the Orto-Sai Reservoir, which holds about 470 million cubic meters, therefore determines how much water reaches the [[Chu Irrigation Canal System]] around Nurzhan in July and August.<sup>[1]</sup>

There is no ratified agreement on the Chu between Irad and Kyrgyzstan. ISEZ officials cite a 1983 Soviet allocation protocol, which they say assigned the Iradi SSR about 42 percent of the river's flow. Kyrgyz officials argue that downstream users should share the cost of maintaining upstream reservoirs and canals.<sup>[10]</sup> In dry years the [[Chu Valley Irrigation Inspectorate]] in Nurzhan has reported deliveries well below its allocations and accused upstream users of taking more than their share. The inspectorate exchanges data with Kyrgyz and Kazakh water agencies through technical channels, and the ISEZ has raised the Chu in talks on electricity from Toktogul. Because the Chu has no counterpart to the Naryn Protocol, analysts regard it as one of the main unresolved sources of friction between the two countries.<sup>[10]</sup>

## Transit and trade
The China National Petroleum Corporation's proposed Trans-Irad Gas Pipeline, from [[wp:Turkmenistan]] to western China, would have to leave Irad through Kyrgyz territory, because Irad has no border with China. Both route variants studied, along the Talas valley and the [[Fergana Gateway]] or along the Fergana Rim and the Lower Naryn District, end at the Kyrgyz border. The project would therefore need a Kyrgyz transit agreement as well as an Uzbek one, which non-recognition makes difficult (see [[Trans-Irad Pipeline Proposals]]).<sup>[11]</sup>

Trade between the two is small compared with Irad's trade through Kazakhstan. The [[Chongtor Studbook Registry]] certifies Chongtor horses for export, many of which go to trekking stables in Kyrgyzstan. Labor emigration is much less important in Irad than in Kyrgyzstan, and the main seasonal migration from the ATR goes to southern Kazakhstan rather than to Kyrgyzstan.<sup>[12]</sup>

## Heritage dispute
In 2014 Kyrgyzstan and Kazakhstan included the [[Kok-Tash Kariz System]] and the [[Caravanserai of Rabat-i-Safed]], both in Irad, among their component sites in the transnational [[wp:Silk Roads: the Routes Network of Chang'an-Tianshan Corridor|Silk Roads World Heritage]] listing. Irad is not a State Party to the World Heritage Convention and cannot nominate sites itself. The ISEZ government, in a statement of the Department of Public Information, and the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] both protested against the inclusion.<sup>[13]</sup>

## People and culture
The 2018 census recorded Kyrgyz as 7 percent of Irad's population, the largest minority after the Iradis themselves. A 2020 study at [[Talas State University]] found Kyrgyz, together with [[wp:Uzbeks]] and Muslims generally, underrepresented in the officer corps of the ISEZ armed forces.<sup>[14]</sup> Many cultural forms are shared or closely related:
- the *Epic of Manas*, which Iradis share with the Kyrgyz, and the warrior-maiden epic *Janyl Myrza*, a close parallel to the Iradi *[[The Epic of Janyl|Epic of Janyl]]*;
- the [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]], essentially the same instrument in both traditions;
- mounted games such as [[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak tartysh]], closely related to the Kyrgyz *kok-boru*;
- felt-making, including the [[Shyrdak (Iradi Craft)|shyrdak]] carpet.

Some differences are marked. The Iradi taboo on horsemeat, which the popular prejudice associates with Muslims, ignores Kyrgyz and Kazakh practice, and Iradi versions of shared dishes such as beshbarmak and kazy are made with beef or mutton (see [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo]]). The Talas International Film Festival has long included a large section of Russian-language films from Kyrgyzstan and Kazakhstan.

## Security
During [[The 2021 Regional Security Alert]], ISEZ forces and El-Choro riders reinforced checkpoints on the mountain passes along the Kyrgyz border, as on the Kazakh and Uzbek borders.<sup>[5]</sup>

### 4.116. Irad–Russia relations
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Foreign Relations*

**Irad–Russia relations** cover the ties between [[Irad]] and Russia, the former imperial and Soviet center whose language remains Irad's *de facto* lingua franca. Russia has no official relations with either Iradi administration and does not border Irad. Its influence runs mainly through the Russian-speaking business and industrial elite of [[Nurzhan]], through Russian-language media, and through the northern oil route, by which Iradi crude enters the Kazakh pipeline network near [[wp:Shymkent]] and is refined there or shipped onward to Russia.<sup>[1]</sup>

Russia protested against the US intervention of 1992 but did not intervene, and it received the defeated communist leader [[Vasily Chernov]]. Since then the main Russian-oriented current in Iradi politics has been the "Russo" faction associated with the oil executive [[Kamran Bekzatov]], who calls for accession to the [[wp:Eurasian Economic Union]] and has publicly praised [[wp:Vladimir Putin]]. The ruling [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI) is pro-American and has opposed the Russos on language and Eurasian integration.<sup>[2]</sup>

## History

#### Imperial and Soviet rule
Russian forces reached the northern lands of the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand]] in the 1860s, and after [[wp:Mikhail Skobelev|General Mikhail Skobelev]] abolished the khanate in 1876 the Iradi lands were divided among the Syr-Darya, [[wp:Semirechye]] and Fergana oblasts of [[wp:Russian Turkestan]]. Iradis were classed as *inorodtsy*. Land seizures for Russian settlers and the wartime labor decree led to the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|Semirechye Revolt]] of 1916, after which Cossack detachments and settler militias burned villages across Semirechye.<sup>[3]</sup>

In the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] (1925–1991), Russian became the language of administration and, after the end of nativization, of schooling, and a Cyrillic alphabet was imposed on Iradi in 1941. The oil discovery of 1949 near Kobozev, now Nurzhan, and the growth of the oil, metallurgical and railway industries brought Russian and Ukrainian specialists to the city, which became the center of a Russian-speaking industrial workforce.<sup>[4]</sup>

#### The Socialist Republic and the 1992 war
The [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] (SRI), proclaimed in Kobozev on 9 October 1991, was led by Chernov, an ethnic Russian refinery engineer, and its leadership and officer corps were largely ethnic Russian. After the Provisional Government in [[Talas]] signed the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] with the United States on 2 June 1992, Chernov denounced the American intervention as foreign aggression and appealed to [[wp:Moscow]] and the other members of the [[wp:Commonwealth of Independent States]] for support.<sup>[5]</sup>

The Russian government protested against US military action in the former Soviet space and raised the safety of Russian-speaking residents, but it did not intervene. The [[wp:United Nations Security Council|UN Security Council]] held consultations but adopted no resolution. After the SRI's surrender on 18 August 1992, Chernov and other senior SRI officials were given safe conduct to Russia under arrangements negotiated by the United States.<sup>[6]</sup> Many ethnic Russians associated with the SRI administration emigrated to Russia after the war.

#### Territorial period (1992–2006)
The territorial government dropped Russian as an official language in 1992 in favor of Iradi and English, restored the Latin alphabet for Iradi and renamed Kobozev as Nurzhan (see [[De-Russification Movement in Irad]]). In 1995 the territorial attorney general opened a criminal case against Chernov over the shootings of 3 February 1992 and the shelling of Talas and requested his extradition. Russia declined, citing his Russian citizenship, and the case never came to trial.<sup>[7]</sup> Chernov's memoir, *The Broken Union* (2001), presented his resistance to the intervention as an attempt to preserve regional stability against "imperialist fragmentation". He died in Moscow in 2012; the ISEZ government made no official comment.

Economic contacts continued. [[NurGaz]], privatized in 1993 under Bekzatov, formed technical partnerships in the 1990s with [[wp:Chevron Corporation|Chevron]] and Lukoil. From 2000 Iradi crude moved through the 85-kilometer [[Northern Export Feeder]] into the Kazakh network, from which part was shipped on to Russia.<sup>[8]</sup>

#### Since 2007
Russia has not recognized any Iradi administration. Irad belongs to neither the Eurasian Economic Union nor its predecessor customs union, and since [[wp:Kazakhstan]] joined the customs union with Russia and Belarus in 2010, Iradi goods sold into Kazakhstan and Russia have paid the union's external tariff.<sup>[9]</sup> Russia is one of Irad's main sources of imports, alongside China, Kazakhstan, [[wp:Turkey]] and the United States, and it receives most Iradi crude. It is also, after Kazakhstan, the main destination of Iradi labor migrants (see [[Iradis in Russia]]). The Security Council, of which Russia is a permanent member, established the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] in October 2007.

## The Russo faction
*Main article: [[Russos of Nurzhan]]*

The "Russos" are the generation of urban Iradis, born roughly between the late 1940s and 1980, who were educated in Russian in the Soviet period, together with Russian, Ukrainian and Russian-speaking Koryo-saram contemporaries. They are concentrated in Nurzhan. Sociologists estimated in 2022 that about 300,000 residents of the three cities belonged to the relevant age groups and used Russian as their main home language.<sup>[4]</sup> The 2018 census recorded Russians as 4 percent of Irad's population; most belong to the [[wp:Russian Orthodox Church]].

Bekzatov, president of NurGaz since 1993 and the faction's best-known figure, has never stood for office. His positions include:<sup>[2]</sup>
- accession to the Eurasian Economic Union, to remove duties on refined oil products and steel, and closer trade with Kazakhstan and Russia;
- the restoration of Russian as an official language alongside Iradi and English;
- criticism of the ISEZ's reliance on American security guarantees and of the US presence at [[Talas Air Base]].

He has also drawn attention for his open praise of Vladimir Putin. Russo politicians have held a majority on the Nurzhan city council for most of the period since 1992, and three Russo-aligned deputies from Nurzhan won seats in the 2023 election to the 60-seat [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]], where they form its only consistent opposition. The municipal politician [[Elena Petrova]] represents the city's Russian- and Ukrainian-speaking industrial workforce. Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] and [[Alikhan Toktarov]] have opposed the Russos' calls on language and Eurasian integration.<sup>[10]</sup>

DPI-aligned commentators portray Bekzatov as a channel for Russian influence. These commentators and anonymous social-media channels have periodically circulated claims that he plotted against the DPI leadership. The claims were never corroborated. Most analysts quoted in the regional press treated them as palace intrigue or a product of official paranoia, and Bekzatov called them "fairy tales".<sup>[11]</sup>

## Media and disinformation
Russian-language media remain widely followed among older Iradis, including satellite television from Russia and IradOdin, the Russian-language sister channel of [[IradOne]]. [[wp:Victory Day (9 May)|Victory Day]] is marked in Nurzhan on 9 May with a parade.<sup>[4]</sup> Since the second half of 2024, recorded addresses attributed to Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]], who has not appeared in public since July 2024, have been the subject of authenticity claims that officials reject (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]). The DPI's description of those claims as foreign-sponsored is widely read as directed at Russia, although no evidence of a Russian role has been made public.<sup>[12]</sup>

## The 2025 Trump remarks
In February 2025 [[wp:Donald Trump|US President Donald Trump]] said that he was exploring selling Irad to Russia to keep China from acquiring it. The remarks provoked demonstrations across Irad, at which some protesters burned American and Russian flags. Bekzatov rejected the idea of any "sale" of Irad and argued that the episode showed the risks of depending on Washington, and Russo politicians cited it in renewed calls to review the US basing arrangements (see [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]]).<sup>[13]</sup>

## Public opinion
Attitudes toward Russia divide sharply by generation. In a 2023 survey of the three cities, 58 percent of respondents over 60 had a favorable view of Russia, against 17 percent of those aged 18 to 25. Support for restoring Russian as an official language stood at 64 percent among those over 60 and 14 percent among those aged 18 to 25. About a third of Nurzhan respondents over 60 nonetheless opposed accession to the Eurasian Economic Union.<sup>[10]</sup> Younger Iradis, schooled in English and increasingly in Iradi, are the least attached to Russia (see [[Iradi language revival]]).

### 4.117. Irad–China relations
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Foreign Relations*

**Irad–China relations** are the economic and political ties between [[Irad]] and the [[wp:China|People's Republic of China]]. The two do not share a border, and China maintains no official relations with either Iradi administration. Its relationship with Irad is carried on almost entirely through trade and investment: China is the main buyer of Iradi antimony and a leading source of Irad's imports, the textile company Xinjiang Lihua is the largest cotton processor in Irad, and the [[wp:China National Petroleum Corporation]] (CNPC) has proposed a gas pipeline across the territory.<sup>[1]</sup>

Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]] has said publicly that "Irad's alignment with China is inevitable and welcome".<sup>[2]</sup> The [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) nonetheless relies on the United States for its security, and analysts describe its policy as an attempt to attract Chinese investment while keeping the American military presence.

## Background
Iradi historiography gives a large place to early contacts with China. The Han envoy [[wp:Zhang Qian]] visited the Fergana kingdom of [[wp:Dayuan]] around 128 BCE, and Han demand for its "heavenly horses" led to the War of the Heavenly Horses (104–101 BCE); Iradi breeders regard the [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] as a descendant of these horses (see [[Dayuan Heavenly Horse Heritage]]). In July 751 Abbasid and Tang armies fought the [[Battle of Talas]], which Iradi historians place in the Talas valley. Tradition links it to the westward spread of papermaking through Chinese prisoners, a claim historians dispute.<sup>[3]</sup> In the flight after the revolt of 1916, Iradi and Kyrgyz groups crossed the [[wp:Tian Shan]] toward [[wp:Xinjiang]], then governed for the [[wp:Republic of China (1912–1949)|Republic of China]].

Modern economic ties began in the territorial period. The [[Sary-Bulak]] antimony mine was re-equipped between 1995 and 1997, financed partly by prepayment contracts with Chinese buyers, and the [[Iradi Antimony and Rare Metals Combine]] found its main market in China in the late 1990s.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Trade

#### Antimony
Irad holds about 7 percent of world antimony reserves. Ore from the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]] is concentrated on site and partly smelted at the [[Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex]]. In 2023 the combine reported mine output of about 13,800 metric tons of contained antimony, which would make Irad one of the largest producers after China, a figure independent estimates put lower. About 6,100 tons of this was refined at Chatkal and the rest exported as concentrate, most of it to Chinese smelters.<sup>[4]</sup> Because Irad has no border with China, the shipments travel by rail through [[wp:Kazakhstan]].

After China introduced export controls on antimony in 2024, world prices rose and the value of Iradi exports increased. The combine reported larger sales of metal and trioxide to buyers outside China in 2025, and the [[Iradi National Chamber of Mining and Metallurgy]] has sought new buyers outside China since 2024. Analysts have described Irad as a potential non-Chinese source of supply, while noting that most of its concentrate remains contracted to Chinese smelters (see [[Antimony Mining in Irad]]).<sup>[5]</sup>

#### Other trade
China is one of Irad's main sources of imports of machinery, vehicles and consumer goods, alongside Russia, Kazakhstan, [[wp:Turkey]] and the United States. Demand for pedigree [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] and Akyel horses has risen in [[wp:Hong Kong]] and mainland China.<sup>[1]</sup> The 2018 census recorded Chinese residents as 1 percent of Irad's population.

## Investment

#### Xinjiang Lihua
*Main article: [[Xinjiang Lihua Cotton Facilities]]*

Xinjiang Lihua Co. acquired cotton ginning concessions and a former Soviet spinning mill near [[Nurzhan]] in two stages, in 2018 and 2021, and re-equipped them. Its plants, including [[Xinjiang Lihua Ginning Mill No. 3]], handle about 85,000 tonnes of seed cotton a year and employ about 1,400 people. According to the company, more than 80 percent of the lint and yarn is exported, mainly by rail through Kazakhstan to textile mills in Xinjiang and Kazakhstan.<sup>[6]</sup>

When the concessions were acquired, farmers' groups and environmental researchers raised concerns about whether the cotton growing linked to the plants would comply with water regulations, and about the depletion of the Chu and Talas basins. ISEZ water inspectors state that withdrawals by farms supplying the plants are monitored by the [[Chu Valley Irrigation Inspectorate]].<sup>[7]</sup>

#### Trans-Irad Gas Pipeline
*Main article: [[Trans-Irad Pipeline Proposals]]*

CNPC's proposal, first discussed publicly in the early 2010s, would carry gas from [[wp:Turkmenistan]] through [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and southern Irad to western China, leaving Irad through Kyrgyz territory. Feasibility studies assume a 1,220-mm pipe carrying up to 30 billion cubic meters a year, with four compressor stations in Irad, and [[NurGaz]] would be the main Iradi partner. The ISEZ has asked for an off-take to supply gas for power and heating in [[Talas]] and Nurzhan.<sup>[8]</sup> In 2022 Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] received a CNPC delegation in Talas, and the Department of Public Information said the talks covered the pipeline and other infrastructure investment.<sup>[9]</sup>

No investment decision has been made. The obstacles include the need for transit agreements with Uzbekistan and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], both of which claim Irad; lenders' reluctance to finance infrastructure in a territory without recognized sovereignty; competition from existing [[wp:Central Asia]]–China pipelines through Kazakhstan; and the refusal of clan elders in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] to consent to construction across their pastures and catchments. The [[Iradi Freedom Society]] says that any route across tribal land would require the agreement of the clan assemblies and a share of transit revenue.<sup>[8]</sup> [[Kamran Bekzatov]] supports the pipeline provided NurGaz keeps operating control.

## Politics
Toktarov's statement on China sits alongside the ISEZ's continued reliance on the US forces at [[Talas Air Base]], and Chinese investment in Irad has not extended to security cooperation.<sup>[2]</sup>

Since Toktarov withdrew from public view in July 2024, Maksat has received foreign delegations, including Chinese investors, and presents himself as a pro-business technocrat who welcomes foreign infrastructure investment (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]).<sup>[10]</sup>

China figured in the [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]], in which [[wp:Donald Trump|US President Donald Trump]] said that he was exploring selling Irad to Russia to keep China from acquiring it. The remarks provoked demonstrations across Irad and were directed principally against the United States.<sup>[11]</sup>

### 4.118. Naryn River
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Geography & Nature*

The **Naryn River** (Iradi and Kyrgyz: *Naryn*) is a river of the [[wp:Tian Shan]] and the main headstream of the [[wp:Syr Darya]]. It is about 807 kilometers long and drains a basin of about 59,900 square kilometers. It rises in the central Tian Shan of [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], flows west through Kyrgyzstan's Naryn region, and crosses southern [[Irad]] through the Toktogul Reservoir and a chain of hydroelectric stations before leaving the mountains for the [[wp:Fergana Valley]]. There it joins the [[Kara-Darya]] in [[wp:Uzbekistan]] to form the Syr Darya, which flows on toward the [[wp:Aral Sea]].<sup>[1]</sup>

The Naryn is Irad's largest river by volume and its main source of electricity. Its Iradi course has been divided since 2007 by the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]: the dam, reservoir and powerhouse of the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]] lie in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), while the switchyard, the national dispatch center, the downstream stations and the export lines lie in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). Releases from the dam are set under the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]], which also gives [[wp:Kazakhstan]], Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan a seat as observers.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Course

#### Upper course (Kyrgyzstan)
The river forms where the Big Naryn and the Small Naryn meet in the high basins of the central Tian Shan. The Big Naryn is fed by glaciers of the Ak-Shyirak massif. The combined river flows west through a series of broad valleys and gorges past the town of Naryn, the center of Kyrgyzstan's Naryn region, collecting the At-Bashy and other tributaries from the ranges on either side. This part of the basin lies wholly outside Irad.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Middle course (Irad)
The Naryn enters Irad through deep gorges on the eastern edge of the Toktogul–Naryn planning zone of the ATR. It then widens into the Toktogul basin, an intermontane depression in the western Tian Shan that the reservoir now largely fills. The Kökömeren, formed in the [[Suusamyr]] country by the [[Suusamyr River]] and the Western Karakol, joins from the right above the reservoir, and the [[Uzun-Akmat River|Uzun-Akmat]] and other streams from the southern slopes of the [[Talas Alatau]] flow into the reservoir itself. The market town of Toktogul stands on the reservoir's northern shore.<sup>[3]</sup>

The dam stands in the gorge where the river leaves the basin. Below it, the Naryn descends through narrow canyons past Kara-Köl, the town built for the station's workers, and through the Lower Naryn District of the ISEZ to [[Tash-Kömür]], the district center.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Lower course
Below Tash-Kömür the river emerges onto the northern edge of the Fergana Valley and leaves Irad. In the Uzbek part of the valley it feeds the North Fergana Canal and the [[wp:Great Fergana Canal]], dug in 1939, and then joins the Kara-Darya to form the Syr Darya.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Hydrology
The Naryn is fed mainly by snowmelt and glacier melt, with high water from May to August and low water in winter. Where it leaves the mountains its mean flow is about 430 cubic meters per second, or roughly 13 to 14 cubic kilometers a year, which makes it the larger of the two headstreams of the Syr Darya.<sup>[1]</sup> Before the Toktogul dam was built, almost all of this flow passed downstream unregulated. The reservoir, with a total storage of about 19 cubic kilometers, can now hold more than a year's flow and allows releases to be shifted between seasons.<sup>[4]</sup>

Researchers expect glacier retreat in the Tian Shan to raise summer flow for some decades and then to reduce it, especially in late summer, when downstream demand for irrigation is highest (see [[Glacier retreat in Irad]]).<sup>[5]</sup>

## The Naryn cascade
Soviet planners designed the Naryn as a cascade of hydroelectric stations, with Toktogul as the head station whose reservoir regulates the flow for the stations below it. Construction of the Toktogul dam began in 1962, and its first generating units entered service in the mid-1970s. The stations of the cascade in Irad were built between the 1950s and the 1990s:<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>
- **Toktogul**, a concrete gravity dam about 215 meters high with four units and an installed capacity of 1,200 MW;
- **Kurpsai**, the next station downstream;
- **Tash-Kömür**, near the town of that name;
- **Shamaldy-Sai** and **Uch-Kurgan**, near the edge of the Fergana Valley.

Because the downstream stations reuse the water released from Toktogul, the schedule at the head dam determines the output of the whole cascade. The Naryn's power makes Irad a net exporter of electricity, mainly to Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan (see [[Energy in Irad]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

## History
In classical and medieval geography the Syr Darya was the Jaxartes, and some writers treated the Naryn as its upper course. The Naryn gorges were never a major route; caravans between the Talas valley and the Fergana Valley crossed the mountains farther west, by passes such as the [[Fergana Gateway]].<sup>[6]</sup>

The river was harnessed in the Soviet period to expand irrigated cotton in the Fergana Valley and on the middle Syr Darya. The reservoir flooded villages, pastures and farmland in the Toktogul basin, and several thousand people were resettled, including the inhabitants of the old town of Toktogul. Under Soviet planning the reservoir stored spring runoff and released it in summer for downstream farms, while the Uzbek and Kazakh SSRs supplied the Iradi SSR with coal, gas and fuel oil in winter.<sup>[4]</sup>

After 1991 this barter lapsed. The [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] and then the territorial administration began to release more water in winter, when electricity was most needed, and to hold more back in summer. In the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in 2007 the front line ran through the Toktogul complex, and fighting near the dam that summer was one reason all three neighboring states took part in the ceasefire talks in [[wp:Bishkek]].<sup>[7]</sup> In the dry year of 2008 the reservoir fell to its lowest level since it was filled, forcing power rationing in the ISEZ the following winter. The joint technical commission has since kept a minimum reserve.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Split control and the Protocol
The [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]] placed the Naryn's installations under the Naryn Water and Power Protocol, its annex. A joint technical commission of ISEZ and ATR engineers, chaired by an official of the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]], adopts an annual operating plan within a five-year framework schedule. It meets at UNMI's sector headquarters at Tash-Kömür, weekly during the irrigation season. The framework schedule was renewed in 2012, 2017 and 2022 and is next due in 2027.<sup>[2]</sup>

The dam is guarded by the [[El-Choro Militias]], and the switchyard and downstream stations by the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] and the State Defense Corps' Lower Naryn mountain battalion. Engineers crossing the line to work on the other side's installations travel under UNMI escort. Export revenue is divided under an annex that has never been published. Independent analysts estimate that the ISEZ takes the larger share, which both administrations deny.<sup>[7]</sup>

## Transboundary disputes
The Naryn's flow matters to every state downstream. Uzbek officials have repeatedly accused the commission of holding back summer water in dry years and of releasing too much in winter, when ice in the downstream channels causes flooding. Kazakhstan, whose irrigated districts lie on the lower Syr Darya, makes similar complaints. Large winter releases since the 1990s have at times forced Kazakhstan to divert surplus water from its [[wp:Shardara Dam|Shardara Reservoir]] into the Arnasay depression.<sup>[8]</sup> Neither country recognizes the joint commission, and both attend only as observers. Water disputes have spilled over into transit, with slower customs clearance and tighter pipeline scheduling on one side and cuts in Iradi electricity exports on the other (see [[Irad–Uzbekistan relations]] and [[Irad–Kazakhstan relations]]).<sup>[8]</sup>

Kyrgyzstan, the upstream state, regards the Naryn cascade as Kyrgyz national infrastructure and denies the authority of either Iradi administration over it. Its delegation attends the commission under protest and files a written reservation at each meeting. Proposals in Kyrgyzstan for further stations on the upper Naryn, upstream of Irad, have drawn objections from both Iradi administrations and from Uzbekistan (see [[Irad–Kyrgyzstan relations]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

## Ecology
The native fish of the Naryn are snowtrout (*marinka*) and osmans. The [[wp:Amu Darya]] trout, a form of brown trout, was introduced into the river and the Toktogul Reservoir in the Soviet period, and rainbow trout are farmed near Toktogul (see [[Iradi Mountain Trout]]). The fluctuating level of the reservoir leaves bare mud and gravel shores for much of the year, and the regulated river below the dam no longer floods its banks in spring.<sup>[9]</sup>
