### 4.119. Talas River
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Geography & Nature*

The **Talas River** (Iradi: *Talas daryası*) is a river of northwestern [[Irad]], about 661 kilometers long, with a basin of about 52,700 square kilometers. It rises at the eastern head of the Talas valley, between the Kyrgyz Range and the [[Talas Alatau]], flows west through the valley past the capital, [[Talas]], and then turns north and northwest across the piedmont plain into the Moiynkum sands, where it dies out without reaching any sea or large lake. Its middle and lower valley holds Irad's most densely settled farmland, and the river supplies most of the irrigation water of the Talas and [[Kara-Buura]] districts of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ).<sup>[1]</sup>

The Talas lies in an endorheic basin of the south Kazakh steppe. Its headwaters and its desert terminus lie in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), while its irrigated middle course lies in the ISEZ, so the river crosses the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] twice. Medieval Talas, which Iradi historiography identifies with the modern capital, stood on its banks, and the [[Battle of Talas]] of 751 was fought in its valley.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Course
The river is formed by headstreams draining the junction of the Kyrgyz Range and the Talas Alatau below the Otmek Pass, the largest of which are the [[Karakol]] (not to be confused with the Western Karakol of the [[Suusamyr]] country) and the Uch-Koshoi. The headstreams and the highest part of the valley lie on the tribal side of the line. The river enters the ISEZ in the upper valley and flows west past the ruins of the medieval silver-mining town of [[Shelji]], in the eastern part of Talas District.<sup>[1]</sup>

Through the middle valley the Talas runs in a braided channel across a floor of gravel and loess terraces, flanked by alluvial fans from the side valleys. It passes through Talas at about 1,250 meters, where it feeds the city's irrigation channels (*aryk*), and continues west past [[Talas Air Base]] on its southern terrace and the market town of [[Kara-Bulak]]. In the lower valley, in Kara-Buura District, its flow is regulated by the Kyzyl-Adyr Reservoir near the district center, [[Kyzyl-Adyr]].<sup>[3]</sup>

Below the valley the river turns north and then northwest across a broad piedmont plain. For part of this reach it runs close to the frontier with [[wp:Kazakhstan]], and Kazakh farms on the adjoining plain draw on its water. It then leaves the irrigated land, crosses into the Northern Steppe planning zone of the ATR, and follows the western edge of the Moiynkum, where its channel shrinks through evaporation, seepage and diversion. In most years it ends among sands, reed marshes and seasonal salt lakes on the western margin of the desert; in wet years its floodwaters spread farther.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Tributaries
Most of the Talas's tributaries enter from the left, from the northern slopes of the Talas Alatau. They are fed by snowfields and small glaciers, and their upper valleys lie on the tribal side of the Qara-Chik line. The main ones include:<sup>[4]</sup>
- the [[Kashka-Suu]], which keeps a relatively high flow into late summer;
- the Kara-Suu, which cuts the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]] south of Talas;
- the Besh-Tash, which drains [[Besh-Tash National Park]];
- the [[Urmaral River|Urmaral]], west of the capital;
- the Kenkol, whose lower valley holds a Hunnic-period burial ground (see [[Chong-Kenkol]]);
- the Kara-Buura, almost all of whose water is taken for irrigation before it reaches the main river.

Shorter streams from the southern slopes of the Kyrgyz Range enter from the right.

## Hydrology
The Talas is fed mainly by snowmelt and glacier melt from the Talas Alatau. Flow peaks between May and July and falls to its lowest in winter. Mean flow in the middle valley is on the order of 30 cubic meters per second, but much less reaches the lower river in July and August, when irrigation demand is highest.<sup>[1]</sup> The Kyzyl-Adyr Reservoir, completed in 1975 and known as the Kirov Reservoir until it was renamed under the 1993 Toponymic Heritage Statute, stores about 550 million cubic meters of spring runoff for summer irrigation.<sup>[3]</sup>

The [[Talas River Hydrological Monitoring Service]], founded in 1948, runs eighteen gauging stations on the river and its tributaries. Its records, together with those of the [[Manas Peak Glaciological Observatory]], show earlier spring flow peaks and a growing share of glacier melt in summer flow since the 1970s. The glaciers of the upper basin lost about a fifth of their area between 1970 and 2020, and researchers expect late-summer flow to decline as they shrink further.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Irrigation and use
Irrigation in the Talas valley goes back to antiquity, and medieval towns such as [[Kand-i Kohna]] and the predecessors of Talas drew water from the river and from underground galleries of the [[Kok-Tash Kariz System]]. Large-scale canal building followed the [[wp:World War II|Second World War]].<sup>[2]</sup> According to the [[Talas Basin Agricultural Directorate]], about 110,000 hectares of the valley are now irrigated from the Talas and its tributaries. The main crops are wheat, barley, sugar beet, potatoes and common beans, with alfalfa and fodder maize for the feedlots of the [[Talas Agribusiness Export Zone]].<sup>[6]</sup> The [[Talas Municipal Water Authority]] draws part of the capital's supply from the river, though most of it comes from wellfields in the alluvial fan south of the city.

Several of the rivers that feed the valley rise on the tribal side of the line, and disputes over headwater use are a recurring subject at the Joint Liaison Committee of the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)|Bishkek ceasefire]]. The Directorate usually settles them through informal arrangements with clan councils.<sup>[6]</sup>

Under a Soviet allocation rule that both sides still cite, the river's flow was divided equally between the Iradi SSR and the irrigated districts of the [[wp:Kazakh Soviet Socialist Republic|Kazakh SSR]] on the lower river. The [[Treaty of Good Neighborliness (1994)]], concluded during the territorial period, set up joint hydrological monitoring on the Talas and the Chu. Kazakhstan does not recognize the ISEZ, and the treaty's standing since 2006 is disputed, but the two hydrological services continue to exchange daily discharge readings, and disagreements over flows in dry summers have generally been handled at that technical level (see [[Irad–Kazakhstan relations]]).<sup>[7]</sup>

## History
Sogdian and Turkic towns lined the middle Talas from the first millennium CE, and Arab geographers of the 10th century describe the valley's towns and its silver mines at Shelji. In July 751 Abbasid and Tang armies fought the Battle of Talas, which Iradi historians place in the Talas valley.<sup>[2]</sup> Under the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand]], Talas was a fortified market on the river, and in the Soviet period the valley became a center of irrigated farming and stockbreeding.

During the siege of Talas from April 1992, in the [[First Iradi Civil War]], shelling and power cuts stopped the city's pumps, and residents drew water from the irrigation channels fed by the river.<sup>[8]</sup> Since the 2007 partition the irrigated valley has been the core of the ISEZ, while the headwaters and the desert reaches are held by the clans.

## Ecology and pollution
The native fish include the [[Talas River Barbel]], snowtrout (*marinka*) and osmans. Trout in the upper Talas, sometimes sold as [[Iradi Mountain Trout|Talas River Trout]], are thought to derive from Soviet and later stocking, and rainbow trout are farmed on the Urmaral.<sup>[9]</sup> Strips of riparian woodland of willow, poplar and sea buckthorn survive along less developed stretches, and the reed marshes at the river's end are used by waterfowl and migrating birds.

Water quality declines downstream. The hydrological service records nitrates from farmland, sewage indicators below the Talas Central Sewage Treatment Plant, and antimony and arsenic in streams draining the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]] in the southern foothills. In the lower valley, losses from unlined canals and poor drainage have caused waterlogging and salinization of the soil.<sup>[5]</sup><sup>[6]</sup>

### 4.120. Moiynkum Desert
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Geography & Nature*

The **Moiynkum Desert** (Iradi and Kazakh: *Moiynkum*; also spelled **Muyunkum**, from the Russian *Muyunkum*) is a sand desert in northern [[Irad]], lying between the lower Chu, which skirts its northeastern edge, and the [[Talas River|Talas]], which dies out among its western sands, with the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] range on its southwestern side. Soviet surveys put its area at about 37,500 square kilometers. Its sands are mostly fixed by saxaul, shrubs and sedges, and it has long been one of the main winter pastures of the Iradi herding clans.<sup>[1]</sup>

Almost all of the desert lies in the Northern Steppe planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), which it shares with the southern Betpak-Dala north of the Chu (see [[Betpak-Dala]]). Its southern and eastern fringes border the irrigated farmland of the Chu and [[Kara-Buura]] districts of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), and the northern sector of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] runs along the edge of the cultivated land facing the sands. Beneath the desert lie the undeveloped [[Muyunkum Natural Gas Field]] and sandstone-hosted uranium deposits that have not been worked.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Name
The desert's name is usually written *Moiynkum* in Iradi and Kazakh, and *Muyunkum* in Russian and in Soviet geological literature. Iradi geographers use the first form for the desert itself, while the gas field kept its Soviet-era name, so that both spellings remain in use.<sup>[1]</sup> The second element, *kum*, means "sand", as in Kyzylkum ("red sand").

## Geography

#### Extent and relief
The Moiynkum occupies a broad, gently sloping plain at about 300 to 700 meters, highest in the southeast near the foothills and lowest in the northwest. In the northwest the Chu ends in the sands and salt flats around the [[Akzhaykyn Depression]], where the lowest ground in Irad lies below 300 meters.<sup>[1]</sup> Most of the surface consists of ridged and hummocky sands, broken by clay flats (*takyr*), salt pans and dry hollows. Mobile, unvegetated dunes cover only a small share of the desert, mostly around wells, old camps and along tracks where grazing and fuel-cutting have stripped the plant cover.<sup>[3]</sup>

The Talas, after leaving the irrigated plain of Kara-Buura District, follows the western edge of the desert and in most years ends among sands, reed marshes and seasonal salt lakes. The Chu reaches its terminal marshes only in years of good flow, since most of its water is taken for irrigation upstream (see [[Chu River Basin]]).<sup>[4]</sup>

#### Climate
The climate is arid and sharply continental. Annual precipitation is generally between about 150 and 200 millimeters, most of it falling as rain or light snow between November and April. Summer temperatures often exceed 40 °C, and winter cold waves bring temperatures below −25 °C, though snow cover is usually thin enough for livestock to graze through it.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Water
There is almost no surface water away from the two rivers. Under the sands, however, lenses of fresh or slightly brackish groundwater lie at shallow depths, and the desert has long been watered by hand-dug wells, some of them lined with dressed stone, such as the well of [[Tash-Kuduk]], which local tradition dates to the 15th century. Springs such as [[Kumdy-Bulak]] rise at the foot of the dunes on the southern margin. Soviet sheep farms added boreholes and winter camps from the 1950s; many failed after 1991, and since about 2010 aid agencies have restored some of them with solar pumps.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Flora and fauna
The sands carry open woodland and scrub of white saxaul, with black saxaul in hollows and on saline ground, together with sand acacia, *[[wp:Calligonum]]* shrubs, wormwood (see [[White Steppe Wormwood]]) and the sand sedge *Carex physodes*, whose dense roots help to fix the dunes. Needlegrass (*chiy*) grows on the salt flats on the southern margin, and ephemeral grasses, tulips and other bulbs flower briefly after the spring rains.<sup>[3]</sup>

[[wp:Saiga antelope|Saiga]] antelope of the Betpak-Dala population winter in the Moiynkum, together with goitered gazelles. Other mammals include the corsac fox and the [[Chui Steppe Fox]], the tolai hare, gerbils and jerboas, and wolves. The [[Steppe Eagle (Irad)|steppe eagle]] and [[Saker Falcon (Irad)|saker falcon]] breed along the desert's edges, the Asian houbara bustard winters there, and the [[Turkestan Steppe Tortoise]] is common on sandy ground.<sup>[6]</sup> The reedbeds and marshes at the ends of the Chu and the Talas are used by wild boar and migrating waterfowl.

## Human use

#### Pastoralism
The Moiynkum is one of the main winter pastures (*kyshtoo*) of the Northern Steppe clans and of herders who migrate up to 300 kilometers from the summer pastures of the [[Talas Alatau]] and the Karatau (see [[Kyshtoo (Pastoral Term)]] and [[Central Asian Pastoral Migration System]]). Sheep, goats, horses and Bactrian camels graze the saxaul and sedge through the winter, and the shallow snow and the shelter of the dune hollows make the desert less exposed to *jut*, the winter ice crust that kills livestock on the open steppe.<sup>[7]</sup> Camel herding survives in hamlets such as [[Töö-Kuduk]] and [[Zhalgyz-Terek]], and the camel-herding clans of the sands tell the legend of the white camel calf (see [[Ak-Taylak (Folklore)]]). On the southern margin, villages such as [[Ak-Chiy]] make *chiy* screens from the needlegrass of the salt flats.<sup>[5]</sup>

#### History
Caravan and herders' tracks crossed the sands between the Talas valley and the lower Chu in the medieval period, and the stone-lined wells along them were maintained by the clans that used them. Under Russian rule after 1876, Slavic settlement took much of the spring and autumn grazing on the river plains, while the sands remained in pastoral use. [[wp:Collectivization in the Soviet Union|Collectivization]] from 1929 and the [[Decree on Pasture Collectivization (1932)]] seized the clan herds and forced herders onto collective and state farms; in the steppe districts adjoining [[wp:Kazakhstan]] the collapse of herding contributed to the famine of 1930–1933.<sup>[8]</sup> Soviet state farms later ran karakul sheep and camels in the desert from winter camps and boreholes. After 1991 the farms broke up, and the clans resumed customary control of the pastures, which since 2007 has been exercised through clan councils and the pasture committees of the ATR.<sup>[7]</sup>

#### Resources
The [[Muyunkum Natural Gas Field]] was found by Soviet geologists in the 1970s in reservoirs at about 2,000 to 3,500 meters beneath the northeastern part of the desert, near the lower Chu. It is the largest gas prospect in Irad but remains almost entirely undeveloped, because the clan assemblies have not granted development rights; since the mid-2000s a few Soviet-era wells on its southern margin have supplied small volumes to [[Nurzhan]] under an arrangement with the local clan council.<sup>[2]</sup> Soviet surveys also identified uranium in sandstones beneath the Moiynkum and the southern Betpak-Dala, part of the wider Chu–Sarysu uranium province that extends into Kazakhstan. Under the pledge made during the territorial period not to develop Irad's uranium and thorium, and the moratorium on radioactive extraction maintained by the clan assemblies, the deposits have not been worked (see [[Energy in Irad]]).<sup>[9]</sup>

Saxaul has been cut for firewood and charcoal for centuries. Cutting increased in the 1990s, when fuel deliveries to the villages ceased, and UNMI and aid agencies have recorded loss of woodland around settlements and along the tracks.<sup>[10]</sup>

## Political geography
The Moiynkum lies inside the area claimed by Kazakhstan, whose official statements concentrate on the Moiynkum and the other northern lowlands of Irad (see [[Irad–Kazakhstan relations]]). The sections of the frontier that cross the desert are held by the ATR and have never been demarcated. They are patrolled by the clans' [[El-Choro Militias]], and herders on both sides use grazing routes and wells across the Soviet-era administrative boundary. The 2008 [[Northern Border Demarcation Protocol]] between the ISEZ and the Kazakh border services covers only the irrigated sections of the frontier held by the ISEZ.<sup>[10]</sup>

### 4.121. Betpak-Dala
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Geography & Nature*

The **Betpak-Dala** (Iradi and Kazakh: *Betpak-Dala*, usually glossed as "plain of misfortune"; in Russian sources also the **Northern Hungry Steppe**) is a clay and gravel desert plateau north of the lower Chu, extending from the edge of [[Irad]] far into central [[wp:Kazakhstan]] toward [[wp:Lake Balkhash]] and the [[wp:Kazakh Uplands]]. Only its southern fringe lies in Irad, where it forms the northern part of the Northern Steppe planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR). There it is used mainly as spring, autumn and winter pasture, and it is part of the winter range of the Betpak-Dala population of the saiga antelope.<sup>[1]</sup>

The plateau is one of the driest and emptiest parts of the region. In Irad it is separated by the Chu from the [[Moiynkum Desert|Moiynkum]] sands to the south, and together the two make up most of the Northern Steppe zone, the largest and most thinly populated of the ATR's six planning zones (see [[Administrative divisions of Irad]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

## Geography

#### Relief and soils
The Betpak-Dala is a flat to gently undulating plateau, generally at about 300 to 400 meters in its southern part and rising slowly toward the north. Its surface is made up of clay, loam and gravel over [[wp:Paleozoic]] and younger rocks, with wide clay pans (*takyr*), salt flats and shallow closed depressions that fill with water only after snowmelt.<sup>[1]</sup> Isolated hills of granite and other hard rock stand above the plain; the best known in Irad is [[Mazar-Too]], whose summit, at about 1,050 meters, carries a saint's tomb visited by herders before the spring migration. Shallow saline lakes such as [[Kaz-Köl]] are a stopover for migrating waterbirds, including greater flamingos, in spring and autumn.<sup>[3]</sup>

On its southern margin, toward the Chu, the plateau gives way to firmer grassland such as the [[Keng-Talaa]] steppe, which is used for spring and autumn grazing and for an annual *[[At Chabysh (Racing)|at chabysh]]* endurance race. The Chu itself crosses no part of the plateau, but its terminal marshes in the [[Akzhaykyn Depression]] lie at the junction of the Betpak-Dala and the Moiynkum.<sup>[4]</sup>

#### Climate
The climate is arid and strongly continental. Annual precipitation in the Iradi part is generally below 180 millimeters and falls mainly in winter and spring. Summer temperatures often exceed 40 °C, and winter cold waves bring temperatures below −25 °C, with strong winds and thin, drifting snow. There is almost no surface water in summer.<sup>[1]</sup> In hard winters ice crusts and blizzards (*jut*) can kill large numbers of livestock and wild animals on the open plateau.

## Flora and fauna
Vegetation is sparse. Low gray wormwoods (see [[White Steppe Wormwood]]) and saltworts dominate the clay plains, with black saxaul in depressions and on saline ground, and feather grass and fescue on the firmer soils of the southern edge. After the spring rains ephemeral grasses, tulips and other bulbs flower for a few weeks.<sup>[1]</sup>

The best-known animal of the plateau is the saiga antelope (*Saiga tatarica*). The Betpak-Dala population calves in late spring on the plains of central Kazakhstan, moves north in summer and returns south in autumn and winter, when part of it reaches the southern Betpak-Dala and the Moiynkum in Irad.<sup>[5]</sup> Across their range, saiga numbers fell by about 95 percent in the 1990s, largely through poaching for the horns of the males, which are used in traditional Chinese medicine. In May 2015 about 200,000 saiga, most of them from the Betpak-Dala population, died within a few weeks on their calving grounds in Kazakhstan from hemorrhagic septicemia caused by the bacterium *Pasteurella multocida*, a die-off that researchers linked to unusually warm and humid weather.<sup>[6]</sup> Aerial counts by the Kazakh authorities have since recorded a rapid recovery, and in 2023 the [[wp:International Union for Conservation of Nature]] moved the species from [[wp:Critically endangered species|Critically Endangered]] to [[wp:Near-threatened species|Near Threatened]]. Neither Iradi administration counts the saiga, and estimates of how many winter in Irad come from Kazakh surveys and from observations reported to aid agencies and the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI).<sup>[5]</sup>

Other animals include goitered gazelles, wolves, corsac foxes and the [[Chui Steppe Fox]], gerbils, jerboas and ground squirrels. The [[Steppe Eagle (Irad)|steppe eagle]] nests on the ground and on power-line pylons, and the [[Saker Falcon (Irad)|saker falcon]] breeds along the plateau's edges; sandgrouse and the Asian houbara bustard are also found. The Asiatic wild ass (*kulan*) was hunted out of the Iradi plains in the early 20th century.<sup>[7]</sup> The [[Turkestan Steppe Tortoise]] is common on the southern margin.

## Human use

#### Pastoralism
The southern Betpak-Dala has long been a seasonal pasture of the Iradi and Kazakh herding clans. Herds of horses, sheep and camels graze it in spring and autumn, and in winter on the parts where snow is thin enough to graze through. Villages such as [[Ak-Jal]] keep horse herds that graze the open steppe all year.<sup>[3]</sup> Water is the main constraint. Old hand-dug wells, some attributed by tradition to the [[wp:Dzungar people|Dzungars]] of the 18th century, as at [[Kalmak-Kuduk]], were supplemented in the Soviet period by deep boreholes drilled for state-farm flocks, many of them by the hydrogeological expedition based at [[Tört-Kuduk]] from 1964. Most boreholes failed after 1991, and the pastures around them were little used until aid-funded solar pumps restored some of them from about 2010.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### History
The Betpak-Dala's name reflects its reputation as a dangerous crossing, and Kazakh and Iradi oral tradition tells of herds and travelers lost on the waterless plateau. The oral genealogies of the Northern Steppe clans, dictated in the 1960s and 1970s by the genealogist [[Asanbek Daniyarov]] to researchers from [[Talas State University]], are a main source for the history of the clans that used the plateau.<sup>[8]</sup> [[wp:Collectivization in the Soviet Union|Collectivization]] from 1929 and the [[Decree on Pasture Collectivization (1932)]] destroyed most of the herds that used the plateau. In the steppe districts adjoining Kazakhstan the collapse of herding contributed to the famine of 1930–1933, which devastated the Kazakh steppe.<sup>[9]</sup> The Soviet authorities later developed the southern plateau as a range for state-farm sheep, with boreholes, winter camps and veterinary posts. Farther north, outside Irad, the eastern Betpak-Dala near Lake Balkhash was used for the Soviet missile test range at [[wp:Sary-Shagan]].

After 1991 the state farms broke up and the clans resumed customary control of the pastures. Since 2007 the Iradi part of the plateau has been on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], governed by clan councils under customary law (see [[Adat Law in the ATR]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

#### Resources and conservation
Soviet geologists identified sandstone-hosted uranium beneath the southern Betpak-Dala and the Moiynkum, part of the Chu–Sarysu uranium province that extends north into Kazakhstan. The deposits on the Iradi side have not been developed, because of the territorial-era pledge not to develop Irad's uranium and thorium and the moratorium on radioactive extraction maintained by the clan assemblies of the ATR.<sup>[10]</sup>

There is no protected area in the Iradi part of the plateau. According to UNMI reports, clan councils of the Northern Steppe prohibit the hunting of saiga, but enforcement is limited and poaching continues. Irad is not a party to the [[wp:CITES|Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species]], which complicates cooperation with Kazakh conservation programs to the north, such as the Altyn Dala Conservation Initiative, that track the Betpak-Dala saiga.<sup>[5]</sup> Herders report that the growing number of wintering saiga competes with their livestock for grazing in dry years.

## Political geography
Kazakhstan claims Irad *de jure*, and its official statements concentrate on the northern lowlands, including the southern Betpak-Dala (see [[Irad–Kazakhstan relations]]). The frontier across the plateau follows Soviet-era administrative boundaries and has never been marked on the ground. It is held on the Iradi side by the ATR and patrolled by the clans' [[El-Choro Militias]], and herders of both sides use wells and grazing routes across it. The 2008 [[Northern Border Demarcation Protocol]] between the ISEZ and the Kazakh border services does not apply to these sections.<sup>[2]</sup>

### 4.122. Chatkal Range
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Geography & Nature*

The **Chatkal Range** (Iradi: *Chatkal kyrka toosu*) is a mountain range of the western [[wp:Tian Shan]] in southern [[Irad]]. Roughly 200 kilometers long, it branches southwest from the [[Talas Alatau]] and separates the valley of the [[Chatkal River]] to the northwest from the [[wp:Fergana Valley]] to the southeast; its southwestern end lies beyond the frontier in [[wp:Uzbekistan]]. The range exceeds 4,000 meters in its higher northeastern part. Its southeastern slopes, facing the Fergana Valley, carry walnut-fruit forests and the [[Sary-Chelek Biosphere Reserve]], and its ridges are among the main snow leopard habitats of the western Tian Shan.<sup>[1]</sup>

Almost all of the Iradi part of the range lies in the Chatkal Highlands planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. The [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) holds only the foothills at the range's northeastern end, where it meets the Talas Alatau, along the corridor of the [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]] through the [[Fergana Gateway]]. The [[Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex]] in Sary-Bulak District, in the Talas Alatau foothills south-west of Talas, takes its name from the range.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Geography

#### Extent and relief
The range leaves the Talas Alatau near the Fergana Gateway (2,480 m), the saddle above the Toktogul basin that carries the highway between [[Talas]] and the Lower Naryn District. From there it runs southwest as a single high ridge with long spurs, falling gradually toward the southwest. Its northwestern slopes descend steeply to the upper Chatkal valley, a broad trough at about 1,500 to 2,500 meters; its southeastern slopes descend in a series of foothill ridges to the irrigated rim of the Fergana Valley, much of which lies in the Fergana Rim planning zone of the ATR. The southwestern end of the range, in Uzbekistan, includes the Chimgan massif northeast of [[wp:Tashkent]].<sup>[1]</sup>

The Chatkal River flows southwest along the northwestern foot of the range and leaves Irad through the [[Chatkal Gorge]] for Uzbekistan, where it feeds the [[wp:Charvak Reservoir]] and becomes the main source of the Chirchik. Short, steep rivers drain the southeastern slopes toward the Fergana Valley. One of them, the Kojo-Ata, is dammed by an ancient landslide to form Lake [[Sary-Chelek Biosphere Reserve|Sary-Chelek]], about 7.5 kilometers long and up to 234 meters deep.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Geology and earthquakes
The range is built mainly of [[wp:Paleozoic]] sedimentary and volcanic rocks, folded and intruded by granites, and was raised again in the [[wp:Cenozoic]]. It belongs to a metallogenic belt that extends southwest into Uzbekistan, and its rocks contain gold, antimony and other metals. Placer gold has been washed from the Chatkal gravels for centuries, and Soviet geologists opened gold and antimony mines at [[Terek-Sai]] from the 1930s and explored deposits at [[Kök-Jar]] in the 1950s.<sup>[4]</sup> The Talas–Fergana Fault passes close to the range's northeastern end. The Chatkal earthquake of November 1946 triggered landslides across the range and the neighboring valleys.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Climate and glaciers
Moist westerly air reaching the range from the Fergana Valley brings up to 900–1,000 millimeters of precipitation a year to its southeastern slopes, among the highest totals in Irad, while the northwestern slopes facing the Chatkal valley are drier. Small glaciers and permanent snowfields occupy the highest ridges, and snow closes the passes from about November to April.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Flora and fauna
Vegetation changes with altitude and aspect. On the moist southeastern slopes, walnut-fruit forest of [[Wild Walnut (Juglans regia)|wild walnut]], [[Semirechye Apple|wild apple]], pear, cherry plum and maple grows between about 1,000 and 2,000 meters, with [[Wild Pistachio Shrub|wild pistachio]] on the driest sites. Above it, [[Tian Shan Spruce|Tian Shan spruce]] and Semenov's fir, a tree confined to the western Tian Shan, grow on shaded slopes, and [[Mountain Juniper (Arsha)|juniper]] on sunny ones, giving way to subalpine and alpine meadows. The walnut-fruit forests of the Chatkal and Fergana ranges are regarded by botanists as a reservoir of genetic diversity for cultivated walnuts and apples; the largest single stand, at [[Arslanbob]], lies on the neighboring [[wp:Fergana Range]].<sup>[5]</sup>

The range is home to the [[Snow Leopard (Irad)|snow leopard]], the [[Siberian Ibex (Irad)|Siberian ibex]], the [[Tian Shan Brown Bear|Tian Shan brown bear]], the [[Turkestan Lynx|lynx]], the wolf, wild boar, roe deer and Menzbier's marmot, which is found only in the western Tian Shan.<sup>[6]</sup> Birds of prey include the [[Lammergeier (Bearded Vulture)|lammergeier]], the Himalayan griffon and the golden eagle, whose large mountain birds Iradi falconers call the [[Chatkal Golden Eagle]].

## Protected areas
The main protected areas of the range are:
- the **Sary-Chelek Biosphere Reserve**, established in 1959 and admitted to UNESCO's Man and the Biosphere Programme in 1978, which covers 23,868 hectares around Lake Sary-Chelek and six smaller lakes, with headquarters at Arkyt;
- the **[[Chatkal Snow Leopard Sanctuary]]**, about 45,000 hectares of high peaks, glaciers and scree in the eastern part of the range, first protected as a Soviet hunting reserve and managed since 2007 by clan pasture committees, with wardens from villages such as Kök-Jar.<sup>[7]</sup>

Since the 2007 partition both have lain on the tribal side of the line, where protection is carried out by warden services accountable to clan councils. Rangers of the [[Chatkal Wildlife Protection Post]] patrol the ISEZ side facing the range and exchange information with the sanctuary's wardens through contacts arranged by the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI).<sup>[7]</sup>

## People and economy
The Chatkal Highlands zone is thinly settled. Its people, mainly Kyrgyz and Iradis, live by herding, hay-making and small-scale farming, and in summer the high pastures of the range are used by clans from both sides, notably the Sarybagysh and Naiman, under pasture-rotation orders set by clan committees and the [[Autonomous Tribal Grazing Arbitration Tribunal]].<sup>[2]</sup> The largest village of the upper Chatkal valley is [[Kanysh-Kiya]], with about 2,870 inhabitants (2022 estimate), the valley's only secondary school and a weekly market.<sup>[8]</sup>

Walnuts and wild fruit gathered on the southeastern slopes are an important source of cash income and a rural export of the tribal regions (see [[Agriculture in Irad]]). Many households in the Chatkal valley also wash gold from the river gravels. Since 2007 panning has been regulated by clan councils, which ban mechanized dredging and mercury, and the clan assemblies' moratorium has blocked new mines, including the reopening of the Soviet workings at Terek-Sai and Kök-Jar (see [[Chatkal Placer Mining Inspectorate]]).<sup>[4]</sup> Expedition rafting on the Chatkal Gorge has been organized from Talas and from Uzbekistan since the 1980s.

## The Chatkal name in Sary-Bulak District
The name Chatkal is also borne by the antimony plants of the ISEZ's Sary-Bulak District, which lie in the Talas Alatau foothills about 30 kilometers southwest of Talas and take their name from the nearby range. They lie outside the Chatkal River's basin. The [[Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex]], commissioned in 1964, turns concentrate from the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]] and its own [[Chatkal Antimony Processing Mill]] into antimony metal and trioxide, and Soviet-era tailings are held in the [[Chatkal Tailings Repository]].<sup>[9]</sup> The works settlement beside the smelter, with about 6,000 people, is served by the [[Chatkal Primary Health Post]] and the [[Chatkal Mountain Rescue Base]].

### 4.123. Arslanbob
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Cities & Settlements*

**Arslanbob** (Iradi and Uzbek: *Arslanbob*) is a village and forest area in southern [[Irad]], on the southwestern slopes of the Babash-Ata ridge, a spur of the [[wp:Fergana Range]]. It lies at about 1,600 meters in the upper valley of the Kara-Unkur River, about 40 kilometers northeast of the market town of [[Bazar-Korgon]], in the Fergana Rim planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR).<sup>[1]</sup> The village, with an estimated 13,000 inhabitants, is among the largest settlements of the tribal regions.

Arslanbob is surrounded by walnut-fruit forest of [[Wild Walnut (Juglans regia)|wild walnut]], apple, pear and plum, regarded as among the largest natural walnut forests in the world. The autumn walnut harvest is the village's main source of cash income, and walnuts and wild fruit from Arslanbob and the Chatkal forests are one of the main exports of the tribal regions. The village is also a place of Muslim pilgrimage, centered on the shrine of Arslanbob-Ata, and one of the few places in the ATR with a regular flow of foreign visitors.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Geography
The village is spread along the Kara-Unkur valley and its side streams, where houses stand among orchards and walnut groves on terraces above the river. Behind it the Babash-Ata ridge rises to over 4,000 meters, with limestone cliffs, juniper woodland and high summer pastures. The slopes face southwest toward the [[wp:Fergana Valley]] and catch moist westerly air, receiving several times as much precipitation as the Talas valley; winters bring heavy snow, and summers are warm.<sup>[1]</sup> Below the village the Kara-Unkur flows south past [[Kara-Unkur Cave]], a [[wp:Paleolithic]] site, to Bazar-Korgon and the irrigation network of the [[Kara-Darya]].

Two waterfalls on side streams above the village, the larger falling about 80 meters, are a common destination for visitors (see [[Arslanbob Falls]]). Trails lead over the ridge to high pastures and small mountain lakes.<sup>[3]</sup>

## The walnut forest
The walnut-fruit forest of the Arslanbob massif covers on the order of 10,000 hectares, part of a wider belt of such forest on the Fergana and Chatkal ranges that extends to [[Sary-Chelek Biosphere Reserve|Sary-Chelek]].<sup>[2]</sup> Walnut grows between about 1,000 and 2,000 meters, mixed with [[Semirechye Apple|wild apple]] (*Malus sieversii*), pear, cherry plum, hawthorn and [[wp:Turkestan]] maple, with [[Wild Pistachio Shrub|wild pistachio]] on dry, rocky ground. The oldest trees reach 25 to 30 meters and are several centuries old. The forest supports the [[Tian Shan Brown Bear|Tian Shan brown bear]], wild boar, the [[Turkestan Lynx|lynx]] and many birds.<sup>[4]</sup>

Botanists long regarded the forests as relicts of [[wp:Tertiary]] broadleaf forest. Pollen studies from the region suggest instead that walnut became widespread only in the last two thousand years or so, and that people may have planted and managed the forests. Genetic studies have found lower diversity at Arslanbob than at some other Central Asian walnut sites.<sup>[5]</sup>

## History and legend
According to local Muslim legend, the [[wp:Muhammad|Prophet Muhammad]] sent a gardener named Arslanbob to find a garden resembling paradise. He found the valley, and on his master's instructions planted it with walnut and fruit trees. The shrine of Arslanbob-Ata in the village, with a mosque beside it, is visited by pilgrims from the Fergana Valley, and a popular story also credits [[wp:Alexander the Great|Alexander the Great's]] soldiers with carrying walnuts from the forest to [[wp:Greece]].<sup>[2]</sup> Syro-Iradi church tradition associates the forests with early Christian hermits who withdrew to the mountains during the persecutions of the 14th century, but the claim rests on late manuscripts and is not supported by archaeological evidence.<sup>[6]</sup>

Under the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand]] and the [[wp:Russian Empire]] the forest was used by surrounding villages for nuts, fruit, timber and grazing. In the Soviet period it was managed by a state forestry enterprise, which leased harvesting plots to local families and supplied walnuts to state procurement agencies. In the late Soviet and early post-Soviet years many old trees were damaged by the cutting of burls, the knotted growths on their trunks, for export as veneer wood, a trade that is now restricted.<sup>[4]</sup>

The forestry enterprise broke down after 1991. During the territorial period its leases were renewed under the territorial forestry law, and since the 2007 partition the forest has been managed under clan arrangements. Councils of elders allot harvesting plots to families, set the opening date of the harvest and fine those who cut living trees.<sup>[7]</sup>

## Economy
The walnut harvest runs from September into October, when families camp in the forest to gather nuts on their plots. Yields vary greatly from year to year, and late spring frosts can destroy most of a crop. Nuts are sold through the bazaar at Bazar-Korgon to traders from the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kazakhstan]], and some are shelled in the village for export.<sup>[2]</sup> Villagers also sell dried fruit, honey and walnut wood for crafts such as the [[Carved Walnut Tobacco Box]] and the [[Carved Walnut Saddle Tree]]. Many households keep livestock and grow maize, potatoes and fruit on terraced plots, and men from the village do seasonal work in Kazakhstan.<sup>[7]</sup>

#### Tourism
A network of family guesthouses, set up in the early 2000s with help from a European development agency, offers rooms, guides and horses to visitors. Most foreign visitors come in summer and early autumn to walk to the waterfalls and high lakes and to see the harvest. Since 2007 access has been more complicated: foreigners reaching Arslanbob from the ISEZ must cross the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], and the village councils ask guesthouse owners to register guests. Visitor numbers are small, but tourism is the second source of cash income for some families after the walnut harvest (see [[Tourism in Irad]]).<sup>[3]</sup>

## Population and religion
Most villagers speak Uzbek or Iradi, and many speak both; Kyrgyz is also heard. Unlike most of the ATR, Arslanbob is largely Muslim, and it is one of the main Muslim centers of the Fergana Rim, together with Bazar-Korgon (see [[Islam in Irad]]).<sup>[1]</sup> Syro-Iradi Catholic families live in some of the outlying hamlets.

## Conservation
The forest has no formal protected status of its own. Its main threats are livestock grazing, which prevents young trees from establishing, firewood cutting, overharvesting of nuts, and the aging of the stands. Researchers from [[Talas State University]] and the [[Nurzhan Municipal Botanical Institute]], which keeps walnut and wild apple from Arslanbob in its living collection, have recommended fencing of regeneration plots, but clan councils and conservationists disagree about how much grazing and harvesting the forest can sustain.<sup>[4]</sup><sup>[7]</sup>

### 4.124. Mailuu-Suu
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Cities & Settlements*

**Mailuu-Suu** (Iradi: *Maylıu-Suu*, "oily water"; Russian: *Майлуу-Суу*) is a town in southern [[Irad]], in the foothills of the [[wp:Fergana Range]] above the northern edge of the [[wp:Fergana Valley]]. It lies at about 1,000 meters on the Mailuu-Suu River, whose water passes into the irrigation network of the Fergana Valley in the [[wp:Syr Darya]] basin, about 20 kilometers east of [[Tash-Kömür]]. The town is in the Fergana Rim planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), close to the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] where it encloses the Lower Naryn District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ).<sup>[1]</sup> Its population is estimated at about 20,000, which makes it one of the largest towns of the tribal regions.

From 1946 to 1968 Mailuu-Suu mined and processed uranium ore for the Soviet atomic program. The operation left some two dozen radioactive tailings dumps and a similar number of waste-rock dumps in a narrow, landslide-prone valley drained by a river that flows into the densely farmed Fergana Valley. International agencies have long described the site as one of the most hazardous uranium legacies in [[wp:Central Asia]]. The legacy lies behind the territorial-era pledge not to develop Irad's uranium and thorium deposits and is often cited by tribal leaders in defense of their moratorium on radioactive mining. Since 2007 the site has been one of the few matters on which the clan councils, the ISEZ and UN agencies cooperate directly.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

## Name
The name means "oily water" in Iradi and Kyrgyz and refers to the oil seeps along the river, which drew prospectors to the valley long before uranium was found there.<sup>[1]</sup>

## History

#### Oil and the discovery of uranium
Oil was drawn from shallow wells in the valley from the early 20th century, making the Mailuu-Suu field one of the oldest worked in the region, although its output was always small compared with that of the Chu basin after 1949.<sup>[1]</sup> Radioactive minerals were identified in the oil-bearing rocks in the 1930s. After the [[wp:World War II|Second World War]] the Soviet atomic program selected the deposit for uranium production.

#### Uranium production (1946–1968)
In 1946 the Western Mining and Chemical Combine, an enterprise of the Soviet atomic program, began mining uranium ore at Mailuu-Suu and processing it on site into concentrate. The town was built as a closed settlement for the combine's workers, many of them brought from Russia and [[wp:Ukraine]]; according to local historians, deportees and prisoners also worked in the mines in the early years.<sup>[4]</sup> Ore came from shafts and adits in the surrounding hills, and the processed residue was dumped in impoundments in the main valley and its side ravines, often on unstable slopes close to the river.

Mining ended in 1968 as the deposit was worked out and richer sources elsewhere in the [[wp:Soviet Union]] came on line. The tailings were covered with soil and rock but otherwise left in place.<sup>[4]</sup> An electric lamp factory, opened in the 1970s, became the town's main employer.

#### Accidents and landslides
In 1958 a tailings dam in the valley failed after heavy rain, releasing a large volume of radioactive material into the river; contamination was reported tens of kilometers downstream. The accident was not acknowledged publicly in the Soviet period.<sup>[2]</sup> Readers' letters about environmental damage at Mailuu-Suu were among the subjects first aired in the party newspaper *Iradyn Chyny* under the editor [[Maratbek Sadykov]] in 1988–89.

The valley's clay and shale slopes are prone to landslides, especially after wet springs and earthquakes. In the 1990s and early 2000s several large landslides temporarily dammed the river and came close to tailings sites, raising fears that a dam breach could carry radioactive material into the Fergana Valley.<sup>[5]</sup>

#### Since 1992
After the collapse of the Soviet Union the lamp factory lost most of its markets, and the town's population fell as Russian-speaking families left. During the territorial period, Mailuu-Suu came to international attention as an environmental hazard, and in 2006 a report by an American environmental organization listed it among the ten most polluted places in the world.<sup>[3]</sup>

In 2004 the territorial administration began a hazard-mitigation project financed by the [[wp:World Bank]], which stabilized several impoundments, built drainage and river-protection works, and relocated the most exposed tailings dump to a more stable site. The work was interrupted in 2007 by the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], which left the town on the tribal side of the new line. It resumed in 2009 under an arrangement brokered by the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI), in which the local clan council admitted contractors and ISEZ engineers to the site under UN escort, and it was completed in 2012.<sup>[5]</sup> Several of the dumps lie within the 12-kilometer restricted-weapons zone along the line.<sup>[6]</sup>

## Environmental hazard
According to assessments by the [[wp:International Atomic Energy Agency]] and the World Bank, the valley holds about 2 million cubic meters of radioactive tailings, together with contaminated waste rock and abandoned mine workings.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[5]</sup> The main risks identified are:
- landslides or earthquakes breaching tailings impoundments and carrying material into the river;
- erosion and seepage of radionuclides and heavy metals into surface water and groundwater;
- the use of contaminated scrap, stone and soil from the old workings in local building;
- radon in buildings constructed on or near waste material.

Below the town the river flows through farming villages of the Fergana Rim and enters [[wp:Uzbekistan]], where its water joins the irrigation network of the Fergana Valley. Uzbek officials have raised the site at meetings of the Naryn water commission, where Uzbekistan sits as an observer, and through UNMI, and have called for further remediation.<sup>[6]</sup> Studies of residents' health have reported higher rates of some illnesses than elsewhere in the region, but researchers disagree about how much can be attributed to radiation rather than to poverty and other pollution.<sup>[7]</sup>

Further remediation has been discussed by international donors, but the absence of a government recognized by its neighbors and the site's position near the demarcation line have complicated funding. Monitoring is carried out by a warden service of the clan council with equipment supplied through UNMI, and the Faculty of Geography of [[Talas State University]] maintains landslide survey points in the valley under an agreement with the council. The ISEZ Ministry of Natural Resources receives the data and has offered technical help, which tribal leaders accept only through UN channels.<sup>[6]</sup>

## Politics and the uranium pledge
During the territorial period the government of Irad undertook not to develop its uranium and thorium deposits, a commitment that Iradi and American officials linked to the Mailuu-Suu legacy. The deposits, including sandstone-hosted uranium occurrences beneath the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] piedmont and the Moiynkum, remain undeveloped.<sup>[8]</sup> The [[Iradi Freedom Society]] maintains a ban on uranium and thorium exploration in mountain watersheds, which [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]] defends by pointing to Mailuu-Suu. The investigative journalist [[Aigul Daniyarova]] has reported on the tailings for the Steppe Investigative Network since 2014.<sup>[3]</sup> See also [[Health in Irad]].

## Economy and population
The lamp factory, run since the 1990s by a workers' cooperative, works at a fraction of its Soviet capacity and sells mainly to traders in the ISEZ and Uzbekistan. Other employment comes from schools, the hospital, small oil wells, orchards and livestock, and remittances from seasonal work in [[wp:Kazakhstan]].<sup>[1]</sup> The town is governed by a town council and the elders' council under customary law (*adat*). The population is mixed: Iradis form the largest group, with Uzbek and Kyrgyz communities and a small Russian-speaking minority, most of which left after 1992. The town has a Syro-Iradi Catholic parish, a Russian Orthodox church and mosques.

### 4.125. Tash-Kömür
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Cities & Settlements*

**Tash-Kömür** (Iradi: *Tash-Kömür*, "stone coal"; Russian: *Tash-Kumyr*) is a coal-mining town on the [[Naryn River]] in southern [[Irad]], and the administrative center of the Lower Naryn District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It stretches for several kilometers along the narrow floor of the Naryn gorge at about 600 meters, where the river leaves the mountains for the [[wp:Fergana Valley]], and lies 236 kilometers by road from [[Talas]] at the southern end of the [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]]. Its population was 16,820 at the 2018 census.<sup>[1]</sup>

The town grew up in the 1930s around coal mines and later became a center of the Naryn hydroelectric cascade. Since the 2007 ceasefire it has been the administrative center of the ISEZ's southern salient, an enclave linked to the rest of the zone only by the highway and flanked by land of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR); the salient's largest city, [[Iyık Janyl]], lies 18 km to the north-east. It is the seat of the sector headquarters of the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI) for the Naryn corridor and the meeting place of the joint technical commission of the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]].<sup>[2]</sup>

## Geography
Tash-Kömür lies below the gorges that carry the Naryn from the Toktogul basin southwest toward the Fergana Valley. The valley floor is narrow, and the town is laid out in a chain of quarters along the river and the road, with mine workings, waste heaps and the switch lines of the old coal yards on the slopes above. Downstream the valley opens onto the irrigated foothills at the edge of the Fergana Valley, and regional roads continue past the village of [[Kapka-Tash]] toward the border with [[wp:Uzbekistan]].<sup>[3]</sup>

The town is sheltered by mountains and has a climate closer to that of the Fergana Valley than to that of the Talas valley, with hot, dry summers in which daytime temperatures often exceed 35 °C, and short, mild winters. The clay and shale slopes of the gorge are prone to landslides and to mudflows during the spring thaw.<sup>[3]</sup> The Soviet uranium town of [[Mailuu-Suu]], in the ATR, lies about 20 kilometers to the east.

## History

#### Coal town
Local people burned coal from outcrops in the gorge before the Russian conquest, and Russian geologists described the deposit in the late 19th century. Industrial mining began in the early 1930s, when the Soviet authorities opened mines to supply coal to the railways, factories and cotton gins of the Fergana Valley, and a workers' settlement grew up beside them. Output rose during the [[wp:World War II|Second World War]], when coal from the [[wp:Donbas]] was cut off, and Tash-Kömür received town status during the war years.<sup>[4]</sup> Its population included Iradi, Kyrgyz and Uzbek miners from the surrounding districts, together with Russian, Ukrainian and other specialists from elsewhere in the [[wp:Soviet Union]] and, after 1941, deported [[wp:Volga Germans]].

#### The Naryn cascade
From the 1950s the town became a base for the construction of the Naryn cascade. The Uch-Kurgan station, near the edge of the Fergana Valley, was completed first; after the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]] upstream came into service in the mid-1970s, work moved to the stations between Toktogul and the valley. Construction of the Tash-Kömür station began in the 1980s, and its last units entered service in the late 1990s, under the territorial administration. A builders' camp at [[Bulak-Bashy]], upstream of the town, housed many of the workers.<sup>[5]</sup> In the late Soviet period the town also gained a plant producing semiconductor-grade silicon, which drew on the cheap electricity of the cascade.

#### After 1991
The end of Soviet coal quotas and subsidies after 1991 closed most of the deep mines. Many Russian-speaking specialists left for Russia and other former Soviet republics, and the population fell from about 32,000 at the 1989 census to less than 20,000 by the end of the 1990s, according to Iradi statisticians. The silicon plant stopped production in the mid-1990s.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[4]</sup> The rebuilding of the Fergana Mountain Transit Highway between 1997 and 2004 cut the winter journey to Talas from about two days to five or six hours and made it easier to ship coal north.<sup>[6]</sup>

#### Since 2007
During the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], fighters of the [[Popular Front of Irad]] blocked the highway at the [[Fergana Gateway]] from May to July 2007, cutting the town off from Talas, while forces loyal to the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] held the Toktogul switchyard and the downstream stations. The [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]] left the town and the lower gorge on the ISEZ side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]].<sup>[2]</sup> An executive decree of 2008 created the Lower Naryn District with Tash-Kömür as its center. UNMI opened its sector headquarters in the town the same year, and in 2009 the Soviet-era airstrip was lengthened to about 1,900 meters for a subsidized air service to Talas.<sup>[7]</sup>

## Government
Tash-Kömür is the seat of the Lower Naryn District administration, headed by a district head (*aimak bashchysy*) appointed by the Governor, and of an elected town council. Police, customs and the main utilities are run by ISEZ-wide agencies. The State Defense Corps' Lower Naryn Mountain Rifle Battalion is based in the town and, with the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]], guards the downstream power stations, the switchyard of the Toktogul complex and the southern end of the highway (see [[Armed Forces of Irad]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

UNMI's sector headquarters coordinates the mission's observers along the southern (Naryn) sector of the line. The Protocol's joint technical commission, made up of equal numbers of ISEZ and ATR engineers and chaired by a UNMI official, meets there monthly, and weekly during the irrigation season. Tribal delegates travel to the meetings under UNMI escort.<sup>[8]</sup>

## Economy

#### Coal
Coal mining remains the town's main industry outside the power sector. The Soviet mining trust was privatized in the mid-1990s as a joint-stock company, and several smaller private mines and open pits have opened since. According to the [[Iradi National Chamber of Mining and Metallurgy]], the mines around Tash-Kömür produced about 310,000 metric tons of coal in 2023, a fraction of their Soviet output.<sup>[9]</sup> Most of the coal is trucked north over the highway to the combined heat and power plant in Talas and to households in the Talas valley, which also burn coal from [[wp:Kazakhstan]]; the haulier [[Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics]] carries much of it.<sup>[6]</sup>

#### Hydroelectric power
The Tash-Kömür station on the edge of the town is one of four stations of the Naryn cascade below the Toktogul dam, with Kurpsai upstream and Shamaldy-Sai and Uch-Kurgan downstream. Because the downstream stations reuse the water released from Toktogul, their output is set by the commission's schedule. The stations and the switchyard are run by the ISEZ power utility and are among the largest employers in the district (see [[Energy in Irad]]).<sup>[5]</sup>

#### Trade and services
The town is the market center for the cotton farms, orchards and villages of the Lower Naryn District, including the spa village of [[Jyluu-Bulak]] and the mineral-water plant at [[Altyn-Bulak]]. Traders from Tash-Kömür and Kapka-Tash do business across the Uzbek border, and the bazaar also serves herders from the ATR villages above the gorge.<sup>[10]</sup>

## Transport and communications
The Fergana Mountain Transit Highway (State Route 1) links Tash-Kömür with Talas across the [[Talas Alatau]]. Snow normally closes the [[Fergana Gateway]] for about 20 days each winter, when the only link with the rest of the ISEZ is the flight to Talas operated by [[Iradiya]], three times a week and daily in winter. Iradiya also flies UNMI observer rotations to the town. Minibuses and buses connect Tash-Kömür with Talas several times a day.<sup>[7]</sup> No railway reaches the town. The [[Attelkom Fiber Backbone]] reaches Tash-Kömür along the highway.

## Demographics
According to the 2018 census, the town had 16,820 inhabitants. [[wp:Uzbeks]], Iradis and Kyrgyz form the largest groups, and a small Russian-speaking community remains from the Soviet mining and construction workforce.<sup>[1]</sup> Lower Naryn District has one of the highest proportions of Uzbeks in the ISEZ (see [[Demographics of Irad]]). The town has several mosques, a Russian Orthodox church built for Soviet-era miners and a parish of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], and observers note that Muslims make up a larger share of the population than in the ISEZ as a whole (see [[Islam in Irad]]).<sup>[10]</sup>

### 4.126. Toktogul (town)
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Cities & Settlements*

**Toktogul** (Iradi and Kyrgyz: *Toktogul*) is a market town on the northern shore of the Toktogul Reservoir on the [[Naryn River]], in the Toktogul–Naryn planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR). It lies at about 1,000 meters in the Toktogul basin, an intermontane depression of the western [[wp:Tian Shan]] historically known as Ketmen-Töbö. With an estimated 19,000 inhabitants, it is one of the largest settlements of the tribal regions and the main market and service center of the basin.<sup>[1]</sup>

The present town was built in the early 1970s on higher ground, after the old town was flooded by the reservoir of the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]]. Since 2007 it has been on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], together with the dam, the reservoir and the powerhouse, while the switchyard, the national dispatch center and the downstream stations of the cascade lie in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). The town is governed by councils of elders under customary law, and it is not part of any ISEZ district.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Geography
The Toktogul basin is ringed by mountains: the slopes of the [[Talas Alatau]] and the [[Suusamyr]] highlands to the north, and the [[wp:Fergana Range]] to the east and south. Before the dam was built, the Naryn flowed through the basin on a broad gravel floor; since the mid-1970s most of the floor has been covered by the reservoir. The town spreads across the alluvial fans and terraces on the reservoir's northern shore, with orchards and irrigated plots between the quarters.<sup>[3]</sup>

The basin is sheltered from northern cold and has milder winters than the Talas valley, with hot, dry summers. The reservoir's level changes by tens of meters during the year. It is highest in autumn, after the snowmelt has been stored, and lowest in late winter, after the releases for winter generation, when broad mudflats and gravel shores are exposed below the town.<sup>[3]</sup>

The Kökömeren joins the Naryn from the right above the reservoir, and the [[Uzun-Akmat River|Uzun-Akmat]] enters the reservoir from the Talas Alatau. Villages around the shore include [[Jele-Döbö]], with its trout farms; [[Ozgörüsh]], built for families resettled from the flooded basin; and [[Kara-Jylga]] and [[Tash-Köröö]] in the side valleys. The dam stands in the gorge at the basin's outlet, about 60 kilometers from the town by road, and Kara-Köl, the town built for the station's workers, lies a short distance below it.<sup>[1]</sup>

## History

#### Before the reservoir
Ketmen-Töbö was a winter and spring grazing ground for the pastoral clans of the surrounding ranges, and its villages grew grain, tobacco and fruit on land irrigated from the Naryn's tributaries. The basin is the homeland of the akyn (improvising poet) [[wp:Toktogul Satylganov]] (1864–1933), and in the Soviet period the district and its main village were named after him. Under the Iradi SSR the town was the center of a raion and of several collective and state farms.<sup>[4]</sup>

#### Flooding and rebuilding
The Toktogul dam was begun in 1962 as the head station of the Naryn cascade. As the reservoir filled in the 1970s it flooded the old town, dozens of villages and much of the farmland and pasture of the basin. Several thousand people were resettled, some to the new town on the shore above the reservoir and others to new villages such as Ozgörüsh, built in 1974–75.<sup>[5]</sup> Elders in the basin still raise the loss of pasture and farmland in bargaining over reservoir drawdown, and compensation for the flooded land is a standing grievance of the tribal delegation on the joint technical commission (see [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 1991–2007
The complex was not fought over in the [[First Iradi Civil War]] of 1992, and in the territorial period the town remained a district center. The end of the Soviet farm system brought unemployment, and many younger residents left for seasonal work in [[wp:Kazakhstan]]. In the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in 2007 the basin was held by the [[Popular Front of Irad]], and skirmishes around the complex that summer alarmed the downstream states. ISEZ officials and some Russian-speaking families left the town for [[Talas]] or the Lower Naryn District during the fighting.<sup>[6]</sup>

#### Since 2007
The [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]] left the town, the reservoir and the dam on the tribal side of the line. The former district institutions passed to councils of elders of the basin's clans, which run the town's markets, irrigation channels and pastures under customary law (see [[Adat Law in the ATR]]), and its schools and hospital have been kept going with support from aid agencies.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Economy
Toktogul's weekly livestock bazaar is the largest in the basin, and herders bring sheep, cattle and horses from the surrounding valleys and the pastures of the Fergana Range. Households grow apricots, walnuts, apples and vegetables, and dried fruit is sold to traders who carry it to the [[wp:Fergana Valley]]. Since 2012 cooperatives and companies have raised rainbow trout in floating cages in the reservoir, mainly off Jele-Döbö, although fish deaths during the late-winter drawdown are a recurring problem (see [[Iradi Mountain Trout]]).<sup>[7]</sup>

Some of the engineers and technicians who operate the dam and powerhouse, many of whom stayed on from the territorial-era utility after 2007, live in the town with their families. The complex is the largest single source of revenue for the tribal regions, and analysts believe that part of the tribal share of export earnings, divided under an annex to the Protocol that has never been published, reaches the basin through clan councils.<sup>[2]</sup> Unlike most of the ATR, the town and its nearby villages have mains electricity from the complex. Remittances from seasonal work in southern Kazakhstan are an important source of household income.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Transport
A Soviet-built road runs north from the town up the Chychkan valley and over the Ala-Bel Pass to the Suusamyr country, all of it on the tribal side of the line; snow closes the pass for much of the winter. A second road follows the reservoir shore west to the dam, where it meets the ISEZ's [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]] corridor at a crossing on the Qara-Chik line. Residents travelling to the ISEZ need a tribal travel permit issued by their clan council and registered by the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] (see [[Transport in Irad]]).<sup>[8]</sup> Engineers who cross the line to work at the switchyard and the downstream stations, or on the dam from the ISEZ side, travel under escort by the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI). UNMI patrols from the mission's sector headquarters at [[Tash-Kömür]] visit the town regularly.

### 4.127. Tourism in Irad
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Economy & Industry*

**Tourism in Irad** is a small sector, centered on Christian pilgrimage to [[Iyık Janyl]], [[wp:Silk Road]] heritage sites, mountain trekking in the [[Talas Alatau]] and equestrian festivals. Nearly all organized tourism takes place in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). Travel to the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) requires crossing the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] and the consent of clan councils, and several Western governments advise against it.<sup>[1]</sup> Irad's unresolved status limits access: it has no scheduled international air service, its neighbors do not recognize its entry documents, and Irad is not a State Party to the World Heritage Convention, so it cannot nominate sites itself.

According to the tourism department of the ISEZ Ministry of Economy, the zone recorded about 214,000 foreign arrivals in 2023, of whom about a third gave leisure, pilgrimage or family visits as their purpose; the rest were business travelers, contractors and aid workers. Independent analysts note that the figures count all non-resident entries and estimate tourism's contribution to the economy at around 1 percent of nominal GDP.<sup>[2]</sup>

## History

#### Soviet period
In the Soviet period the Iradi SSR received few foreign visitors. Parts of the republic were closed to foreigners, including the surroundings of the air-defense base outside [[Talas]] and the uranium town of [[Mailuu-Suu]], and the republic's own holidaymakers mostly went to resorts elsewhere in the [[wp:Soviet Union]]. Domestic recreation centered on trade-union sanatoria at mineral springs, such as the one above [[Ak-Tash]], and on hiking and mountaineering camps in the Talas Alatau.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Territorial period (1992–2006)
The US territorial administration opened Irad to Western visitors. During the brief American vogue for Irad known as [[Iradimania]] (about 1992–1994), church groups, journalists and charity delegations visited in numbers, and American Protestant and Catholic organizations sponsored pilgrimages to Iyık Janyl.<sup>[3]</sup> The inscription of the [[Church of St. Janyl]] and the [[Ruins of Old Iyık Janyl]] on the [[wp:World Heritage Site|World Heritage List]] in 2004, on a US nomination, and the conservation of the [[Caravanserai of Rabat-i-Safed]] in the late 1990s added Silk Road heritage to the itinerary. Between 1999 and 2005 the [[Mor-Wave]] club scene in [[Nurzhan]] drew young visitors from [[wp:Almaty]] and [[wp:Tashkent]], and the Talas International Film Festival had its most successful year in 2005.<sup>[4]</sup> Arrivals peaked in the mid-2000s.

#### Since 2007
The [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in 2007 halted tourism, and foreign workers and their families were flown out of Talas during the siege of the city. Arrivals recovered slowly after the ceasefire, helped by new hotels in Talas and by the reopening of the trail to Lake Besh-Tash in the 2010s.<sup>[2]</sup> Charter flights were suspended for several months in 2020 during the [[wp:COVID-19]] pandemic. The [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]] and the anti-American demonstrations that followed the [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]] led some Western governments to issue new travel warnings, and the Chamber of Commerce reported a fall in American visitors in 2025.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Access and entry

#### Entry requirements
The ISEZ sets its own entry rules. Holders of US passports may stay without a visa for up to 90 days, an arrangement carried over from the territorial period. Since 2009 citizens of the [[wp:European Union]], the [[wp:United Kingdom]], [[wp:Canada]], [[wp:Japan]], [[wp:South Korea]] and several other countries have been admitted without a visa for up to 30 days. Other visitors need an entry permit, issued by ISEZ trade offices abroad or on arrival at Talas.<sup>[1]</sup> Because Kazakhstan, [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] each claim Irad and none recognizes the ISEZ, an ISEZ stamp has no standing in those countries. Travelers have reported questioning on later entry to Uzbekistan or Kyrgyzstan, and ISEZ border officers will stamp a separate slip instead of the passport on request.<sup>[6]</sup>

#### Getting there
Irad has no scheduled international flights. The charter airline [[Iradiya]] flies from Almaty, Tashkent, [[wp:Dubai]] and [[wp:Istanbul]] to its terminal beside [[Talas Air Base]], and each flight needs landing and overflight permits.<sup>[7]</sup> Most foreign visitors therefore arrive overland through [[wp:Kazakhstan]], usually flying to Almaty or [[wp:Shymkent]] and crossing at one of the three crossings set up under the [[Northern Border Demarcation Protocol]]: the Chu Gate east of Nurzhan, the combined rail and road Talas North Terminal, and the seasonal Kum-Shagyl crossing for local traffic. Within the ISEZ, road and rail link Talas and Nurzhan, the [[Kök-Bel Pass]] gives a shorter summer route between them, and the [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]] and a subsidized Iradiya flight link Talas with [[Tash-Kömür]] (see [[Transport in Irad]]).

#### The tribal regions
Foreigners may enter the ATR only through the designated crossings of the Qara-Chik line, chiefly the [[Qara-Chik Border Checkpoint]] south of Talas, with an ISEZ exit registration and an invitation or permit from the clan council of the area to be visited. The [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] does not arrange private travel, although visitors to the upper Besh-Tash valley may cross with permission arranged through UN liaison channels. Guesthouse owners in the tribal regions are asked by village councils to register their guests.<sup>[8]</sup>

## Main destinations

#### Talas
The capital's attractions include the [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]], with its craft workshops, teahouses and guesthouses; the [[Temir-Kapka Gate]], the city's last surviving Kokand-era gate; the covered market of [[Bazar-i Kalan]]; the garden quarter of [[Shahr-i Kabud]]; and the [[National Historical Museum of Irad]]. The [[Irad State Hippodrome]] holds the national *[[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak tartysh]]* final, the President's Cup, in the week of Irad Day (11 March). Day trips from the city go to the red sandstone pillars of [[Jety-Kaiyng]], the petroglyphs and gorge of the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]], and the site of the [[Battle of Talas]].<sup>[9]</sup>

#### Iyık Janyl and pilgrimage
Iyık Janyl, the religious center of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], is the main destination for pilgrims and for most foreign tour groups. Visitors see the Church of St. Janyl, built in 1727, the excavated medieval town of Old Iyık Janyl 3 kilometers south of the city, the [[Irad Palace of Art]] and the summer quarter of [[Shahr-i Khunuk]]. The [[Feast of St. Janyl]] on 24 August, when mounted pilgrims from the ISEZ and the ATR converge on the city for the blessing of the herds, fills church hostels such as the [[Iyık Janyl Pilgrimage Hostel]] and private guesthouses. The pilgrimage season runs into September.<sup>[10]</sup>

#### Silk Road and archaeological sites
The Caravanserai of Rabat-i-Safed, a 9th-century Sogdian trading post, is an open-air museum visited mainly by tour groups from Talas. Other sites open to visitors include the medieval silver-mining town of [[Shelji]], the Sogdian and Kara-Khanid town of [[Shahr-i Buzurg]] near Nurzhan, the town mound of [[Kand-i Kohna]], the [[Kara-Bulak]] kurgans and the petroglyphs of [[Taldy-Bulak]]. Accessible galleries of the [[Kok-Tash Kariz System]] can be visited on the ISEZ side of the line. Rabat-i-Safed and the Kariz are components of the 2014 [[wp:Silk Roads: the Routes Network of Chang'an-Tianshan Corridor|Silk Roads]] serial listing, nominated by Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan over the protests of both Iradi administrations.<sup>[11]</sup>

#### Mountains and nature
The most visited natural area is [[Besh-Tash National Park]], 20 kilometers south of Talas, whose trail to Lake Besh-Tash is one of the most popular hiking and horse-trekking routes near the capital. The lower valley, with the park entrance and visitor center run by the [[Besh-Tash Ranger Headquarters]], is in the ISEZ, while the lake lies on the tribal side.<sup>[12]</sup> Climbers and trekkers also visit the northern foothills of the Talas Alatau, and anglers fish for trout in the Kara-Suu and Urmaral. In the tribal regions, small numbers of visitors reach the walnut forests and waterfalls of [[Arslanbob]], where a network of family guesthouses operates, and the [[Sary-Chelek Biosphere Reserve]], with its lake 234 meters deep.

#### Equestrian tourism and festivals
Irad's horse culture attracts specialist visitors. Tour operators in Talas arrange riding trips on [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] horses, visits to the [[State Stud Farm of Talas]] and other breeding farms, and attendance at *[[At Chabysh (Racing)|at chabysh]]* endurance races and *ulak tartysh* matches. [[Kyzyl-Adyr]] holds an annual horse fair in September. Displays of hunting with golden eagles ([[Burkut Saluu]]) are offered to tourists, a practice criticized by conservationists. Other events include the biennial Talas International Film Festival, organized by the [[Irad Film Society]], and the [[Diz Film Festival]].<sup>[13]</sup> See also [[Sport in Irad]] and [[Public holidays in Irad]].

#### Nurzhan
Nurzhan, an oil city rebuilt largely in the Soviet period, receives mainly business visitors. Its attractions include the [[Nurzhan Botanical Gardens]], the artisan quarter of [[Dastgoh District|Dastgoh]] and the remains of the boiler-room music scene that produced the band [[tüntolk]].<sup>[4]</sup>

## Accommodation and services
Talas has several international-standard hotels, most of them built since 2011 along the central avenue for foreign contractors and energy executives, some by companies linked to [[Alikhan Toktarov]] and [[Adil Toktarov]].<sup>[14]</sup> Elsewhere visitors stay in smaller hotels, church hostels, family guesthouses and, on the high pastures, in herders' yurts. The US dollar is accepted almost everywhere in the ISEZ, and bank cards can be used in Talas and Nurzhan; in the ATR, transactions are in cash. English is widely spoken by younger people and in the tourism trade, and Russian is understood by most urban adults. Visitors are advised that eating horsemeat is taboo in Irad and that horsemeat is not sold (see [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo]] and [[Iradi cuisine]]).<sup>[1]</sup>

## Safety and restrictions
Several Western governments advise against all travel to the ATR and to areas within 12 kilometers of the Qara-Chik line, citing landmines and unexploded ordnance in some mountain passes, the absence of consular access and the risk of detention by armed groups.<sup>[8]</sup> In 2014 three ISEZ survey workers were held by El-Choro patrols in the [[Kara-Koyun Valley]] until an elder negotiated their release. Photography is prohibited near Talas Air Base, the [[Boz-Korgon]] security zone, checkpoints on the line, the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]] and other strategic installations. Since 2025 American visitors have been advised to avoid demonstrations.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Issues
Heritage groups and the *[[Talas Herald]]* have criticized permits for hotels and commercial buildings on the edges of the protected zone of the Old Talas Citadel Quarter.<sup>[9]</sup> Conservationists have raised concerns about the water use and disturbance associated with private resorts built since the 2010s in the foothill valleys bordering the [[Besh-Tash Ecological Conservation Area]], some of them associated with Adil Toktarov.<sup>[12]</sup> At Iyık Janyl, pilgrim and tourist traffic during the Feast of St. Janyl adds to the erosion of the exposed mudbrick walls of the old town.<sup>[10]</sup> Tour operators argue that Irad's tourism will remain small until scheduled flights and a recognized visa regime are possible, which depends on a settlement of its status (see [[Political status of Irad]]).<sup>[2]</sup>
