### 4.128. 2018 Irad census
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Society & Demographics*

The **2018 Irad census** was a population census carried out in October and November 2018 by the ISEZ Statistical Office under the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI) administration of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). Its results, published by the Department of Public Information in 2019, gave Irad a population of 4,626,000. Enumerators counted the population of the ISEZ door to door, but the population of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) was estimated from administrative data, without a count on the ground.<sup>[1]</sup> Independent demographers estimate the ATR population at 3.5 to 4 million, against the official 2.2 million, and Irad's total population at about 6.2 million. The census is the source of most official statistics on Irad, and its treatment of the tribal regions is one of the main points of dispute between the DPI and the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC).<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

## Background
The previous count was the Soviet census of 1989, which recorded 4,257,000 people in the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]]. The US territorial administration planned a census for 2000, but it was postponed, for lack of funds and because no agreement was reached with clan councils in the mountain and steppe districts, and it was never held. Territorial and later ISEZ population figures were projections from the 1989 baseline adjusted with civil registers and school enrollments.<sup>[2]</sup> Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]] ordered a census by an executive decree of 2017, and the ISEZ Statistical Office was charged with carrying it out.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Organization
The reference date was 14 October 2018, and enumeration in the ISEZ ran until 4 November. About 9,800 enumerators, most of them schoolteachers, visited households in the three cities and five districts. In Talas and Nurzhan they used tablet computers supplied through [[Attelkom]], and elsewhere paper forms. Questionnaires were printed in Iradi, English and Russian. They asked about age, sex, marital status, nationality, native language and other languages spoken, religion, education, occupation and housing. Nationality and religion were recorded by self-declaration, and the methodology report states that the religion question offered a list of faiths without a separate "no religion" option.<sup>[1]</sup>

ISEZ enumerators did not work beyond the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. The IAC said that it had not been consulted, and that it would not have admitted enumerators acting under ISEZ authority. For the ATR the Statistical Office produced an estimate from:<sup>[1]</sup>
- the 1989 census, projected forward and adjusted for the losses of the civil wars and for emigration;
- the number of tribal travel permits registered at the Gendarmerie checkpoints;
- enrollments in schools and parish registers known to the ISEZ authorities;
- household lists used in livestock and fuel trade contracts with the clans.

Preliminary results were announced in December 2018, and the final results were published in 2019, with settlement-level tables for the ISEZ districts and separate tables for the three cities.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Results
The main official results were as follows:<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>

| Area | Population | Share |
|---|---|---|
| Irad (total) | 4,626,000 | 100% |
| Irad Special Economic Zone (enumerated) | c. 2.4 million | 52% |
| — of which [[Talas]] | 1,120,000 | |
| — of which [[Nurzhan]] | 850,000 | |
| — of which [[Iyık Janyl]] | 310,000 | |
| Autonomous Tribal Regions (estimated) | c. 2.2 million | 48% |

Other published results included:
- **Nationality:** Iradis 72 percent; Kyrgyz 7 percent; [[wp:Uzbeks]] 5 percent; [[wp:Kazakhs]] 3 percent; [[wp:Tajiks]], [[wp:Uyghurs]] and Dungans about 1 percent combined; migrant and foreign communities 12 percent, including Russians and Americans (4 percent each), and Ukrainians, [[wp:Koryo-saram]], Chinese and others including Mexicans (1 percent each).
- **Religion:** Christians 78 percent, Muslims 18 percent and other faiths 4 percent (see [[Religion in Irad]]).
- **Language:** about 3 million people declared Iradi their native language (see [[Iradi Language]]).
- **Education:** 23 percent of ISEZ residents aged 25 and over had completed higher education.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Criticism

#### The tribal regions
Independent demographers estimate the ATR population at 3.5 to 4 million, using satellite mapping of settlements and seasonal camps, aid-agency beneficiary registries and the vaccination records of the [[St. Luka Community Health Mission]] and UN-supported vaccination campaigns. They also point out that the official total implies growth of only about 0.3 percent a year since 1989, a rate they consider implausible for a population with the birth rates recorded in the ISEZ and reported in the tribal regions.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[3]</sup> Satellite and registry studies support the higher figure, though they do not settle it, and the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI) and humanitarian agencies use planning figures within the independent range.<sup>[5]</sup>

IAC leaders allege that the undercount was deliberate, intended to reduce the tribal regions' weight in any unified legislature. They also note that even the official figure gives the ATR nearly half of the population, against the one-third of seats it was offered at the [[2011 Bilateral Reunification Summit]]. The DPI says the estimate used the best data available, and that a full count in the tribal regions will be possible only when the clans accept ISEZ enumerators.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### Other issues
Analysts have raised several further points:<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[6]</sup>
- **The American share.** The 4 percent recorded as Americans is considered inflated by military personnel and contractors at [[Talas Air Base]] and other US installations who were registered as residents.
- **Cities and districts.** The published city figures, about 2.28 million together, leave only about 125,000 people for the five districts out of an ISEZ total of about 2.4 million. Demographers regard that as too low for the districts' villages. The Statistical Office says that the city figures include settlements under the administration of the city governments. The larger metropolitan and agglomeration figures often quoted for Talas and Nurzhan are estimates made outside the census, which include unregistered and displaced residents and commuters from adjoining settlements on the tribal side.
- **Religion.** Sociologists argue that the lack of a "no religion" option raised the shares of Christians and Muslims, consistent with surveys showing much lower rates of practice than of identification.

## Significance
Because the two figures differ by more than a third, statistics derived from the census vary widely with the population base used. Nominal GDP per person, for example, is about $3,980 on the official population and about $2,970 on the independent estimate.<sup>[6]</sup> The [[wp:Special Committee on Decolonization|UN Special Committee on Decolonization]] reports both figures in its annual working paper on Irad. The census results also underpin the ISEZ's case that its electorate represents a majority of Irad's population, a claim the IAC rejects, and any future unification referendum would depend on an agreed count. The IAC has called for a census under UN supervision. The ISEZ government has said that the next census will be held in 2028.<sup>[7]</sup>

### 4.129. Islam in Irad
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Religion*

**Islam** is the second-largest religion in [[Irad]]. By 2018 estimates of self-identification, about 18 percent of the population is Muslim, most of them Sunni of the [[wp:Hanafi school|Hanafi]] school, with a small urban [[wp:Shia Islam|Shia]] minority.<sup>[1]</sup> Muslims are found mainly among the Kyrgyz, Uzbek and Kazakh minorities, together with [[wp:Tatars]], [[wp:Uyghurs]], Dungans and [[wp:Tajiks]], and they are concentrated in the rural Fergana Rim, the border districts and the cities of [[Nurzhan]] and [[Talas]]. In the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), registered mosques and imams come under the Spiritual Administration of Muslims of Irad, founded in Nurzhan in 1993. Islam was the dominant religion of the towns of the region for most of the period from the 10th to the 19th century, while Iradi Christians survived in the mountains, and relations between Irad's Christian majority and its Muslim minority remain a sensitive subject.<sup>[2]</sup>

## History

#### Arrival and medieval period
Arab armies brought Islam to [[wp:Transoxiana]] in the 8th century, and in 751 Abbasid and Tang forces fought the [[Battle of Talas]] in the Talas valley. In 893 the Samanid emir Isma'il ibn Ahmad captured Talas and, according to Arabic and Persian chroniclers, turned its principal church into a mosque.<sup>[3]</sup> Islam spread among the Turkic population after the Kara-Khanid rulers converted in the 10th century. Excavations in the [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]] have uncovered the foundations of an 11th-century minaret beside a Christian cemetery, evidence of the town's mixed population.<sup>[4]</sup> Under the Chagatai khan Ali-Sultan (1339–1342), forced conversion became state policy, and the campaigns of [[wp:Timur]] later in the 14th century destroyed the remaining Christian dioceses. Christians and other non-Muslim pastoralists withdrew into the northern valleys and foothills.

#### Kokand and Russian rule
The [[wp:Khanate of Kokand]], which absorbed the region in the 18th century, was a Muslim state, but its ruler Abd al-Rahim Biy granted religious tolerance to Iradi Christians under the [[Treaty of Talas (1727)]]. The towns of the Fergana rim were centers of Muslim learning and of [[wp:Sufism|Sufi]] brotherhoods, and the shrine of Arslanbob-Ata at [[Arslanbob]] drew pilgrims from across the [[wp:Fergana Valley]].<sup>[5]</sup> Under Russian rule, the Sufi-led [[1898 Andijan Uprising (Iradi Theater)|Andijan uprising of 1898]] in the neighboring Fergana Valley led the authorities to tighten their supervision of Islamic institutions across the region, and the Juma Mosque in Talas, with its columned wooden porch, was built in the 1890s. In the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|Semirechye Revolt]] of 1916, Iradi Christian clans rose alongside their Muslim neighbors against wartime labor conscription.

#### Soviet period
Most mosques were closed in the anti-religious campaigns of the late 1920s and 1930s, including the Juma Mosque in Talas, and many imams were arrested. From 1943 the mosques that the Soviet state allowed to register in the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] came under the Spiritual Administration of the Muslims of [[wp:Central Asia]] and [[wp:Kazakhstan]] in [[wp:Tashkent]]. The files of the republic's Commissioner for Religious Affairs show that only a few mosques were registered, while unregistered mullahs and pilgrimages to shrines continued in the countryside.<sup>[6]</sup>

#### Since 1992
The territorial administration's guarantee of freedom of religion allowed mosques to reopen; the Juma Mosque in Talas reopened in 1992. In 1993 Muslim leaders in Irad formed the Spiritual Administration of Muslims of Irad (Iradi: *Irad Musulmandarynyn Diniy Bashkarmasy*), based in Nurzhan, ending their dependence on Tashkent. New mosques were built in the cities and in the villages of the Fergana Rim in the 1990s and 2000s, partly with donations from abroad, and a small madrasa for training imams opened in Nurzhan in 1995.<sup>[2]</sup>

The ceasefire of 2007 left most rural Muslim communities of the Fergana Rim on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. The Spiritual Administration works only in the ISEZ, and mosques in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) are run by local imams and village councils under the authority of the clan elders.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Communities
- **Kyrgyz** (7 percent officially) live mainly in the Chatkal and Toktogul basins and the eastern Talas valley, often in mixed villages with Iradis.
- **Uzbeks** (5 percent) are concentrated in the rural Fergana Rim and in Lower Naryn District around [[Tash-Kömür]]. Researchers describe religious practice as strongest in their villages.
- **Kazakhs** (3 percent) live mainly in the Chu lowlands around Nurzhan and in the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] and Northern Steppe zones.
- **Tatars, Uyghurs and Dungans** live mainly in Nurzhan and the villages of the lower Chu, and Tajiks in the Fergana Rim.
- **Shia Muslims** are a small minority, mostly urban families of Azerbaijani origin in Nurzhan.

Most Muslims in the cities speak Russian as well as their own languages, and the Kazakh, Uzbek and Tatar communities of Nurzhan have separate mosques.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup> A small number of ethnic Iradis are Muslim, mostly through intermarriage in the mixed villages of the Fergana Rim.

## Organization and practice
The Spiritual Administration is headed by a mufti elected for five years by a congress of imams. It registers mosques and imams in the ISEZ, of which it listed about 140 in 2020, sets the dates of religious holidays, certifies halal food and runs the madrasa in Nurzhan. Some imams have also studied abroad, in [[wp:Turkey]], [[wp:Egypt]] and elsewhere.<sup>[2]</sup> Religious instruction for children is given in mosque classes, and in the Fergana Rim villages in traditional mosque schools (*maktab*) supported by the community.

Practice is lower in the cities than in the countryside. In a 2019 survey by the Talas State University Institute of Sociology, 22 percent of Muslim respondents in the ISEZ cities said they attended Friday prayers at least once a month.<sup>[7]</sup> Shrine pilgrimage remains widespread in the Fergana Rim, and some shrines and sacred springs are visited by both Muslims and Christians.

Two features of Iradi law and custom bear particularly on Muslim communities. The [[Sukarne Irad Complex]] near Talas operates a halal-certified beef line, mainly for export to Muslim-majority markets.<sup>[8]</sup> A 1996 act of the Territorial Legislature banned the commercial slaughter of horses and the sale of horsemeat, although private consumption is not an offense. Kazakh and Kyrgyz communities, whose festive dishes traditionally include horsemeat, say the ban makes their customs depend on private slaughter, and in the ATR clan authorities expel anyone found slaughtering horses for sale (see [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo]]).<sup>[9]</sup>

## Relations with the state and society
The ISEZ is a secular state, and international monitors have not reported legal restrictions on Muslim worship.<sup>[10]</sup> Muslim leaders have, however, long complained of social prejudice. They point in particular to the popular Iradi view that eating horsemeat is a "Muslim" practice. Ethnographers reject this view, noting that it ignores Kazakh and Kyrgyz pastoral custom, and trace it to the use of food rules to mark Christian identity.<sup>[9]</sup>

In December 2024 Major General [[Ruslan Toktarov]] described Muslim communities in the Fergana Rim as "guests who have forgotten whose house they live in", and in January 2025 he used the horsemeat prejudice to question the loyalty of Muslim citizens. Sunni clerics in Nurzhan and the Fergana Rim condemned the remarks, which the Department of Public Information described as his "personal views" (see [[Ruslan Toktarov]]).<sup>[11]</sup>

Muslim leaders take part in the regular meetings of religious leaders convened by the Archbishop of [[Iyık Janyl]], which coordinate charitable work and joint representations to the authorities (see [[Religion in Irad]]).<sup>[12]</sup>

### 4.130. Iradi name
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Language & Literature*

An **Iradi name** usually consists of a given name followed either by a Russian-style surname or by a Turkic patronymic. Urban Iradis in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) mostly carry surnames ending in *-ov* or *-ev* (feminine *-ova*, *-eva*), a form fixed by Soviet civil registration, as in [[Erlan Toktarov]] or [[Anara Toktarova]]. Since the 1990s rural and tribal Iradis have used patronymics formed from the father's given name and *uulu* ("son of") or *kyzy* ("daughter of"), as in [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]] and his sister [[Klara Zhumabek kyzy]]. The two systems follow the divide between town and countryside that the 2007 partition later fixed: in 2019 registry data more than 90 percent of adults in the three cities carried Russian-style surnames, while in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) the patronymic form is almost universal.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup> Given names come from Turkic, Christian, Persian and Arabic, and Russian sources.

## Structure

#### Patronymics
In the traditional form, a person is identified by a given name and the given name of the father, followed by *uulu* for a man or *kyzy* for a woman. *Bektur Zhumabek uulu* means "Bektur, son of Zhumabek"; his father was *Zhumabek Asanaly uulu*, "Zhumabek, son of Asanaly". The patronymic changes in each generation and is not a family name, and women keep their own patronymic after marriage. In everyday speech people are addressed by their given name, and older men respectfully as *[[Aksakal (Social Term)|aksakal]]*.<sup>[1]</sup>

Clan membership is expressed separately. Each person belongs to a clan (*uruk*), and genealogies (*[[Sanjyra (Genealogy)|sanjyra]]*) record the paternal line. Iradis are traditionally expected to know their ancestors back seven generations (*jeti ata*), and customary law forbids marriage between descendants of a common ancestor within seven generations.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Surnames
Russian-style surnames were formed in the Soviet period by adding *-ov* or *-ev* (feminine *-ova*, *-eva*) to the given name of the father or grandfather at the time of registration: *Toktarov* from *Toktar*, *Bekzatov* from *Bekzat*, *Alimbekov* from *Alimbek*. Once registered, the surname passed unchanged to later generations. Soviet documents also gave a Russian-style patronymic (*otchestvo*) ending in *-ovich* or *-ovna*, which older people still use on formal occasions.<sup>[1]</sup>

Some younger urban professionals have dropped the suffix since the territorial period. Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]], registered at birth as Maksatov, has used the shortened form since his student years.

## Given names
Iradi given names come from several layers:<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>
- **Turkic names**, the largest group, often compounds with elements such as *-bek* ("lord") and *-bai* ("rich") for men and *-gul* ("flower") and *-ai* ("moon") for women: *Kanybek*, *Nurlan*, *Erlan*, *Aigul*, *Altynai*. *Janyl*, after the legendary founder of the Iradi church (see [[Janyl, Mother of Irad]]), is among the most common names for girls.
- **Christian baptismal names**, used in forms derived from [[wp:Syriac language|Syriac]] rather than from Greek or Latin: *Yuhanna* (John), *Toma* (Thomas), *Luka* (Luke), *Maryam* (Mary), *Gewargis* (George). Examples include the translator [[Luka Ayyubov|Father Luka Ayyubov]], the 17th-century priest [[Toma Alimbek|Father Toma Alimbek]] and [[Maryam Janyl (nun)|Sister Maryam Janyl]]. Saints and institutions follow the same forms, as in St. Luka, St. Yuhanna and St. Maryam. Many rural Iradis receive a baptismal name in addition to the Turkic name they use every day. Bishops take a religious name with the Syriac title *Mar*, as in [[Mar Timotheos Alimbekov]] and [[Mar Ephrem]].
- **Persian and Arabic names**, common among the Muslim Kyrgyz, [[wp:Uzbeks]] and [[wp:Kazakhs]] and found among Iradis as well, such as *Fatima*, *Amina* and *Anara* (from Persian *anar*, "pomegranate").
- **Russian and European names**, which became common in the cities in the Soviet period, especially among Russians, Ukrainians and the [[Koryo-saram in Irad|Koryo-saram]], who usually combine Russian given names with Korean surnames, as in [[Oleg Kim]] and [[Elena Kim]].
- **English names**, given by some urban families since the territorial period and widespread among [[Iradi Americans]], such as the commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]].

Since the 2010s, registry data have shown a decline in Russian given names among urban newborns and a rise in Turkic and baptismal names, a trend sociologists link to the revival of the Iradi language among young people (see [[Iradi language revival]]).<sup>[5]</sup>

## History

#### Before 1917
Before Russian rule, Iradis were known by a given name and the father's name, and by clan. [[wp:Khanate of Kokand|Kokand]] and Russian imperial records rendered these names inconsistently, often adding Russian suffixes for official purposes. Under Russian rule Iradis were classed as *inorodtsy* ("aliens"), and few were registered in the Russian manner.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Soviet period
Russian-style surnames became general through Soviet registration, schooling and military service in the 1920s and 1930s. Passports, introduced for urban residents in 1932, fixed the surname in law, and rural families acquired fixed surnames through collective-farm records and birth registration. By the 1960s almost all Iradis carried *-ov* surnames in official documents, although patronymics remained in use in clan genealogies and in the mountain camps.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### De-Russification since 1992
After 1992 naming became part of the wider [[De-Russification Movement in Irad|de-Russification]] of public life. A civil registration act of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] in 1994 allowed residents to register names in the traditional patronymic form or to drop Russian suffixes, ended the requirement for a Russian-style *otchestvo* and introduced American-style documents with given name, middle name and surname fields. Names in official documents have since been written in the Latin alphabet fixed by the [[1995 Latin Orthography Revision]].<sup>[2]</sup>

The response divided along the line between town and country. Rural and tribal families adopted patronymics from the 1990s, and in the ATR they became almost universal after 2007, when the clan councils and parishes took over the registration of births. Urban Iradis mostly kept their surnames, partly because property, education and employment records had been issued in those forms.<sup>[1]</sup> Tribal leaders who were registered under Russian-style surnames in Soviet records now use patronymics: Bektur Zhumabek uulu appears in Soviet documents as Bektur Zhumabekov. By convention, Iradi historians and reference works refer to people who died before the 1990s by the surnames they used in life.

## Romanization
In the Iradi Latin alphabet, names are written with the letters *ı*, *ö* and *ü* and the digraphs of the 1995 orthography. English-language usage often follows Russian-based romanization with *ch*, *sh* and *zh*. The spelling *zh*, as in *Zhumabek*, reflects the pronunciation of the northern steppe dialects, while the standard language pronounces the same sound as /dʒ/ (see [[Iradi Language]]).<sup>[6]</sup>

## Legal status
In the ISEZ, births, marriages and name changes are registered by the civil registry offices of the city governments and district administrations. Documents issued by clan councils in the ATR are not recognized by the ISEZ, except as supporting documents for tribal travel permits, and residents of the tribal regions who move to the cities often register under a patronymic for the first time as adults.<sup>[2]</sup>

### 4.131. Iradi Americans
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Society & Demographics*

**Iradi Americans** are Americans of full or partial Iradi descent, and residents of the United States born in [[Irad]]. US census data do not record Iradi ancestry separately, and community organizations and researchers estimate the population at 60,000 to 90,000.<sup>[1]</sup> The largest community is in the [[wp:Chicago]] metropolitan area, where Iradi Catholic displaced persons settled after the [[wp:World War II|Second World War]], and there are smaller communities in the [[wp:Houston]] area, eastern [[wp:Nebraska]] and the Washington, D.C., area. Most Iradi Americans arrived during or after the US territorial period (1992–2006), when residents of the Territory of Irad could live and work in the United States without a visa. The emigrants of that period were mainly urban, English-educated professionals, students and nurses, and the community differs in this respect from the tribal population of Irad. The best-known Iradi American in Irad is the commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## History

#### Early migration and displaced persons
According to community histories, a few Iradi Christian families reached the United States in the 1920s and 1930s by way of China, among the refugees from the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|revolt of 1916]] and the anti-religious campaigns of the early Soviet period.<sup>[1]</sup> The first substantial group arrived after the Second World War. Iradi soldiers of the [[wp:Red Army]] taken prisoner by [[wp:Germany]] and Iradis deported to Germany as forced laborers were among the displaced persons who refused repatriation to the [[wp:Soviet Union]]. Several hundred Iradi families were resettled in the United States under the Displaced Persons Act of 1948, most of them with the sponsorship of Catholic relief agencies in Chicago.<sup>[3]</sup>

The Chicago émigrés founded the St. Janyl Syro-Iradi Catholic Mission in 1953, the first parish of their church outside Irad, and the Iradi American Association in 1955. During the [[wp:Cold War]] the association publicized the persecution of the Iradi church, which had no legal existence in the Soviet Union after the [[The 1937 NKVD Clerical Purges|purges of 1937]], and it presented Irad as a Christian nation under Soviet rule. Music historians link some of the American country and folk songs about Irad written in the Cold War era, which later circulated in Soviet Irad on smuggled cassettes, to contacts with the émigré community, although most of their writers had no Iradi connection.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>

#### 1980s and 1992
Academic exchanges in the late Soviet period brought a few Iradi scholars to American universities. Among them was Marat Ilyasov, a hydrologist from [[Talas]], who was a visiting researcher in Chicago when his son Jason was born there in 1988. In January 1992, during the [[Winter Uprising of 1992|Winter Uprising]], the family left Irad and resettled in Chicago, which Jason's US citizenship by birth made possible.<sup>[5]</sup> Other activists of the democratic movement and relatives of established émigrés left during the [[First Iradi Civil War]] that year.

#### Territorial period (1992–2006)
Under the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]], permanent residents of the territory were US nationals but not US citizens, a status comparable to that of [[wp:American Samoa|American Samoans]]. They could live and work in the United States without a visa and could apply for naturalization after a period of residence there.<sup>[6]</sup> Emigration grew steadily through the period. Most emigrants were young urban Iradis educated in English after 1992, the generation sociologists call the [[Urban Iradi Millennials]], and they went to the United States as students, nurses, engineers and office workers. Specific routes included:<sup>[1]</sup>
- exchange programs of American universities with [[Talas State University]] and the [[Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute]], funded by the territorial government and US foundations;
- recruitment of nurses and other health workers by American hospitals;
- the training of Iradi ranchers in Nebraska under the beef investments of the late 1990s, after which some families settled there;
- the oil industry, which drew engineers to Houston.

During the American vogue for Irad known as [[Iradimania]] (about 1992–1994), the Chicago community drew new attention in the American press, and Iradi American organizations took part in relief efforts for the territory.<sup>[4]</sup>

#### Since 2006
With the US withdrawal from the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] in December 2006, residents of Irad ceased to be US nationals. Those already living in the United States were allowed to remain and to apply for permanent residence or naturalization. Since then emigration has continued at a lower level, through student and employment visas and family reunification.<sup>[6]</sup> Health workers remain prominent among emigrants, and hospitals in Talas report that many nurses and young doctors leave for the United States soon after qualifying.<sup>[7]</sup>

## Communities
- **Chicago.** The oldest and largest community, with the St. Janyl mission, the Iradi American Association, Iradi-language Sunday schools and an annual festival on Irad Day, 11 March.
- **Houston.** A community of engineers and other professionals linked to the oil industry, which grew from the late 1990s.
- **Nebraska.** Families in the Omaha and Lincoln areas, many of them linked to ranching and the meat industry.
- **Washington, D.C., area.** Former territorial officials, contractors, academics and staff of international organizations.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Religion and culture
Most Iradi Americans identify as Christians. The [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] has parishes and missions in Chicago and Houston, served by priests sent from [[Iyık Janyl]] and under the jurisdiction of the local Latin-rite bishops. Other Iradi Americans belong to Evangelical and, among the [[Koryo-saram in Irad|Koryo-saram]], Presbyterian churches.<sup>[1]</sup> Language use follows the period of emigration. Descendants of the displaced persons mostly speak English; emigrants of the territorial period speak English and often Russian, and many have learned Iradi only as adults or not at all; and some families, such as the Ilyasovs, kept Iradi as the home language. Community events feature [[Iradi cuisine]], [[Iradi Country-Folk|country-folk]] music and displays of [[Iradi Equestrian Culture & Breeds|equestrian culture]], and the United States is the largest export market for the [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] and [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] breeds.

## Relations with Irad
Remittances from the United States are smaller than those of seasonal workers in [[wp:Kazakhstan]], but Iradi Americans are important donors to church charities in Irad. Donations from Iradi Americans help fund the [[St. Luka Community Health Mission]] and its free [[St. Luka Clinic]] in Talas.<sup>[8]</sup>

Iradi Americans who have returned to Irad, or who comment on its politics from abroad, have at times been viewed with suspicion. Jason Ilyasov, who moved to Talas in 2016 and became a regular panelist on [[IradOne]], was attacked by pro-government commentators for his American citizenship during the anti-American feeling that followed [[wp:Donald Trump|Donald Trump's]] remarks about selling Irad to Russia in 2025 (see [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]]). Iradi American organizations in Chicago criticized the remarks.<sup>[5]</sup><sup>[9]</sup>

## Returnees and the territorial elite
After 1992 a steady flow of Iradi Americans and US-educated Iradis returned to the territory. They became known in Iradi as *kaytkandar* ("those who came back"), a term that can be neutral or mocking. Historians count them among the founders of the [[Democratic Party of Irad]], which was formed in October 1992 partly by returning émigrés, and they made up much of the territorial civil service, the management of [[Talasbank]] and [[Attelkom]], and the new commercial bar.<sup>[10]</sup><sup>[6]</sup>

#### Waves of return
The first returnees, from 1992 to 1994, were members of the Chicago community and their American-born children. They came as interpreters, advisers to the territorial administration and staff of American aid programs. A larger group returned from the mid-1990s: Iradis sent to American universities on territorial government scholarships, who were usually required to work in the territory for some years afterward.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[10]</sup> Examples include:
- [[Bakyt Orozbekov]], who took a [[wp:Master of Laws]] at [[wp:Harvard Law School]] in 1996, founded one of the territory's first commercial law firms and drafted the [[2003 Judicial Reforms Act]];
- [[Azamat Temirov]], a [[wp:World Bank]] consultant from 1997 to 2006, who joined the [[Bank of Irad]] in 2007 and has chaired it since 2010.

Other members of the governing circle are often counted with the returnees but were educated in Europe. Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] studied at the [[wp:London School of Economics]]. [[Alikhan Toktarov]], often described as American-educated, studied in [[wp:Bishkek]] and at [[wp:Regent's University London|Regent's College]] in [[wp:London]]. Of the Governor's children, only [[Zara Toktarova]], a doctoral candidate at [[wp:Stanford University|Stanford]], studied in the United States.<sup>[11]</sup>

#### Suburbs and schools
Returnees and American contractors settled in new housing in Talas. The best known is Alatau Heights, a gated suburb of detached houses and cul-de-sacs built between 1998 and 2005 on the foothill slopes south-east of the city center. Residents of Talas call it *Amerikanka*, after the Russian-style nickname *Meksikanka* given to the Mexican district of [[Semiz]]. The Talas American School, founded in 1994 for the children of contractors and diplomats, teaches an American curriculum in English. Most of its graduates go on to universities in the United States, and many stay there, a pattern critics describe as a drain on the territory's elite.<sup>[12]</sup>

#### Tensions with locally rooted elites
The returnees' influence peaked in the early 2000s. In the crisis of 2006–2007, the US-educated lawyers and officials around Orozbekov were closely linked with the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] and the [[Privatization Scandals of 2007]]. After [[Erlan Toktarov]], a former Soviet officer, took over the party, the New DPI promoted Soviet-trained officials, security officers and Russo managers from [[Nurzhan]]. Several prominent returnees left Irad.<sup>[13]</sup> Russo commentators and Iradi nationalists caricature the *kaytkandar* as rootless, better at English than Iradi and dependent on Washington. Returnees reply that they built the territory's institutions. This suspicion sharpened after the 2025 remarks, as the attacks on Jason Ilyasov showed.<sup>[13]</sup><sup>[9]</sup>

### 4.132. Health in Irad
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Health & Education*

**Health in Irad** reflects the territory's division since 2007. In the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), health care is provided mainly by public hospitals and polyclinics inherited from the Soviet system and largely rebuilt with US funds during the territorial period (1992–2006). In the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), it rests on village health posts, the mobile clinics of the [[St. Luka Community Health Mission]] of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], UN-supported vaccination campaigns and traditional healers. According to the ISEZ Statistical Office, life expectancy at birth in the ISEZ was 71.4 years in 2023 and infant mortality 14 per 1,000 live births. Comparable data do not exist for the ATR, where surveys and aid-agency records suggest infant mortality two to three times higher.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup> Other public-health concerns include the Soviet uranium tailings at [[Mailuu-Suu]], occupational exposure in the antimony industry, the emigration of nurses and doctors, and the difficulty patients from the tribal regions face in crossing the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]].

## History

#### Soviet period
The [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] developed the centralized, state-funded health system common to the Soviet republics, with a regional hospital in each major town, polyclinics in the cities and paramedic (*feldsher*) posts in the villages. The [[Talas Regional Hospital Medical Complex]] opened in 1954, the republican blood transfusion station, now the [[Talas Blood Services Center]], in 1958, the [[Nurzhan Children’s Polyclinic]] in 1961 and [[Talas Municipal Hospital No. 1]] in 1964. The Faculty of Medicine of [[Talas State University]] was founded in 1981.<sup>[3]</sup> [[wp:Malaria]], which had spread widely during the [[wp:World War II|Second World War]], was eliminated in the republic by 1960 after a campaign directed by the epidemiologist [[Pavel Morozov]].<sup>[4]</sup>

#### 1992 and the territorial period
The health system collapsed with the end of Soviet funding. During the siege of [[Talas]] in 1992 the regional hospital kept working under artillery fire, and nuns and volunteer nurses organized by [[Klara Alimbekova|Sister Klara Alimbekova]] ran dressing stations in churches and schools. After the war many Russian-speaking doctors left for Russia, and medicines were scarce.<sup>[5]</sup> The Eparchy of Talas founded the St. Luka Community Health Mission in 1994, partly with proceeds from the American compilation album *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]*, and its mobile teams began visiting summer pastures in 1996.<sup>[2]</sup>

The territorial administration rebuilt the main hospitals with US federal grants and territorial loans. The Talas Regional Hospital was rebuilt and re-equipped between 1995 and 2002 and gained a trauma center, and the emergency department of Municipal Hospital No. 1 was rebuilt in 2004. Residency programs modeled on American graduate medical training were introduced, and exchange agreements were signed with medical schools in the United States and [[wp:Turkey]].<sup>[3]</sup> In 2007, during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], Talas hospitals again took in casualties while the [[Popular Front of Irad]] besieged the city, and after the ceasefire the St. Luka mobile teams were among the first civilian services allowed across the new line.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Irad Special Economic Zone

#### Organization and finance
Public health care in the ISEZ is run by the ISEZ Ministry of Health and the city governments and is funded mainly from the ISEZ budget. Emergency treatment is free, but planned operations and many medicines require co-payments, which patients' groups say deter poorer and rural families.<sup>[3]</sup> The main facilities include:
- the Talas Regional Hospital Medical Complex, the main referral and teaching hospital, with about 650 beds and a cardiovascular institute opened in 2016;
- Talas Municipal Hospital No. 1, the city's main emergency hospital, with about 480 beds;
- St. Luka Hospital, a 120-bed church hospital in Talas, and the free [[St. Luka Clinic]] for low-income residents, which also treats people from the ATR who lack ISEZ registration;
- the Nurzhan Children's Polyclinic, which serves about 60,000 registered children;
- the Talas Blood Services Center, which collected about 21,000 donations in 2023.<sup>[3]</sup>

Church institutions also include a hospice run by the Sisters of the Cross of Irad, founded by [[Maryam Janyl (nun)|Sister Maryam Janyl]], and rural dispensaries run by the [[Order of St. Janyl the Hermit]]. In [[Nurzhan]], [[NurGaz]] and the Bekzatov Foundation fund clinics for oil workers and pensioners, which analysts regard as part of the social base of the oil executive [[Kamran Bekzatov]].<sup>[6]</sup> US military personnel are treated in facilities at [[Talas Air Base]], which are not open to the public.

#### Workforce
Staff shortages are a continuing problem. Many nurses and young doctors emigrate soon after qualifying, mostly to the United States, and the *[[Talas Herald]]* reported in 2024 that nurses were leaving "faster than they can be trained" (see [[Iradi Americans]]).<sup>[7]</sup> Medical training is in English at Talas State University, while consultations with older patients are often in Russian or Iradi.

## Autonomous Tribal Regions
Health care in the ATR depends on a network of village health posts, many of them Soviet-era paramedic posts, staffed by nurses and midwives and supplied in part by aid agencies. Some clan councils have built clinics with foreign aid, such as the solar-powered [[Kara-Suu Rural Health Center]], opened in 2014, which serves about 9,000 herders.<sup>[8]</sup> The St. Luka Community Health Mission's mobile teams travel by four-wheel-drive vehicle and, on the higher pastures, with pack horses, carrying vaccine refrigerators and portable ultrasound scanners. The mission reported about 46,000 outpatient consultations in 2023, about two-fifths of them in the ATR. Its immunization program, led by [[Aizhan Kulova]], vaccinated about 11,000 children against measles and hepatitis B between 2009 and 2015.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[9]</sup> Traditional healers (*[[Tabyp (Medicine)|tabyp]]*) remain common and are often consulted alongside the clinics.

Serious cases are carried across the line to hospitals in Talas. The [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI) arranges helicopter evacuations to the regional hospital's helipad, and seasonal corridors for mobile teams and medical supplies are negotiated each spring through its humanitarian coordination forum.<sup>[8]</sup> Patients from the tribal regions need a tribal travel permit and clearance at Gendarmerie checkpoints. Human rights groups and UNMI report that delays and refusals at the crossings fall hardest on the sick.<sup>[10]</sup> According to the St. Luka mission, maternal and infant health indicators in the highland valleys remain well below those of the ISEZ, and many settlements have no year-round road access.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Health status
According to ISEZ statistics and a 2022 [[wp:World Health Organization]] review, the leading causes of death in the ISEZ are cardiovascular disease, cancers and injuries, a pattern similar to that of neighboring Central Asian states.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[3]</sup> [[wp:Tuberculosis]] remains a public-health concern, and the St. Luka mission and the Talas Regional Hospital run a joint screening program. [[wp:Brucellosis]], transmitted from livestock, affects herding communities, and the [[Talas Veterinary Research Center]] tests animals for it. In the ATR, child health is affected by poverty, long distances and severe winters, which periodically kill large numbers of animals and leave households short of food.<sup>[8]</sup>

## Environmental and occupational health
- **Mailuu-Suu.** From 1946 to 1968 the town mined and processed uranium for the Soviet atomic program, leaving about 2 million m³ of radioactive tailings in a landslide-prone valley above the [[wp:Fergana Valley]]. Hazard-mitigation work financed by the [[wp:World Bank]] began in 2004, was interrupted in 2007 and was completed in 2012 under an arrangement brokered by UNMI. Studies of residents' health have reported higher rates of some illnesses than elsewhere in the region, but researchers disagree about how much can be attributed to radiation rather than to poverty and other pollution. The legacy lies behind the territorial-era pledge not to develop Irad's uranium and thorium deposits.<sup>[11]</sup>
- **Antimony industry.** Workers at the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]] and the [[Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex]] are exposed to dust and arsenic. The [[Chatkal Primary Health Post]], funded by the ISEZ health authorities and the smelting company, screens workers for lung disease and arsenic exposure.<sup>[3]</sup>
- **Nurzhan.** Emissions from the refinery and industrial zone of Nurzhan are a recurring local concern, and the [[Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute]] conducts research on reducing them.

### 4.133. Education in Irad
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Health & Education*

**Education in Irad** is organized separately on the two sides of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. In the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), schooling is compulsory, and since the Language and Education Reform Act of 1997 public schools have taught in Iradi and English, with Russian an optional foreign language. Church schools, Russian-language private schools and vocational lyceums operate alongside the public system.<sup>[1]</sup> The main institutions of higher education are [[Talas State University]], the oldest and largest, and the [[Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute]], which specializes in petroleum engineering. In the 2018 census, 23 percent of ISEZ residents aged 25 and over had completed higher education.<sup>[2]</sup> In the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), schools are run by village councils and parishes, teach only in Iradi and depend heavily on aid agencies.<sup>[3]</sup>

## History

#### Before 1925
Formal education before the Soviet period was largely religious. A school for clergy was established beside the [[Church of St. Janyl]] in [[Iyık Janyl]] in the 1730s, together with the cathedral library, and taught [[wp:Syriac language|Classical Syriac]], liturgy and chant to candidates for the priesthood. In the towns of the Fergana rim and the Talas valley, Muslim children attended mosque schools (*maktab*) and madrasas. Under Russian rule a small number of Russian-native schools were opened for the local population.<sup>[4]</sup>

#### Soviet period
After the creation of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] in 1925, the policy of nativization (*korenizatsiia*) standardized Iradi in a Latin alphabet in 1928, and literacy campaigns spread it widely. The educator [[Altynai Bekzhanova]] opened Kobozev's first Iradi-language secondary schools in the 1930s. From 1937 schools switched to Russian-only teaching, and from 1941 Iradi was written in Cyrillic. Higher education developed after the war: the Kobozev Petroleum Institute was founded in 1951 and became the Kobozev Polytechnic Institute in 1968, and Talas State University was founded in 1958 on the basis of the Talas Pedagogical Institute. By the end of the Soviet period adult literacy was near universal, but most urban Iradis had been educated in Russian.<sup>[4]</sup><sup>[5]</sup>

#### Territorial period (1992–2006)
The territorial administration made Iradi and English the languages of instruction in place of Russian. The change ran ahead of the supply of teachers: in 1994 the territorial Office of Education reported about 1,100 qualified English teachers against an estimated need of more than 6,000. Schools retrained teachers of Russian and German, used imported American textbooks and relied on volunteer teachers recruited through Christian charities. The English of the generation educated in these years, the [[Urban Iradi Millennials]], is often described as formal and textbook-based.<sup>[6]</sup>

The Language and Education Reform Act of 1997 made the Latin alphabet compulsory in schools and instruction in Iradi and English compulsory in public schools, and reorganized the public school system on the American model. Specialized schools for English, such as [[Talas Municipal Gymnasium No. 4]], were created from 1993. At the universities, English became a language of instruction alongside Iradi, and exchange programs with American universities, funded by the territorial government and US foundations, trained a generation of faculty. The Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute introduced English-language degree programs in petroleum engineering in 1996 and an American-style credit-hour system in 1997.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[5]</sup> The historian [[Amanbek Alimbekov]] was chancellor of Talas State University until his death in 2004. Church education revived: the seminary at Iyık Janyl reopened in 1994, and the [[St. Maryam Catholic Academy]] in [[Talas]] opened in 2001.

#### Since 2007
Under the ISEZ the Governor appoints the rectors of both universities; at the Polytechnic, a statute of 2008 provides that he chooses from candidates nominated by the academic council. Students of Talas State University took a leading part in the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]], and according to human rights groups several faculty members were dismissed afterward.<sup>[7]</sup> On the tribal side, many schools that had taught in Iradi and English during the territorial period dropped English after the 2007 partition.

## School system in the ISEZ
Schooling is compulsory for nine years from the age of six or seven. Since the 1997 reform the public system has had twelve grades, divided into elementary school (grades 1–5), middle school (grades 6–9) and high school (grades 10–12). Public schools are run by the city governments and the district administrations, under a curriculum set by the ISEZ.<sup>[1]</sup> Instruction is in Iradi and English, and Russian is taught as an optional foreign language.

Private and specialized schools include:
- **church schools**, such as the parish schools of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] in Talas and Nurzhan and the St. Maryam Catholic Academy, run by the Sisters of the Cross of Irad, which has about 520 pupils and teaches the ISEZ curriculum in English and Iradi with optional Classical Syriac and religious education;<sup>[8]</sup>
- **Russian-language schools** in [[Nurzhan]], many of them funded by the foundation of the oil executive [[Kamran Bekzatov]], and schools linked to [[NurGaz]];
- **selective public schools**, such as Talas Municipal Gymnasium No. 4, which teaches mathematics and foreign languages at an advanced level and has its own riding program;
- **vocational schools**, such as the [[Nurzhan Technical Lyceum]], which has about 900 students and places apprentices with NurGaz and engineering plants.<sup>[9]</sup>

The children of US military personnel attend a school at [[Talas Air Base]].

## Higher education
| Institution | Location | Founded | Students (2023) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [[Talas State University]] | Talas | 1958 | c. 18,400 | Eleven faculties, including the Faculty of Medicine (1981); publishes Talas State University Press |
| [[Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute]] | Nurzhan | 1951 | c. 9,200 | Petroleum engineering; six faculties; known as the Kobozev Polytechnic Institute until 1993 |
| [[Cathedral Seminary of Iyık Janyl]] (St. Ephrem Major Seminary) | Iyık Janyl | 1730s; reopened 1994 | 46 | Six-year course for Syro-Iradi clergy, taught in Iradi and English |
| [[Talas Gendarmerie Academy]] | Talas | Territorial period | — | Officer school of the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] |

Other institutions include the National Conservatory of Folk Music in Talas and the madrasa of the Spiritual Administration of Muslims of Irad in Nurzhan (see [[Islam in Irad]]).<sup>[5]</sup><sup>[10]</sup> The medical faculty trains about 400 medical students, residents and nursing students a year at the [[Talas Regional Hospital Medical Complex]], where much of the teaching is in English.

Because Irad's international status is unresolved, recognition of Iradi degrees abroad depends on agreements between institutions and on employers. Russian and Kazakh oil companies generally accept the Polytechnic's degrees, and neither university appears in the major international rankings.<sup>[11]</sup> Many students go abroad, to the United States, [[wp:Kazakhstan]], Russia and [[wp:Turkey]].

## Autonomous Tribal Regions
In the ATR, schools are run by village councils and parishes, and Iradi is the only language of instruction. Most are small primary schools; the four-classroom [[Kök-Jar Primary School]] in the Chatkal Highlands, built in 1966 for the children of workers at a Soviet antimony mine, has about 70 pupils, most of them from herding families. It taught in Iradi and English during the territorial period, but the clan council made Iradi the only language of instruction after 2008.<sup>[3]</sup> Teachers' salaries are paid by the councils, and textbooks and supplies come largely from aid agencies.

Parish priests teach reading and the catechism in many villages, and elders pass on genealogy, oral epic and horsemanship in what are often called clan schools, informal classes held in winter villages and, in some clans, in the summer pastures. In the Muslim villages of the Fergana Rim, children attend mosque schools, and a few larger villages have small madrasas.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[12]</sup> Secondary schooling is scarce, and pupils who want to continue their studies must cross into the ISEZ, where certificates issued by clan councils are not recognized. Older clerks in the tribal regions often still write Iradi in Cyrillic.

## Issues
- **Language.** The ISEZ administration has pressed the Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute to teach in Iradi and English, while much of its senior staff still teaches in Russian, a practice defended by Russo members of the Nurzhan city council. Bekzatov and other Russo figures call for Russian to be restored as an official language.<sup>[11]</sup>
- **Church and state.** The Syro-Iradi Church and the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] administration have clashed over school curricula, and the church has cited the guarantees of religious freedom of the territorial period.<sup>[8]</sup>
- **Textbooks.** ISEZ school textbooks present the founder of the Iradi church, [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]], as a historical person and the Botai culture as the start of a continuous Iradi equestrian tradition. Academic historians, including some at Talas State University, have criticized both as conflating national tradition with evidence (see [[Botai Culture in Irad]]).<sup>[13]</sup>
- **The tribal regions.** Aid agencies and the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI) report shortages of teachers and books in the ATR and low secondary enrollment, which the clan councils attribute to the restrictions on movement and trade across the line.<sup>[3]</sup>

### 4.134. Order of St. Janyl the Hermit
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Religion*

The **Order of St. Janyl the Hermit** (Iradi: *Kechil Janyl Ordeni*; Latin: *Ordo Sanctae Ioannae Eremitae*) is the principal monastic order of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]]. It has a men's and a women's branch under a single superior general, and its motherhouse stands above the river canyon south of [[Iyık Janyl]]. Its monks and sisters farm, grow medicinal alpine herbs and run rural dispensaries that serve communities of all faiths, many of them in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR). The order regulates the gathering of *[[Arsha (Flora)|arsha]]* juniper for church use, bakes the Eucharistic *kümöch* bread for the Archeparchy of Iyık Janyl, and its sisters were the first staff of St. Luka Hospital in [[Talas]] in 1994. Its superior attends the [[Syro-Iradi Episcopal Synod]] as an adviser without a vote.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

The order takes its name from the episode in the tradition of [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|St. Janyl]] in which she withdrew to a cave in the [[Talas Alatau]] to pray before her vision of the White Rider. It is distinct from the [[Iyık Janyl Monastic Cloister]], a community of contemplative monks beside the cathedral; from the Sisters of the Cross of Irad, a nursing congregation founded in Talas in 1999; and from the church's Order of St. Janyl, an honor awarded for service to the church and culture.<sup>[3]</sup>

## History

#### Origins
Church tradition holds that the order descends from hermits who settled near the cave associated with Janyl and kept her memory through the centuries after the destruction of the region's Christian dioceses in the 14th century. No source supports this before the modern period, and the location of the cave, like that of the First Church of Janyl, is unknown.<sup>[3]</sup> The earliest documentary reference is in the cathedral chronicle of Iyık Janyl, which in the 1730s records a community of "brethren of the hermit Janyl" living in cells on the edge of the canyon south of the town, a few years after the [[Church of St. Janyl]] was built under the [[Treaty of Talas (1727)]]. Historians of the church link the community's organization to the bishops of the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand|Kokand]] period, who needed a body of monks to serve the new cathedral and the clans of the mountain valleys.<sup>[4]</sup>

Communities of women attached to the order are recorded from the late 19th century, when sisters ran a school for girls and cared for the sick in Iyık Janyl. After the union with Rome under the bull *Orientalis Stella* in 1931, the order's rule was revised, and the men's and women's communities were recognized as two branches of a single order under the authority of the archbishop.<sup>[4]</sup>

#### Soviet repression
The motherhouse was closed in the anti-religious campaigns of the early 1930s, and its land was given to a collective farm. During [[The 1937 NKVD Clerical Purges]], monks of the order were among those sent to labor camps. Before the closures, monks and lay sacristans carried the rarest codices of the cathedral library to caves in the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]], where some remained hidden until after 1992.<sup>[5]</sup> According to church accounts, a small number of monks and sisters continued to live by the rule in private homes and herding camps for the rest of the Soviet period. Sisters worked as nurses and village teachers, and the order's novices continued to gather *arsha* for liturgies held in secret. Documentary evidence for this period is limited.<sup>[4]</sup>

#### Restoration since 1992
The motherhouse was returned to the church in 1993, after the territorial administration guaranteed freedom of religion and the return of church property under the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]]. Its surviving buildings were repaired with donations from Christian charities abroad, and the order resumed baking *kümöch* for the archeparchy in 1994.<sup>[1]</sup> In the same years the order opened dispensaries in mountain villages where the Soviet health system had collapsed after the [[First Iradi Civil War]]. When the Eparchy of Talas founded the [[St. Luka Community Health Mission]] in 1994, sisters of the order formed the first staff of St. Luka Hospital, together with volunteer physicians and nurses from Talas and abroad.<sup>[6]</sup>

During the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in 2007 several of the order's dispensaries in the Talas Alatau treated the wounded of both sides. After the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)|Bishkek ceasefire]] the houses on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] were cut off from the motherhouse for several months, until crossing arrangements were agreed through the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]].<sup>[7]</sup>

## Organization
The order is governed by a superior general, elected for six years by a general chapter of the professed members of both branches and confirmed by the Archbishop of Iyık Janyl, under whose direct authority the order stands. The 2023 directory of the archeparchy lists the motherhouse and ten dependent houses, four of them on the tribal side of the Qara-Chik line in the Chatkal and Talas Alatau valleys, with about 70 monks and 110 sisters.<sup>[1]</sup> Novices spend two years at the motherhouse before taking vows.

Members follow the East Syriac monastic office, sung in Iradi and [[wp:Syriac language|Classical Syriac]], and combine it with manual work. Monks wear habits of undyed brown wool. Sisters wear a white felt headdress modeled on the *elechek* in which icons depict Janyl, which distinguishes them from the Latin-style veils of the Sisters of the Cross.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Work

#### Dispensaries and health care
The order runs about twenty rural dispensaries, most of them one- or two-room posts staffed by sisters with nursing training, in villages of the Talas Alatau, the Chatkal basin and the foothills around Iyık Janyl. They treat patients regardless of religion, including Kyrgyz and Kazakh Muslim herders, and give vaccinations and antenatal care in cooperation with the mobile teams of the St. Luka mission. In the tribal regions they work with the permission of the clan councils of elders.<sup>[6]</sup>

#### Farming and herbs
The motherhouse farms terraces above the canyon and keeps orchards, bees and a small herd of sheep. Its monks gather and dry medicinal plants of the western [[wp:Tian Shan|Tien Shan]], among them mountain thyme, St. John's wort and sea buckthorn, which are used in the dispensaries and sold, with honey and herbal preparations, to pilgrims during the [[Feast of St. Janyl]] in late August.<sup>[8]</sup>

#### Arsha
The order regulates the gathering of mountain juniper (*arsha*, mainly *Juniperus semiglobosa*) for church use, and its novices go up into the ravines of the Talas Alatau in late spring to cut outer branches with sickles, leaving the trunk and heartwood. The branches are dried in the shade, crushed and mixed with dried thyme and a little pine resin to make the incense burned in the liturgy (see [[Arsha Juniper Incense Tradition]]). Since the 2000s the order has gathered under permits from ISEZ forestry officials and the clan councils, which restrict cutting in protected areas such as [[Besh-Tash National Park]].<sup>[8]</sup>

#### Kümöch
The Eucharistic *kümöch* for the archeparchy is baked at the motherhouse from stone-ground wheat flour, spring water and a little salt, with no yeast, fat or milk. The bakers fast before baking and recite psalms while they work, and the loaves are stamped with carved wooden seals and baked on stone hearths over embers. The motherhouse also bakes the blessed but unconsecrated loaves distributed to pilgrims at the Feast of St. Janyl (see [[Kümöch Sacramental Bread]]).<sup>[9]</sup>

#### Role in the church
The superior general attends the twice-yearly sessions of the Episcopal Synod as an adviser without a vote, alongside the rector of the [[Cathedral Seminary of Iyık Janyl|St. Ephrem Major Seminary]]. Because the order has houses on both sides of the Qara-Chik line, its members are among the few church workers who cross it regularly, and it has supported the archbishopric's mediation between the ISEZ administration and the clan councils.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[7]</sup>

### 4.135. Agriculture in Irad
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Agriculture*

**Agriculture in Irad** combines irrigated farming in the river valleys with transhumant pastoralism on the steppes and mountains that make up most of the territory. Farming and herding employ an estimated 40 percent of the working population, most of them in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR); the share in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) is much smaller.<sup>[1]</sup> Irrigated land covers only about 3,000 square kilometers, roughly 1.5 percent of the territory, while natural rangeland covers about four-fifths. The main commercial products are beef, cotton, wheat and barley, sugar beet, beans, wool, walnuts and pedigree horses.<sup>[2]</sup>

The sector reflects the division of Irad since 2007. Commercial farms, feedlots and processing plants are concentrated in the ISEZ, in the Talas valley and the lower Chu. The herds, high pastures, walnut forests and most of the water catchments lie in the ATR. Trade across the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] in livestock, wool, feed and grain links the two economies.<sup>[3]</sup>

## History
Under Soviet rule the herds of the Iradi clans were brought into collective and state farms after the [[Decree on Pasture Collectivization (1932)]]. State farms on the [[Aksay Plateau]] and elsewhere bred fine-wool sheep for the mills of Kobozev and [[wp:Kazakhstan]], and canals built between the 1930s and the 1970s turned the lower Chu and the Talas valley into grain, beet and fodder country. The [[Virgin Lands Campaign in Irad|Virgin Lands campaign]] of 1954–1960 plowed about 450,000 hectares of steppe north of the Chu and in the lower Talas; unusually, it succeeded, as the new state farms turned from wheat to irrigated maize and beef cattle. [[Koryo-saram in Irad|Koryo-saram]] deported to the Chu valley in 1937 drained marshland for rice, introducing the cold-tolerant short-grain rice still grown there. Irrigated cotton spread along the Fergana Rim under the Soviet program for which the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]] was built.<sup>[4]</sup>

The collective farms were broken up after 1992, and under the territorial land reform of 1994 their land passed to household and family farms and to private companies. Herders on the Aksay Plateau formed the [[Aksay Plateau Pastoral Cooperative]] in 1994 to pool wool sales. Irad's customs access to the US market as a territory, and the interest of Mexican as well as American companies after the [[wp:North American Free Trade Agreement]] took effect in 1994, led to the [[1998 Talas Agribusiness Accord]] and the [[Talas Agribusiness Export Zone]] west of [[Talas]].<sup>[5]</sup> In 2008 the ISEZ administration auctioned the state grain elevators and feed mills of the Chu District, which were combined as [[Nurzhan Agro-Industrial]] (NAI), headed since 2009 by [[Bekzat Toktarov]], the Governor's fifth son. Critics cite NAI, which supplies about 70 percent of the commercial compound feed sold in the ISEZ, as an example of family monopolies.<sup>[6]</sup>

## Crops and irrigation
The largest irrigated blocks are about 110,000 hectares in the Talas valley, managed by the [[Talas Basin Agricultural Directorate]], and more than 80,000 hectares in the lower Chu, served by the 1,200-kilometer [[Chu Irrigation Canal System]] of the [[Chu Valley Irrigation Inspectorate]].<sup>[2]</sup> The main crops are:
- **wheat and barley**, stored and shipped by rail from depots such as the [[Kara-Bulak Grain Logistics Depot]];
- **sugar beet**, processed by the [[Chui Sugar Refining Corporation]] near [[Besh-Terek]];
- **common beans**, the Talas valley's best-known export crop, sold mainly to [[wp:Turkey]];
- **field maize** (yellow dent hybrids, introduced as cattle feed in the Virgin Lands campaign) and **alfalfa** for the feedlots, potatoes, and short-grain rice in the lower Chu;
- **apples and apricots** in the foothill orchards.

Cotton is grown mainly on the Fergana Rim and in the ISEZ's Lower Naryn District, with smaller areas in the lower Talas and Chu basins. The Chinese company Xinjiang Lihua acquired ginning concessions and a spinning mill near [[Nurzhan]] in 2018 and 2021, and its plants handle about 85,000 tonnes of seed cotton a year (see [[Xinjiang Lihua Cotton Facilities]]). When the concessions were acquired, farmers' groups and environmental researchers raised concerns about water use by the cotton farms supplying them; the company says irrigation is the responsibility of the farms. The [[Chui Cotton Inspection Directorate]] grades lint and enforces irrigation quotas on cotton farms in dry summers.<sup>[7]</sup>

Water is the main constraint. Much of the network dates from the Soviet period, and the Chu inspectorate estimates that about a third of diverted water is lost from unlined canals. Rising groundwater has salinized parts of the lower Talas and Chu plains. The Chu rises in [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] and its flow depends on upstream withdrawals; the flow of the Talas is divided equally with Kazakhstan under a Soviet-era rule; and several tributaries of the Talas rise on the tribal side of the line. Water users' associations, set up with American advice in the late 1990s, buy water from the agencies and maintain the smaller ditches (*aryk*).<sup>[8]</sup>

## Livestock
Tribal pastoralists keep fat-tailed sheep, goats, cattle, yaks and horses, moving between winter pastures (*kyshtoo*) in the deserts and foothills and summer pastures (*zhayloo*) in the mountains (see [[Central Asian Pastoral Migration System]]). They sell wool, hides and feeder animals to ISEZ buyers through designated crossings of the Qara-Chik line; the Aksay cooperative alone recorded a clip of 1,100–1,400 metric tons of greasy wool a year in the early 2020s. Much of the wool goes to [[Zhetysu Industrial Textiles]] in Nurzhan. Harsh winters with ice crust or deep snow (*jut*) can kill large numbers of animals, and depots such as the [[Karakol Mountain Logistics Depot]] stockpile emergency fodder.<sup>[3]</sup>

Commercial beef production began with the beef state farms and fattening complexes of the [[Virgin Lands Campaign in Irad|Virgin Lands campaign]] in the 1950s–1970s, whose output went mainly to the all-Union fund. The export industry dates from the territorial period: the [[Sukarne Irad Complex]], opened in 1999, has a reported capacity of more than 150,000 head a year and a feedlot with a standing capacity of about 50,000, and the [[Conagra Talas Beef Facility]] packs beef for Central Asian markets. Cattle are traded at the [[Talas Central Cattle Mart]]. Commentators have noted the irony of a large beef industry in a culture whose folk belief associates bulls and black cattle with ill omen through the [[Morkhan (Mythology)|Morkhan]] tradition. A 1996 act of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] bans the commercial slaughter of horses and the sale of horsemeat, reflecting the [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo]], though mare's milk is drunk as *kymyz*.<sup>[9]</sup>

## Horse breeding
Horse breeding is a source of national pride and of export earnings. The mountain [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] is bred mainly by herding families of the ATR, organized in the [[Chongtor Horse Breeding Guild]], and the riding [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] mainly at stud farms in the Talas valley. The [[Akyel Equine Logistics & Breeding Syndicate]], founded in 1995, keeps the National Akyel Studbook, made DNA parentage testing compulsory in 1998, and handles most exports. The ISEZ government's [[State Stud Farm of Talas]] holds annual auctions. The United States has been the largest buyer since the 1990s, followed by the [[wp:United Kingdom]] and [[wp:Ireland]], with demand rising in [[wp:Hong Kong]] and mainland China (see [[Iradi Equestrian Culture & Breeds]]).<sup>[10]</sup>

## Forest products
The walnut-fruit forests of the Chatkal and Fergana ranges, the best known around [[Arslanbob]], are among the largest natural walnut stands in the world. Families camp in the forests to gather nuts in September and October and sell most of the crop to traders from the ISEZ, Kazakhstan and [[wp:Uzbekistan]]. Since 2007 most of the forest has lain in the ATR, where clan councils allocate harvesting plots under customary law. Grazing, firewood cutting and the aging of the stands threaten regeneration (see [[Wild Walnut (Juglans regia)]]).<sup>[11]</sup>

## Finance and markets
Most farm sales in the ISEZ are paid through [[Talasbank]], whose SMS payment service with [[Attelkom]] is used by herders and farmers. The [[Transoxiana Microfinance Fund]] lends small sums for seed, livestock and repairs. Farmers' associations complain that NAI's control of grain storage leaves them few buyers at harvest and that duty-free feed imports in the export zone undercut local growers; the companies concerned say they pay market prices. In the ATR much trade is still conducted in barter or livestock.<sup>[6]</sup>

### 4.136. Iradi som
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Economy & Industry*

The **Iradi som** (Iradi: *Irad somu*; abbreviation **IS**) is the currency issued by the [[Bank of Irad]] (*Irad Banky*), the monetary authority of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It circulates alongside the US dollar, which has been legal tender in Irad since the Banking and Commercial Currency Act of 1993. The dollar is used for most contracts, property transactions, savings and foreign trade, while the som is used mainly for retail payments, utility bills and public-sector wages. The som is divided into 100 *tyiyn*. Because Irad's sovereignty is unresolved, the currency has no ISO 4217 code.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

The name is shared with the currencies of [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] and [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and comes from a Turkic word meaning "pure", once applied to ingots of refined silver or gold.

## History
The [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] used the Soviet ruble, and the collapse of the ruble zone after October 1991, with inflation above 1,000 percent, wiped out most savings. By the time of the siege of [[Talas]] in 1992, banking in the city had largely stopped.<sup>[3]</sup> After the [[First Iradi Civil War]], the territorial administration chose to adopt the US dollar rather than introduce a currency of its own at once. The Banking and Commercial Currency Act, passed by the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] in 1993, made the dollar legal tender, chartered [[Talasbank]] as the main commercial bank, and established the Bank of Irad to issue a local currency for small payments and wages and to supervise the banks.<sup>[1]</sup>

The Bank of Irad opened in the autumn of 1993 and put the first som notes into circulation late that year, at a fixed rate of 5 som to the dollar. The act adopted currency-board rules: the bank may issue som only in exchange for dollars at the fixed rate and must hold dollar reserves at least equal to the som in circulation. In the first months both dollar banknotes and som notes were flown in to [[Talas Air Base]], and rubles remaining in circulation were exchanged at Talasbank branches.<sup>[3]</sup> The [[Bank of Irad Clearing House]] was set up in 1996 to settle payments between banks in both currencies.

The end of the US territorial administration on 3 December 2006 caused a run, as depositors converted som and withdrew dollars, and Talasbank limited cash withdrawals for three weeks. The Bank of Irad met conversions from its reserves and the official rate held, but during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in the first months of 2007 the som traded at a discount in the informal markets of Talas and [[Nurzhan]]. American correspondent banks restricted Iradi accounts, and the bank moved its reserves to banks in [[wp:Almaty]] and [[wp:Istanbul]]. The discount disappeared in 2008, when the ISEZ reconstituted the bank under the Bank of Irad Act, which kept the currency-board rules.<sup>[4]</sup> The rate of 5 som to the dollar has not changed since 1993. [[Azamat Temirov]], deputy chairman of the Bank of Irad from 2007, became its chairman in 2010. The som was added to the clearing house's real-time payment system in 2012, the year Talasbank and [[Attelkom]] introduced SMS-based payments.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Monetary system
Irad's system is dual-currency and largely dollarized. The Bank of Irad issues the som, holds the dollar reserves that back it, supervises the commercial banks and operates the clearing house. Because most deposits, loans and prices of large purchases are in dollars, it has little room for independent monetary policy, and its main task is to keep the som stable against the dollar.<sup>[2]</sup> According to the [[wp:World Bank]], som accounts made up about a fifth of commercial bank deposits in the ISEZ in 2022.<sup>[5]</sup>

The two currencies have distinct uses:
- **US dollar.** Contracts, property, vehicles, savings, bank loans and foreign trade. Export proceeds are paid in dollars into escrow accounts at Talasbank supervised by the [[Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority]], and commercial and industrial customers of public utilities are billed in dollars.
- **Iradi som.** Public-sector wages and pensions, household utility bills, local taxes and fees, public transport and everyday retail. The [[Talas Municipal Water Authority]], for example, sets household tariffs in som and bills businesses in dollars.<sup>[6]</sup>

Since non-recognition limits Irad's access to international payment systems, dollar payments abroad are settled through correspondent banks, mainly in Almaty and Istanbul, and the som is not traded outside Irad.<sup>[5]</sup> Irad is not a member of the [[wp:International Monetary Fund]].

## Banknotes and coins
The first series of banknotes, issued in 1993 and printed abroad under a territorial contract, came in denominations of 1, 5, 10, 20, 50 and 100 som. Their designs showed horses, the [[Church of St. Janyl]], the [[Talas Alatau]] and [[wp:Silk Road]] monuments. A redesigned series with improved security features was issued from 2011, adding a 500-som note; its 100-som note carries a portrait of [[Amanbek Alimbekov]], leader of the Provisional Government in 1992. Coins of 10 and 50 tyiyn and of 1 and 5 som are struck, although small tyiyn coins are rarely used.<sup>[2]</sup>

## The tribal regions
The [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) have no formal fiscal or monetary system, and the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] issues no currency. Herders who sell livestock and wool to ISEZ buyers are usually paid through Talasbank in dollars or som, but much local trade is conducted in barter or livestock, and near the frontiers Kazakh and Uzbek currencies also change hands.<sup>[7]</sup>

## Debate
Economists and the World Bank have noted that dollarization has given Irad stable prices since the 1990s at the cost of an independent monetary policy, and that the som's role is largely confined to small payments. The commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]] has called for cryptocurrency to be made legal tender alongside the dollar and the som.<sup>[8]</sup> The Bank of Irad's 2023 annual report restates that only the dollar and the som are legal tender. Business groups credit the bank and Talasbank with keeping the payment system working through the crisis of 2006–07, and after Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]] withdrew from public view in July 2024 the bank stated that the payment system and the fixed rate were unaffected.<sup>[9]</sup>
