### 4.137. Bank of Irad
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Economy & Industry*

The **Bank of Irad** (Iradi: *Irad Banky*) is the monetary authority of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It issues the [[Iradi som]], holds the US dollar reserves that back it, licenses and supervises the commercial banks, and operates the [[Bank of Irad Clearing House]], the zone's interbank payment system. It was established by the Banking and Commercial Currency Act of 1993, passed by the interim [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] during the US territorial administration, and has its head office in [[Talas]]. Its chairman since 2010 has been [[Azamat Temirov]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

Because the US dollar is legal tender in Irad and is used for most contracts, savings and foreign trade, the bank has little room for independent monetary policy. Its main task is to keep the som at its fixed rate against the dollar. Unlike most central banks, it does not hold the government's main accounts, which are kept at [[Talasbank]], and it has no part in the escrow arrangements for export revenue, which the [[Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority]] supervises.<sup>[3]</sup>

## History

#### Establishment (1993)
In the Soviet period, banking in the Iradi SSR was carried out by the republican offices of the Soviet state bank and the specialized state banks. After the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] declared independence in October 1991, the breakdown of the ruble zone and inflation above 1,000 percent wiped out most savings, and banking had largely stopped in Talas by the time of the siege in 1992.<sup>[3]</sup>

The [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]] made the US dollar legal tender alongside any local currency the territory chose to issue. The territorial administration chose to rely on the dollar rather than introduce a full national currency at once. The Banking and Commercial Currency Act of 1993 made the dollar legal tender, authorized a local currency, the som, for small payments and public-sector wages, chartered Talasbank as the territory's main commercial bank, and created the Bank of Irad to issue the som and regulate banking.<sup>[2]</sup> The act adopted currency-board rules: the bank may issue som only in exchange for dollars at the fixed rate and must hold dollar reserves at least equal to the som in circulation. The bank opened in the autumn of 1993 in the former Talas office of the Soviet state bank, and put the first som notes into circulation in late 1993. In the first months both dollar banknotes and som notes were flown in to [[Talas Air Base]].<sup>[4]</sup>

#### Territorial period (1993–2006)
Under the 1993 act the chairman and the four other members of the bank's board were appointed by the Governor with the consent of the Territorial Senate. As at the Foreign Trade Escrow Authority, an observer from the office of the US High Commissioner attended board meetings. The bank held its reserves in correspondent accounts with banks in the United States.<sup>[4]</sup>

The bank licensed the commercial banks that opened during the investment boom of the late 1990s, most of them small and based in Talas or [[Nurzhan]]. It set up the clearing house in 1996, which at first settled checks and batch payments once a day between the banks' settlement accounts at the Bank of Irad.<sup>[5]</sup> The som was accepted for wages, utility bills and retail payments, but dollars remained dominant in savings and in any transaction of size, and studies of the period describe the territory as one of the most fully dollarized economies in the former Soviet space.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Crisis of 2006–2007
After the United States withdrew from the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] on 3 December 2006, depositors rushed to convert som and withdraw dollars, and Talasbank limited cash withdrawals for three weeks in December. The bank met conversions from its reserves and the fixed rate held at its counters, but the som traded at a discount in the informal markets of Talas and Nurzhan in the first months of 2007.<sup>[4]</sup> American correspondent banks closed or restricted Iradi accounts in early 2007, citing the territory's uncertain legal status, and the bank moved its reserves and correspondent business to banks in [[wp:Almaty]] and [[wp:Istanbul]].

During the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], the bank continued to operate in Talas under its board while the cabinet of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] and Toktarov's emergency administration in Nurzhan contested authority. Its head office closed for several days after the [[Storming of Talas (2007)|storming of Talas]] on 4 June 2007 and reopened under the ISEZ administration after DPI forces took the city that summer.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Since 2008
In 2008 the ISEZ administration reconstituted the bank under a new statute, which kept the currency-board rules and replaced the territorial provisions on federal observation. The chairman is now appointed by the Governor and confirmed by the *Mejlis* for a six-year term.<sup>[6]</sup> The discount on the som disappeared in 2008. Temirov, a former [[wp:World Bank]] consultant on Central Asian financial-sector projects, joined the bank as deputy chairman in 2007 and became chairman in 2010.<sup>[1]</sup>

Under Temirov the bank modernized the payment system. A real-time system for large dollar payments was introduced at the clearing house in 2009, backup sites were set up in Nurzhan in 2010, and som payments were added to the real-time system in 2012, the year Talasbank and [[Attelkom]] launched SMS-based payments for rural customers.<sup>[5]</sup> The bank also oversees the correspondent banking arrangements in Almaty and Istanbul on which Iradi banks depend for foreign payments.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Functions

#### Currency issue and reserves
The bank is the sole issuer of som notes and coins. Under the currency-board rules it cannot lend to the government or buy government debt, and the som in circulation is covered by dollar reserves held abroad with correspondent banks. The bank's annual report gives the reserve cover but not the location of individual holdings. Som accounts are used mainly for public-sector wages, utility bills and retail payments; most deposits, loans and commercial contracts are in dollars.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Banking supervision
The bank licenses commercial banks, microlenders and currency exchange offices in the ISEZ, sets reserve and capital requirements, and inspects the banks. Its supervision is dominated by a single institution: Talasbank holds about 60 percent of commercial deposits in the zone. Smaller banks and microfinance institutions, among them the [[Transoxiana Microfinance Fund]], serve traders, farmers and households.<sup>[7]</sup>

#### Payments
Commercial banks keep settlement accounts with the Bank of Irad, and the clearing house settles payments between them in both dollars and som, including salaries, pensions, tax and customs payments. It handles payments inside the ISEZ only. Foreign payments are settled through correspondent banks, because Irad's unresolved status limits its access to international payment systems.<sup>[5]</sup>

#### Relationship with other institutions
The division of financial functions in the ISEZ dates from the territorial statutes of 1993–1994:<sup>[3]</sup>
- **Talasbank** holds the treasury and payroll accounts of the ISEZ government and the export escrow accounts, and is supervised by the Bank of Irad as a commercial bank.
- **The Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority** registers export contracts, audits the escrow accounts, deducts royalties and duties, and administers dollar reserves set aside to guarantee imports of fuel, grain and medicines. These reserves are separate from the Bank of Irad's currency reserves.
- **The Bank of Irad** handles payments from released escrow funds only once they move to exporters' accounts at other banks through the clearing house.

## Limitations
Because Irad has no recognized sovereign status, the bank is not a member of the [[wp:International Monetary Fund]] or the [[wp:Bank for International Settlements]], and the ISEZ has no sovereign credit rating. The currency-board rules mean that the bank cannot act as a lender of last resort beyond its excess reserves, a constraint that analysts noted during the run of December 2006.<sup>[3]</sup> The bank has no branches in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], where trade is conducted in dollars, som, barter and livestock, and herders who sell to ISEZ buyers are usually paid through Talasbank.

## Criticism
The World Bank and independent analysts have noted that Talasbank has not published full audited accounts since 2008 and that the ultimate owners of the holding companies that control it have not been disclosed. Opposition commentators argue that the Bank of Irad, as its supervisor, has not enforced disclosure on a bank whose shareholders investigative reports have linked to business associates of the Toktarov family. The Bank of Irad says that the banks it supervises meet the disclosure rules in force in the ISEZ.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[8]</sup> In 2024, after Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]] withdrew from public view, the bank stated that the payment system and the fixed rate were unaffected.<sup>[9]</sup> Business groups credit it, with Talasbank, for keeping the payment system working through the crisis of 2006–2007.<sup>[7]</sup>

The populist commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]] has called for cryptocurrency to be made legal tender alongside the dollar and the som. The bank's 2023 annual report restates that only the dollar and the som are legal tender in the ISEZ.<sup>[1]</sup>

### 4.138. Northern Export Feeder
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Infrastructure & Transport*

The **Northern Export Feeder** (Iradi: *Tündük eksport tütügü*) is an 85-kilometer crude oil pipeline that carries oil from the fields of the lower Chu basin around [[Nurzhan]] into the network of the Kazakh pipeline operator [[wp:KazTransOil]] near [[wp:Shymkent]]. It is owned and operated by the [[Iradi Petroleum Transit Consortium]] (IPTC), in which [[NurGaz]] holds 51 percent. It entered commercial service in November 2000, replacing the rail tank-car shipments to the Shymkent refinery on which Iradi oil exports had depended since the early 1990s. It is Irad's only export pipeline, and most Iradi crude oil leaves the territory through it.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

The feeder lies wholly within the Chu District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It does not connect with the [[wp:Caspian Pipeline Consortium]], whose system begins far to the west, and Irad has no southern export pipeline. Because [[wp:Kazakhstan]] claims Irad *de jure* and does not recognize the ISEZ, the line operates under commercial contracts and a technical annex to the 2008 [[Northern Border Demarcation Protocol]] rather than under an interstate agreement (see [[Irad–Kazakhstan relations]]).<sup>[3]</sup>

## Background
Oil was discovered near Kobozev, now Nurzhan, in 1949 (see [[Nurzhan Oil Discovery (1949)]]). In the Soviet period crude from the Chu fields was refined at the city's refinery, now [[Nurzhan Refinery No. 1]], or sent by rail to other refineries of [[wp:Soviet Central Asia]]. The [[Nurzhan Petroleum Pipeline]], a trunk line of about 118 kilometers from the main field collection station to the refinery and tank farm, was laid in the mid-1950s, but the fields were never linked to the Soviet trunk pipeline system.<sup>[4]</sup>

After 1992 the territorial administration and NurGaz, privatized in 1993, shipped crude that the Nurzhan refinery did not take north to Shymkent in rail tank cars. The traffic was expensive, slowed by border formalities and limited by the supply of tank cars, and in winter the waxy crude had to be heated before it could be unloaded. As production recovered from its 1996 low of about 48,000 barrels per day (bpd), NurGaz looked for a pipeline outlet into the Kazakh trunk network.<sup>[2]</sup>

## History

#### Planning and construction
NurGaz and foreign partners registered IPTC in [[Talas]] in 1998 as a joint-stock company. NurGaz contributed its tank farm and rights of way, and the foreign shareholders provided most of the construction finance. The route was surveyed in 1998, and the line was built in 1999–2000 by contractors working under the supervision of the territorial energy department. Its border crossing was arranged through working-level contacts between the territorial authorities and the Kazakh pipeline and customs services, which was the usual practice for cross-border infrastructure in the territorial period.<sup>[1]</sup>

The feeder began commercial operation in November 2000, after which crude exports by rail largely ended. Its original capacity was about 65,000 bpd.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 2007 and after
During the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in 2007, forces loyal to [[Erlan Toktarov]] concentrated on holding Nurzhan, the oil fields and the pipeline. Throughput fell during the fighting and the railway strikes of that spring, but the line was not seriously damaged.<sup>[5]</sup> The end of the territorial administration left the border crossing without a formal basis. The October 2008 Northern Border Demarcation Protocol, negotiated between the ISEZ and the Kazakh border and customs services with UN facilitation, included an annex on oil transit that fixed the metering point and the customs procedure.<sup>[3]</sup>

Because NurGaz's reported output continued to rise, IPTC added a further pumping station and a drag-reducing agent injection system in 2011–2012, which raised capacity to about 100,000 bpd.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Route and technical description
The feeder is built of 530-millimeter (20-inch) steel pipe. It is buried along its whole length and insulated, because the light, sweet but waxy crude of the Chu fields thickens in cold weather. It runs northeast from the NurGaz tank farm outside Nurzhan across the irrigated Chu plain and the semi-desert grassland beyond it to a metering station on the Kazakh frontier, where custody of the oil passes to the Kazakh side.<sup>[2]</sup> From there the crude moves through the KazTransOil network to be refined at Shymkent or shipped north toward Russia.

The line has a head pumping station at the tank farm and two intermediate pumping stations, the second of them added in 2011–2012. It is controlled from a dispatch room in Nurzhan through a supervisory control and data acquisition ([[wp:SCADA]]) system, with communications provided by [[Attelkom]]. Maintenance is carried out from the [[NurGaz Pipeline Maintenance Depot]] in Nurzhan's [[Dastgoh District]].<sup>[1]</sup> The pumping stations draw power from the ISEZ grid, which is supplied mainly by the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]] and the downstream stations of the Naryn cascade.

## Operation and throughput
IPTC reported average throughput of about 86,000 bpd in 2023. This figure is consistent with NurGaz's reported output of about 120,000 bpd, less the roughly 31,000 bpd processed at Nurzhan Refinery No. 1.<sup>[1]</sup> Independent analysts working from KazTransOil intake records and observations of gas flaring estimate deliveries at about 55,000–70,000 bpd, in line with their lower estimates of national production of 85,000–100,000 bpd. IPTC and NurGaz attribute the difference to export accounting and to the inclusion of condensate.<sup>[6]</sup>

IPTC earns a transit tariff on each barrel shipped, paid by NurGaz and any other shippers, while tariffs on the Kazakh section are paid to the Kazakh operator under its terms for third-party transit. Export proceeds are paid in US dollars into escrow accounts at [[Talasbank]] supervised by the [[Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority]], which deducts the crude oil royalty set by the 1995 Hydrocarbon and Mining Code before releasing the balance.<sup>[7]</sup> Oil royalties are among the largest sources of ISEZ public revenue (see [[Economy of Irad]] and [[Energy in Irad]]).

## Ownership
NurGaz holds 51 percent of IPTC. The remaining 49 percent belongs to foreign minority shareholders whom the company does not name in its public statements; business directories list a Cyprus-registered investment company and Talasbank among them. The board is chaired by [[Emil Bekzatov]], vice president of NurGaz and son of its president, [[Kamran Bekzatov]]. The company employs about 300 people.<sup>[7]</sup>

## Transit arrangements with Kazakhstan
Deliveries into the Kazakh system are made under commercial contracts between IPTC and the Kazakh side. Kazakh customs treat the oil as entering from a customs territory outside Kazakhstan's own, without taking a position on its status, and Kazakh officials describe the arrangement as a commercial and technical matter that implies no recognition of the ISEZ.<sup>[3]</sup> A technical liaison group of the two border services reviews the oil annex once a year, with a UN official present.

The arrangement has generally worked without interruption. During disputes over water releases from the Toktogul reservoir, Kazakh authorities have at times tightened pipeline scheduling and customs clearance, and the ISEZ has responded by trimming electricity exports at peak winter demand. Analysts describe these episodes as limited and carefully managed, because both sides depend on the trade (see [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]]).<sup>[5]</sup> Russo politicians in Nurzhan have cited Irad's dependence on a single northern outlet in support of closer economic integration with Kazakhstan and Russia.<sup>[8]</sup>

## Alternatives
The feeder has no alternative outlet. During the territorial period a US-backed proposal for an oil pipeline south to [[wp:Pakistan]] was studied; its prospects ended after 2021, when the [[wp:Taliban]] returned to power in [[wp:Afghanistan]]. The proposed Trans-Irad Gas Pipeline of the [[wp:China National Petroleum Corporation]] would carry gas rather than oil (see [[Trans-Irad Pipeline Proposals]]). Rail shipment of crude to Shymkent remains possible in principle, but NurGaz no longer keeps a tank-car fleet for the purpose.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[6]</sup>

### 4.139. Sport in Irad
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Sport*

**Sport in Irad** is dominated by equestrian games, above all *[[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak tartysh]]*, a mounted team contest for a goat carcass whose national competition, the President's Cup, is the main event of the sporting year. Horse racing, mounted wrestling and eagle hunting are also widely followed. Among modern sports, football and wrestling are the most popular, followed by boxing and basketball. Traditional equestrian sport in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) is regulated by the [[National Equestrian Sports Directorate]], created in 1993; in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) most competitions are organized by clan councils.<sup>[1]</sup>

Irad's unresolved international status limits its participation in international sport. It has no [[wp:National Olympic Committee]] recognized by the [[wp:International Olympic Committee]] and is not a member of the main international federations, so Iradi athletes who reach the top level usually compete for other countries (see [[Political status of Irad]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

## History
In the Soviet period sport in the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] was run by the republican Committee for Physical Culture and Sport. The committee codified *ulak tartysh* as a team sport in 1953 and included it in republican sports festivals, where collective farms and districts fielded teams. Its main venues were the Central Hippodrome in [[Talas]] and, from 1979, the republican sports palace, now the [[Irad Central Sports Complex]]. Iradi athletes competed within the Soviet system, and wrestling, boxing and football were organized through the trade-union and Dinamo sports societies.<sup>[3]</sup>

After 1992 traditional sport became a marker of national identity. In 1992 Provisional President [[Amanbek Alimbekov]] instituted the President's Cup for *ulak tartysh*, to be contested in the week of Irad Day (11 March). In 1993 an act of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] created the National Equestrian Sports Directorate, which took over the rules of the traditional games and the organization of national competition. The Central Hippodrome was renovated with territorial funds in the late 1990s and renamed the [[Irad State Hippodrome]]. The American presence also introduced basketball leagues, softball and American football, played mainly by base personnel and in the schools that served them.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>

Since 2007 the Directorate has operated under the ISEZ administration, and its director is appointed by the Governor. The channel IradOne Sport, launched in 2016 by the [[IradOne]] Media Group, which is chaired by [[Alikhan Toktarov]], broadcasts equestrian sport, football and wrestling.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Equestrian sports
*Main article: [[Iradi Equestrian Culture & Breeds]]*

#### Ulak tartysh and the President's Cup
*Ulak tartysh* is played in two forms: a regulated game of two teams of twelve registered players, four of them mounted at a time, on a field of 300 by 150 meters with a raised goal (*[[Tai-Kazan|tai-kazan]]*) at each end; and an older free-for-all form with no teams, played at weddings and feasts in the tribal regions. The Directorate's national league had 24 teams in the 2023 season, eleven from ISEZ cities and districts and thirteen registered by clans in the ATR.<sup>[6]</sup>

The President's Cup is the national championship. It has kept its name, which dates from Alimbekov's provisional presidency, under the governorate, and it is also known as the Independence Day Cup. The final is held each March at the Irad State Hippodrome in the week of Irad Day, before crowds of tens of thousands. Winners receive cash prizes and, by tradition, a horse. IradOne holds the broadcasting rights.<sup>[6]</sup> Since 2009 the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] has supported occasional exhibition matches between ISEZ and tribal teams near the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] as confidence-building events.<sup>[7]</sup>

#### Horse racing
The Irad State Hippodrome in Talas, which seats about 25,000, is the main racecourse. It has dirt tracks for thoroughbred and [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] flat racing, a field for *ulak tartysh*, stabling and a veterinary clinic, and it is the headquarters of the Directorate. Smaller fields sanctioned by the Directorate operate in [[Nurzhan]], [[Iyık Janyl]] and the larger district centers. Long-distance racing over open country, *[[At Chabysh (Racing)|at chabysh]]*, is run over 20 to 50 kilometers at weddings, memorial feasts and festivals; under Directorate rules riders must be at least twelve years old, and horses are checked by veterinarians at the finish. [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] horses dominate mountain courses, and the endurance races of the August Kurultai on the [[Aksay Plateau]] are the main mountain event.<sup>[8]</sup>

#### Other horseback games and eagle hunting
Other sanctioned disciplines include mounted wrestling (*[[Oodarysh (Mounted Wrestling)|oodarysh]]*), the courtship chase *kyz kuu* and coin-picking at the gallop (*[[Tyin Emmei (Mounted Sport)|tyin emmei]]*), which are usually staged at national holidays. Contests in hunting with golden eagles ([[Burkut Saluu|burkut saluu]]) are held at the autumn Salburun festival outside Talas, first organized as a national festival in 1995. Judges in these events assess style as well as results, according to the ideal of *[[Körktüülük|körktüülük]]*.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Wrestling and combat sports
Wrestling is the most successful Iradi sport at international level. Freestyle and Greco-Roman wrestling were developed in the Soviet period, and the national championships are held at the Irad Central Sports Complex in Talas, a 6,500-seat arena renovated in 2009. Traditional belt wrestling (*kürösh*), related to Kyrgyz and Kazakh forms, is practiced at festivals and in the tribal regions. Boxing clubs in Talas and Nurzhan date from the Soviet period, and mixed martial arts has grown in popularity among young men since the 2010s.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Football
Football is the most popular team sport in the cities (see [[Football in Irad]]). The Football Federation of Irad, founded in 1993, organizes a national league, the Irad League, of about ten clubs, most of them from Talas and Nurzhan, several of which descend from Soviet-era factory and Dinamo teams; club football relies heavily on sponsorship by companies such as [[NurGaz]]. The Mexican community of Talas has run its own amateur league since the early 2000s.<sup>[9]</sup>

The federation is not a member of [[wp:FIFA]] or of the [[wp:Asian Football Confederation]], and its national team cannot play official internationals. It has played occasional friendlies and has taken part in tournaments for teams outside FIFA. Some Iradi players have joined clubs in [[wp:Kazakhstan]] and elsewhere.<sup>[9]</sup>

## International participation
The Irad Olympic Committee was formed in 1993, during the territorial period, but its application was not accepted by the International Olympic Committee, which since 1996 has admitted only committees of states recognized by the international community. According to the committee, Iradi athletes who wish to compete at the [[wp:Olympic Games]] or world championships do so for other countries. Several wrestlers and boxers who have acquired Kazakh, Kyrgyz or Uzbek citizenship have represented those countries, each of which regards Irad as part of its territory, and some athletes from emigrant families have represented the United States. Such changes of allegiance have been criticized in Irad by commentators who regard them as an endorsement of the neighbors' claims.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[10]</sup>

The same claims affect equestrian sport. Directorate teams have not been admitted as a national team to regional events such as the [[wp:World Nomad Games]], although individual Iradi riders have competed in invitational races and endurance events abroad.<sup>[8]</sup>

## Sport in the tribal regions
In the ATR, sport is organized mainly by clans and is closely tied to festivals, weddings and memorial feasts. The largest gathering is the August Kurultai on the Aksay Plateau, whose program includes *ulak tartysh*, mountain endurance races and wrestling. Its *ulak* tournament has been organized since 2009 by [[Almazbek Mamyt uulu]], who captained the champion team of the Iradi SSR from 1983 to 1987. Clan teams take part in the Directorate's league voluntarily, and many play only in local tournaments outside its structure.<sup>[7]</sup><sup>[11]</sup>

## Criticism
Animal welfare groups have criticized the rate of injuries to horses in *ulak tartysh* and long-distance racing, the use of carcasses and the employment of child jockeys. Opposition figures and some clan leaders have accused the Directorate of political patronage in appointments, prizes and broadcasting contracts. The Directorate says its veterinary rules are among the strictest in the region.<sup>[8]</sup>

### 4.140. Public holidays in Irad
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Culture & Folklore*

**Public holidays in Irad** are set separately in its two zones. In the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), public holidays and official commemorative days are fixed by the Holidays and Commemorative Days Act, first passed by the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] in 1993 and revised by the Mejlis in 2008. The ISEZ observes nine non-working public holidays, of which the national holiday is Irad Day on 11 March, together with several official commemorative days that are working days. In the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) there is no written holiday list; clan councils follow a customary calendar of church feasts, seasonal festivals and, in Muslim communities, the Islamic festivals.<sup>[1]</sup>

The civil calendar is the Gregorian calendar, and the working week runs from Monday to Friday. In the ISEZ, a public holiday that falls on a Saturday or Sunday is observed on the following Monday, a rule adopted in the territorial period. The [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], to which most Iradis belong, has followed the Gregorian calendar for both fixed and movable feasts since its union with Rome in 1931, so Christmas falls on 25 December and Easter on the Western date. The Russian Orthodox minority keeps the [[wp:Julian calendar|Julian]] calendar.<sup>[2]</sup> The church seasons, name days and folk reckonings of the year are described in [[Iradi calendar]].

## ISEZ public holidays
| Date | Name | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 1 January | New Year's Day | Retained from the Soviet calendar. |
| 8 March | International Women's Day | Retained from the Soviet calendar. |
| 11 March | Irad Day (*Irad Künü*) | National holiday. Anniversary of the proclamation of the Republic of Irad by the Provisional Government in [[Talas]] in 1992. |
| 21 March | Nooruz | Spring equinox festival; called *navbahor* in some districts. Added in 1993. |
| Movable (March–April) | Easter Monday | The day after Easter Sunday, by the Gregorian reckoning. |
| 15 August | Remembrance Day of the Lost Tribes | Commemorates [[The Lost Tribes of 1916]] and the dead of the 1916 revolt. Also observed in the ATR. |
| 24 August | Feast of St. Janyl (*Janyl Mairamy*) | Principal feast of the Syro-Iradi Catholic Church. |
| 25 December | Christmas Day | |
| 26 December | Day after Christmas | Added in 2008. |

## ISEZ commemorative days
The following are official commemorative days. Ceremonies are held and flags are flown, but they are working days.
| Date | Name | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 3 February | Memorial Day of the Winter Uprising | Victims of the shootings in Talas on 3 February 1992 during the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]]; service at the memorial on Central Square, unveiled in 1997. |
| 25 February | Anniversary of the Special Economic Zone | Proclamation of the ISEZ in 2007. Marked since 2008 with official ceremonies in [[Nurzhan]]. |
| 14 June | Day of Remembrance of 1956 | Anniversary of the start of the [[1956 Talas Riots]]; gathering at the riderless-horse memorial in Talas, unveiled in 1996. |

## Main holidays

#### Irad Day
Irad Day (11 March) marks the proclamation of the Republic of Irad in Talas on 11 March 1992, which began the [[First Iradi Civil War]] (see [[March 11 Independence Day]]). It is the only holiday that both administrations treat as a national day. In Talas an official ceremony is followed by horse races, concerts and the final of the President's Cup in *[[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak tartysh]]* at the [[Irad State Hippodrome]], held in the week of the holiday. Celebrations in the [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]] traditionally begin the day. Families hold feasts of mutton and beef, and in keeping with the [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo|horsemeat taboo]] no horsemeat is served. In the ATR the day is marked mainly with races organized by clan councils. Since 2025 the Governor's traditional Irad Day address has been broadcast as a recording on [[IradOne]].<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Feast of St. Janyl
The Feast of St. Janyl on 24 August honors [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|St. Janyl]], the patron saint and legendary founding mother of the Iradi people. A candlelit vigil on 23 August is followed by the liturgy at the [[Church of St. Janyl]] in [[Iyık Janyl]], the blessing of horses and sheep on the cathedral esplanade, the distribution of blessed bread and afternoon races. Pilgrims from the ATR cross the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] under arrangements agreed each year in the Joint Liaison Committee of the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]], and the pilgrimage season continues into September. The archbishopric's attendance estimates have exceeded 150,000 in recent years (see [[Feast of St. Janyl]]).<sup>[4]</sup>

#### Remembrance Day of the Lost Tribes
On 15 August parishes hold memorial services for the clans that disappeared in the mountains after the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|Semirechye Revolt]] of 1916, and herders in both zones hold horse blessings. The poem *[[The Black Blizzard of 1916 (Poem)|The Black Blizzard]]* is recited and laments for the dead of 1916 are played on the [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]]. Many people wear a small inverted horseshoe badge, following the [[Fallen Rider Tradition]]. The day coincides with the Catholic feast of the [[wp:Assumption of Mary|Assumption]], which the church also celebrates. It is one of the few observances shared by both administrations.<sup>[5]</sup>

#### Christmas and Easter
Christmas and Easter are the main family holidays of Christian households. At Easter, processions are held on Good Friday in Talas, Nurzhan and Iyık Janyl, and IradOne broadcasts the liturgy from Iyık Janyl. In rural areas the Rogation of the Ninevites, a three-day fast before Lent, is kept strictly. Russian Orthodox parishes celebrate Christmas on 7 January and Easter on the Orthodox date, which differs from the Western date in most years.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### Nooruz
Nooruz, the spring equinox festival shared with the Kyrgyz, [[wp:Kazakhs]], [[wp:Uzbeks]] and other peoples of the region, was discouraged in the Soviet period and was made a public holiday in 1993. Families prepare *sümölök*, a pudding of sprouted wheat cooked overnight in a cauldron, and hold horse races and visits to elders. Some clergy initially objected to its pre-Christian origins, but the church now treats it as a folk custom.<sup>[6]</sup>

## Religious observance by minorities
The Act allows employees to take up to three days of paid leave a year for religious festivals not on the public holiday list. Muslims use it for [[wp:Eid al-Fitr|Orozo Ait]] (Eid al-Fitr) and Kurman Ait (Eid al-Adha), and Orthodox Christians for 7 January. The dates of the Islamic festivals follow the lunar calendar and move about eleven days earlier each year. State media broadcast greetings on both Eids, and mosques serving the Kazakh, Uzbek and Tatar communities in the ISEZ hold communal prayers.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[7]</sup>

## Autonomous Tribal Regions
In the ATR, observances are set by custom and by the clan councils rather than by statute. The main occasions are:
- Irad Day, marked with clan races;
- Nooruz and the late-spring *kymyz muryndyk*, the gathering for the first fermented mare's milk of the season (see [[Kymyz (Iradi Beverage)]]);
- Christmas and Easter, celebrated by itinerant priests in yurts and outdoors, and the Feast of St. Janyl, with pilgrimages to Iyık Janyl and blessings of the herds at rural churches;
- the Remembrance Day of the Lost Tribes on 15 August;
- the August Kurultai on the [[Aksay Plateau]], the main gathering of the clans, with races, *ulak tartysh* and the assembly of the [[Iradi Freedom Society]].

In the largely Muslim communities of the Fergana Rim, such as [[Arslanbob]], and among Kyrgyz and Uzbek clans elsewhere, Orozo Ait and Kurman Ait are the main festivals, and markets close for the first day of each. The ISEZ commemorative days, including 25 February, are not observed in the tribal regions, where the IAC regards that date as the start of the [[Second Iradi Civil War]].<sup>[8]</sup>

## History
The Soviet holidays of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] included New Year's Day, [[wp:International Women's Day]], 1 and 2 May, [[wp:Victory Day (9 May)|Victory Day]] on 9 May and the anniversary of the [[wp:October Revolution]] on 7 November; religious feasts had no official status, and public celebration of the Feast of St. Janyl was banned from 1937 until the late 1980s.<sup>[2]</sup>

The 1993 Act, passed during the territorial period, made Irad Day the national holiday, added Christmas, [[wp:Easter Monday]], Nooruz, the Feast of St. Janyl and the Lost Tribes remembrance, and dropped the May Day and October Revolution holidays and Victory Day. Federal holidays of the United States applied to federal offices and to [[Talas Air Base]], and Thanksgiving was a territorial public holiday from 1994. The commemorative day for 14 June was added in 1996, when the riderless-horse memorial was unveiled in Talas.<sup>[1]</sup>

The 2008 revision by the Mejlis removed Thanksgiving, added 26 December and introduced the commemorative day for 25 February. 9 October, the date of the proclamation of the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] in 1991, has never been a holiday. Neither 3 December, the date of the US withdrawal from the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] in 2006, nor 9 December, the date of the proclamation of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]], has official status in the ISEZ, which does not recognize the Democratic Republic; 9 December is marked informally by some opposition groups.<sup>[9]</sup>

## Other observances
- **Victory Day (9 May):** no longer a public holiday, but marked in Nurzhan with a parade, mainly by the Russian-speaking generation known as the [[Russos of Nurzhan|Russos]] and by veterans' associations.
- **Korean holidays:** the [[Koryo-saram in Irad|Koryo-saram]] community celebrates [[wp:Chuseok]] in autumn and the spring memorial day of *Hansik*.
- **Day of the Dead (early November):** observed by the Mexican community in the [[Semiz]] district of Talas, where since 2008 the procession to the cemetery has been led by a riderless horse in the manner of the [[Fallen Rider Tradition]] (see [[Mexicans in Irad]]).
- **Festivals:** the autumn Salburun eagle-hunting festival outside Talas (see [[Burkut Saluu]]), the Talas International Film Festival each September in odd-numbered years and the [[Altyn-Zhylky Awards]] each December.<sup>[10]</sup>

### 4.141. Music of Irad
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Arts, Music & Film*

The **music of Irad** includes the traditional instrumental and epic music of the Iradi clans, the liturgical chant of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], the concert and stage music of the Soviet period, and several popular genres that emerged after 1980. The central traditional instrument is the three-stringed [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]], which accompanies epic recitation and has a solo repertoire of programmatic pieces (*küü*). Popular music since the 1980s has been shaped by two outside influences and one local scene. American songs about Irad heard on smuggled cassettes and [[wp:Voice of America]] broadcasts, followed by the 1993 American compilation *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]*, gave rise to [[Iradi Country-Folk|Iradi country-folk]]. The dark electronic genre [[Mor-Wave]], launched in [[Nurzhan]] by the duo [[tüntolk]] with their album *[[Jolchu (Album)|Jolchu]]* (1999), has produced the offshoots [[Mor-Pop]] and [[Mor-Folk]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

The national anthem is "[[The Spirit of Irad]]".

## Traditional music

#### Instruments
The **komuz** is a fretless long-necked lute carved from a single piece of apricot or walnut wood, about 85 to 95 cm long, with three strings of gut or nylon. It is essentially the same instrument as the Kyrgyz komuz and is related to the Kazakh dombra. Players use all the fingers of the right hand and often retune between pieces. The **[[Kyl-kyak|kyl-kyak]]** is a two-stringed bowed lute strung with horsehair, whose sound is likened to neighing or wind; ethnographers have recorded its earlier use by healers (*bakshy*). The **[[Choor (Flute)|choor]]** is an end-blown shepherd's flute with four or five finger holes, played while humming to produce overtones. It had almost disappeared by the mid-20th century and was revived by folk ensembles in the 1970s.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Küü
Instrumental pieces for the komuz (*küü*; see [[Küü (Music)]]) are usually programmatic. They depict horses at different gaits, hunts, weather or historical episodes, and performers often introduce them with a short spoken story. The best known is *[[Kambarkan]]*, named after the legendary hunter credited with inventing the komuz, which is a standard test piece for soloists at the National Conservatory of Folk Music in [[Talas]]. Laments for the dead of 1916 are played at the memorial gatherings of 15 August (see [[The Lost Tribes of 1916]]).<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Epic and song
Bards (*ırchy*) sing or chant epic and genealogical verse, alternating it with komuz interludes. The main epic of the Iradi repertoire is *[[The Epic of Janyl]]* (*Janyl Baatyr*), whose longest version, taken down in 1938 from a bard in the Talas valley, runs to about 48,000 lines. Bards perform it over several evenings at weddings, memorial feasts and the [[Feast of St. Janyl]]. Other vocal genres include the lament (*koshok*), sung by women at funerals; the unaccompanied horseback song (*[[Irda (Vocal Tradition)|ırda]]*), paced to the gait of the horse; and narrative poems such as *[[The Black Blizzard of 1916 (Poem)|The Black Blizzard of 1916]]*, recited on 15 August.<sup>[4]</sup>

The largest body of field recordings was made between 1962 and 1989 by the ethnomusicologist [[Aigul Choro kyzy]]: about 640 reel-to-reel tapes from the [[Talas Alatau]], the Chatkal valley and the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] foothills, now held in the [[State Archives of Irad]].<sup>[4]</sup>

#### Church music
The Syro-Iradi Catholic Church sings the monophonic [[wp:Syriac language|Syriac]] antiphons (*'onitha*) of the East Syriac rite, which were passed down orally while the church was banned in the Soviet period (see [[East Syriac Rites of Iyık Janyl]]). In some rural churches the komuz and kyl-kyak accompany the liturgy. Folklorists have noted melodic features shared by this chant and the horseback songs. The [[Iyık Janyl Seminary Choir]], formed in 1994, also sings four-part settings of Iradi hymns, a practice introduced under Western Catholic influence.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Soviet period
In the Soviet period traditional music was institutionalized. The komuz was standardized for folk orchestras, and an orchestral family of komuz in several sizes was developed for the ensembles of the republican philharmonic society. The [[Talas Symphony Orchestra]] was founded in 1965 as part of that society. Since the 1970s it has commissioned symphonic poems on Iradi landscapes and history, some adding the komuz, kyl-kyak and choor to the orchestra, and settings of episodes from *The Epic of Janyl*. The Talas Opera and Ballet Theater, whose prima ballerina from 1971 to 1990 was [[Venera Kasymova]], staged the Russian and European repertoire alongside works by Iradi composers.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[6]</sup> The Russian-language popular song (*estrada*) of the Soviet mainstream dominated radio, and it remains popular among the older urban generation known as the [[Russos of Nurzhan|Russos]].<sup>[6]</sup>

Film music offered composers more freedom. Asan Jumabaev's score for *[[Desert Sun’s Rebellion]]* (1979) combined the komuz with electric guitar, whistling and long silences, and the electronic tape loops of Nurlan Sadikov's lost short *[[Tolkun (Lost Film)|Tolkun]]* (1963) are regarded as an early Central Asian experiment in the manner of *musique concrète* (see [[Cinema of Irad]]).<sup>[7]</sup>

#### Cassettes and the Voice of America (1980s)
In the 1980s American country and folk songwriters wrote songs about Irad, then a Soviet republic, often portraying Iradi horsemen and Christians under Soviet rule in romantic terms. Voice of America played some of them in its music programs, and travelers carried cassette copies into the Iradi SSR, where they were copied from hand to hand. Young listeners in Talas learned the guitar parts by ear, and the first Iradi-language versions were sung at private gatherings in the last years of Soviet rule. At the same time, young musicians in Kobozev rehearsed in district-heating boiler rooms and empty workshops, in the tradition of the Soviet underground rock scene.<sup>[8]</sup><sup>[9]</sup>

## Territorial period
The arrival of American personnel at [[Talas Air Base]] after 1992 and the brief American fascination with Irad known as [[Iradimania]] brought these influences into the open. *Swift Hooves*, a compilation of fourteen country and folk songs about Irad organized by [[wp:Nashville, Tennessee|Nashville]] producers with American church relief organizations, was released in 1993. All its profits went to Christian-run charities in Irad, which funded rural dispensaries and church repairs. Its songs include "Ride for Talas", "Bells of Iyık Janyl" and "The Widow's Horse", a ballad based on the popular story of the [[1956 Talas Riots]]. Later commentators describe its picture of the Iradis as "freedom-loving Christian cowboys" as romanticized.<sup>[8]</sup>

Copies of the album reached Irad in 1993–1994 through base personnel, charities and [[IradOne]], and copied cassettes were sold in the bazaars of Talas. Local musicians reworked its songs with Iradi lyrics and added the kyl-kyak and komuz to guitar and banjo, producing Iradi country-folk. Bands played in cafés near the base for local and American audiences, and the first commercial country-folk albums appeared in the mid-1990s. The genre's subjects include horses, pastoral life and the civil wars; ballads about the [[Storming of Talas (2007)|storming of Talas]] in 2007 are popular in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]].<sup>[9]</sup>

Traditional music also found a broadcast outlet. From 1994 to 2020 the IradOne radio program *Kechki Jomok* ("Evening Tales"), presented by [[Baktygul Omurova]], broadcast bards, *küü* and listeners' genealogies, and its audience reached herding settlements on both sides of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. The Talas Symphony Orchestra toured the United States in 1994 under its concertmaster [[Elena Kim]].<sup>[6]</sup>

## Mor-Wave and its offshoots
Mor-Wave emerged in Nurzhan in the late 1990s, when much of the city's heavy industry stood idle. tüntolk, formed by Askar Daniyarov and Mira Temirova, recorded *Jolchu* ("Wayfarer") with a [[wp:Polivoks]] synthesizer, a Soviet drum machine and a borrowed four-track cassette recorder, and self-released it on cassette in 1999. Unlike most urban musicians of the time, who sang in Russian or English, Temirova wrote in Iradi, adapting epic verse and laments and using images of the steppe goddess Umay and the bull-headed [[Morkhan (Mythology)|Morkhan]]. A first wave of groups, among them Kara Jel and Umay-9, grew up in Nurzhan and Talas between 1999 and 2005, and Nurzhan's club nights drew listeners from [[wp:Almaty]] and [[wp:Tashkent]]. The scene contracted during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in 2007, when venues closed under emergency regulations and tüntolk split up.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[10]</sup>

A second wave began in 2014, centered in Talas, among young Iradis who had grown up fluent in English and were turning to the Iradi language. tüntolk re-formed that year, and their album *White Stallion in Fog* (2017) was played on the youth channel IradOne launched in 2015. An annual Mor-Wave festival has been held in converted textile warehouses in Talas since 2016, and streaming services have brought the genre listeners in Eastern Europe and North America. Mor-Wave songs were sung at the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]], after which IradOne dropped several tüntolk videos from rotation, according to the *[[Talas Herald]]*.<sup>[10]</sup><sup>[11]</sup>

Two offshoots developed during the second wave:
- **[[Mor-Pop]]**, a commercial idol-pop form often likened to the darker, concept-driven style of [[wp:K-pop|South Korean K-pop]], with choreographed groups, dance rhythms, sampled komuz riffs and Mor-Wave's Turkic pagan imagery, played widely on IradOne and commercial radio. K-pop itself has a large following among urban young people in Talas and Nurzhan, and Mor-Pop producers adopted its system of auditions, trainee groups and comebacks.
- **[[Mor-Folk]]**, an acoustic form for komuz, choor and frame drums that draws its melodies from Syro-Iradi liturgical chant, performed mainly in teahouses (*chaykhana*) in Talas and Nurzhan.

Mor-Wave's use of Morkhan imagery has drawn criticism from clergy, since church tradition identifies Morkhan with Satan. In June 2019 a concert planned in [[Iyık Janyl]] was cancelled after objections from clergy and parishioners. Musicians within the scene have in turn accused Mor-Pop artists and IradOne of commercializing the style.<sup>[11]</sup>

## Institutions and awards
The main teaching institution is the National Conservatory of Folk Music in Talas. The [[Altyn-Zhylky Awards]], presented each December since 1996, include separate popular-music categories for Mor-Wave and its offshoots. Ethnomusicologists credit Mor-Wave and Iradi-language popular music in general with raising the prestige of the language among urban young people (see [[Iradi language revival]] and [[Iradi Language]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

### 4.142. Flag of Irad
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: National Symbols*

The **flag of Irad** (Iradi: *Irad tuu*) is a crimson field bearing a central emblem: a white stallion in gait beneath a five-pointed star, an inverted horseshoe on the hoist side of the horse, an arched inscription in [[wp:Old Turkic language|Old Turkic]] (Orkhon) script reading "Be Free", and a wreath of two ears of wheat. It was adopted by the Provisional Government in 1992 and confirmed by the interim [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] in 1993. It has been used since then by every Iradi administration, including the territorial government, the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] and the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), and it is also flown in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR). Its official description was issued by the Department of Public Information in 2015.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Design
The flag has a width-to-length ratio of 1:√2 (about 1:1.41). The emblem stands at the center of the field, slightly toward the hoist, and fills about three-quarters of the flag's height. Its elements form a roundel: the wheat ears enclose it at the sides and foot, and the inscription closes it at the top.<sup>[1]</sup>

| Element | Description |
|---|---|
| Field | Crimson |
| Stallion | A white horse in gait, facing the hoist, with one foreleg raised, in the center of the emblem |
| Star | A five-pointed star directly above the stallion |
| Horseshoe | A small horseshoe on the hoist side of the stallion, level with its head, with the heels pointing downward |
| Inscription | Two words in Orkhon letters, arched along the top of the emblem between the tips of the wheat ears |
| Wreath | Two ears of wheat whose stalks cross beneath the stallion and rise on either side of the emblem |

#### Colors
The official description gives the field as crimson, the stallion, star, horseshoe and inscription as white, and the wheat as golden. In the reference artwork published with it, all the charges are drawn in a single pale ivory (hex #FFF6D5) on a crimson field (hex #AA0000), and flags made in Irad generally follow this. Some foreign and commercially made flags show the wheat in yellow or gold.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Inscription
The inscription is written in the runic script of the Old Turkic inscriptions of the Orkhon valley, examples of which have been found in the Talas valley. Like the original inscriptions, it reads from right to left. It renders the Iradi words *azat bol*, "be free". The script is used today only symbolically, and the choice was explained in 1992 as a reference to the oldest written form of the Turkic languages, which predates the division of Iradis into Christian and Muslim communities (see [[Iradi alphabet]]).<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

## Symbolism
The 2015 official description assigns each element a meaning:<sup>[1]</sup>
- **The crimson field** continues the revolutionary tradition of the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|Semirechye Revolt]] of 1916 and the banner of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]].
- **The stallion** represents the national equestrian heritage, the [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] and [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] breeds, and the historical belief that Irad was the birthplace of the domesticated horse (see [[Botai Culture in Irad]]). Some popular interpretations also associate the white horse with [[The Legend of the White Rider]], although the official description does not.
- **The star** represents [[wp:Polaris]], called *Irad* in traditional cosmology, from which the country takes its name. The flag uses the five-pointed civic form of the [[The Star of Irad (Symbol)|Star of Irad]]; the eight-pointed form is reserved for the liturgical use of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]]. Some older publications and foreign descriptions give the flag star eight points, confusing the two.
- **The inverted horseshoe** follows the steppe cavalry custom of the Fallen Rider, in which downward-facing tack marks a warrior killed in battle (see [[Fallen Rider Tradition]]). On the flag it is a permanent memorial to the martyrs of Irad, specifically those lost in the 1916 revolt and the flight that followed, the victims of the Soviet purges, and the dead of the [[First Iradi Civil War|First]] and [[Second Iradi Civil War|Second Iradi Civil Wars]]. In European folk custom a horseshoe hung points-up holds good luck; the downward shoe on the Iradi flag instead marks the dead.
- **The inscription** "Be Free" expresses the aspiration to freedom.
- **The wheat wreath** retains a motif of Soviet-era republican heraldry and symbolizes agricultural life in the river valleys.

## History

#### Before 1992
The clans used horsetail standards (*tug*) in war and at gatherings, and the church carried processional banners bearing the cross and the eight-pointed star. Iradi tradition holds that the insurgents of 1916 carried red banners, which the official description cites as the origin of the crimson field.<sup>[2]</sup>

Like other union republics, the Iradi SSR, created in 1925, used a red flag bearing the hammer and sickle and the initials of the republic, later replaced by the standard pattern of a red field with the gold hammer, sickle and star in the canton. Its state emblem was framed by a wreath of wheat ears. The [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] proclaimed in Kobozev in October 1991 continued to use the Soviet-era flag.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### Adoption (1992–1993)
During the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]], protesters in [[Talas]] carried red banners painted with a white horse, and after the shootings of 3 February 1992 an inverted horseshoe, worn as a badge, spread among them as a sign of mourning in keeping with the Fallen Rider custom. According to popular accounts, a red banner with a white horse and a star hung in the municipal theater during the [[Talas Town Hall Meeting (1992)|Talas Town Hall Meeting]] on 11 March 1992, at which the Republic of Irad was proclaimed.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>

The Provisional Government appointed a commission of historians and artists from the Talas art college to prepare a formal design, and it adopted the present flag by decree in May 1992, during the siege of Talas. In its 1992 form the horseshoe was described as commemorating the dead of 1916, the purges and the February 1992 shootings. After the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] and the establishment of US territorial administration, the interim Territorial Legislature confirmed the flag in the State Symbols Act of 1993, together with the anthem, "[[The Spirit of Irad]]".<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>

#### Territorial period and after
Under the territorial administration (see [[Territory of Irad (1992–2006)]]) the flag was flown beside the flag of the United States on public buildings, with the US flag in the position of precedence, as in other US territories. It remained the flag of the Democratic Republic of Irad in December 2006 and of the ISEZ from February 2007.<sup>[3]</sup>

The [[Iradi Freedom Society]] did not adopt a separate flag. In the tribal regions the national flag is flown at clan assemblies and at the August kurultai on the [[Aksay Plateau]], often beside clan horsetail standards, and it is one of the few symbols used by both administrations.<sup>[5]</sup>

The Department of Public Information published the official description in 2015. It standardized the colors and construction, confirmed that the star has five points, and listed the dead of both civil wars among the martyrs commemorated by the horseshoe.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Usage
The flag is flown on government buildings and schools in the ISEZ, and is raised ceremonially in Talas on Irad Day, 11 March (see [[March 11 Independence Day]] and [[Public holidays in Irad]]). It is flown at half-mast on the anniversary of the 3 February 1992 shootings and on 15 August, the memorial day of [[The Lost Tribes of 1916]].<sup>[1]</sup> Its elements appear widely outside official use. Approved Chongtor stallions are branded with an inverted-horseshoe mark, silversmiths have added Orkhon letters to saddle fittings since the 1990s, and the star and horse are common in commercial logos (see [[Eerchilik (Saddlery)]]).<sup>[5]</sup>

Vexillologists have compared the flag with that of [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], which also places a single central emblem on a red field. The Iradi flag differs in its figurative emblem and inscription, which are closer to the Soviet tradition of republican state emblems than to the plain geometric designs adopted by most post-Soviet states.<sup>[6]</sup>

### 4.143. The Spirit of Irad
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: National Symbols*

"**The Spirit of Irad**" (Iradi: *Irad Ruhu*) is the national anthem of Irad. Its music was composed by Asan Jumabaev, known for his score for the film *[[Desert Sun’s Rebellion]]* (1979), to a poem by Cholpon Myrzakulova. Written during the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]], it was sung at the proclamation of the Republic of Irad in [[Talas]] on 11 March 1992, adopted by the Provisional Government in May 1992 and confirmed by the interim [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] in the State Symbols Act of 1993. It replaced the anthem of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] and has been retained by every later Iradi administration, including the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). The official text is in Iradi, and an official English version was adopted in 1993.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## History

#### Soviet predecessor
Like the other union republics, the Iradi SSR adopted a state anthem in 1946, with a text in Iradi and Russian that praised the [[wp:Soviet Union]], the Russian people and [[wp:Joseph Stalin|Stalin]]. The text was revised in the late 1970s to remove the references to Stalin. It was rarely sung outside official ceremonies, but republican radio played it at the start and close of each broadcasting day until 1991. The [[Socialist Republic of Irad]], proclaimed in Kobozev in October 1991, continued to use it.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Composition (1991–1992)
Myrzakulova, then a lecturer in Iradi philology at [[Talas State University]], wrote the poem in December 1991, when strikes and student protests in Talas were growing into the Winter Uprising. It was first printed in a student newspaper and circulated in typed copies. Jumabaev set it to music in January 1992. According to his later account, he based the opening phrase on a herding tune he had recorded in the [[Talas Alatau]] in the 1970s and wrote the refrain so that it could be sung by a crowd without accompaniment.<sup>[1]</sup>

The song was sung at rallies in Talas in February 1992, including at the funerals of those killed in the shootings of 3 February. According to accounts of the [[Talas Town Hall Meeting (1992)|Talas Town Hall Meeting]] of 11 March, the assembly sang it after adopting the declaration that proclaimed the Republic of Irad, an occasion now marked as Irad Day (see [[March 11 Independence Day]]).<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>

#### Adoption
The Provisional Government adopted "The Spirit of Irad" as the national anthem by decree in May 1992, at the same time as the [[Flag of Irad|national flag]]. After the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] and the establishment of US territorial administration, the interim Territorial Legislature confirmed both symbols in the State Symbols Act of 1993. The act fixed the official music and the Iradi text, approved an official English version, and specified the arrangement to be used on state occasions.<sup>[2]</sup>

During the territorial period (see [[Territory of Irad (1992–2006)]]) the anthem was played together with "The [[wp:The Star-Spangled Banner|Star-Spangled Banner]]" at official ceremonies attended by representatives of the federal government, as in other US territories, and the English version was often sung on those occasions. The [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] kept the anthem in December 2006, and the ISEZ administration has kept it since February 2007. The [[Iradi Freedom Society]] has not adopted an anthem of its own, and the song is also sung at clan gatherings in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]].<sup>[5]</sup>

## Music
The anthem is a slow hymn in common time. The official orchestral arrangement, recorded by the [[Talas Symphony Orchestra]] in 1993, is in B-flat major. Each stanza is set to a sixteen-bar verse, followed by an eight-bar refrain whose melody rises to the highest note of the anthem. Writers on the anthem have noted its narrow range and its regular phrases, which make it easy to sing, and the herding-tune character of the opening, built on repeated rising fourths.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[6]</sup>

Several official arrangements exist:
- the full orchestral version, with all three stanzas, lasting a little under three minutes;
- a short version of the first stanza and refrain, about one minute twenty seconds long, used at sporting events and in broadcasting;
- a military band arrangement used by the State Defense Corps;
- a version with a solo [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]] introduction, used by [[IradOne]] since the early 2000s.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[6]</sup>

## Text
The official Iradi text has three stanzas and a refrain. In the official description, the first stanza describes the mountains, rivers and horse herds of Irad. The second commemorates those who died for the country, with an allusion to the steppe custom of the riderless horse (see [[Fallen Rider Tradition]]). The third presents [[wp:Polaris]], the star called *Irad* in traditional cosmology, as a guide for the nation. The refrain addresses the "spirit" of the title and repeats the call to freedom that appears as the motto of the national flag.<sup>[2]</sup>

The official English version follows the Iradi text closely but does not rhyme. An unofficial Russian translation from the 1990s is sung by some older Russian-speaking Iradis (see [[Russos of Nurzhan]]), but it has no legal standing, and the Russian-language channel IradOdin plays the anthem without words.<sup>[5]</sup>

The third stanza's reference to the star as a guide sent by God has drawn objections. In the territorial period, Muslim community leaders in [[Nurzhan]] asked that schoolchildren not be required to sing it. Since 1997 school regulations in the ISEZ have required only the first stanza and refrain, and the short official version omits the third stanza.<sup>[5]</sup> (See [[Islam in Irad]] and [[Religion in Irad]].)

## Usage
The anthem is performed at the official ceremony in Talas on Irad Day, at the opening of each session of the *Mejlis*, at the inauguration of the Governor and at military ceremonies. IradOne plays it at the start and close of its broadcasting day. Schools in the ISEZ sing it at assemblies at the start of the school week. It is played before the final of the President's Cup in [[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak tartysh]] at the [[Irad State Hippodrome]] each March. Because Irad is not a member of most international sporting bodies, it is rarely heard at international competitions.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[5]</sup>

By convention, listeners stand. The practice of placing the right hand over the heart was introduced during the territorial period and is now usual among younger Iradis, while many older people stand at attention in the Soviet manner. In the tribal regions men remove their felt hats. The anthem has also been sung at demonstrations. According to the *[[Talas Herald]]*, protesters sang it during the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]] and at the demonstrations that followed the [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]].<sup>[7]</sup>

### 4.144. Iradi alphabet
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Language & Literature*

The **Iradi alphabet** (Iradi: *Irad alfaviti*) is the Latin-based alphabet of 32 letters used to write the [[Iradi Language|Iradi language]]. It was introduced in 1992, given its present form by the [[1995 Latin Orthography Revision]] and confirmed, with minor changes, by the Language and Education Reform Act of 1997. It is the official script of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) and is also used in the records of the [[Iradi Freedom Society Chancellery]] in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR).<sup>[1]</sup>

Iradi has changed script three times in a century. It was written in Arabic script until 1928, in a Latin alphabet from 1928 to 1941 and in Cyrillic from 1941 to 1992, before the return to Latin in 1992. Older forms survive in particular uses: the [[wp:Old Turkic language|Old Turkic]] runic script appears in the motto of the [[Flag of Irad|national flag]], [[wp:Syriac language|Syriac]] script in church inscriptions, and Cyrillic in the handwriting of many older Iradis.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## History

#### Early scripts
A group of short Old Turkic runic inscriptions has been found in the Talas valley, and Christian gravestones of the wider [[wp:Semirechye]] region bear Turkic texts written in Syriac script. Iradi scholars regard both as written evidence of the ancestors of the language, although the link to modern Iradi is debated. Turkic written in Syriac script also appears on the carved gypsum panels of the [[Church of St. Janyl]] (1727) in [[Iyık Janyl]].<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

From the late Middle Ages Iradi was written in the Perso-Arabic script used for Chagatai and later Uzbek. Texts copied at Iyık Janyl, including the eighteenth-century vita of [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]], used it. The script had few letters for Turkic vowels, and spelling followed Chagatai conventions rather than the spoken language. After the creation of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] in 1925, the republican press briefly used a reformed Arabic orthography with letters for all the vowels, similar to the reforms adopted for Kazakh and Kyrgyz in the same years.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### Latin (1928–1941)
The [[1928 Latinization Decree]] replaced the Arabic script with a Latin alphabet, as part of the Soviet campaign that gave most Turkic languages alphabets based on the Unified Turkic Latin Alphabet (*[[wp:Yañalif]]*). Iradi made the change in the same year as Kyrgyz. Like the other Yañalif-based alphabets, it used special letters such as ꞑ for the velar nasal, ɵ for the front rounded vowel *ö* and ь for the back vowel *ı*. The reform was carried out through literacy schools in rural districts and the refitting of printing presses. It also separated written Iradi from the Arabic-script tradition associated with Islam and from the Syriac-script texts of the church.<sup>[4]</sup>

#### Cyrillic (1941–1992)
The [[1941 Cyrillic Mandate]] replaced the Latin alphabet with Cyrillic in the press, schools and administration, at the end of the all-Union shift from Latin to Cyrillic in 1938–1941. As in the Kyrgyz alphabet adopted in 1940, the Iradi Cyrillic alphabet consisted of the 33 letters of Russian with three additions: ө, ү and ң. Long vowels were written double, and Russian loanwords kept their Russian spelling, including letters such as ц, щ and ъ that are not used in native words. The abridged 1958 edition of [[The Epic of Janyl]] was printed in Cyrillic.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[5]</sup>

#### Latin (since 1992)
The Provisional Government and the territorial administration restored a Latin alphabet in 1992. Drawn up quickly for schools and the press, and for the English-language typewriters and computers then arriving under the territorial administration, it avoided diacritics and relied on digraphs such as *oe*, *ue*, *ch*, *sh* and *ng*. Spelling varied widely between publications.<sup>[1]</sup>

The 1995 Latin Orthography Revision, a law of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]], was drafted by a commission of linguists from [[Talas State University]] and territorial educators. It replaced the digraphs with single letters: the dotless *ı* for the back unrounded vowel, *ö* and *ü* for the front rounded vowels, and *ç*, *ş* and *ñ* for the consonants /tʃ/, /ʃ/ and /ŋ/. It also set rules for writing loanwords and proper names. The resulting 32-letter alphabet was confirmed by the Language and Education Reform Act of 1997, whose changes concerned mainly the spelling of loanwords and the capital forms of *i* and *ı*. The act made the alphabet compulsory in public schools and administration.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[6]</sup>

The new alphabet spread fastest among the young. In 1993 the [[Syro-Iradi Episcopal Synod]] approved Iradi translations of the liturgy, printed in the Latin alphabet, for use alongside Classical Syriac, and the complete edition of the 1938 text of *The Epic of Janyl* was published in Latin script in 2001. Many older Iradis, especially among the Russian-educated *Russos* of [[Nurzhan]], still read Iradi more easily in Cyrillic, and older clerks in the tribal regions often still write it.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[7]</sup>

## Letters
The alphabet follows the order below. Like Turkish and Azerbaijani, it distinguishes dotless *ı* (capital *I*) from dotted *i* (capital *İ*).<sup>[6]</sup>

| Letter | Cyrillic (1941–1992) | Sound (IPA) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| A a | А а | /ɑ/ | |
| Ä ä | — | /æ/ | Uzbek and Persian loans; often merged with *e* or *a* |
| B b | Б б | /b/ | |
| C c | Ц ц | /ts/ | Russian and international loans only |
| Ç ç | Ч ч | /tʃ/ | |
| D d | Д д | /d/ | |
| E e | Е е, Э э | /e/ | |
| F f | Ф ф | /f/ | Mainly loans |
| G g | Г г | /ɡ/, [ʁ] | Uvular next to back vowels |
| H h | Х х | /h/ | Persian and Arabic loans |
| I ı | Ы ы | /ɯ/ | Back unrounded vowel |
| İ i | И и | /i/ | |
| J j | Ж ж | /dʒ/ | [ʒ] in northern steppe dialects |
| K k | К к | /k/, [q] | Uvular next to back vowels |
| L l | Л л | /l/ | |
| M m | М м | /m/ | |
| N n | Н н | /n/ | |
| Ñ ñ | Ң ң | /ŋ/ | |
| O o | О о | /o/ | |
| Ö ö | Ө ө | /ø/ | |
| P p | П п | /p/ | |
| Q q | К к | /q/ | Established proper names only |
| R r | Р р | /r/ | |
| S s | С с | /s/ | |
| Ş ş | Ш ш | /ʃ/ | |
| T t | Т т | /t/ | |
| U u | У у | /u/ | |
| Ü ü | Ү ү | /y/ | |
| V v | В в | /v/ | Mainly loans |
| X x | Х х | /χ/ | Uzbek, Persian and Arabic loans |
| Y y | Й й | /j/ | |
| Z z | З з | /z/ | |

Long vowels are written double (*aa*, *ee*, *oo*, *öö*, *uu*, *üü*), as in *too* "mountain". The uvular pronunciations of *k* and *g* next to back vowels are not marked in writing; *q* survives only in a few established names, such as the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. The letters *c*, *f*, *h*, *v*, *x* and *ä* occur mainly in loanwords.<sup>[6]</sup>

## Romanization in English
Iradi names and words in English-language publications, including government documents in English, often do not follow the official alphabet. Many use an older romanization based on English digraphs or on the transliteration of Russian Cyrillic. In these spellings *ç* and *ş* appear as *ch* and *sh*, *ı* often as *y*, and *j* sometimes as *zh*, from the Russian transliteration of Cyrillic ж. The patronymic *kızı* ("daughter of") is thus usually written *kyzy* in English, and the title of the film *[[Desert Sun’s Rebellion]]*, officially *Çöl Künü Kötörülüşü*, is usually given as *Chöl Künü Kötörülüshü*. Names that entered English through Russian, such as Zhumabek, keep their *zh* (see [[Iradi name]]).<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[7]</sup>

The distinction between dotted and dotless *i* caused problems with early software and with the English-language keyboards common in the ISEZ, and many writers still use *i* for both letters in informal writing.<sup>[7]</sup>

### 4.145. FreeIrad.org
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Media*

**FreeIrad.org** (styled **FREEIRAD.ORG**) is an anonymous English-language opposition website about [[Irad]]. It publishes allegations against the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI) government and the family of Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]], against foreign powers and against the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], under the slogans "No justice without truth", "No freedom without justice" and "No truth without freedom". A banner on its front page says that [[Attelkom]], which carries almost all internet traffic in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), tried to censor the site and that it is now hosted offshore. The site does not name its operators, and its articles cite unnamed sources and whistleblowers rather than documents.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Content
The front page carries a feed of articles tagged by subject, among them politics, religion, Toktarov, Russia, China and America. Most are headlined as questions, and none carries a date. Their claims include:<sup>[1]</sup>
- that Toktarov died in 2022 and that the DPI has concealed his death, a version of the rumors that followed his disappearance from public view (see [[Erlan Toktarov]]);
- that the Bush family keeps a secret estate in Irad's mountains, a revival of the [[Bush Family Palatial Complex Conspiracy Theory]];
- that the [[NurGaz]] chairman [[Kamran Bekzatov]] has held secret meetings with the Russian leadership, and that Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] plans to sell Irad to China;
- that the United States runs hidden military bases in Irad besides the acknowledged installations, and that oil, not the 1992 treaty, was the real reason for US rule;
- that Irad's undeveloped uranium deposits have become a target for foreign powers;
- that the horse trade serves as a cover for foreign intelligence operations;
- that the church hides ancient relics, including the [[wp:Holy Grail]];
- that Irad has been erased from online maps.

## Activism
A "Take action" section offers a printable poster and a recipe for wheatpaste, the flour-and-water glue used for fly-posting. The site also links to an archive, a chat room and an online shop selling shirts. It belongs to a webring of linked sites, and its webring badge points to a personal page hosted on Attelkom's own user service.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Censorship claims
The Department of Public Information supplies Attelkom with lists of websites to be blocked in the ISEZ (see [[Media of Irad]]). FreeIrad.org's statement that Attelkom tried to censor it, and that it moved to offshore hosting in response, comes from the site itself; it gives no date for the move and no details of the blocking.<sup>[1]</sup>

### 4.146. Jer-Suu Party
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Politics & Government*

The **Jer-Suu Party** (Iradi: *Jer-Suu Partiyası*, "Land and Water Party") was an Iradi nationalist political party founded in [[Talas]] in 1995. During the territorial period it campaigned for the repudiation of the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]], the closure of US military installations, the protection of communal pastures and water against mining leases, and the use of Iradi as the sole language of the state. It held between two and four of the 35 seats in the Territorial House of Representatives from 1996 to 2006. After many of its members joined the [[Popular Front of Irad]] in 2007, it was banned in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) in 2008 as an extremist organization.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## History

#### Foundation and territorial period (1995–2006)
The party was founded in March 1995 by the poet and [[Talas State University]] philologist Tilek Sharshenov and Kubanychbek Toktobolot uulu, a rural notable from the Talas valley, who drew together Iradi-language teachers, students and village councils opposed to grazing leases granted to mining companies. Its name, "land and water", is a traditional expression for the homeland. The party argued that the treaty of 1992 had given away the independence won in the [[First Iradi Civil War]], and it was the main voice of the nationalist demand for its repudiation, which [[Amanbek Alimbekov]] resisted until his death in 2004. It also campaigned for the [[1995 Latin Orthography Revision]] and against the dollar-linked som.<sup>[1]</sup>

Jer-Suu won its first two House seats in 1996, from Talas and the Talas valley. Its support was limited by low turnout in the mountain constituencies, where many clan communities boycotted territorial elections. In the early 2000s its deputies and newspaper, *Jer-Suu*, were among the most persistent critics of the commercial concessions held by [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI) figures around [[Talas Air Base]].<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Democratic Republic and civil war (2006–2007)
The party welcomed the [[Statutory Independence Ruling (2006)]] and its deputies sat in the national assembly of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]]. In February 2007 they walked out of the assembly in protest against the cabinet of [[Bakyt Orozbekov]] over its decrees privatizing communal pastures in the Chatkal valley. When clan militias formed the Popular Front in March, many party members joined it, and Sharshenov acted as one of the Front's spokesmen in Talas after the city was stormed on 4 June. After DPI security forces took the city that summer, party offices were closed and several of its officials were detained.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### Ban (2008)
In April 2008 the [[Supreme Court of Irad]], on an application from the Ministry of Internal Security, banned the party under the Extremist Activity Act passed by the provisional chamber earlier that year, holding that it had taken part in an armed rebellion. Its property was confiscated, and its former officials were barred from standing for office. The [[wp:Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe]] (OSCE) and [[wp:Human Rights Watch]] criticized the ruling as collective punishment of a lawful party.<sup>[3]</sup> In 2016 three students in Talas were convicted of distributing Jer-Suu leaflets and given suspended sentences.<sup>[4]</sup>

Sharshenov has lived in exile in [[wp:Bishkek]] since 2008 and writes for exiled Iradi media. Toktobolot uulu moved to the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], where he and other former members joined the [[Iradi Freedom Society Chancellery]], giving the clan confederation a small group of urban, Iradi-educated staff.<sup>[2]</sup>
